translations.text: Discourses on instruction in conduct, delivered by the blessed Mar Philoxenus, bishop of Mabbug.
Discourses on instruction in conduct, delivered by the blessed Mar Philoxenus, bishop of Mabbug.
In these he explains the whole order of discipleship: how a person should begin as a disciple of Christ,
and by what rules and practices he should proceed until he reaches spiritual love,
from which perfection is born, through which we become children bearing the likeness of Christ, as Paul the apostle said.
The first discourse is the basis of this whole volume, by the grace of our Lord.
Our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ has invited us in his living gospel to approach wisely the task of keeping his commandments,
and to lay the foundation of his teaching properly within us, so that we may raise the building of our conduct upright.
For anyone who does not know how to begin building this tower that rises to heaven with understanding cannot complete it and bring it to a wise conclusion.
For knowledge and wisdom guide, arrange, and accomplish everything—its beginning, its completion, and its establishment.
The person who begins in this way is called wise by the word of our Savior. He says, “Everyone who hears these words of mine and acts on them
is like a wise man who dug deep and set his building on rock. The rain fell, the rivers came,
and the winds blew and beat against that house, but it did not fall, because its foundations had been laid on rock.
But anyone who hears and does not act is like a foolish man who set his building on sand.
Even weak things, if they strike his building, bring it down. We are therefore obliged,
according to the word of our Teacher, not only to be constant hearers of the word of God, but also constant doers.
For someone who acts without hearing is better than someone who listens constantly but is devoid of deeds, as the word of Paul the apostle teaches us:
“It is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the law who are justified.
For if Gentiles who do not have the law do by nature what the law requires, these people, although they do not have the law,
are a law to themselves. They show the work of the law written on their hearts,
and their conscience bears witness concerning them.” For hearing the law is good, because it leads to deeds.
Reading and studying the Scriptures is also good, because it cleanses our hidden mind of evil thoughts.
But if someone constantly reads, hears, and studies the word of God without bringing his reading to completion through the labor of deeds,
the Spirit of God has already spoken against this to him through the blessed David, rebuking him and reproaching his wickedness,
and forbidding him to presume to take even the Holy Scripture into his unclean hands. For it says, “God said to the sinner:
“What have you to do with the books of my commandments, you who have taken my covenant on your lips? Yet you have hated my discipline and thrown my words behind you.”
Together with the rest of what is written after these words. For someone who constantly reads but is far from putting it into practice—his reading is an accusation against himself.
And he deserves a harsher judgment, because, although he hears every day, every day he scorns and despises what he hears.
He is therefore like a dead person, a corpse without a soul. For even if ten thousand trumpets and horns sound in a dead person’s ear, he does not hear.
So too the soul that is dead in sins, and the mind that has lost the remembrance of God,
through the deadly delusion of its thoughts, does not hear the cries of the divine voices.

The trumpet of the spiritual word does not stir it. Instead, it is sunk in the sleep of death and finds it pleasant. Though it is dying in its death, it does not perceive this so as to turn back and seek life for itself.
Just as someone who is naturally dead does not perceive his death, so someone who by his own will is dead to the knowledge of God does not feel his death.
Nor does he perceive his destruction, so as to take measures and seek a way to find life for himself.
Thus God too, when he saw the deadness of the Jews, who had willingly stopped their ears and shut their eyes,
and had made their hearts insensitive to the remembrance and knowledge of God, stirred Isaiah to awaken them.
He called out to him to cry out in their ears, saying, “Cry out with your throat, and do not hold back. Raise your voice like a trumpet,
and show my people their wrongdoing and the house of Jacob their sins.” And elsewhere the prophet himself said, “He said to me, ‘Cry out.’
And I said, ‘What shall I cry out?’ ‘All flesh is grass, and all its beauty is like the blossom of the field.’”
Like grass and blossom dried up by the sun, which neither rain nor all the water flowing from springs can moisten,
once it has lost its natural moisture, so the people have become dead to all the life of the Spirit.
Like grass and blossom, they grow hot and dry up before the noonday heat of error and the burning heat of evil deeds. For the soul dies to the remembrance of God.
And when it dies, all its powers of discernment die with it, and its thoughts of meditation on heavenly things cease.
Though the soul is alive by nature, it dies by its own will. Though it exists in its created form, it is lost through its own freedom.
The disciple of God must therefore have the remembrance of his master Jesus Christ firmly fixed in his soul and meditate on him night and day.
He must wisely consider where to begin, and how and from where to raise the courses of his building,
and how to begin and finish his building, so that he will not be laughed at by everyone passing along the road,
as our Lord said about the man who began to build a tower and could not finish it, becoming an object of laughter and mockery to everyone who saw him.
Who is this man who began building the tower, about whom our Savior spoke, if not the disciple who sets out on the way of Christ’s gospel?
The beginning of this disciple’s building is his promise and covenant with God, in which he promises to leave the world and keep the commandments.
And let us begin, run, and finish, gathering and bringing from everywhere the precious stones of good conduct,
to build this tower that rises to heaven. For the foundation has been spread out and laid, according to Paul's words: it is Jesus Christ our God.
Everyone builds on this foundation as he wishes, because the foundation once stooped down in its love,
to receive everything placed upon it, until the day of revelation comes, when everyone's work is examined and tested.
And he who is the foundation at the foot of the building rises and becomes the judge and head at the top of the building.
As Paul himself said: “If anyone builds on this foundation with gold or silver,
or precious stones, or wood, or hay, or stubble, everyone's work will be revealed.
For that day will reveal it, because it is revealed by fire, and the fire will distinguish what sort of work each person has done.”
For by gold, silver, and precious stones, Paul represents righteous conduct and its beautiful qualities.
Among these, faith is like gold, and abstinence is like silver, along with fasting, ascetic discipline, and the other labors of righteousness.
Like precious stones are love, peace, hope, pure intentions, and holy thoughts,
and a mind that soars wholly in the Spirit and, in all its movements, continually bears awe of God and wonder at the greatness of his being,
and an intellect gripped by silence, trembling before God's mysteries, which cannot be explained or expressed.
These thoughts, movements, heavenly flights, and spiritual ways of life are what Paul calls precious stones.
But error and wickedness, together with the service of every lust, he calls wood, hay, and stubble.
As long as the building is fixed in the earth, everyone builds and raises upon it whatever he wishes, until the day that distinguishes everything is revealed,
and he comes of whom it was said that he holds a winnowing shovel in his hand, cleans his threshing floors, and gathers the wheat into storehouses,
but burns the chaff with unquenchable fire. He reveals himself as a judge and cultivator, he who planted the tree of our humanity in the world,
holding in his hand the axe of judgment. Every tree that does not bear the fruit of good deeds
he cuts down and throws into the fire. When that fisherman appears who cast his net into the sea of the world and filled it with fish, large and small,
which are the races and families of humanity, the peoples and tribes of mortal beings, the different languages and countless nations,
then he will draw up his net and bring it to the shores of the sea, as he himself said. He will select the good fish and put them into his containers,
which are the living storehouses of his kingdom, but he will throw the bad ones outside into the outer darkness, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.
For these things are reserved to happen at that time, when the chief Shepherd is revealed in the glory of his kingdom.
For the time of testing is one thing, and the time of instruction another; the time of calling is one thing, and the time of separation another.
And just as there is no examination in this time of learning, so too there will be no learning in that time of examination.
Therefore, my beloved, let us listen to the living voice of God, who has called us to give us eternal life.
For his utterances are full of life, and they give life to whoever listens to them. From life, living words are spoken.
And from living words, life is given to those who listen to what they say with living hearing.
But because we ought to explain and discuss each of these subjects in its proper place,
and make known in our discourse which comes first and which follows it, and how these good things are observed and brought to completion one after another,
we have set down this introduction to encourage the reader toward the wealth of subjects that follow.
For someone beginning on the path of Christ’s commandments ought to know where to begin,
and which should be the first stone in the building of his discipleship, which stone should be second, and which third.
Otherwise, not knowing the proper order and not having learned where to begin, he may not know where or how to finish either.
And through ignorance of his discipleship, he may put the last things first and the first things last, and place some of these in the middle.
For if the farmers and laborers of this world know the seasons for sowing and planting, and other seasons for harvesting and gathering fruit,
and observe the order of the seasons so that their work will not be spoiled and thrown into confusion, how much more ought the sower and laborer of the Spirit,
and the disciple of truth, to know what is appropriate for the beginning of his discipleship, and where he ought to begin.
Then, when he has laid the first stone in its proper order in the foundation of his discipleship, he can raise the entire rest of the building according to the rules.
For builders and architects also act this way: when they begin the foundation of their building
with strong blocks and large, good stones, even if they place something inferior in the building,
the sound foundation can receive and support weak materials.
But if they place weak and small stones below in the foundation, and strong and large ones above, their entire building collapses and falls.
Again, let us take this same illustration from the teachers who provide children with a complete education,
who impart their teaching to them in order, without transgressing or confusing the rules and progression of human learning.
Rather, they know which things to teach first and which afterward, until the learner reaches the full extent of the course of instruction.
Again, in all the crafts of this world, this progression is recognized among them as a rule:
which tasks are given to apprentices to perform when they first begin learning the craft.
In keeping with their limited ability, their masters show them how to perform the small tasks belonging to the crafts.
so that if a mistake happens, the loss will be small. Likewise, those who learn the art of athletic training
have an established order for the forms of combat with which they begin,
and for the stages through which they progress and advance in the art of athletic training. First they demonstrate how to take their stance facing one another.
After this they lay their hands on one another, and in this way they practice and approach full combat.
Likewise, those who are chosen for worldly military service learn this art of warfare in this same order.
Their instruction is not confused or disordered. Rather, each of the things they learn is learned in its proper place
and in its proper order, as with everything else in the world, whose beginning, middle, and end are known.
Now, judging from the analogies in these examples we have presented, this order is even more appropriate for us.
We need to know the first way of life and the one that follows it. For here we learn spiritual athletic training,
and we have been chosen for the service of those in heaven. Just as those chosen to serve before earthly kings
learn the king’s rules and customs from those who have preceded them—even how to walk, how to look, and how to use their voices,
and even the limits to observe when speaking before him—the later arrivals learn from the earlier ones,
and those newly chosen learn from those who preceded them. So here too, a person who is chosen
to serve Christ, whether by his own deliberate choice or through a promise made by his parents,
must learn this service from those who preceded him, either from the Holy Scriptures or from spiritual people
who have walked this path according to its rules, who began with hard work, finished in the Spirit, and were made perfect in love.
For the desires that wage war against us at the beginning of childhood are known, as are those in the middle of childhood,
those at the end of the period of childhood, those at the beginning of youth, those in its middle,
and those at its end; and likewise those in the period after youth,
following exactly that same earlier order, until the end of this period.
Likewise, it is known which passions wage war against us in old age, until our departure from the world,
and which of these arise in us during infancy and childhood through natural movements and impulses,
before the power of free choice becomes active in us and we attain the knowledge that distinguishes good things from evil things.
We must also know, when we carry out our practices and labors, which passion fights against which,
and which desire struggles against which, and, when we have finished performing a good deed, which evil is stirred up against us.
And how, when one desire is defeated, another gains the victory.
And how, when we have subdued the desires of the body, the battle against the soul’s passions is stirred up against us.
And how, when we have stripped off evil outwardly, it returns to clothe us inwardly in our thoughts.
And when we have killed it in the members of our body, it lives within the living impulses of the soul.
And when we have cut it off and cast it outside us, it enters and hides in us, so that it may be within us.
And which passion is born in the soul from the body’s fasting, which from abstinence, and which from singing aloud.
And which from prayer in silence, which from giving up possessions, and which from disregard for clothing.
And which passion is born in us from universal compassion toward everyone, and which passion is stirred up against us when our way of life surpasses our brother’s.
And which passions arise in us from understanding thoughts, and which from words of instruction.
And which from words handed down in writings, and into which passion we fall when we have completely overcome gluttony.
And which is stirred up against us when we have achieved victory in the battle against sexual immorality.
And which passion is born in us from obedience to superiors, and which from obedience to everyone.
And which thoughts arise in us when we resist obedience.
And by what instruction the thought that refuses to obey its teachers is brought to an end.
And by what attitude we can uproot from ourselves our presumption that we possess knowledge.
And which passions are overcome by which, and which desires are brought to an end by which.
And what the struggle is for those at the bodily level, what it is for those at the level of the soul, and what it is for those at the spiritual level.
And what those at the bodily level ought to do when they wish to overcome the desires of the body.
And what those at the level of the soul should do to overcome and defeat the soul’s passions, and what those at the spiritual level should do
to escape the stumblings that befall spiritual people in the realm of the spirit, and how far the struggle extends in each of these ranks.
And how we can know when the stirring of desire comes from ourselves, and how and when it comes upon us from outside through the adversary’s incitement.
And by what means the desire born from ourselves is overcome, and by what means the desire that the enemy stirs up against us is overcome.
And whether the same desire is overcome by one method at all times, or whether we also need different methods to overcome it at different times.
And how and by what means we can discern whether our desires are overcome by us through the strength of our endurance or through the grace of God.
And which struggle is stirred up against us among many people, and which when we are in solitude.
And how the soul becomes clearer and purer, and what place helps the body's labor.
And what we should begin with first when we approach discipleship to Christ.
And what passion is stirred in us by the praise that leaders give us, whether for our knowledge or for our conduct.
And what passion is stirred when we are praised for our great austerity.
And through what thoughts we recognize the entrance of the passions, and how we should guard ourselves so that they do not disturb us when they take hold of us.
And what attitudes we should adopt when we overcome their assault, and how we can acquire humility.
And through what thoughts we can remove pride from ourselves, which is the opposite of humility.
And through what attitudes we maintain endurance within our souls, and what the renunciation of the body is.
And what renunciation of the world is, and what the renunciation of the soul is.
And how, when we have renounced the wealth of visible things, we acquire the wealth of Christ's gifts.
And what commandments we should keep at the beginning of our discipleship.
And how we should obey our teachers, who counsel us and teach us good things, without looking at their shortcomings.
And what strength our soul receives from each of the good things we practice, and how we should conduct ourselves.
With good manners in the dwellings of our brothers, and to what extent fasting should be practiced.
And how, at each time, we should increase or decrease the food for our bodies accordingly.
And how and to what extent we should endure when the battle of desire rises against us.
And what we should do when we want to extinguish the passions of the soul within us.
And through what meditation we can uproot hostility from our souls.
And how and from where pure prayer is born within us, and what contemplations draw us into wonder at God.
And how we can always stir sorrow for God's sake within our souls, and how many feelings and contemplations belong to this sorrow for God's sake.
And how, when we enter stillness, we should guard our thoughts against wandering toward things outside ourselves.
And what harm a person suffers from fellowship with heretics.
And how our heart becomes dulled through conversations and encounters with other people, and grows dark, losing the remembrance and contemplation of God.
And we should know what bodily fasting is, what fasting of the soul is, what spiritual fasting is, and what purity of the body is.
And what purity of the soul is, and what purity of the spirit is, and what the renunciation of the body is, and what the renunciation of the soul is.
And which is that of the spirit, and what are the different kinds of stillness: bodily, of the soul, and spiritual.
And how the soul is taught to fast from evil things, just as the body fasts from food.
The disciple of Christ must learn and know these things and many others like them,
so that he may walk confidently on the path of his service and carry out the wishes of the heavenly King, before whom he serves.
For if those who learn worldly crafts carefully learn all the secrets of those crafts,
and strive to know all the forms of work involved in each of them,
how much more must someone chosen for this craft of the spirit—if it is right to call it a craft—
know all the roads and paths, the aims and purposes of the mysteries of this divine way of life,
and know that, although he is a bodily human being, he has been chosen to work at spiritual things and has been made worthy by God's grace of the heavenly way of life.
And further, while still living in the flesh in this world, he is to walk on a path above his nature.
Therefore, if we are disciples, we must ask questions and learn as disciples all the things through which we find our life.
And just as apprentices learn crafts from their masters, so we too must learn and receive instruction from spiritual masters.
For no one can become a master unless he first becomes a disciple.
Nor can he help and benefit others unless he gathers for himself the benefits that come from others,
submitting himself to receive and learn from everyone, and considering everyone higher and more exalted than himself.
For because our nature is created, and we came into being by the Creator's will when we did not exist, we can also acquire anew the knowledge of good things.
And just as we came into being from nonexistence, so too we become righteous after being sinners.
But when someone has completely stripped off the world, then he fully clothes himself in Christ's way of life.
For until he strips off his filthy garment and cleanses himself of the stains of evil through tears of repentance, he cannot put on the purple robes of the knowledge of Christ.
For someone stained by thoughts or deeds of wrongdoing must first heal his wounds
and cleanse the blemishes of his soul and body, and then come to the banquet hall of the divine mysteries,
clothed in the spiritual garments belonging to the banquet. For this reason it is all the more fitting
that everyone who becomes a disciple of Christ should lay the foundation of his discipleship from his very childhood,
so that throughout his upbringing he may acquire habits of goodness, and the world may not exhaust the strength of his soul and body,
and he then approach this new service like an old, worn-out vessel.
But as our Lord said, new wine is put into new wineskins, and both are preserved.
So, at the beginning of our youth, while we are still a fresh planting, let us pour into our souls the new wine of Christ’s teaching.
While our strength remains within us and our freshness has not grown old through sins, let us do this so that we can bear the fervor of love for holy teaching.
Then, as we preserve it, we may be preserved by it from all evils.
Especially while our soul’s strength has not been drained and carried away into the toil of alien pursuits.
Anyone who begins this way of life in his youth ought to be under the watchful care of teachers,
obeying their words and not judging their shortcomings.
Those teachers, in turn, should place themselves in the position of tutors entrusted with raising the children of the heavenly King.
For their Father is a king, their Brother is a king, and their Mother is a queen. And just as those who raise the children of an earthly king
show boundless care for their upbringing, with vigilance and diligence, so that through these children they may please their parents,
and also please the children themselves when they attain royal honor, so too a teacher who has disciples
should consider himself to be raising the King’s children, and should be alert and watchful over their protection, both in private and in public,
and over their upbringing. We ought to act like physicians toward ourselves and toward one another.
For there is no physician who, when an illness strikes his own body, does not attend to it before treating the illnesses of others.
And if others become sick, the rule of the medical profession requires him to hasten to restore their health.
In this same manner of physicians, we ought first to learn the causes of illnesses,
and then administer medicines, so that the medicine does not make the illness worse.
For by God’s grace we received both soul and body when we were formed at our creation, and we are required to care for both.
The body’s own nature makes demands on us concerning bodily illnesses and sufferings, and concerning its food, drink, and clothing.
Its natural needs themselves draw us to care for it, and we cannot neglect it, even if we wish to.
For the pressure of its sufferings drives us to seek its healing, and the demands of its needs drive us to supply its necessities.
But concerning the healing of our soul, the command of God’s word urges us to treat its illnesses and heal its sufferings,
to satisfy its hunger with the food of teaching, and to give it the knowledge of God to drink,
to clothe it in the garment of faith, to put on its feet the readiness of hope, and to train it in good habits,
in the perfection of all virtues, and in obedience that is ready to carry out God’s commandments.
So that, when our hidden lives are holy and our outward lives are pure, we may be vessels prepared for the Spirit of God, for him to dwell in us purely and holily.
When, with knowledge and wisdom, we treat the illnesses that afflict us and heal the wounds of sin in our souls.
For there is not a single illness caused by sinful desires for which a medicine has not been given to us from the word of God to heal it.
For just as medicines are mixed and prepared by physicians for bodily illnesses,
medicines against the passions of sin have been prepared and made ready by the Spirit of God,
so that anyone who feels an illness may find a medicine at his side and bring help to himself from close at hand.
For, as a general rule, everything is healed by its opposite, so that the opposing action of the medicine may fight against the harm caused by the illness.
For illnesses caused by cold are treated with warming remedies.
And for those caused by heat, cooling substances are supplied to bring relief.
Likewise, dryness also heals those caused by moisture.
And for those that arise from moisture, drying substances are given as treatment.
Take an example from this, then, discerning person who wishes to heal the illnesses of the soul.
Do for your soul what the art of medicine does for the body.
For this reason the working of visible things is set before our eyes, to serve as an instructive demonstration of hidden things,
so that, in the same way that the body is healed, we may heal the soul of the illnesses caused by evil deeds.
We must prepare against each individual passion of sin a medicine that is the opposite of the illness.
Against doubt, faith; against error, truth; against conjecture, certainty.
Against deceitfulness, honesty; against guile, simplicity; against cunning, innocence.
Against turmoil, serenity; against harshness, gentleness; against surliness, kindness.
Against bodily desire, spiritual desire; against pleasure, suffering; against the joy of the world, the joy of Christ.
Against songs, spiritual hymns; against amusement, sighs and weeping; against gluttony, fasting.
Against intoxicating drink, thirst guided by discernment; against rest, labor; against enjoyment, hardship.
Against fleshly pleasure, the pleasure of thoughts that rejoice in the Spirit; against talking, stillness.
Against worldly conversations, silence; against slackness, diligence; against slowness, swiftness.
Against heedlessness in one's thoughts, alertness of mind; against discouragement, perseverance.
Against cruelty, compassion. Against malice of mind, goodness of soul.
Against arrogance, humility. Against boasting, lowliness. Against love of honor, submission.
Against praise, reproach. Against wealth, poverty. Against possessions, dispossession.
Against hostility, peace. Against hatred, love. Against anger, reconciliation.
Against rage, peacefulness. Against envy, love. Against malicious jealousy, love for humanity.
Against curses, blessings. Against a blow on the cheek, turning the other cheek to the one who strikes us.
Against distress, joy. Against reliance on ourselves, confident hope in God.
Against bodily passions, spiritual passions. Against bodily sight, spiritual sight.
Against fine clothing, soiled clothing. Against pride, humility.
Against negligence, diligence. Against thoughts that dwell on food, a mind that meditates on heavenly things.
Against the sight of everything visible, remembrance of everything invisible. Against this present world,
seeking the world to come. Against love for bodily parents, love for spiritual parents.
Against attachment to the human race, the attachment of our mind to our heavenly kin. Against a city and a house on earth,
a dwelling in Jerusalem above. All these things, then, and others like them, are treated by their opposites
and healed by their opposites. Whoever longs for spiritual things must renounce bodily things.
For until one desire dies in us, another does not come to life in us. That is, until bodily desire dies,
spiritual desire does not come to life in our thoughts. For the death of either one brings the other to life.
For whenever the body, with all its desires, is alive in us, the soul, with all its desires, is dead.
But when the soul shares in life in the Spirit, and all its members come to life with it,
which are its thoughts, then the person rises from the dead and lives the new life of the new world.
For until we take off the old person, we cannot put on the new, spiritual person.
And even when we put him on through grace, we are still unaware of him. For all these ailments that we have listed
are treated with these medicines. From now on, it is up to the sick person to recognize his illness
and become his own physician. For each of these ailments that we have listed, he should apply the medicine that opposes it.
For look: beside the ailment lies the remedy that heals it, and beside the sore is the medicine that cures it. For if you want to heal your ailments,
Look, the medicines that heal them are beside them. Only recognize your pains, and learn about the medicinal roots that heal them.
From the brief outline I have drawn for you, understand the rest through your own diligence.
For instruction does not teach you everything, so that you will not become sleepy and idle.
But if the things already written, or those yet to be written, seem to you too difficult for your strength,
call on God to help you, and from him you will receive grace to help you in the battle in which you are engaged.
Let us therefore proceed with God's help and, as far as we are able, outline each of these passions in a few words.
That is, as grace provides, for my own help and for the benefit of others.
We will arrange the subjects in order, one after another, and show where the disciple ought to begin,
and how he should proceed and ascend through all the stages of the spiritual life until he reaches the lofty stage of love.
From there he ascends to the stage of perfection, and then the spiritual realm of Christ's joy receives him.
Once he stands there, he is freed from the passions, escapes from desires, and subdues all his enemies under his feet.
Then a person speaks boldly the words of the apostle: "It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me." To him be glory forever. Amen.
Here ends the first discourse, on the purpose of the book.
Notes on the Syriac text
Next, the second discourse, in which he teaches which commandment a person approaching discipleship to Christ ought to observe first.
Anyone who wishes to approach the way of life of discipleship to Christ in the proper order ought, before everything else, to hold firm faith within his soul.
This faith believes God without questioning, accepts his words, and does not investigate his nature.
It listens to his utterances and does not judge his deeds. For faith believes God in everything he says,
without seeking testimony and proofs to establish the truth of his word. This sure proof is enough for it: that it is God who speaks.
For signs, testimony, and proofs are required when a human being does or says something.
But when it is God who speaks, and the Lord of all says that he will act, we are required to believe,
since the fact that it is God who speaks and acts is enough to convince our faith. But if we would judge his decisions,
that is not permitted. For how can a human being, who is a created thing, judge the will of his Maker?
For just as a vessel cannot blame its craftsman for making it this way, or judge any of his actions,
so too a human being, who is a rational vessel, has no right to blame the craftsman who made him.
For even if he possesses speech endowed with knowledge, it was not given to him to judge his Maker’s will, but to praise the knowledge that fashioned him.
For a rational human being is even further from examining his Maker than a speechless tool is from investigating its craftsman.
For we received speech from God our Creator to give thanks, and he placed thoughts of knowledge within us so that we might marvel at his works.
And so that we might perceive it, he gave us the perception of wisdom. And so that we might taste its benefits, he placed within our souls a sense of discernment.
And so that we might see him through his works, he gave us the eye of faith, which gazes upon his hidden things.
For God is beyond the investigation of our thoughts, and his governance also surpasses the examination of reason.
For his works also go hand in hand with his nature: just as his nature cannot be investigated, neither can the deeds of that nature be examined.
For his decisions cannot be put on trial by asking why he willed this way and acted this way.
For just as he cannot be put on trial by us for why he made us in this form, fashioned us with this arrangement of parts, and placed us in the world,
so none of his decisions can be blamed by us by asking why he willed and acted this way.
“Whoever approaches God,” it says, “must believe that he exists and that he rewards those who seek him.”
For Paul entrusted this rule to anyone who wishes to approach God, and laid this obligation upon him to fulfill:
to believe simply that God exists. And whoever believes that he exists does not investigate since when or how.
Likewise, if he hears his will, his word, and his teaching, let him acknowledge that it is God’s will, and let him listen to and believe God’s voice and command.
But to judge why, in what manner, and for what reason it is so is the insolent investigation of a soul that has not perceived God.
For everyone who approaches God ought to acquire the mind of a child.
And as a child is toward his father and mother, so should he also be toward God and his governance.
And just as a child receives instruction from a teacher without scrutinizing his words or examining his teaching,
and does not judge in his thoughts what he teaches him, because the thoughts of his own soul lack the ability
to judge what he hears, so a human being ought to be toward God,
neither investigating him with his words nor judging his deeds in his hidden thoughts.
For he is a child, and like a child he should listen to his teaching and receive it in faith.
For this is also why God gives us birth anew: to teach us that we are children.
And as newborns, we have been born from the world into faith. For a childbearing womb has been placed in our midst,
which is baptism, in which the Spirit is mingled. And we are born through faith.
And just as a natural infant born from the womb remains in all its natural infancy and knows nothing of the world,
and neither investigates nor examines, neither thinks nor speaks, except for [?], through the natural movements of life alone,
being far removed from all thoughts, so also this infant of the Spirit, whom, instead of a natural womb,
the womb of baptism brings to birth, should not investigate the one who gave him birth.
He should listen to his words with simplicity and be a child toward his teaching, receiving the utterances without attempting to investigate them.
And just as that natural infant learns the names of things in the world without understanding their significance,
so here too let us receive the names and words, and leave the mystery of their meaning to God.
For we are children in relation to that knowledge, and infants in relation to the inexpressible wisdom of God, since our Savior's word has also called us this.
He says, “Let the children come to me, and do not stop them, for the kingdom of God belongs to those who are like them.”
And again he said elsewhere, “Whoever does not receive the kingdom of God like a child will not enter it.”
For just as children have trust concerning the things of the world,
so our trust should be toward the utterances spoken to us by God.
For this is also how a child responds to a word he hears from his father.
Whatever his father promises him, he believes without doubt that he will give it to him. He does not regard his word as false, nor does he investigate it.
For he does not examine it, test its force, and establish its truth,
and only then accept it. Nor, indeed, does he know how to distinguish whether what his father promises him is beyond his father's means.
Instead, he confidently accepts from him everything he tells him, without doubting.
And if he sees purple robes on a king's son, or a crown set on his head, he demands that his father give them to him, believing in the simplicity of his mind
that he will give them to him, because he thinks his father can do anything.
And if he sees a snake or a scorpion, in his childishness he does not hesitate to stretch out his hand toward them.
He asks his father or mother to give them to him, making his childish desire known by his crying as well.
His constant insistence with them, his shouting, and his crying testify that he asks with all the strength of his nature.
He believes that his father's authority holds even against the harm caused by a dangerous crawling creature.
And there is no doubt in his soul suggesting that what he wants might not be given to him.
It was therefore according to this example of children that our Lord commanded all who receive his kingdom to be.
As they accept and believe God's promises to them, like children.
For our Lord proclaimed and revealed his kingdom to bodily beings, saying, “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near.”
You have heard a voice proclaiming the kingdom. Believe it and do not doubt, especially once you have learned that it is the voice of God.
Do not ponder within yourself what that kingdom is like, nor investigate those spiritual places in your thoughts.
Do not adopt a bodily way of thinking when you hear about places without bodies.
Do not invent images in your mind of those glorious dwellings that the Son's ascension has prepared.
Nor should you arrange by your own knowledge what God's knowledge has already established.
For you were not called to investigate the kingdom, nor to prepare and establish it,
but only to be an heir and an invited guest in it, and to delight in the abundance of its spiritual blessings.
For you have heard the voice of Jesus speaking to you about the kingdom: “Repent; the kingdom of heaven has drawn near.” For he told you to repent,
not to become an investigator of the kingdom. For it is near you if you draw near to it.
Drawing near to it does not happen through verbal inquiries that investigate what the kingdom is like, how great it is, and what it resembles.
Rather, it happens when a person observes the kingdom's laws and fulfills the commandments entrusted to us by the kingdom's authority.
And you have heard all these things through faith concerning God: that he exists from eternity and forever,
and that he exists by his own being, without having come into being from anything else, and that he is not a single person,
but a self-existent nature, believed in and confessed in three persons.
Furthermore, concerning the persons, the word of faith teaches you to affirm that the one who begot was not divided,
and the one who was begotten was not severed. Rather, the Father exists together with his offspring by nature and from eternity,
along with the Holy Spirit, who is of the same nature as they are. And you have confessed only that they exist.
But how, and since when, or how great and how far, and in what form and order, and what their likeness is,
and how they are three while not being separate from one another, and how they are called three while being in one another,
and how the Son was begotten without being severed from the Father, and how the Father begot him without his going outside him,
and how, although they exist in being from eternity and forever, they are not called three self-existent beings—these things and others like them
are received through faith, and without faith no one can hear them. For a person cannot endure them.
Nor can ordinary hearing, unless faith is present beforehand and receives them.
Likewise, concerning spiritual natures and the heavenly orders, faith can accept everything that is said about them.
For how is faith not required when Scripture calls them truly spiritual beings,
yet elsewhere speaks of them as composite beings and assigns to their composition forms that differ from one another?
For the scriptural account has told us of wings and faces belonging to the seraphim,
and of other forms belonging to the cherubim, differing from one another. Which of these accounts are we to affirm?
For the two contradict one another, if the wording is understood only in its outward sense.
Are we to believe that they are spirits? Are we to affirm that they are composite beings?
Are we to accept that their structure consists of different forms? We accept all these things by faith,
because they are spoken by God. The backs of the living creatures, it says, were full of eyes as they turned about.
Through this statement we have learned that a spiritual nature sees with its whole being and hears with its whole being,
and senses with its whole being, thinks with its whole being, tastes with its whole being, and understands with its whole being.
And with its whole being it desires according to the desire of its nature. It does not hear with one part while not hearing with another,
or see with one part but not with another. Rather, its whole being is hearing, and its whole being is sight. Whatever it is, it is with its whole being.
Its hearing is not confused by its sight, even though it sees with the same part with which it hears, and tastes with the same part with which it thinks.
And these faculties are believed to exist in this way without being confused with one another or canceling one another out.
But in composite natures the opposite of these things is found: a being hears with one part,
sees with another, tastes with another, smells with another, senses with another, and thinks with yet another part.
Corresponding to the composition of its organs, the activity of its senses is also divided.
But above, among these spiritual natures, each is a unified whole in all its movements,
with no distinct bodily parts within it: head, feet, hands, faces, back or front,
length or breadth, color or forms differing from one another. For these natures have no composition made up of such bodily parts.
The absence of an eye does not mean the absence of the eye’s sight, and the absence of an ear does not mean the absence of the ear’s hearing.
The absence of a bodily palate does not mean that they lack the ability to taste spiritual things. Nor does their lack of wings mean that they do not fly.
Nor does their lack of feet mean that they do not move. Nor does their lack of the organs of the heart mean that they do not think.
Rather, they possess all the functions of bodily organs, although they have no composite bodily organs.
And how their activity takes place without organs is beyond the power of our understanding to grasp.
Rather, it is through what has been given to us by God—I mean faith—that we understand these things.
And although they do not fall at all within the scrutiny of human thought, we accept them without doubt.
For in this way we learn through faith even that they exist. And not only they, but also the self-existent nature that made them:
we accept through faith that it exists. For our entire teaching has its foundation in faith.
For although the appearance and course of created things give discerning people understanding and instruction about their Maker,
nevertheless, faith precedes even this. Indeed, because faith was absent, even this proved false for many.
And, to put it briefly, everything that is spirit, and the entire world of spiritual beings,
faith sees it, and faith perceives it. For if we do not receive faith into our soul,
we have no way to understand anything beyond what is visible. And faith is not needed for visible things,
because the sight of the eye sees them. For they are bodily things, and a human being looks at them bodily.
But the entire spiritual world is perceived by faith. And it is as though, if there is no faith, that world does not exist.
Consider how great the power of faith is: without it, all the spiritual things that exist are as though they did not exist.
And not only living creatures or spiritual places, but even Being itself, which exists,
is as though it did not exist for us if we have no faith. For this reason Paul looked into the mystery of our teaching
and said, “Whoever approaches God must believe that he exists.”
For he instructed the disciple to take faith upon himself and then approach discipleship to Christ.
For Paul knew that spiritual nature does not fall within the scope of the bodily senses, nor is even its existence known through them,
because it is subject to none of the bodily senses. For this reason he instructed us in his teaching simply to believe that it exists.
For the Maker divided all bodily nature into five forms: some of it to be seen, some to be heard,
some to be smelled, some to be tasted, and some to be touched. And he gave human beings five senses,
so that through them they might experience the world in its many variations. And beyond these five senses
that I have mentioned, a human being has no way to experience anything of the bodily world. Nor does the world itself exist beyond these.
But everything else that is spiritual, whether Being or creation, is subject to none of these five forms,
and is experienced through none of these five senses. For this reason our Lord too, when he gave us this grace by which we might perceive it,
First he handed down faith to us, so that through it we might perceive him; then he revealed himself to us.
For this reason blessed Paul said, “Faith comes from hearing, and hearing comes from the word of God.”
For Paul taught us to receive faith through hearing the word of God.
Although faith was planted in us at our creation by God our Creator, it had become corrupted and changed from faith into error.
It was like natural wisdom, which was also given to us at our creation, but which we changed; and instead of God's wisdom,
we gathered worldly wisdom within it, and through God's wisdom we substituted something other than God.
As Paul himself said, “In the wisdom of God, the world did not know God through wisdom.”
In the same way, the natural faith within us had also turned into error.
And these things, which the Creator gave us for our benefit, proved to be harmful among us,
because we changed their beneficial arrangements and used them in ways contrary to their purpose.
For our faith believed in what it should not, and our wisdom knew what it ought not.
For where faith was not needed, there we employed faith.
For what the bodily eye sees and all the bodily senses perceive,
our faith understood as though it were something else, and we formed an opinion about it that took one thing for another.
And because this entire order of faith—the faith that the Maker had planted in our nature—had become corrupted, the word of God
was planted in us a second time, and the power within us was awakened through Christ's teaching.
For this reason, throughout all his sayings, he urges that faith should be in us.
He says, “Truly I tell you, if you have faith like a mustard seed, you will say to this mountain, ‘Move from here,’ and it will move.
And nothing will be too difficult for you.” … He taught us that through faith nothing is too difficult for us.
Accordingly, everything is overcome by the power of faith, in keeping with the command expressed in Christ's word.
For through faith signs occur, wonders are performed, and mighty deeds are accomplished.
And marvels are carried out. For faith alone accomplishes everything that is above nature:
whether the resurrection of the dead, the restoration of the sick to health, the healing of diseases, or the cleansing of lepers;
whether the opening of blind eyes, the running of the lame, or the straightening and restoration of all the other bodily parts;
whether speech for those with speech impediments, hearing for the deaf, or the driving out of demons. Faith accomplishes all these things.
A mountain is moved from its place by faith. The sea and rivers were crossed on foot by faith.
Through the power of faith, all of nature obeyed a human being’s command.
In short, faith gives a human being the power of God, so that when someone believes, they can do whatever they wish through the power of their faith.
For faith transforms the weakness of the body into its own strength.
It turns a human being’s lowly command into a command of God that is obeyed.
For faith looks at what does not exist as though it exists, and considers what exists as though it does not exist.
This too is a likeness of the power of God, of whom Paul said, “He calls things that do not exist as though they exist.”
And the prophet said, “He rebukes the sea and dries it up, and makes all the rivers dry.”
And again, “He looks at the earth, and it trembles; he rebukes the mountains, and they smoke.” ... And Isaiah also said:
“All the nations are considered as nothing to him.” These things, then, the Spirit of God spoke about the power of God:
He called things that did not exist into existence, and he calls what exists and changes it into nothing.
Faith too imitates this very power, not only in signs and wonders,
bringing into being things that do not exist, in imitation of God, and removing and destroying things that exist through the power of God,
but also in looking at things considered nonexistent because they are hidden as though they were plainly visible.
And the things that exist, with which we occupy ourselves and which we use, it considers nonexistent.
For it sees their dissolution in advance. Before they have passed away, it has already made them pass away; while they still stand, it has already dissolved them.
Though they are visible, to faith they are as though invisible. Though their pleasures are tasted, to faith they are as though nonexistent.
Though all created things are in motion, to faith they are at rest.
When it sees death, it does not acknowledge that it is death. It considers wealth to be poverty.
Everything that exists in the world, even in the world’s very nature, it regards as nonexistent,
because the world’s course will come to an end and its affairs will cease.
But it brings things that are far away and distant from it, and sets them close before itself.
It beholds them face to face. Without a veil, it looks at all hidden things and beholds all secret things.
For the kingdom of heaven is far beyond bodily sight, but the eye of faith beholds it.
Those dwellings in the Father’s house are physically far from us, but faith already dwells in them.
That spiritual light rests gloriously within its realm, and faith walks in it.
And in it faith sees. The garment of our glory is in heaven, and our faith is already wrapped in it.
Our wealth and our spiritual possessions are there, and our faith trades in them. Our true city is in heaven.
And faith already dwells in it. Our kindred, our family, and our fathers are in that place.
And faith speaks with them and is always in their company. The table of our delight is prepared there.
And faith continually delights in it. The spring that gives us the water of life flows there.
And faith drinks from it at all times. The hosts of life and the ranks of light are
in the land of life, and faith glories with them. But why am I speaking about created works,
which, though glorious, are nevertheless creatures? Though they are great and wonderful, they came into being and were fashioned only recently.
And though they are now far from us because they are hidden, we are destined to draw near to them when we become spiritual, in keeping with the order of their realm.
What shall we say about these things, when God himself, the self-existent nature, who is remote and far from everything, is near to faith?
However far we may go from him, he is not far away. However far he may withdraw from faith, he is not remote.
And though he is beyond everything, he is close to faith.
And though he is within all created works, those that speak and those that are silent, those that live and those without sensation, wherever he is,
faith is beside him. For this is the nature of faith’s vision: that we should see what cannot be seen,
know what has not been known, and perceive what cannot be perceived,
and behold and draw near to what is infinitely remote. And the more subtle, hidden, and inward
and spiritual, exalted, and inexpressible the nature that faith seeks to see, the more brightly its own vision shines.
For faith is accustomed to show its proven worth in things that are exceedingly great, because it considers it a disgrace
to linger over little things and be held back among created works. For this reason it passes through everything
and stops at nothing except the Creator. For the limits of created works cannot
bear and contain the power of faith, because there is not one created work in which faith believes.
And if it believes in one, it believes that it was made, not that it exists. But faith’s own true quality is tasted only in God.
For it casts everything aside and places all natures on this side of itself, while it draws near to meet the Maker.
For faith makes present things pass away and brings things that are to come. Faith is the language of God.
Faith is the Creator’s command. Faith commands and, like God, is obeyed in everything.
It gives a sign, and all created things answer it. The power of faith is the power of God,
because faith’s power is received from God. For faith is the mistress of created works.
Just as a mistress commands her servant women and they obey her, so faith also commands created things, and they obey it.
And this is what is wonderful: not only do created works obey faith, but even the Creator himself does not resist its will.
It receives everything it seeks. Whatever it asks of him, he gives it. It calls to him, and he answers it.
For the Giver’s door stands open to faith’s requests, as he himself said: “Whatever you ask, without doubting, you will receive.”
For faith indeed gives commands in God’s house, like a mistress of riches and a steward of possessions.
Wonderful and exalted is the mystery of faith, and no one can explain its mystery.
And it is so great that it is God’s dwelling place: faith, which is not in heaven, nor merely a matter of sound and words,
but is revealed through the soul’s genuine testing and through the fixed and steadfast resolve of its thoughts, while it does not deny itself.
Rather, in this too it resembles God, of whom Paul said, “He cannot deny himself.”
So faith too, like him, does not deny itself. It does not admit doubt about itself, and conjecture finds no place in it.
Fear does not enter its domain. It accomplishes everything it wishes, and whatever it seeks is given to it.
Anyone who approaches God must hold this faith within.
For faith has no thoughts that undo one another, nor ideas that cancel one another out.
Faith does not regret what it does and says, nor does it reproach itself,
once it has spoken and asked for what it wishes. And just as there is no regret in God
over anything he does or says, so there is no regret in faith over what it accomplishes,
so that in this too it may resemble God. As for faith, its command is an authoritative command.
It prays confidently, and in accordance with its confidence, its prayer is immediately fulfilled in deeds.
There are also times when faith does not first pray and then give a command concerning something, but speaks with authority, in the likeness of God.
And just as nothing can resist God’s command, so nothing can resist faith’s command either.
There are times when faith prays, and in its very prayer reveals itself.
And there are times when, without praying, it commands with authority and receives an answer. Elijah did not pray before Ahab and then receive a hearing.
But the faith within him commanded with authority, and whatever he said immediately came to pass.
His word ruled over all created beings and works more powerfully than a king’s command over the cities of his dominion.
“As the mighty Lord lives, before whom I stand,” he said, “there will be neither dew nor rain during these years until I say so.”
It is not written that he prayed and then spoke. The moment creation heard his word, it was brought under the direction of his command.
All created works obeyed the command of a mortal human being as though it were the word of God.
The clouds obeyed him. He called to the earth, and it answered him. He commanded the air, and it no longer displayed its changes.
Before the word of Elijah’s faith, all creation became a subject maidservant, serving in awe of the command spoken to it by its mistress.
On another occasion, as it is written, he commanded the military captains who had come up to take him away, together with the others accompanying them.
He spoke with divine authority, and God’s fire came down from heaven and burned them all.
“If I am a prophet, as I said,” he declared, “let fire come down from heaven and consume you and the fifty men with you.”
Immediately, without delay, fire blazed down from heaven upon the unclean men, and the prophet’s word was fulfilled in deed.
In other places, however, it is written that faith prayed and was then heard.
For example, it is written that he bent down, placed his face between his knees, and sent his disciple to look toward the sea.
Again, when he raised the widow’s son, he prayed and stretched himself out, and then raised him. In this prayer too,
faith was revealed. For if he had not believed that he would raise him, he would not have taken the boy from his mother,
carried him upstairs, and laid him on his bed. Again, he also spoke with authority to his disciple: “Ask whatever you wish, and I will give it to you,
before I am taken away from you.” And just as the disciple asked and the master commanded, the Spirit carried it out in deed.
The gift rested upon Elisha. But when he was offering sacrifices on Mount Carmel before the eyes of Ahab
and all Israel, he cried out, “Answer me, Lord! Answer me, Lord, so that all this people may know that you are the Lord and I am your servant,
and that I have done everything at your command.” He received no answer and brought down no fire until he prayed.
The reason for this is clear: why they prayed on one occasion and commanded with authority on another.
For in the one case their weakness was evident, and in the other the power of God that was with them was revealed.
For when they prayed and pleaded, they were shown to be weak human beings.
But when they commanded and were obeyed without prayer, it became known that God’s power accompanied their command.
On one occasion they spoke as human beings, and on another as servants of God.
That is, like gods in the flesh. For the faith within them made them heavenly gods.
And in this too they resembled Christ, who is God. For sometimes he acted as one who has authority,
while at other times he made a request and then acted. For he did not raise Lazarus until he had prayed.
And he did not bless the bread and distribute it to the crowds until he had looked up to heaven. And until he had spat, put his fingers into the ears of that deaf man, and looked up to heaven,
he did not command him to be opened. But he healed the others with an authoritative command,
without looking up to heaven or asking his Father. For with an authoritative command he raised the young man, the widow’s son.
He called aloud to the daughter of the synagogue leader, and immediately she arose. He commanded the sea, and it grew calm, and the wind, and it was restrained.
He merely said, “Fill the jars with water, and draw some out and bring it to the master of the banquet.” And the deed did not lag behind his will.
“I say to you,” he said to the mute spirit, and immediately it departed from the person.
“I am willing; be cleansed,” he said to the leper, and just as he willed, the leprosy immediately fled from the body.
For Jesus too performed miracles in this manner, so that in this too he lowered himself to the level of those whom, in his grace, he called his brothers.
So that they would not be distressed that they were not heard until they prayed, he too humbled himself and prayed, and then was heard.
For the Lord took upon himself equality with his servants, so that what is written might be fulfilled: that he had to become like his brothers in everything.
For he gave them authority to speak with authority and receive an answer, so that by this they might be recognized as servants of God,
and so that he might also give faith the boldness to do whatever it wishes. So too Joshua son of Nun:
he commanded the sun and the moon with authority, and they were halted. Each stood still at its place along its course.
Joshua stretched out his hand, it says, and spoke with the authority of faith: “You, sun, remain at Gibeon,
and you, moon, in the valley of Aijalon.” And the sun was halted and the moon stood still until the people had taken vengeance on their enemies.
And why do I speak about the prophets, when faith displayed victories like these through the whole people, women and children alike?
For faith cried out as it had been commanded, and the walls could not withstand its voice.
For everywhere faith displayed victories like these, and throughout all the Holy Scriptures it performed these miracles.
Whoever has perceived the power of faith and experienced it in action knows that it has done these things,
and also believes that it does things like these. So you too, whoever wishes to become a disciple of God,
acquire faith, the mistress of all possessions. For this will be the beginning of your discipleship.
Make it the foundation in the building of your tower, and however high it may reach, it will not fall.
For a building whose foundation is faith is not shaken by waves or winds.
Jesus too laid this faith as a foundation through Simon, and just as our Lord made it the beginning,
so also the disciple who approaches instruction in the proper order must begin with it first.
For Jesus made it the foundation of the whole church. You, then, make it the foundation of your own conduct.
He built upon it the virtuous conduct of the whole world. You, then, build upon it the victories and conduct of your soul.
He laid it down to be a foundation for all the generations after his coming.
And you, make it the beginning of your life in God. See how great its power is,
since it is sufficient to bear all humanity. For Jesus too, who laid it as the foundation of the building of his church,
did so because he had already seen its invincible might, its unfailing firmness, its strength that does not weaken, and its victory that cannot be put to shame,
and its power that cannot be brought low, its prowess that cannot be weakened, and its command that cannot be resisted,
and its verdict that cannot be reversed, its word that cannot be proved false, and its authority that cannot be treated with contempt.
For it was this faith, mistress of victories, that Jesus made the foundation of his church and the beginning of the building of his holy body,
to teach everyone to begin with it, and to teach the disciple to make it the foundation of all his conduct.
For he established it as the foundation of his church not only to show its power, but also to teach everyone
who wishes to begin the new building of his discipleship to make it his starting point.
And throughout the rest of his entire building, it will support and raise all the courses of good deeds.
For not one of the good stones is raised into the structure of this tower unless faith raises it.
And there is no life in any of the limbs of virtue unless the life of faith is in them.
For just as all the limbs of the body are dead without the life of the soul,
so all the practices of righteousness are dead without the life of faith.
And just as the limbs live through the soul, so deeds live through faith.
And just as, even if the limbs of the body are healthy and strong, as long as the soul is not in them,
they are inactive, and their beauty and health do them no good, so too, even if one's practices are laborious and severe,
and a person is vigorous in the race of righteousness, as long as faith is absent from the limbs of his deeds, his labor is empty.
And just as all the limbs receive sensation from the life of the soul,
so that through its life each one of them may move according to its natural order and perform the function that belongs to it: the eye to see,
the ear to hear, the palate to taste, the nostrils to smell, the hand to touch, the foot to walk, and the whole body to move and act
and stir with living movements, in every posture, through the functioning of all its members.
The members that make up works of righteousness are likewise.
As long as they lack the life of faith, they are dead and idle.
For fasting is not fasting if faith does not accompany it. Nor are charitable gifts counted as such if they are not given in faith.
Nor does compassion amount to anything if faith does not accompany it.
Neither do abstinence and asceticism, unless faith is mingled with them; nor humility and submission, unless faith sustains them;
nor strict confinement, if faith does not accompany it. For a good deed with which faith is not mingled is not even counted as a good deed.
Righteousness that is not mixed with faith loses its name and is emptied of its labors.
Just as the shadow of a body is not called a body, nor is the shadow of a hand or foot called
by the name of any of these members, so too the body of righteousness, which lacks the life of faith,
is not called a body, nor is fasting called fasting, nor are asceticism or abstinence
given the names of genuine members. For without faith they are all a shadow and a dead body.
They cannot be called a genuine body, because they exist only in appearance and labor in someone else’s vineyard.
For faith is the fence around the plants of Christ’s commandments.
Every plant found within this fence belongs to Christ and is planted in his vineyard.
But the plants outside this fence are called wild plants.
They either bear no fruit at all, or, if they do produce fruit, beasts with teeth and birds strip it off and destroy it.
And if the fruits happen to remain, they are spoiled and have no nourishing power.
For this is the vineyard for which the master of the house hired workers.
Everyone he saw standing outside it he considered idle, and he urged him to come and work in his vineyard.
For through faith the good things already present are preserved, and those not yet present are acquired.
For faith gathers treasures and guards treasures. It hides precious possessions,
and it guards precious possessions. It serves as the foundation, and it serves as the architect. It is spread out beneath the foundation courses.
And she rises with the courses of masonry. She forms the limbs, and she gives the limbs life. She plants spiritual plants.
And she tends the spiritual plants. She becomes a fence around the plants, and she is the spring that waters them.
She is the one who gives birth, and she is the one who nurtures. She is the body, and she is the soul within the body.
She scatters seeds, and she reaps and gathers crops. She plants trees,
and she picks and gathers fruit. … For faith is everything, because she is capable of being everything.
So hold fast to this faith, disciple. Persevere in this truth, and do not grow slack.
And everything you believe, you ask for and receive from Christ, who promised to give.
To him be glory, and to his Father and his Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.
The second discourse on faith is finished.
Notes on the Syriac text:
The Third Discourse on Faith
Come again, disciple, and hear the lovely victories of faith.
Come, listen to your mother's voice, for through her sweet melodies she gives you life.
Come, suck the living milk of instruction from the living breast of the mother who gave you birth.
Come, stand beside the spring that gives the generations drink, for whoever does not drink from it will not have his thirst quenched.
Come, sit at the table filled with the food of life, for whoever is not nourished from it
has no life in his life. Come, incline your ear and listen. Come, open your eyes and see
the wonders revealed through faith. Come, carve out new eyes for yourself.
Come, prepare hidden ears for yourself. You are invited to hear hidden things; you need hidden ears.
And you have been called to see spiritual things; you need spiritual eyes.
Come, see yourself as something you are not, and be renewed before you are renewed.
For the Creator created you as a new creation, and faith helped him in making you.
He brought you to a wondrous transformation and a heavenly formation, and faith was with him when he was forming you.
For in the beginning, when he was creating creatures and fashioning his works, wisdom was with him,
as Solomon said: “The Lord laid the foundations of the earth by his wisdom, and established the heavens by his understanding.”
By his knowledge the depths were split open, and the clouds sprinkled water. And again Wisdom said:
“When he established the heavens, I was with him; when he made a circle over the surface of the depths, and when he strengthened the clouds above,
and when the springs of the depths grew strong.” For Wisdom was with God in his first works.
But in this second creation, faith was with him, in this second birth.
He took faith as his helper. Faith accompanies God in everything.
Without it he does no new things today. For it would have been easy for him to give you birth from water and the Spirit without it.
Yet until it is professed, he does not give you birth anew. He could have renewed you and changed you from old to new.
Yet until he takes faith from you as a pledge, he does not change you or renew you. Faith is required of the person being baptized.
Then that person receives treasures from the water. For without faith,
everything is ordinary. Faith came, and despised things appeared glorious.
Without faith, baptism is water. Without faith, the life-giving mysteries are bread and wine.
The old person is seen just as he is, if there is no eye of faith to see him.
The mysteries are ordinary, and the wonders of the Spirit are despised, if there is no eye of faith to see them.
For the power of faith cannot be tasted by testing words. Rather, faith is tasted in and through itself.
Faith is not perfected by what the ear hears. Rather, it is confirmed from within by the power of the soul.
For the ear receives only the report of faith. But the practice of faith
is born from thoughts. For the spring from which faith flows is a pure mind
and a simple thought in which there is no “this and that.” For the thought of faith is single, and there is nothing in it that fights against anything else in it.
Faith gazes in secret, watches closely, and examines the power hidden in things. For faith is further within than knowledge.
What knowledge does not see is revealed to faith, which is further within than knowledge.
For because knowledge could not do the work of faith, knowledge went out, and faith entered in its place.
For knowledge is outside, concerned with works, while faith is within, concerned with the work.
Knowledge investigates the wisdom hidden in creation, while faith investigates the hidden things of the mysteries.
Knowledge examines the power of roots and fruits and of all the food given to the body.
But faith examines the power hidden in the life-giving mysteries, which are the food of the soul.
For however subtle knowledge becomes, it still creeps among bodily things. It wanders and roams in the visible world.
Faith, however, does not remain within this creation, nor can the power of deeds receive it so that it may dwell in them.
The tongue cannot taste the power of faith, nor can speech tell of its beauties or sketch and portray its likenesses.
For its power is not tasted through sound, nor is it known through speech, nor through that part of thought which turns toward the body.
Rather, within the holy of holies of the hidden, spiritual mind, there the mysteries of faith are shown and hidden things are revealed.
For the part within us that is more glorious than the whole human being is alone capable of perceiving faith.
For the deeds of faith are seen outwardly, and its words are heard with the ears.
Its power, however, is tasted inwardly in the mind. For not even if you see the dead rising or the eyes of the blind being opened,
or demons coming out, have you yet seen the power of faith.
For how have you seen the power of faith in a body rising, when, look, it also raises the soul from the dead?
And how have you tasted its power in the healing of bodily eyes, when, look, it also creates eyes for spiritual beings?
And how do you see its authority in demons coming out, when, look, it also drives natural thoughts out of the soul?
For the power of faith is shown to those outside through outward deeds.
But the person himself tastes it through the soul’s power. Faith does not give the mind a taste of itself through anything else.
Rather, without anything else acting as an intermediary, faith itself encounters the mind and lets it taste its power.
Inwardly, within the soul, outward signs do not serve as intermediaries for tasting faith.
Rather, faith itself dwells in the soul and delights it, enlightening its thoughts and filling them with joy.
It makes the light of its nature dawn within, and the soul marvels at the new light spread over it.
For until faith turns the soul’s vision back and gathers it in from every direction, it does not show the soul the beauty of its nature.
For the soul cannot even see faith while dividing its gaze among other things.
For the soul’s natural vision becomes impoverished whenever it is divided and looks outside itself.
And it cannot contemplate the clarity of faith’s light.
For faith gives such power to the soul that becomes a pure dwelling place for it:
that the soul looks at things not as they are, but as it wishes to see them.
For look, you carry in your hands the glowing coal of the mysteries, which by its nature is ordinary bread.
And through it faith beholds the body of the Only Begotten, though the eye of faith does not look as the bodily eye does.
Rather, faith compels bodily sight to see what is invisible to it. For bodily sight sees bread, wine, oil, and water.
But faith compels sight to see spiritually what it cannot see physically. That is, instead of bread,
it is to taste the body; instead of wine, it is to drink blood; and instead of water, it is to see the baptism of the Spirit.
And instead of oil, the power of Christ. For faith possesses the power of God.
It has the will and authority of God, and it gathers benefits from wherever it wishes.
Faith approaches the bones of the saints and sees them as living rather than dead.
It speaks with them as with the living and appeals to them concerning its needs.
For faith reveals to the dead body what it needs to receive from the giver who grants requests.
And it appeals to him: “Through your mediation, may I receive this gift,” paying no attention to the fact that he is deprived of life,
silent in speech, without a sound, inactive in conduct, and a stranger to all natural movements.
For it does not seek to have him as its mediator on the level of these things. It knows that, in terms of nature,
not only in his death, but even in his life, he is incapable of being a mediator between the Creator and his creatures.
But through that which is above nature and has been mingled into the saints from the power of Christ,
and remains with them even when they lie within their graves—it is to this that faith looks.
It appeals to the dead as to the living and speaks with the silent as with those who can speak.
For the eye of faith casts off the sight of all visible things and puts on the hidden sight of all spiritual things.
It moves among everything that is inward, within the body. For a person stands in one place and contemplates another.
He lives bodily in the lower world, but through his faith he dwells in the world above.
Faith hears about the resurrection of the dead and the renewal of human bodies, and regards them as though they had already risen and been renewed.
It has received a promise concerning the world of life, the kingdom of light, and the places of glory,
and concerning spiritual delights, tastes of blessedness, and the explanation of mysteries,
and concerning our becoming like the angels. It regards all these things that it has heard as certain.
For faith is an intermediary between things past and things to come. For the things that happened before us,
and the things that are to happen after us—we receive knowledge of them all through faith.
As Paul says: “By faith we understand that the worlds were formed by the word of God.”
“And the things that are seen came into being from things that are not seen.”
For if a person has no faith, he can deny everything recorded in the Holy Scriptures.
And he can say of all hidden things, which truly exist, that they do not exist at all.
And because they are not seen, there is no immediate refutation of his doubt. For faith
does not even need testimony to confirm what it hears. For demonstrations and testimonies are required for knowledge
and for someone who wants to see and touch before he believes. For faith does not arise from miracles.
For just as God does not need to be convinced through mighty deeds and miracles about the things that will come into being through him,
since everything is revealed and clear to his foreknowledge, so faith does not need miracles either.
For how could it need what it itself produces?
Indeed, mighty deeds, signs, miracles, and everything of this kind come about through faith.
How, then, could it need what it itself produces, so that its testimony might confirm its belief in hidden things?
