For just as God has no need of his works,
in the same way faith has no need of the miracles performed through it. For faith needs nothing:
neither seeing nor touching, neither signs and miracles nor proofs and testimonies,
but only to hear the word of God and to know that it is God who is speaking. Immediately it accepts and does not doubt.
For none of the righteous has pleased God without faith, as Paul’s teaching testifies.
He began with Abel and recounted them all, proceeding one by one down to the revelation of Christ.
He showed that they all pleased God through faith. And, laying down a clear rule for all disciples, he said:
“Without faith no one can please God.” And again he said:
“All these died in faith and did not receive what had been promised to them, because God had looked ahead to our benefit, so that they would not be made perfect without us.”
For until their death, according to the apostle’s words, faith accompanied them throughout their lives.
Through it they performed mighty deeds while they were in the world.
And through it they hoped and waited to receive the promises to come and to obtain what he had promised them—
the one whose word they followed. For faith is the soil that receives the seed of the word of God.
And just as a farmer's seed produces no crops if he has no field,
so God's word produces no spiritual benefits among us if there is no soil of faith to receive it.
And again, just as the eye receives the sun, so the vision of faith receives the spiritual light of Christ's commandments.
And just as the sunlight, although it reveals everything, allows nothing to be seen without an eye to receive it,
so also God's command, although it accomplishes everything, does not take effect among us without faith.
For the sun is bright by nature, and God's word is powerful in the one who speaks it. But just as
the sun's natural light becomes powerless for blind eyes and reveals nothing,
so God's command seems weak within a soul that has no faith.
For faith is a discerning eye that sees everything
and examines it as it really is. And because visible things are small in its sight, it leaves them behind and gazes at things that are unseen.
It examines things that are above nature and beyond the senses, and comes to know them.
For even our name has been given to us from faith, because it gave us birth out of error into the knowledge of God.
And for this reason, everyone who approaches Christ and becomes a disciple of his gospel takes his name from faith and is called a believer.
For since faith is our mother and the one who gave us birth, it is fitting that we should be named after the one who gave us birth.
And this is the wonder: how far the greatness of faith has reached, so that, just as from the name of God and his Christ, a name may also be taken from faith by
human beings. For from God's name we are called godly, and from Christ's name
we are named Christians, and from the name of faith we are called believers.
For this is the name that has set us apart from all religions and separates us from all teachings of error.
For no one is called a believer except someone who has been born of true faith, which is his mother and nurturer.
For since all our teaching looks in hope toward things to come and fixes its gaze on the expectation of unseen things,
and these things in which we have been instructed are not apparent or known to the bodily senses,
it is fitting that we have been called believers because of these things, since the hope of all our blessings rests on faith.
And if faith is taken away, not one of these things of ours can be believed. For whether it is our mysteries here
or the blessings promised to us in the world beyond, faith is what holds and safeguards them.
For if someone examines all the mysteries of the church's worship with bodily eyes, without faith, he considers them ordinary and contemptible.
And the things of this world appear, in their outward form, more powerful and glorious than ours.
For look: on our side is poverty, and on the world's side, wealth; on our side, contempt, and on its side, glory.
On our side is humility, and on its side, exaltation; on our side, lowly status, and on its side, prominence.
On our side is dispossession, and on its side, possessions; on our side, hunger, and on its side, fullness; on our side, deprivation,
and on its side, abundance; on our side, afflictions, and on its side, comforts; on our side, subjection,
and on its side, command; on our side, a narrow road, and on its side, a broad road.
On our side is a single garment prescribed by the commandment, and on its side, varied finery in clothing.
On our side is a word that forbids us even a day's provisions, and on its side, treasures accumulated for generations and years.
On our side, we are to appear in utter contempt and dishonor, and on its side is an appearance of grandeur and honor.
All these things, and others like them, make the world appear glorious and superior in every respect to these things of ours.
If we take faith, which is our true wealth, out of the picture—as our teacher Paul also testified about this when he said,
"If in this life we hope in Christ, we are more miserable than all other people."
And again, elsewhere he says, "We are fools for Christ's sake, weak, lowly, and dishonored, and we have nothing."
And although we possess nothing among the things of the place where we live, in what is ours we possess everything,
as the apostle himself says again: "Although we have nothing, we possess everything."
In short, not one of these things of ours can be seen in this life except by the eye of faith, which alone sees them.
For our wealth is not visible here, nor our authority, nor the distinct ranks of our deeds,
nor our honors, nor our comforts, nor our kingdom, nor the halls where we will rest,
nor the hidden and sealed blessings kept for us, nor heaven, the city where we dwell,
nor Zion, the land of life, which thirsts and longs to receive her children, nor the treasures in our storehouses,
nor the wealth of our heavenly possessions, nor our freedom, which is above all subjection,
nor the fullness of all good things that we are to receive. For all these things of ours are hidden in this life,
and they are not visible to people who live according to the flesh. Believers, however, have perceived them through faith alone.
And they see everything that is invisible, and listen to sounds that cannot be heard by the bodily ear.
And they touch what cannot be felt by the physical hand, and taste things that cannot be tasted by the palate of the mouth.
For the perception of the spiritual blessings promised to us lies deeper within than all the bodily senses.
And if we lack spiritual senses—that is, faith, which perceives these blessings—it is as though they do not even exist.
But if you say, “Look, our mysteries here are glorious,” consider that without faith
their glory cannot be seen. And everything that we take from the world and use,
according to the tradition handed down to us, belongs to the world if we look at it with the world's eye.
But if we contemplate it in faith, it is above the world. For the buildings of our houses of prayer belong to the world,
because their structure is taken and assembled from the world. Spiritually, however, they are above the world,
because they are representations of that church of the firstborn who are enrolled in heaven, which is the free Jerusalem, the mother of us all.
And all the altars, together with the other vessels used in the service of the mysteries, and everything with which we perform the mysteries handed down to us,
belong to the world by their nature. But because of the greatness of the things celebrated through them, they are lofty and exalted,
and we regard them as above nature, because they are likenesses of the living, spiritual powers in heaven,
through whom the service of God's hidden mysteries and his purposes are accomplished.
Furthermore, the holy mysteries themselves, which we celebrate for the salvation of our lives,
are originally taken from the world. For the bread and wine that are offered on the spiritual altar come from it.
But when the altar receives them, as the womb received the Word, it makes them become something above the world:
the living body and blood of God, who is above the world.
Likewise, the water and oil through which the mystery of our baptism is accomplished are taken from here, from the world.
But when the time comes for those invited to grace to be born in them and from them,
the baptismal font of ordinary water and oil becomes a womb and a power that give birth to spiritual beings,
so that, like Christ rising from the tomb after three days, the dead sinner who descended into the font rises from it alive.
And corresponding to our Lord's being raised after three days, he is renewed through three immersions in the three names.
And just as our Lord, after his resurrection, passed from the bodily way of life that preceded his crucifixion to a spiritual way of life,
so too the person who is raised from the baptismal font as from a tomb walks in new life, according to Paul's teaching.
We bury our dead like everyone else.
And the outward appearance of our funeral rites and burial is no different from that of pagans and Jews.
But we, in the hope of faith and in expectation of the resurrection of the dead, entrust our departed to life, not to death.
And according to our faith, we send them to heaven, not to Sheol.
But those who go astray, because they have no hope of faith, send their dead to death and destruction.
For the mysteries of believers are great and exalted, if someone approaches them with a mind shaped by faith.
For because the bodily eye is too limited to see our mysteries, we have been given another eye, that of faith,
which is capable of contemplating them and seeing them as they will be, not as they are.
And the things promised to us that are far from us, it sees close at hand and does not consider distant.
Have you understood, then, you who wish to become a disciple of Christ, that everything belonging to us is established through faith?
And without faith, neither we, nor the things belonging to us, nor the things that come from us, nor those promised to be given to us
are visible, and they are as though they did not exist. Therefore, at the beginning of your discipleship, acquire faith for yourself.
And go after God. For you will not even agree to keep his commandments unless you first believe him.
For faith is planted in your nature and placed within you by the Creator, so that you may believe him through the faith he has placed in us.
Therefore, do not turn the power of faith in the opposite direction and use it to believe in things that do not exist,
and, instead of believing in things that are true and endure forever, believe in something that is neither true nor lasting.
For all the things here exist in outward form; they pass away and dissolve, according to the teaching of Scripture.
But all the things to come that are promised to the faithful endure forever, neither passing away nor decaying.
Therefore, do not use the faith within you to believe in something that passes away and consider it enduring.
Instead, use faith in its proper order, and through it believe in spiritual things. For even those who used to worship idols,
and considered stones, wood, and all the natural things in creation to be gods, had faith within them.
But they altered its proper order, and instead of using it to believe in God, they used it to believe in manufactured idols.
And they called them gods of error, though they do not exist.
For faith is faith as long as it rests on things appropriate to it. But if it believes in other things that are contrary to it,
and regards them as something they are not, it is no longer faith but error.
For this reason God placed faith in your nature: so that you would believe in him alone,
and, for his sake, believe whatever he wants you to believe, and nothing else.
For through that likeness placed within us, knowledge of God is naturally present, as the blessed Paul said:
“Knowledge of God is manifest in them, for God has revealed it in them.” Through that same likeness, faith too is naturally fixed in the thoughts of us all.
But just as knowledge of God was fixed within them, even though they did not worship his nature or honor his being, but worshiped his name
and honored it in all created things because of that natural knowledge, so too, through the faith placed within us, we believe all sorts of things,
and our will turns our faith wherever it wishes, directing it to look at the natural impulses within us.
For if our will wishes, it believes in God through faith.
And if it wishes, through that same faith it affirms idols and demons. And if it desires that world of rest,
it believes that it endures forever, and longs and yearns for it. And if it wishes, it believes in this world, which passes away,
as though it were enduring, and loves it and runs after it.
For the will is the ruler of faith, as it is of all the other natural impulses within us.
It governs everything, whether the outward senses or the inward thoughts.
For just as eyes have been given to us to see the beauties of created things,
and ears to hear the divine commandments, and hands to reach out toward good deeds,
and feet to run to beneficial gatherings, yet the will turns them toward the opposite,
and instead of the good things for which the limbs and senses were made, it uses them for evil and hateful things,
so too with the faith placed in our nature, through which we are to believe in God and affirm his spiritual promises:
the authority of the will has turned it around, and through it the will believes in demons instead of God, and affirms bodily things instead of spiritual things,
and visible things instead of invisible things, and things that pass away and perish instead of things that do not pass away.
But you, disciple, use faith in its proper good order, and do not turn it toward error.
Through it believe in God and his promises, and do not use it to believe in the world and its comforts.
For everything visible is temporary, and everything invisible is eternal, as Paul also taught.
Believe in God, then, and hope that eternal good things will be given to you by him. Let faith be the beginning of your journey.
For if you do not believe in invisible things, you cannot abandon visible things.
And if you do not believe that Christ’s promise is true, and that the good things he has promised to all who go forth following his gospel are real,
you will not leave what you hold on to and run after the blessings he has promised you.
“Unless,” he says, “a person renounces his father and mother, his brothers and sisters, and the whole world,
and even his own life, he cannot be my disciple.” Hear this voice, disciple, and leave the world.
This good news, which promises spiritual blessings, should alone draw you away from the ways and practices of the world.
For you have heard this voice. Believe him and be his disciple, and no one else’s.
There must be no other reason for your departure from the world. Otherwise, your departure will not succeed.
For as the first cause is, so too will be all the others that follow it.
For many abandon the world's way of life for one reason or another,
and come forward to become Christ’s disciples, but not for that one true reason. Because of this, their discipleship does not succeed.
Instead, they become like diseased limbs in the healthy body of Christ’s discipleship,
and they also hinder the healthy limbs from carrying out the ministry of the Spirit and from observing all our Lord’s commandments.
It would have been better for them to remain in the world than to become an example of laxity among spiritual people.
For the world's entire way of life is sick and feeble in spiritual matters, but the body of Christ’s discipleship is healthy and sound.
Whoever cuts off the limbs of his own person from that diseased body,
and comes to be joined to this living body, should be brought into fellowship with the body solely by his love for its way of life.
There should be no other reason for this joining. Yet there are many who, whether because of servitude,
or debt, or pressure from parents, or a wife’s clamoring, together with other unhealthy reasons—
reasons by which many are forcibly driven—come to become disciples of Christ.
When they come, they are with him in outward appearance, but in reality they are with the world.
They are here deceitfully, only as far as the eye can see, but there in their actions and thoughts.
They are here out of habit, but there by choice. Here, submission to compulsion leads them; there, their own free choice holds them.
In short, their shadow is here, but their body is in the world.
Here they stand only in image and likeness, but there in their actual persons,
becoming a cause of stumbling both to themselves and to their brothers.
They eat Christ’s bread by taking it wrongfully, not justly. Although they hired themselves out to him, they work for another,
and they feel no shame. Although he called them, they obeyed another who opposes him.
And while everyone takes them in and carries them as his own, they are ungrateful for his grace and despise his commandments.
They become a stumbling block instead of a source of edification, and a spectacle of losses instead of gains,
and a cause of stumbling in the place of truth, and an image full of deceit among visions of help.
For those who are like this, it would have been better, according to Christ’s word, if they had not been born; or, if they had been born,
if they had remained in the diseased condition of worldly conduct in which they had been, rather than coming to make others sick along with themselves,
and, besides being dead to God themselves, putting living members to death along with them.
But you, disciple of God, flee from such people. Let faith alone be the reason for your departure from the world,
so that the whole building of your deeds may rise in keeping with the foundation you have laid.
For when your deeds draw strength from your original faith, the faith that brought you out of the world,
they are all brought to fulfillment through that faith, kept in sound health, and maintained in uprightness,
and they hasten to meet God’s unseen gaze, reaching fulfillment and perfection through the encouragement that faith gives.
For as long as faith looks upward, the course of conduct advances diligently, and the path of labors
runs swiftly. For that eye of faith which you opened at the beginning, and through which you saw Christ’s promises from afar—
take care not to close it because of any of the circumstances that confront you once you have begun the course of your journey,
lest a stumbling block suddenly come upon you and you fall on the path you are walking.
But just as those who begin a journey along a road in the natural world walk with the same sight with which they began until they reach the end of the road,
taking care that their eyes do not grow drowsy on their journey and obstruct the sight that guides them, so you too, disciple,
who have begun to travel the road to heaven, must preserve until the end the sight you had at the beginning of your journey.
For the more the eye of your faith contemplates the things to come, the lighter the labors of your way of life become for you,
and your soul takes delight in the hardships of your good deeds. And just as the foot is kept from stumbling as long as the eye is open to see,
so weariness is absent and far removed from the soul as long as faith’s sight is sound and it contemplates and looks upon heavenly things.
For a soul deprived of the gaze of faith is either asleep or dead.
The soul that drives faith away from itself entirely is a dead soul.
But the soul that retains the name of faith, yet does not always have its eye open to contemplate spiritual things,
is a sleeping soul, submerged in the sleep of weariness. When it labors, it does not perceive it, and when it acts righteously, it does not know it.
And while it runs, it is unaware of its running. And just as someone who is asleep does not perceive what is happening beside him,
so neither is someone whose vision of faith has gone out aware of the good things accomplished through it.
Rather, like a blind man who is led by someone else, he too is drawn along by the force of habit,
or because he cannot change the forms of toil to which he holds. And he goes on in the place where he is.
For it is not fitting for a disciple of Christ to have his good deeds sustained by human law,
lest, when the laws are abolished, or their framers wish to change them,
his own good deeds also be torn apart and scattered. For the one who set the contest before us is not a human being.
For this reason, human laws should not govern us in the struggle of this contest either,
but only the will of Christ himself, who sets the contest before us. This, then, is the beginning of your departure from the world,
you who are beginning your journey on the road to heaven and have, through faith, stripped off the garment of deluded thinking,
which is entangled in the affairs of the world, goes astray, and regards what does not exist as though it existed.
Take care, then, not to change in your faith, always remembering the words of Paul.
Through them, strengthen your faith and cleanse your thoughts of the filth of error, in accordance with what he said:
“Whoever approaches God must believe that God exists.” To him be glory forever. Amen.
The third discourse, on faith, is finished.
Notes on the Syriac text:
The fourth discourse: On faith, and on how a person can accept Christ’s commandments in simplicity.
Our Lord gave us an easy and simple beginning in his gospel: true and steadfast faith, which arises naturally in a simple mind,
so that through this very faith we may obey him and keep his commandments.
In this way, all the righteous people of old who were called by God also heard his word in simplicity and accepted his promises in faith.
For by simplicity I do not mean what is regarded in the world as foolishness, but the singleness of an undivided mind,
which is ready to listen rather than judge, and to accept rather than investigate, just as an infant receives sounds from its nurse.
Or again, like a child who receives instruction in reading from his teacher, without judging or investigating
what is said to him. For just as an infant’s capacity is too small to investigate human learning,
so the capacity of our understanding is too small to grasp the explanations of divine mysteries.
And so, only through faith and simplicity can a person listen and accept.
This is how Abraham too was called and went out to follow God, without passing judgment on the voice that came to him,
and without being held back by family and relatives, homeland and friends, or any of the other human ties.
For the moment he heard the voice and knew that it was God's, he disregarded everything and set out.
He listened to it simply and assented to it in faith, with that natural simplicity which is unpracticed in evil.
Like a child following his father, he ran toward the voice of God.
Everything became insignificant in his eyes as soon as he heard the word of God. For he also possessed natural knowledge and discernment.
But here he showed his discernment in this: that he ought to obey God who had called him, as a servant obeys his master,
and as a created thing obeys its maker. Nor did he give the knowledge he possessed any authority here
to investigate and inquire why and for what purpose he had been called by God.
"Leave your land and your relatives," he said, "and come to the land that I will show you." And he did not reveal to him
which land it was, so that his faith might shine all the more and his simplicity might be seen.
Although it appeared that he was leading him to the land of Canaan, he promised to show him another land, the land of life that is in heaven.
As Paul also testifies, "He was waiting for the city that has a foundation, whose designer and maker is God."
And again he said, "It is clear that they longed for a land better than the land of Canaan, namely, the one in heaven."
And to teach us clearly that it was not the land of the bodily promise that God was promising to show Abraham, he settled him in Haran
after bringing him out of Ur of the Chaldeans, and did not lead him to the land of Canaan immediately after his departure.
And again, so that Abraham would not be thought to have heard news of a reward and therefore to have set out in response to God's voice,
he did not tell him from the beginning the name of the land to which he was leading him.
Look, then, disciple, at this departure, and let your departure be like it. Do not delay in responding to the living voice of Christ who has called you.
For just as he called Abraham alone there, so here through his gospel he calls everyone who is willing,
and invites them to set out after him. For when he said, "Whoever wishes to come after me,
let him deny himself, take up his cross, and come after me," he extended a common call to all humanity.
And whereas there he chose Abraham alone, here he invites everyone to become like Abraham.
Again, with the holy apostles too, he repeated what he had done with Abraham. Look also at their faith.
which resembles Abraham’s faith. For just as Abraham obeyed the moment he was called,
so, as soon as he called the apostles, they obeyed and followed him. He saw them, it says, casting nets into the sea.
He called them, and immediately they left their nets and their father and followed him.
Even before they heard him say, “Unless someone leaves his father and mother
and everything he has and follows me, he cannot be my disciple,” they left everything and followed Jesus.
For it was not lengthy instruction that made them disciples, but simply hearing the word of faith.
For because the faith within them was alive, the moment it received the living voice, it obeyed Life.
They immediately ran after him and did not lag behind him. By this they showed that they had been disciples even before they were called.
For this is the way of faith that is mingled with simplicity: it does not receive instruction through a multitude of persuasive arguments.
Rather, just as a healthy, clear eye receives the ray sent toward it without devices or techniques,
but, the moment it opens, freely beholds its light because its natural sight is sound,
so too the eye of faith, set within the pupil of simplicity, as soon as it hears the voice of God,
recognizes it, and the light of its word shines within it. It joyfully moves toward him and receives him.
As our Lord himself said in his Gospel, “My sheep hear my voice and follow me.”
For wherever natural faith is preserved in its integrity, the person in whom this faith is preserved is a sheep belonging to the Shepherd.
Likewise, it is written about Matthew that our Lord saw him sitting at the tax office and called him.
Immediately he left his business, together with all his possessions, and followed him.
Again, it is written about Philip that he said to him, “Follow me,” and immediately he followed him.
With this clarity and simplicity, then, the apostles followed the word of Christ.
The world could not hold them back, nor could human customs restrain them.
Not one of the things considered important in the world could hold back these souls that had become aware of God.
For nothing in the world is stronger than the word of God for a person who has the life of faith within him.
But in someone in whom the word is weak because of the deadness of his soul, the mighty word is weakened, and the sound teaching of God becomes sick within him.
For wherever a person’s life is directed, all the activity of his life turns in that direction.
For someone who lives for the world directs the entire activity of his thoughts and senses toward the world.
And whoever is alive to God turns his soul, with all its impulses, toward God's mighty commandments.
For the weight of love for earthly things did not hang upon those who were called, so they immediately obeyed the voice that called them.
For the bonds of the world are a weight upon the mind and its thoughts.
And everyone who is bound and entangled in them hears the voice of God's call with difficulty.
But the apostles were not like this, nor did the righteous and the fathers follow this pattern.
Instead, they obeyed like people who were alive and went out like people who were light, not bound by the weight of anything.
For who can bind and hinder a soul that is aware of God?
For it is open and ready, so that whenever the light of the divine voice comes, it may find the soul prepared to receive it.
Our Lord also called Zacchaeus from the fig tree, and immediately he came down quickly and welcomed him into his house,
because he had been waiting to see him and become his disciple, even before he called him.
And this is the wonder: although our Lord had not spoken with him, and he had not seen him in person, he believed in him through what others said.
For the faith within him had been preserved in its natural life and health.
For by hearing the report about him and believing him, he showed his faith. And by promising to give half his possessions to the poor,
and to repay fourfold whatever he had taken by fraud, he thus made the simplicity of his faith shine within him.
For if Zacchaeus's mind had not at that moment been filled with the simplicity that befits faith,
he would not have made this generous promise to Jesus, nor would he have taken what had been gathered through years of toil
and brought it out and distributed it in so short a time. For what greed had gathered, simplicity was pouring out.
And what had been acquired through cunning thoughts, purity of soul was scattering; and what oppression had obtained and acquired,
faith was renouncing and crying out that it did not belong to her.
For God alone is faith's possession, and she will not consent to acquire other possessions alongside him.
For all possessions are insignificant to faith, apart from that one enduring possession, which is God.
Indeed, faith has been placed within us for this very reason: that she may find and possess God alone, and that everything apart from him
may be a loss to her. For the holy Scriptures have shown us that it is with this disposition that a person draws near to God:
with faith and simplicity. For this reason, Adam and Eve too, as long as they remained in the simplicity of their nature, and the faith within them
had not been dulled by bodily passions, accepted and kept God's commandment as soon as they heard it.
For God said to Adam, “Do not eat. If you eat, you will die.”
“But if you keep the commandment, I will give you everlasting life.” And he accepted it in faith and kept it.
In his simplicity he did not question the commandment: “Why did he keep us from one tree,
and give us authority over all the others, and promise to give me life if I keep the commandment?”
Because of his simplicity, Adam did not question or investigate these things. But when the enemy’s counsel came and found simplicity,
it taught that simplicity cunning and deceit. And in that one simple thought it sowed another, opposing thought,
so that he who had been one person, wholly in harmony with himself in his simplicity,
would be divided between two thoughts, willing and unwilling, judging and being judged,
and wavering over whether to act or not. The counsel offered to him made that innocent and simple man
a judge of God’s commandment to him. And because he lost his simplicity, he did not succeed in his judgment either.
For he foolishly judged that an enemy should be obeyed more than a friend, and a murderer more than a giver of life,
and the one who taught evil more than the one who had become their teacher of good.
For as long as they remained in simplicity, they obeyed God’s commandment.
But once they wanted to become cunning, they became receptive to the devil’s counsel.
For cunning is on Satan’s side, but simplicity belongs with those who are Christ’s.
For no one who wants to be cunning and deceitful can become Christ’s disciple as his teaching requires.
For a mind full of cunning is constantly tearing down and building up opposing thoughts, binding and loosening,
affirming and declaring false. At one moment it judges something good, but at another it rejects it
and chooses something else instead. For a mind trained in cunning is a passageway for confused thoughts,
and it does not remain with any one of them so as to trust it and rely on it. Simplicity, however, is the opposite of cunning in everything,
as its very name testifies: it contains no thoughts that cancel one another out.
For simplicity has received a name that is fitting for God. We also call God simple in the words of our confession about him,
because there are no combinations or divisions into bodily parts in him. Likewise, someone who is not skilled in evil
is called simple by us in ordinary speech, because there is no [?] of evil in his mind.
He does not know how to look for and devise a way out of the things he encounters in the world, nor how to use cunning to harm his enemies.
Nor to offer a rebuttal to what is said against him, nor to devise schemes and set ambushes.
Nor to act deceitfully and harm others. Simplicity does not know how to do these things or anything like them.
For this reason, God's mysteries have always been entrusted to simplicity, and it has been found worthy of divine revelations.
Likewise, it is well known that when the apostles were chosen, they were simpler than anyone else.
Indeed, Jesus chose them for this very reason: to mock the world's wisdom through their simplicity,
and through their lack of education to show that the knowledge of the learned and the scribes was empty.
As Paul also said, “God chose the foolish people of the world to put its wise people to shame...”
And again he said, “Has not God made the wisdom of this world foolish?” And again he said,
“Since, in God's wisdom, the world did not know God through wisdom, God was pleased, through the foolishness of preaching,
to save those who believe.” Again, he said to some of his disciples who were boasting of worldly knowledge,
“Consider your calling too, my brothers: not many among you are wise by human standards.”
By what I have said, I do not mean to show that there is no wisdom in Christ's teaching,
but that Christ's wisdom is a wisdom above the world, to which the world's wisdom is opposed in every respect,
just as darkness is opposed to light, bitterness to sweetness, and sickness to health.
For divine wisdom does not excel in these things—in the study and contemplation of earthly thoughts. Rather, all its meditation concerns spiritual things.
Its impulses and thoughts are above the world, as the apostle also testified about himself,
saying, “I am unlearned in the wisdom of the world, but in my knowledge I possess wisdom that is above the world.”
And to teach that not everyone is capable of hearing and receiving the wisdom he possessed, he proclaimed,
“We speak wisdom among the mature, but not the wisdom of this world, nor of the rulers of this world, who are passing away.
Rather, we speak God's wisdom in a mystery”—a wisdom that not one of the world's wise people
is even able to hear. For the world's wisdom is not capable of being a foundation and receiving the building of God's wisdom.
For this reason, our Lord established simplicity as its foundation.
For who does not know how simple that first pair was, the ancestors of the human race?
And just as they were simple concerning the entire way of life of the world, because they had neither experienced nor been involved in any of its affairs—
since the very course of the world's affairs had not yet been revealed—so close were they.
to divine visions; and God constantly spoke with them face to face,
and was always present with them in close conversation, taking them here and there.
He led them from the place from which they came and in which they had been formed, and brought them into Paradise and settled them there.
And in the likeness of a human being, he showed them everything in a familiar way.
They did not ponder in their minds concerning the one who was showing them these things: where, indeed, was his dwelling?
And since when had he existed? Had he been made? And if he had been made, who had made him? And why had he created us?
And for what reason had he placed us in this Paradise and given us this law?
These things were far from their minds, because simplicity does not think about such things, but is wholly and entirely absorbed
in listening to what it hears. Its entire thought is bound up with the word of the one speaking to it,
just as a child is with the word of whoever is speaking to him.
So, then, God also placed simplicity in the first ancestors of our race.
And it was simplicity that received the commandment. For simplicity comes before faith,
because faith is the daughter of simplicity, whereas unbelief is the offspring of cunning.
For someone who is crafty and cunning does not readily assent to what he hears. But a simple person hears and believes every voice.
But if it is the simplicity that belongs to the purity of nature, it receives only those things that are spoken by God.
For just as the earth, in the constitution of its nature, was appointed by its Creator for this purpose:
to receive seeds and plants useful for human needs—whereas its production of thorns and thistles does not belong to its nature,
but was something it subsequently received from its Maker through a sentence of judgment—so too simplicity has been placed in our very nature by the Maker.
But cunning and craftiness are things we acquire afterward through the experiences we encounter.
The birth of every human being also bears witness to this: in all who are born, simplicity is active before cunning.
While they are infants and children, they are full of innocence and purity.
But when they have spent some time in the world, through their gradual upbringing and the events they encounter, they learn cunning and craftiness.
Thus, if someone were to take away a one-year-old infant and go out and raise him in the wilderness, where there is no human interaction
or experience of worldly affairs, and he were to see absolutely nothing of these things belonging to human society,
he would be found to remain in all the simplicity of nature, even when he reached full manhood,
And this person can very easily receive divine visions and spiritual insights.
And he becomes a vessel well prepared to receive divine wisdom. And I think that this was the condition of
that remarkable herald, John the Baptist, too. Because he was in the wilderness, according to the testimony of Scripture,
until the day of his appearance to the children of Israel, he was able to receive and learn divine mysteries,
and to receive the power of baptism in the Spirit, and things that not one of the earlier prophets had perceived.
Through the simplicity of nature in which he had been brought up, he received these things in the wilderness. Above all,
before the abolition of the curse and the death of sin, and before the dividing wall of hostility was broken down—
the wall that Scripture says was broken down through Christ’s cross—he had already received the things that came after the cross.
And for this reason grace led him to go out into the desert and remain in the simplicity of nature,
so that he could receive knowledge of mysteries that are above nature.
In this same way, then, when God redeemed the people from Egypt, he too brought them out into the desolate wilderness,
where simplicity is acquired. And I am convinced that he brought them out into that wilderness for this reason:
so that, by being kept away from human practices and customs, and from the cunning and worldly wisdom they had acquired in the land of Egypt,
the simplicity of nature might become habitual among them, so that they could receive divine teaching with clarity.
Although there are indeed many other reasons why he brought them out into the wilderness, nevertheless, the foremost of them all
appears to be this one, to anyone who knows how to look into the mysteries of divine providence.
And because those who came out of Egypt were unwilling to strip themselves of the wickedness and cunning they had learned in Egypt,
but opposed God’s promise to them in every way, he kept them in the wilderness for forty years,
so that wickedness might be destroyed along with those who served it, and cunning might perish along with those who had acquired it from Egypt.
And the generation born and brought up in the wilderness, whose entire upbringing was in simplicity, in keeping with the character of the place,
was to enter and inherit the promised land. For it is fitting that those brought up in the wilderness should be simple.
And this follows from simplicity: it listens to and obeys God’s commandments.
And if someone thinks that they believed because they saw signs and wonders in the wilderness,
and because they feared the punishment that came upon those before them,
it turns out that those who came out of Egypt saw more wonders than they did.
For along with all the other mighty deeds performed in Egypt, they also saw the dividing of the sea,
and that fearsome crossing, and then how the sea closed up again and covered the Egyptians who had entered it.
And the miracle that took place at Marah, where the water was sweetened by a piece of wood and became drinking water for them.
In short, those who came out of Egypt witnessed all the miracles in Egypt and in the wilderness,
and those that took place in between. But that younger generation, which was born in the wilderness,
saw only those miracles that remained continually with them: the pillar, the cloud, and the rock that flowed with water,
and the quail that came up from the sea. Although the miracles they saw were far fewer than those seen by the people who came out of Egypt,
in their innocence they persisted in the fear of God far more than those who had seen great and numerous signs.
And to know that all the mighty deeds that took place and the miracles that were performed could not uproot and remove from them the evil practices they had learned in Egypt,
while the generation born in the wilderness, because of its innocence, kept entirely away from them, understand this from the following:
After they had arrived and reached inhabited land, at the end of those forty years, when they camped opposite Midian
and wished to enter the lands of the nations, at the sight of the women whom the Midianites had adorned and placed before them,
the remnant of the people who had come out of Egypt indulged in sexual immorality with them.
As Holy Scripture also makes known, the people saw the daughters of Midian and indulged in sexual immorality, devoted themselves to Baal-peor, and worshiped idols.
Those who did this, as Scripture says, were the survivors of those who had come out of Egypt.
A plague, it says, took hold of them, and twenty-four thousand of them died.
Scripture says that here the number of those six hundred thousand who came out of Egypt was brought to its end. And God said
that they would not enter and see the promised land. From the fact that they alone out of all the people died, we understand
that they alone also committed sexual immorality. Moses, it says, and all Israel were sitting before the Lord at the entrance to the tent of meeting.
And Zimri son of Salu, chief of the tribe of Simeon, entered the chamber to be with Cozbi, a daughter of the chiefs of Midian,
in the sight of Moses and all Israel. Then Phinehas rose from there
and displayed the triumph of zeal. For from this very fact—that it was among the surviving remnant of the people who came out of Egypt
that the plague raged—we ought to know that they alone took part in that wicked act.
And all the rest of the people, who were born in the wilderness and were brought up in purity and innocence through the fear of God,
were sitting at God's entrance and, together with Moses, asking for mercy in repentance.
And I have reason to believe this from what happened when the calf was cast.
For there too, when Moses came down from the mountain and saw the people's confusion, he knew that this eagerness did not belong to them all,
but only to some of them. He filed down the calf with a file and scattered its powder over the surface of the water.
When the people drank from it, the waters became examiners of their thoughts. And those in whose thoughts the calf had already taken shape,
and who had urged the carrying out of this evil deed—it is written that the calf's mark appeared on them.
And they were the ones killed by the swords of the Levites. From the outcome of their deaths we understand
also the beginning of their error. Because they had urged it on and had been the first to go astray, they were overtaken
also by the punishment decreed by Moses' pronouncement, through the calf's mark that appeared on their persons.
So too here: since only twenty-four thousand fell in that sudden death,
and Scripture says that with them the number of those who had come out of Egypt was completed,
we should understand from this that they alone had given themselves fully to sexual immorality.
Let us learn of their sexual immorality from the sentence passed on them, and from their sudden death let us recognize that the sexual immorality too was theirs.
They remembered the worship of idols in Egypt, and as soon as they saw it in Midian, they gave themselves fully to it.
But the simplicity of the innocent who had been born in the wilderness kept them close to the Lord.
In the purity of their hearts they sat at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting. With souls far removed from depravity,
and with thoughts free from evil deceit, they asked the Lord for mercy. And because of this,
the bodily promises made to Abraham were fulfilled in them too. Simplicity entered and inherited the promised land,
and ignorance stood within the boundaries of his inheritance, which had been promised to the ancestor of their people.
The wholeheartedness they had toward the Lord was what gave them victory in their battles against the Amorites.
For after they crossed the Jordan, Joshua commanded them to go around Jericho seven times over seven days,
and on the seventh day to go around seven times, while he went before them with the priests carrying horns and the ark of the Lord.
In simplicity, all the people walked behind Joshua and behind the ark, like children following their fathers.
Why should I speak of all the rest of the people, when Scripture indicates to us that simplicity and purity were found in Joshua to an even greater degree?
It says that the young man Joshua did not leave the tent, but remained there continually in Moses' service.
And he who kept away from going out and coming in among the crowds was all the closer to simplicity.
For if cunning and wickedness are gathered from association with many people,
it is clear that simplicity and innocence are acquired through being brought up and living in solitude.
The more a person lives in solitude, the more he acquires simplicity.
Even the customary ways of the world bear witness to this for us.
For all those who were brought up in quiet seclusion, who did not go out on the roads
or associate and converse with many people, are found to be especially innocent and simple,
and to have preserved within them the righteousness from which uprightness is born.
So too blessed David joins uprightness to innocence in his words: “The innocent and upright have joined me, because I have waited for you.”
Again, the prophet himself bears witness to the innocence of his soul, describing how he was with God.
He says, “I was innocent and did not know; I was like an animal with you.” For I lowered myself to such complete ignorance
that, like an animal in relation to a human being, which cannot judge any of his actions or ways
because its nature lacks reason and discernment, so was David’s knowledge in relation to God.
Just as an animal is guided by a human being, so he submitted himself to be guided by the will of God,
and not to judge his will in any way, as he makes clear in the words that follow, saying:
“Because I was like an animal with you in complete innocence, you comforted me with your counsel
and led me after your glory.” Again he said, “I did not investigate what is with you in heaven, or what your will is on earth.
For I did not grasp the distinctions in your providence: while I was trying to understand that you had willed this, your will desired something else.
Because I was bewildered by the changes in your works, I ran and took refuge in simplicity, and I became with you an animal
that knows nothing, so that your will alone might be my guide, and your knowledge might guide me on the path of life.
And you will give me, through the care of your wisdom, everything needed for spiritual and bodily life.”
Again, in the same psalm, he shows that God’s grace abounds especially toward the innocent. He says, “God is good to Israel,
to the pure in heart.” He links purity with the vision of God, because “Israel” is interpreted as “one who sees God.”
The person who is simple and clear in heart is able to become one who sees God.
As our Lord also said in his gospel, “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God.”
Again, the prophet David himself shows that a mind far removed from the cunning of human teachings,
He understands God's righteousness more fully and gains courage of spirit and confidence to contend with everything.
For he says, “Because I have not learned scholarly knowledge, I will enter in the Lord's might, and I will remember your righteousness alone.”
And, explaining in what respects he was uneducated and simple, and in what respects he was knowledgeable and wise, he said:
“My learning, from my youth until now, has been to declare your wonders.”
Again, when he describes the purity of his thoughts, he compares them to hands.
He compares their freedom from wrongdoing to the washing of hands. “I have washed my hands clean,” he says.
That is, “I have scrubbed and purified my thoughts, and I have remembered your altar, Lord.”
Again he said, “I have walked with integrity of heart within my house. How long will it be before you come to me?” And again he said:
“No one who practices deceit shall dwell within my house.” And it is well known that deceit is made up of cunning. Again he said:
“Examine me, Lord, and test me; probe my innermost being and my heart.” And again he said, “I alone have purified my heart
and washed my hands in innocence.” Along with these things, his very selection also bears witness that he was chosen from a place that teaches simplicity.
For he was chosen from following the sheep, as he himself also acknowledges and recalls his selection
in one of his psalms: “He chose David his servant,” he says, “and took him from the sheepfold and from following the nursing ewes.”
And, explaining that his kingship too was conducted with simplicity, he said, “He shepherded them with integrity of heart.”
It is clear that integrity is simplicity and sincerity. The book of his history also gives us an indication of his simplicity:
in the conduct of worldly affairs, a counselor who advised him about human matters was constantly at his side. For Ahithophel
is identified by Scripture as David's counselor. Yet it is easy for us to see the simplicity of blessed David from other things as well.
He himself also makes this known when speaking with Jonathan, saying, “There is no evil in my heart, yet your father is hunting me down to take my life.”
And again, what Jonathan said to his father, “He placed his life in your hands,
fought a battle, and killed the Philistines,” teaches us about David's simplicity.
Again, when the men with him advised him to kill Saul, he persisted in that same simple disposition.
For their advice that he should kill his enemy belonged to the world's cunning and craftiness.
For this is the habit of those who are full of worldly cunning: to devise schemes and remove their opponents from their path.
David, however, persisted in his simplicity and compassion.
And we can find many things in the Holy Scriptures that reveal the simplicity and integrity of heart of this man of God.
And again, what the Lord said to Samuel, “I have found for myself a man after my own heart,” testified to the purity of David’s heart.
And purity of heart, as is well known, is born of simplicity. He himself also asked in prayer, “Create in me a pure heart, O God.”
Along with these, let us also consider all the other upright and righteous people, who all pleased God through simplicity.
For concerning those first disciples of the apostles, after our Lord’s ascension into heaven,
it is written that they all lived together and were of one mind and one soul.
They broke bread at home and received their food with joy.
In the sincerity of their hearts they praised God, and no one said that the possessions he owned were his own.
For everything they had was held in common. And it is clear that equality like this
is born of simplicity. Their praise rose to God from the sincerity of their hearts.
And their receiving food together with joy, without the one who had brought much expecting to be fed more
than another who had contributed nothing to the common stock, came from purity of mind. The account also showed
that blessed Joshua was more sincere than all the people because of his constant upbringing within the tabernacle.
And this man, who was far simpler and purer than all the people, who was brought up in quiet within the tabernacle,
was chosen for that renowned leadership after the great Moses.
And that simplicity is more readily found among those brought up in a tent or within a house
than among all the others who are accustomed to going out and coming in is also attested by the story of Jacob and Esau.
“Esau,” it says, “was a man skilled in hunting, a man of the open country; but Jacob was a blameless man who lived in a tent.”
From their deeds we can also understand the difference between their minds.
For everywhere the Scriptures call Esau wicked and deceitful, one who harbors anger and holds a grudge.
“He kept his anger forever,” it says, “and preserved his resentment for all time.”
Again, it spoke of his anger toward Jacob’s descendants: “He committed violence and raged against them.”
Again, when he armed himself to go out to meet his brother with four hundred men, this too revealed his lasting anger.
For when Jacob returned from Haran after twenty years, he was demanding repayment from him for the blessing.
And if Jacob’s humility and God’s hidden providence had not changed his anger into kindness, he would have done what he had set out to do.
Jacob, however, is seen to be the opposite of this in everything, whether toward his parents or in Laban’s household.
For his actions show us that he is simple and obedient.
For this reason, Holy Scripture too has made all his simplicity known to us in a single statement: “Jacob was an innocent man,
who lived in a tent.” Again, because of his simplicity, he would not even have thought of stealing the blessing if his mother Rebekah had not taught him.
But when he heard of the course of action that would benefit him, he was persuaded in the simplicity of his mind and raised no difficulty.
And so that no one should suppose that his simplicity was natural stupidity, see how he is on his guard against his father’s curses,
and responds intelligently to the matters before him. “Look,” he says, “my brother Esau is a hairy man, and I am a smooth-skinned man.
Perhaps my father will feel me, and I will seem to him like someone mocking him, and you will bring curses upon me rather than blessings.”
But his mother, in faith, affirming those earlier promises that had been revealed to her,
and what had been spoken to her when she went to inquire of the Lord, when she was told that the older would be the younger’s servant,
answered him: “Let your curses fall on me, my son. Only listen to me and do what I command you.”
Immediately he obeyed his mother like a little child, and she prepared and gave him the food Isaac longed for,
and wrapped skins around his hands and his neck, in the places that were within reach of touch.
In his simplicity, he did not question anything that was happening to him. Rather, like a little child placed before his nurse, who does whatever she wishes with him,
so this man too, through his simplicity, was compliant before his mother.
Again, when he took the food and brought it in to his father, he repeated like a little child what Rebekah had put into his mouth,
neither adding nor taking anything away. And when the time for marriage came, he did not take a step toward it of his own will.
Instead, in his innocence, he looked to his parents’ command. Esau, however, being crafty in wrongdoing,
because he wanted to distress and embitter his parents in return for their having plotted against him, went and took wives for himself from the daughters of Canaan,
who continually embittered the spirits of Isaac and Rebekah.
And when he saw that his parents’ hatred toward him had increased because of his wives’ constant uproar,
being concerned not to be deprived of his material inheritance, he also approached this matter craftily, and went and took as his wife Basemath, the daughter of Ishmael.
As one might say, he sought to receive a dressing along with the wound. He did this not as a discerning son who regretted what he had done before,
but because he was afraid that Isaac would exclude him from the inheritance of the wealth and possessions that he loved.
Likewise, his distress over the birthright and the blessings was not because he had lost the spiritual promises contained in them,
but because he had been deprived of the larger share of the property that firstborn sons customarily received.
And because he saw that his father's love for him had changed—that love because of which he had expected to receive something more as an inheritance—
For all these things about Esau teach anyone who knows how to examine them about his depravity and wickedness.
Along with these things, we also find here the simplicity of their father Isaac.
For although all his love had been directed toward Esau, and he loved him as his firstborn, as soon as he became aware of God's providence,
which is above nature, and Rebekah came in and disclosed to him what had been said to her when she went to inquire of the Lord,
his love immediately shifted away from Esau, and he directed it toward Jacob, who was worthy of it.
Let us also look at Jacob's own obedience: like a little child, he obeyed his parents in everything.
“If Jacob too takes wives like these from the daughters of Canaan,” Rebekah said, “what good is life to me?”
Isaac called Jacob and commanded him, saying, “Do not take a wife from the daughters of the Canaanites.
Instead, go to Laban son of Bethuel, your mother's brother, and take a wife from there.”
He obeyed and readily set out, suddenly having no further need of all the comforts of his father's house.
Like a stranger who owned nothing, he began his journey.
He asked them for nothing for his needs: no animal to carry his baggage, no servants to attend him, and no splendor for display,
along with the other things that are mere show, to which so many people today are attached.
Instead, he left them with his staff, carrying blessings and good promises as his provisions in place of these human things.
His own words also make this clear, when he gives thanks to God for what he has received
and asks to be rescued from his brother. He says, “With my staff I crossed this Jordan,
and now I have become two camps. Rescue me from the hands of my brother Esau, for I am afraid of him.”
Let us also hear the words he spoke in the place where God appeared to him, and from them we will see his simplicity even more clearly.
He said, “Truly the Lord is in this place, and I did not know it.”
What did you suppose, innocent Jacob? That God was confined only to the place where your parents lived,
and did not reveal himself and appear everywhere to those worthy of his revelation? Let us also see how many times his wages were changed in Laban's household.
As his words finally rebuked that crafty man: “You changed my wages ten times, but the Lord did not allow you to harm me.”
Again, when he worked for him in exchange for his younger daughter, Laban secretly brought him another in her place.
He deceived him in his simplicity, and he did not realize it. And when he demanded an explanation of why deceit had been practiced on him,
As soon as he presented an appeal to him, even though it was deceitful, his simplicity listened and accepted it.
For how many times did Laban, in his wickedness, seek to cheat him!
He changed his behavior toward him through many tricks, in his bitterness and deceitfulness.
Yet Jacob’s serenity was not disturbed, his simplicity was not unsettled, and his innocence did not turn to cunning.
And just as he carefully guarded these qualities of his, God also took care of the things that concerned him.
This is an illustration that offers clear instruction to everyone who wishes to work with the Lord:
He should not turn his thoughts away from meditation on God and occupy them with devising schemes by which to harm his enemies.
Instead, disciple, remain serene in your mind. It is for the Lord to know how to direct your life
and to do for you what benefits you. You have heard about some who are preparing to harm you,
others who sit in ambush to take your life, and others who have become workers intent on tearing down what you have built;
others who tarnish your reputation and disparage your conduct;
others who scheme to throw you to the ground from the height where you stand, and others who make mocking gestures;
others who speak against you in ridicule and contemptuously pour insults upon you; and others for whom you have become a byword and a tale,
whose entire conversation consists of insults against you. Through all these things, remain in your simplicity.
Do not turn backward from the place toward which you are looking, and do not cease your secret communion with God.
Do not let the pull of these things outside you overcome the hold of the hidden anchor on which your life depends.
Instead, hold fast to the hope that does not prove false—Christ—in keeping with Paul’s assurance to us that we should hold fast to the hope promised to us.
This is for us like an anchor that holds our soul so that it will not be shaken.
For just as an anchor cast down below, by its weight, holds a ship steady among the waves,
so that it does not drift and wander off its course, so too may the hope promised to us in heaven—
which is a hidden anchor placed above us, submerged and concealed from us in the highest heaven—hold our thoughts close to it
and secure the ship of our soul, so that it does not drift and wander amid the billows and waves that strike it from the world
and go off the course of its voyage. Remain, then, in your simplicity amid the things you have heard,
and do not let those who speak against you change you into someone like themselves.
For this is why the enemy gathers these people and lines them up against you: to turn your mind away from its gentleness.
and disturb and unsettle your serenity, and turn your simplicity into cunning, so that you become like those who fight against you.
You will be filled with anger like them, become a vessel of wrath like them, and put on the clothing of wickedness.
And when your mind descends from that simplicity which looks single-mindedly toward the One, and you turn your attention to many things and hear what is being said against you,
through these things the enemy finds you just as he wishes, and you become ready and easy prey within his reach.
But you must persevere in simplicity, which is a vessel of righteousness.
For just as a physical vessel receives whatever falls into it,
so simplicity too is a pure and precious vessel that receives the various kinds of righteousness.
So, in these things I have told you, look to innocent Jacob, whose story I have outlined for you.
And whenever contentious speech arises to disturb your simplicity, and you become aware of the enemy's schemes that seek to hinder you,
reflect on this blessed man, and consider his whole disposition from beginning to end.
For this is why these things and others like them are written in the Scriptures:
to support the soul that is wavering and about to fall, and to comfort thoughts overwhelmed by the clamor of the one who provokes them.
See how much Esau and Laban schemed to harm Jacob, while the Lord was actively working on his behalf in all his affairs.
And while he remained quiet and did not trouble himself about confronting his enemies' schemes, God was turning their cunning plans back upon them.
And instead of losses, he brought gains his way. For Jacob was occupied with his innocence, and God was seeking good things for him.
He conducted himself in every matter like a child in his simplicity, and the Lord in his wisdom made his ways prosper.
Laban rushes about and schemes to cause him loss, but Jacob is unaware. The innocent man is unconcerned; the pure-hearted man does not know.
But on his behalf God acts as the one who sees and knows everything. Whatever Laban tied, the Lord untied.
He devised a scheme to cause Jacob loss; the Most High scattered it. He found a way to increase his own possessions and diminish Jacob's;
God found another way to counter him. For while Jacob remained quiet, the Judge became his advocate.
And while he went about his affairs in simplicity, God guided his ways with wisdom.
These things about Jacob are written for you, and they are yours, if you persevere in the simplicity of Jacob's mind
and in the purity of that innocent man's soul. For the simple belong to the Lord. Do not be ashamed of simplicity.
The crafty and cunning are instruments of the adversary. Do not long for cunning or take pleasure in it.
For cunning is soil that produces wickedness, while simplicity is a field that bears the fruit of righteousness.
And for this reason, everywhere the Lord speaks with simplicity, and in it his wishes find rest.
It becomes a dwelling place and a recipient of his revelations. For Eli and his sons were sleeping inside the temple of the Lord.
And when the Lord wished to speak with human beings, he passed over old age, trained in wisdom and experienced in worldly affairs,
and youth, which had acquired cunning in evil deeds, and came to simplicity and spoke with it.
He chose conversation with it for himself. “The Lord called Samuel,” it says.
“Samuel, Samuel”—twice. And simplicity got up and ran to old age.
The child did not know who had called him. Instead of answering God, he ran to give Eli an answer.
He did this three times, because he had not yet experienced divine revelations.
But when Eli understood that the Lord had called him, he instructed him to answer as one answering the Lord, and not to run to him.
“Eli understood,” it says, “that the Lord had called the boy.” And old age sent childhood to the Lord to learn his wishes.
And cunning became dependent on simplicity, to learn through it the wishes of the divine nature. For Eli was pleading with Samuel,
and asking him to reveal everything he had heard from the Lord, and not to hide a single word from him.
And because he saw that he himself had not been considered worthy for the Lord to speak with him, he appealed to the child to reveal the divine mystery to him.
Between the divine nature and knowledge, simplicity became the interpreter. Childhood received and answered.
And a boy only a few years old, who was not acquainted with matters of human conduct,
had the knowledge of God revealed to him, because the Lord dwells among the innocent and speaks with the simple. He chose the uneducated,
those who, when they learn a word, do not think it is their own, but know who spoke it and offer thanks to him.
And the word of God that comes to them does not become material for pride and empty boasting.
They do not exalt themselves over what belongs to God as though it were their own. Nor do they say, “The word of wisdom we possess is our own.”
The simple and innocent do not think such things. Rather, in their simplicity they acknowledge that whatever they possess belongs to the Lord.
And for this reason, everywhere we have found it to be so: God rejected cunning and chose simplicity.
For since a person wise in spirit is not easily found, one who through personal experience gains a taste of the knowledge of life,
the simplicity of human nature is therefore acceptable to God, because it is his gift,
and his original shaping of our nature. For when God created us in the beginning, he placed simplicity within us.
Simplicity, then, occupies the middle ground. And there are those who rise from it to the learning of spiritual things.
And he becomes wise in spirit. There is also one who descends from it to learning and studying the things of this world.
This person is called clever and resourceful, if things are called by their exact names.
Those who are educated and whose entire study concerns bodily things are not called wise.
Nor are those whose simplicity has been trained in spiritual things called clever and resourceful.
Rather, those who gather their knowledge from the world are named resourceful and clever.
But those who are trained in spiritual things are called wise and understanding.
For wisdom belongs to God alone, and to the person whose search is directed toward God.
For knowledge of the world does not deserve to be called wisdom, strictly speaking.
Nor does God's wisdom deserve to be called resourcefulness and cleverness, when understood with discernment.
For there is no contrivance in this wisdom, nor does it consist of a combination of different thoughts.
For even this question is beyond words: why God delights in simplicity and chooses it over the wisdom of the world.
Yet even the wisdom of the world is a gift from God, as the apostle said: “In the wisdom of God,
the world did not know God through wisdom.” From this it is clear that if wisdom were not present in the constitution of our nature,
and wisdom had not been placed in all created works, we would not even be able to gather wisdom from the world.
So even the wisdom of the world is a gift from God. Why, then, did he reject it and choose simplicity?
Clearly, then, it is because our own effort is involved in it.
And because, when those who acquire it gather it, their gaze is directed toward the world, not toward God.
And again, they pursue it with the intention of being considered wise.
In short, human passions fill their souls when they investigate and seek this wisdom among created works.
And because they coupled their search with toil, distress, and personal exhaustion
to discover this knowledge, they supposed it was their own, considering the labor they had undertaken for it.
For this reason the Lord rejected the wise people of the world and chose the simple in their place.
And again, the wisdom of the world is opposed to divine wisdom in every respect.
There is no way for them to mingle with one another, just as light does not mingle with darkness.
Thus, even if one of the world's wise people wishes to become wise in spiritual things, he first casts off the thoughts belonging to that wisdom.
and all the self-assurance of his former knowledge; and he stands at the beginning of the path of the first stage, which is simplicity and childlikeness,
and faith that hears and accepts with innocence. Then he begins this journey along the path of Christ’s wisdom.
And in proportion to his progress and his eagerness to advance, wisdom herself also reveals herself to him.
Simplicity, however, is a gift of nature, and it belongs to the Creator.
Nothing of our own is mixed into it—that is, nothing from our will or from our labor.
For this reason, her gift rests within his gift, and his wisdom dwells in the place that he himself has prepared.
Just so, here too he stooped down to Samuel, left shrewdness behind, and spoke with him; and the high priesthood [?], and he came to him.
Now Holy Scripture does not reproach Eli for many evil deeds, but only for this: that he was negligent and did not rebuke his sons.
He himself did not share in their wicked deeds. And as for anyone saying that he behaved like them in his youth,
Scripture did not accuse him of this, nor did it say, “You committed this wickedness in your youth, and now your sons are acting like you.”
Rather, the Lord said to Samuel, “Look, I am doing something in Israel that will make both ears of everyone who hears it ring,
because of the wickedness that Eli heard his sons were committing in the tent of meeting, yet he did not rebuke them.”
The whole accusation against Eli concerns his negligence and his failure to make his rebuke proportionate to his sons’ wrongdoing.
For it is written that he rebuked them, but it was a feeble, lax rebuke, not what all that wrongdoing required.
For this alone was the charge against Eli the priest: his negligence, not evil deeds of his own.
Even though this was so, God preferred youth to him and held converse with childlikeness and simplicity.
For, as Scripture makes known, Samuel was brought up within the Lord’s temple,
like Joshua son of Nun and Jacob. For they too were brought up in the tent, as our discussion showed above.
And it is remarkable how the Lord called his creation from these two places:
either from among those accustomed to the wilderness or from among those brought up within the tent.
For simplicity is acquired in both these places.
For God set apart David and Moses, along with the others, from the wilderness for his work of governance.
But Samuel, Joshua, and Jacob he chose from an upbringing in the tent.
So from this too we know that simplicity is dear to God.
It is the beginning of the path of those who have drawn near to God. Yet we can also look at simplicity again.
Holy Scripture also indicates to us that Abel, the first righteous man, was more innocent than Cain.
For both of them brought offerings to the Lord. The offering of innocence was accepted, while that of wickedness was rejected.
Cain became angry with the Lord and with Abel: with Abel because he envied him, and with the Lord because he had rejected his offering.
Had he been innocent, he would not have been envious; and had he been pure, he would not have been angry with the Lord either.
Again, we see Cain’s cunning in the outlet he found for his wickedness.
When he planned to kill his brother Abel but could not because Abel was near his parents,
he told him to go out to the plain. Abel, in his innocence, listened and agreed like a child.
In his simplicity he suspected no evil, nor did he wonder in his heart why Cain was calling him out to the plain.
For he was not even aware of Cain’s hatred toward him, because innocence does not know how to perceive such things.
Instead, he dealt with him in innocence of heart and brotherly love, and readily obeyed wherever he called him.
But here too, look at the deeds of innocence, and consider the offenses of cunning and wickedness.
Strive to be on the side of the innocent, those who have pleased God in every age.
Reject cunning as something that does not suit you and is not fitting for the discipleship in which you stand.
For just as the clothing appropriate to your way of life is well known, and everyone laughs at you if you wear the opposite,
so the clothing of innocence is fitting for your soul; and if you wear that of cunning, discerning people will reproach you.
Even the banquet itself will not admit you in this clothing.
Along with these, let us also consider Joseph the chaste, whose respect for his father and love for his brothers
sprang from his innocence. For his brothers envied him, but he was unaware of it; they plotted to kill him, but he did not know.
His father instructed him to go and visit his brothers, and he readily obeyed him.
He saw dreams that revealed his greatness and their subjection, and in his innocence he came and disclosed their subjection to them.
The innocent man did not realize that cunning was adding to its wickedness, and that hatred was growing in his brothers through hearing these things.
When the aged Jacob saw the innocence of his son Joseph, he rebuked him so that he would not disclose these things—not because he did not believe they would happen.
For Scripture says that he kept these words in mind, because he believed they were going to come true.
Rather, he rebuked Joseph’s innocence so that, by disclosing his dreams, he would not increase his brothers’ hatred toward him.
For he carried provisions and brought them to his brothers, going from place to place asking about them.
And he does not realize that he is running toward murderers, not toward his brothers.
He saw them and, in his simplicity, was filled with joy; but at the sight of him, they were filled with gloom and anger.
And while simplicity was thinking good thoughts and increasing its love at the sight of the brothers, the envy that cunning had given birth to
was growing ever stronger and greater, and murder was being planned. They planned evil and carried out evil.
But look at the outcome of both, and see which one God favored.
For while simplicity, which did not know how to conceal its dreams, was being borne in honor on a chariot,
craftiness lay on the ground before it. Simplicity gave commands, and craftiness obeyed it.
For simplicity was growing in the wisdom of God, while craftiness was increasing in wickedness.
“I have seen that there is no one as wise and discerning as you,” the king of Egypt said to that simple man.
For simplicity is close to wisdom, and understanding of God is akin to innocence.
Simplicity is a vessel that receives divine revelations. The blessed Paul, too, rightly rejects cunning.
He says, “We do not conduct ourselves with cunning, nor do we falsify the word of God.
Rather, by openly revealing the truth, we present ourselves before the consciences of all people.”
See, Paul too has taught you that deceit accompanies cunning, and that it is a vessel for every evil.
For this reason Paul too flees from it. And what disciple would not reject it,
if the apostle rejected and cast it out, placing it outside the pure teaching of Christ? For it is not compatible with that teaching.
For just as evil is the opposite of good, so cunning is the opposite of simplicity.
And again, in another place, Paul writes to his disciples, “Did I perhaps, like a cunning man, catch you by deceit?”
Here again he linked deceit with cunning. And again, in another statement, he accuses the heretics and shows that their entire teaching rests on cunning.
He says, “Let us not be children who are shaken and shifted by every wind of deceitful human teachings,
by those who cunningly devise schemes to lead people astray. Rather, let us be true in our love, so that everything about us may grow in Christ.”
Again, our Lord too made it known that the heretics are devious and cunning.
For he said, “Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravenous wolves.”
And this too—when someone is one thing but appears to be another—is the work of cunning.
For although they were wolves, they appeared in sheep’s clothing: cunning taught them to act this way.
For cunning serves both of them: it produces evil and makes evil grow.
It also devises ways to teach evil to others, and conceals it where concealment is called for.
