And where it knows that disclosure is appropriate, it reveals it. For evil is blind, but cunning has eyes.
Again, in another place, our Lord taught his disciples to beware of the cunning of the Pharisees and Sadducees.
“Beware,” he said, “of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees, and of the leaven of Herod.”
And so that you may know that here he calls cunning and evil “leaven”:
in another place, when the Pharisees told him, “Herod wants to kill you,” he called him a fox because of his cunning.
“Go,” he said, “tell that fox.” For because he lacks the strength to accomplish what he wants by authority,
he devises crafty schemes so that cunning may take the place of strength for him, just as cunning also takes the place of strength for a fox.
“I go of my own will,” he said, “but your cunning cannot make me depart against my will.”
“I perform signs,” he said, “today and tomorrow, and on the third day I am brought to completion.”
So then, it was against Herod’s cunning and the evil of the Pharisees—
who teach one thing while doing another—that our Lord warned his disciples.
For our Lord was not warning them against the teaching of Moses that the Pharisees taught,
but against their own traditions, which they devised in their cunning to serve as material for their dishonest trade.
And against their presenting themselves to people as righteous and as concerned for the honor of God,
while secretly dishonoring him by their deeds; and their making their prayers long so that they might devour widows’ houses;
and their disfiguring their faces so that they might appear to be fasting; and their washing the outside of the cup and the dish.
That is, they adorn and beautify their outward appearance, while within they are full of wrongdoing and every kind of filth.
And outwardly they adorn themselves with humility and modesty for people’s eyes to see,
while secretly they are full of greed, deceit, depravity, and a desire for every kind of lust.
For it was against this teaching of the Pharisees that our Lord instructed his apostles to be on their guard.
All these things that happen through deceit and are carried out under a false appearance are born of cunning.
But what does our Lord command his disciples to do instead of these things?
To be innocent as doves toward good things, and shrewd as snakes in dealing with evil things.
For faith, simplicity; against error, shrewdness. Innocent, so that they may find their lives.
And astute, so that they may not lose their lives. For simplicity is useful to us for acquiring good things.
But so that we do not lose what we have acquired, we need astuteness. Toward God, sincerity of mind.
But toward people who scheme to take the things of God away from us, astuteness of thought.
Our Lord therefore rightly commanded us to be innocent as doves toward one another and toward him,
and shrewd as snakes against those who devise ways to deprive us of spiritual things.
For even the snake's shrewdness is directed toward human beings, not toward itself.
In its natural shrewdness, it surrenders its body to blows but protects its head from injury, since injury to the head brings death upon its whole body.
Again, to the disciples who inquisitively asked which of them was greatest in the kingdom of heaven,
and with a calculating mind desired to rise in rank above one another, he taught the simplicity of children,
which has no desire for power or leadership, and whose thinking has no experience of love for worldly honor.
He said, “Truly I tell you, unless you turn and become little children, simple like children, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven.”
And again, “Whoever does not receive the kingdom of God like a child, with innocence of heart and simplicity, will not enter it.”
Again, Paul too teaches about this simplicity, not only that we should have it toward God and toward one another,
but he also commands those who are slaves in the natural order to honor their masters with simplicity, without deceit or inquisitiveness.
He says, “Slaves, obey your masters in everything, not only when you are being watched, like those who seek to please people,
but with fear and trembling and simplicity of heart, as toward Christ.” Again, he also commands those who give
to show simplicity in their gifts. He says, “Let the one who gives do so with simplicity, and the one who leads, with diligence.”
For if inquisitiveness is found in those who give, they become investigators of the recipients' conduct.
For this reason, the gift is withheld—the gift that simplicity gives without calculating.
For this is the habit of simplicity: not to calculate and then give, but to distribute and give generously to everyone.
Our Lord also taught this very simplicity when he said, “Give to everyone who asks you.”
Again, Paul himself prays for those who give, that the fruits of their righteousness may increase and that they may distribute gifts to the needy with simplicity.
He says, “May God, who gives seed to sowers and bread for food, himself supply and multiply your seed,
and increase the fruits of your righteousness, so that you may be enriched in everything with complete simplicity, which brings about, through us,”
Thanksgiving to God. Look, here too Paul prayed in simplicity for his disciples to become rich.
And from this, he says, thanksgiving to God grows and becomes stronger.
And again he said, “You have obeyed the confession of Christ’s gospel; and submit yourselves in your simplicity with them and with everyone.”
And again he said, “I am afraid that perhaps, just as the serpent deceived Eve by its cunning,
so your minds may be corrupted and turned away from simplicity toward Christ.”
Here again he taught us that whoever believes in Christ ought to remain faithful to his teaching in simplicity.
By these words he also indicates that Eve herself did not accept the deceit of the tempter’s craftiness until she abandoned simplicity toward God’s commandment.
And again, that holy greeting which Paul commands his disciples to give one another at the end of all his letters—
simplicity brings it forth, and purity of mind gives it. And again he said, “Let us live by the Spirit and follow the Spirit.
And let us not be conceited, opposing one another and envying one another.”
A person’s living by the Spirit and following the Spirit comes about through simplicity and purity of mind.
It is therefore good for Christ’s disciples to pursue simplicity and concern themselves with purity of mind.
And let us not envy those who devise evil and are cunning in obtaining the world’s honors and comforts.
For look, we have learned from all the Scriptures of the Old and New Testaments
that a person draws near to God through simplicity, and simplicity becomes God’s dwelling place.
Along with the teaching of the Scriptures, experience of actual deeds also shows us this:
righteousness is closer to simplicity than to craftiness. For crafty and cunning people,
even if they undertake labors and appear to conduct themselves righteously, are held captive by other passions.
And they persevere in their labors for this reason: to nourish the evil passions stirring in their souls.
For they scheme to capture either honor, glory, or power
through the way they carry out their labors. Simplicity, however, has no such thoughts as it performs its labors.
Rather, it is guided either by the good law it has received and holds fast to, or by fear of breaking that law,
or love for God sustains it in its afflictions, if it has reached this point. For until it reaches the measure of love,
fear guards and supports simplicity. So do not be ashamed, disciple, of this good gift.
Instead, hold fast to it from the beginning of your discipleship until the end, and in all good things it will be found with you.
For in simplicity and faith you obeyed God and left the world; you did not dispute with him or question him about what he told you.
For if you had become sophisticated, you would not have obeyed him. And if you had listened to his word with cunning thoughts, you would not have gone out to follow God, who called you.
Nor would any of those who were called and obeyed God have listened to his word
and gone out in obedience to his command when he called them to follow him or to become servants of his providence
in one of its forms toward humanity. For from simplicity of nature comes an abundance of spiritual understanding.
Notice that even this world's learning can be received by a simple mind.
For because childhood is very simple, it accepts the world's learning and stands in awe of teachers.
But as it grows in stature and becomes sophisticated in human affairs, it despises teachers and scorns learning.
In the same way, simplicity also receives the teaching of the Spirit, while being filled with reverence for him,
the teacher, and carefully guarding the teaching so as not to forget it. But if someone wishes to approach sophistication,
and through it, desires, he immediately scorns the teaching and despises God.
Let us therefore hold on to this good gift and guard it carefully, and let all our conduct be marked by purity of heart.
Let us reject sophistication, keep far from cunning, rebuke wickedness, and guard against deceit.
Let us keep far from hidden malice, flee from slander, and cast away from us the tongue that strikes in secret.
With a simple mind and a pure understanding, let us praise the Holy Trinity, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, forever. Amen.
The first discourse on simplicity is finished.
Notes on the Syriac text:
Another discourse, the second, on simplicity.
We ought always to direct our discourse toward spiritual benefits in this place, which is a marketplace for such gains.
For I see that you too are eager to hear helpful discourse, not something intended for entertainment and as an occasion for shouting.
For words composed to entertain the ear or to stir up shouted praise among the listeners—
these are not wanted at all in this place of chastity. Rather, what is spoken here should also be in keeping with the place.
For the place where we are gathered is a place of spiritual benefit and help.
Let us therefore speak a simple word in this place, one that brings a shared benefit to the speaker and to those who listen.
For it is written that the one who hears the word should share all good things with the one who teaches it to him.
Our previous discourse spoke about simplicity and sincerity.
Now I wish to speak again about this helpful subject, for it is something appropriate to us.
Simplicity belongs to us, and there is no way for us to live a life of good works without it.
For just as the body's members cannot see without the eye, so good works cannot be practiced without simplicity.
And just as all the body's members are darkened when the eye is blind, so all good things are clouded when simplicity is lost.
For simplicity is especially fitting for this monastic way of life.
And sincerity of mind is particularly appropriate to those who have left the world and come outside it.
For where none of the world's ways are found, the world's cunning is not needed either.
For here among us there is no buying and selling. Among us there is no bargaining for fleeting profits.
Here there is no question of who will become greater than his brothers and appear to have more authority than his companion.
Here no one wrongs another or is wronged, because among us there are no grounds for wrongdoing.
Here there are no fields and vineyards to divide, nor lands to separate by boundaries.
Here no one wishes to become richer than his brother or to enjoy a greater abundance of worldly possessions than his companion.
Here no one wishes to be seen in splendid clothes, for we all have the same clothing of mourning and humility.
Here no one is a slave to his stomach, wishing to obtain elaborately prepared foods for himself.
For we are all fed from one plain table.
Here no one wishes to snatch away his brother's honor, for we are all commanded to honor one another.
Here no one brings a case against his companion, for we all plead our case against one, for the sake of one.
Here there is not one person wishing to build and another longing to lay out mansions, for we all share the same cramped dwelling of confinement.
Here no one wishes to enlarge his dwelling and furnish himself with gilded dining halls, for each of us has a sleeping place confined to a small space,
on the ground, in humility. And where these things are completely rejected, the world's cunning should not be found either.
For where the world's way of life is cast out and discarded, its craftiness should also be rejected.
For where the body's material concerns are despised, the cunning that fights on their behalf should also be scorned.
Where the old self is crucified with all its practices, craftiness, which is the old self's advocate, should also be crucified.
Where deceit is rejected, cunning, the mother of deceit, should also be rejected.
Where someone drives deceit out and casts it away, its fathers and those who gave birth to it must also depart.
For in a community where there is no deceit and falsehood is not practiced, guile and craftiness, the parents of these things, must also be despised.
Where the humble garment of hair is worn, the simplicity that suits it must be honored.
For linen clothing does not suit our way of life, nor are garments with designs and ornaments fitting for our order.
In the same way, and even more than these things, guile does not suit our discipleship,
nor does craftiness suit our way of life. Adorning the head does not suit us; that belongs to the frivolous and the corrupt.
Likewise, neither does deceit, which was the adversary’s first invention.
For guile is the possession of the devil and all his servants.
But simplicity is the wealth of Christ and all his disciples.
Craftiness is suited only to worldly conduct and to those who have devoted themselves to robbing and plundering others,
and to oppressing and abusing their fellow human beings. They are the ones who need cunning. For, it is said, wisdom does not dwell in a soul steeped in evil,
says Solomon the wise. Nor does knowledge of the Spirit dwell in a body that loves sin.
For a soul steeped in evil is full of guile, because guile itself is an inventor of evil things.
For whoever wishes to serve his desires hurries to become a disciple of guile, so that through its teaching,
and through the wicked tricks it shows him, he may devise ways to conceal his evil deeds and invent an excuse in his mind for the shameful things he does.
For where desires are rejected and human passions are driven far away, their root must also be uprooted.
And whatever nurtures them must also be cut off and cast away. For there is no guile in heaven. There is no craftiness for evil
in Gabriel and Michael. There is no cunning or shameful trickery in those spiritual regions.
There is no darkness of deceit in that radiant Jerusalem, the city of life. No one there schemes to prevail through falsehood,
because falsehood is not even practiced in that place. No one there learns to conceal his shameful deeds,
nor does anyone use guile to hide his evil deeds. And just as these things do not exist in that dwelling place of spiritual beings,
neither should they be found in our dwelling place, which is a model of that place.
For this conduct is a likeness of spiritual beings. This way of living is a model of heavenly beings.
This conduct of yours, you who are clothed in bodies, corresponds to that of those beings on high who have no bodies.
It is fitting for you to say what Paul proclaimed: “Although we live in the flesh, we do not do the works of the flesh.”
For to the eyes you appear bodily, but all your service is spiritual.
You are angels with bodies, spiritual beings clothed in flesh.
Your life is pure, clear, serene, and holy. The likeness of the heavenly life of spiritual beings is imprinted upon it.
The entire way of life of Jesus’ disciples rests on simplicity. If you take simplicity away from it, you throw that way of life into confusion.
Simplicity is our pride, and whoever possesses it is wise.
For just as in the world a simple person is called foolish by fools, so in this spiritual place,
a cunning person deserves to be called foolish by the discerning, because he has acquired in this place a possession unsuited to it.
And he has found within it something that does not belong to it. No one seeks to find trees, crops, and plants among the waves of the sea.
Nor does anyone seek to see waves and billows on dry land.
Rather, each is sought in its own place, and there it is found. Likewise, it is not fitting for cunning to be found in the serene place of spiritual people.
For the place for cunning is the world, which is full of evils. And just as singing is unfitting among mourners,
and weeping at a banquet, so it is unfitting for evil craftiness to be found in a place of simplicity.
For in a place of spiritual gains, the presence of cunning is a loss for spiritual people.
For you are not speaking with your brother as a craftsman. What need do you have of cunning?
You are not sitting in ambush inside the monastery to kill a righteous person in secret. What use do you have for craftiness and deceit?
Why are you proud, fool, of something that condemns you? Why do you boast about something that brings you shame?
What greatness do you gain from something that is your disgrace? Why are you proud of a possession that is not yours?
You took cunning from the world. Through it you stand accused of having all the world’s evils with you as well.
For a tree’s fruits accompany it, and cunning is a tree whose roots are evils.
Wherever it is found, all evils are there with it.
Even if they are not seen in outward actions, they are present in hidden thoughts.
For cunning is a sickness of the soul, just as simplicity is its true health.
Where have you ever seen a sick person proud of his sickness, or a suffering person boasting about his pains?
For a cunning monk ought to be ashamed, because he has been found in a condition unworthy of him.
For just as relations with a prostitute are a shameful disgrace for him,
Thus he ought to be ashamed if cunning is found in him, for it is the likeness of a prostitute.
For cunning within the soul is like a prostitute in the marketplace.
Just as she speaks with all men and puts on every kind of face,
so that she may appear to each person to be like him, so cunning too appears in the changing forms of every kind of thought,
and prepares borrowed and embellished faces, so that through them it may show itself to each person as someone like him.
And what the apostle rightly wrote, “I became all things to all people, so that I might win everyone,”
is put into practice by cunning in the opposite way: it becomes all things to all people so that it may destroy everyone, and ridicule and laugh at everyone.
And if these are the deeds of cunning, how can it be fitting for a disciple of Christ?
And how can it be right for it to be found among guileless monks?
Look with the eye of knowledge and understand that all evils spring from cunning.
Deceit is within it; falsehood is found in it; slander is close to it.
Mockery is its friend. Deception is its very nest. It is the dwelling of an evil [?].
Leading people astray and turning them aside are its teachings. It is in partnership with theft.
It is the advocate of adultery. It exhausts itself in defense of sexual immorality. Favoritism is its ostentatious garment.
Ambushes are forged by it. It makes itself ready to give false testimony. It is the mother of lying denials.
To put it briefly, all evils have appointed it their advocate, to plead their case.
Some it conceals; for some it exhausts itself in their defense; of some it denies that they ever happened,
multiplying its pleas and pretending to breathe its last. Some evils it gives different faces,
saying, “They did not happen for this reason,” and, “It was not done with this intention.” Every kind of lying speech is gathered within it.
It accompanies judges when they want to steal. Rulers make use of it when they want to take bribes.
It accompanies evildoers when they are brought to trial. A woman who wants to depart from the lawful path in relation to her husband
takes it along as her companion, and then goes out into the wandering ways of depravity. Students learn it,
and then begin lying to their teachers. Advocates who speak before judges compose their speeches from its wealth,
and their evasions are forged in its furnace. It spreads the nets of injustice. It stretches snares across the paths of travelers.
It conceals deceitful traps. It digs pits of destruction. It demands payment from them a second time on a debt document that has already been paid.
Until deceit approaches her, she does not know how to plead her own case.
Deceit prepares her to lie, and itself teaches her how to lie. Deceit prepares an evil intention.
But as for how she should put it into practice, cunning becomes her counselor.
She begins to walk in deceit along the path opposed to truth, and calls to cunning, “Come along with me,” and then sets out.
Cunning is the scribe of all evils, a ready advocate for all shameful deeds.
It represents them all, pleads on behalf of them all, and makes a defense.
It is as though cunning were saying this to evil: “You, evil, do as much evil as you wish.
Let all your members delight in the pleasures of desire. Let the body of all your senses be pampered with the things it loves.
Let all your varieties gather their flavor within them, and let them grow and ripen.
Indulge yourself as much as you desire, and do not hold back. Pamper yourself, and do not begrudge yourself anything.
Do wrong as much as you find pleasing. Act wickedly and commit sexual immorality as much as you wish. Fill yourself with wrongdoing, and do not be afraid.
Perfect yourself in every shameful deed, and do not tremble. Do not let reports of the laws frighten you.
Do not let the threat of judgment shake you. Do not be terrified by the voice of rulers. Do not let the shouting of masters frighten you.
I will plead against them all on your behalf. I will speak in your defense before all your accusers.
It is easy for me to weave praise for you out of the accusations against you, and out of the things by which others expect to condemn you,
I will weave you a crown of victory. All my thinking is on your behalf. In thoughts concerning you
I am immersed night and day, so that whenever I am needed, I may speak in your defense.
I ponder this at every moment. But you, evil, delight in pleasures, while I study the book that will acquit you.
Do not worry about how or what you will say before judges. I have become your spokeswoman.
I will silence your accusers. I will overcome the justice that speaks against you.
I will silence the uprightness of those who judge your offenses. I am your tongue, O evil.
I have prepared myself to be a speaking mouth for you. Every tongue that wishes to plead a case against you—I will stand up and condemn it.”
For these encouragements are offered to wickedness by cunning, and it supplies her with this speech
to entice her to step into wrongdoing. Cunning, then, is the evil of evil itself, and the strength of sin,
and the life of the body of shameful deeds. If there were no cunning, perhaps evil would stop for fear of being condemned.
And from fear of the judgment prepared for her by justice. Cunning, then, is worse than all other evils.
For cunning is sin’s tower. When sin attacks along the roads and robs everyone,
she runs to her refuge in cunning, so that a wind may go out in her place to meet her accusers.
She hides in it as in a tower from the scouts of justice, who go out to track her footsteps.
See what an evil your boasting rests on, you miserable disciple!
And what are you proud of, you wolf wrapped in a lamb’s skin? If your cunning is within you, every kind of wrongdoing is with you.
If craftiness is in your soul, every kind of sin lives in you. If your life rests on the snares of deceit, every kind of evil makes its home in you.
Your foul deeds are not openly visible because cunning itself conceals them.
For this is what cunning promises anyone who becomes its disciple: that it will be a covering for his sin.
This does not suit you—it is the mother of all evils.
Nor does this evil, which has become a nest for all evils, belong in your spiritual way of life.
But you, upright disciple, rejoice in your simplicity, through which you have run the path of righteousness.
Do not be ashamed to be called a child, for this name suits you.
This title is fitting for you, because it makes known your freedom from wrongdoing. For the name “child”
indicates his innocence, and the title “simple” proclaims that there is no deceit in him.
For just as each of the craftsmen of the world, or those who serve in the army of an earthly kingdom,
has a name by which his position is known and his craft distinguished, so too this is the disciple’s title: to be called simple.
Who could grant you the privilege of bearing a name by which God is called? For the name “simple” indicates something undivided.
For a simple person has no deceit in him. No hidden plot takes shape with him, falsehood does not flourish in him, and deception is not found in him.
Slander does not dwell in him. He does not secretly strike his companion, does not seek to do evil, and does not devise ways to cause harm.
He harbors no deceit against his neighbor and plans no evil against his brother who sits peacefully with him. Instead, he is a clean and pure vessel.
His companionship is a companionship of light. And just as, in a child by nature, none of these evils
is stirred up, so too none of them stirs in someone whose mind is simple.
For a child, because of his childhood, does not think up evil things, and a simple person, because of his simplicity, does not dwell on foul things.
For all good things are gathered under the name of simplicity, just as all evils are contained under the title of cunning.
For simplicity is a cultivated field that receives the seed and the plantings of all the virtues.
Cleverness, however, is ground full of thorns and thistles—that is, divided and empty thoughts.
And just as the growth of good seed is hindered in a field full of thorns and thistles,
so the divided thoughts of cleverness hinder the simple growth of faith.
And just as good seed grows healthily in ground cleared of the growth of thorns,
so too the word of truth grows and flourishes healthily within a simple mind.
For simplicity does not pass judgment on what faith says, nor does it investigate why God commanded things this way.
It has no objection to what it is told to do. Instead, it listens straightforwardly, accepts readily, and observes simply.
For simplicity is free of strain in all its actions.
It is not worn down by thoughts that bind and undo one another. For the practice of righteousness is easy for simplicity.
And it travels the path of toil without hesitation. For this reason our Lord also, to his disciples,
taught the innocence of children, so that he might give them simplicity. For he rejected the clever and chose the simple.
He sent away the cunning and the scribes, and brought the uneducated and ordinary people close to himself. Annas was cunning.
Caiaphas was clever. The Pharisees were skilled. The scribes were deceitful.
And our Savior's choice rejected all these. In place of Caiaphas he chose Simon for himself, and in place of Annas, John.
In place of the scribes, Andrew; in place of the Pharisees, Matthew; in place of the knowledgeable, Philip.
In place of the cunning, Bartholomew; in place of the clever, James—a band of simple people in place of an assembly of cunning people.
Those who knew nothing, in place of those who thought they knew everything. For truth always
prevails through simplicity, and faith has shone forth through childlikeness. And after our Lord had rejected the assemblies of the educated,
and the companies of the clever and cunning, and had chosen those fishermen, ordinary people without education,
he again taught them too to increase their simplicity, and not merely remain at that original measure of their childlikeness.
He took a child and stood him among them. Looking at them all, he said to them,
"Unless you turn and become like this child, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven."
Our Lord did this because he saw that they wanted to depart from their simple way of thinking by asking for honor,
and to gain rank one above another. Simple people do not make a request like this.
But the question arose from a mind that wanted to probe with cunning.
Our Lord restrained this outburst of confused questioning and spoke to his disciples, rebuking and correcting them:
“If you belong to me, be simple. If you long for the kingdom of heaven, become like this child.
Since you wish to receive the life to come, remain pure.
If you wish to become wise through the word of life, continue in your ignorance. For I do not want you to turn from simple people into crafty people.
Rather, turn from simple people into wise people. For whoever strives to become crafty instead of simple goes downward.
But whoever strives to grow from a child into a wise person goes upward. A crafty person does not accept my teaching.
That is why I chose you: because you are children. For I rejected craftiness in others.
Take care that it does not arise in you, so that I do not reject you because of it. Let this child be an example to you.
Just as he desires nothing from the world and asks for nothing that people possess—neither rank nor honor, neither wealth nor authority—
but only his food and clothing, which he needs in his childhood, so you too must become children like him,
innocent and simple like him, so that you may be my chosen disciples and I may find you as you were when I chose you.”
See, then: our Lord Jesus too urged us toward simplicity through this commandment.
He instructed us to be pure and innocent. For we should not be ashamed of simplicity and shrink from it,
as we would from worldly things that are of no use to us, nor should simple people be despised in our eyes,
or regarded by us as good for nothing. For they are not wanted by this world, but they are useful and wanted for the kingdom of God.
For what is rejected by human beings is chosen in God's sight, just as the apostles too were rejected by the whole world.
And our Savior Jesus himself was also hated and rejected by all the Jews.
So too, whoever rejects simple people and for this reason despises and scorns them—
this insolent person's lot is assigned with that of the Jews, scribes, and Pharisees who rejected Christ and his disciples.
Consider what punishment Christ's word decreed against anyone who causes one of them to stumble. Take care not to cause them to stumble.
Although this saying also bears other meanings—“Whoever causes these little ones to stumble,
it would be better for him if a millstone turned by a donkey were hung around his neck and he were drowned in the depths of the sea”—nevertheless, it applies still more
to those people, so that no one should dare to mock the simplicity of the innocent.
For when you ridicule, deride, and mock his simplicity, criticize his quietness, and scorn his innocence,
And he seemed to you idle and useless. The clamor of your insults against him forces him to strip off and throw away his innocence,
and to renounce his simplicity, as though you had given him cause to be ashamed and to flee from that childlikeness because of which he seemed foolish to the insolent.
And instead of being what he was, he became what he was not, because of your shouting against him
and your insults against him. You caused him to stumble in his former way of life, so that he would abandon it
and adopt other ways in its place that are opposed to his innocence. Though he had been quiet, he would reject this,
and value and choose speech rather than silence, cunning rather than his former simplicity, and craftiness rather than his lack of learning.
And you would make him hot-tempered and angry instead of gentle and peaceable. Because you have thus caused him to stumble, and your shouting has forced him
to exchange his good qualities for bad ones, it would have been better for you to have a millstone turned by a donkey hung around your neck
and to be thrown into the depths of the sea than to cause one of these little ones who believe in the Son to stumble.
Notice that our Lord himself also called them little ones, because they make themselves smaller than everyone else.
And he did this to teach you not to despise them because they eagerly seek lowliness,
but rather to let them become greater in your eyes for this very reason. For the appearance of the simple and uneducated is ordinary, and their bearing is unrefined.
Anyone who wishes to despise them takes their appearance as a reason to look down on them,
because they do not have a mind that knows how to arrange their outward appearance before other people and present them outwardly to the world as knowledgeable and distinguished.
But you should take this very thing as all the more reason to esteem them.
Let their lowly condition be a reason for you to honor them, and their insignificance a basis for praising them.
For wherever faith is preserved in its integrity and is not corrupted by cunning thoughts, it honors and exalts simplicity,
and loves and supports it, even when its appearance is contemptible.
Learn from practical experience itself how dear the simple are to believers,
and how beloved those who are uneducated and ordinary for Christ’s sake are to the whole company of Christ’s disciples.
Understand it also from this: the crafty people of the world eagerly approach those who are unlearned in the faith,
and cunning people and rulers bow before the simplicity of Christ. Look and see the great people of the world,
how lovingly they embrace simplicity, and how they bow before and cherish a lack of learning.
The greater the measure of simplicity someone displays, the greater and more honored he becomes in their eyes.
For the people of the world do not go out to the spiritual birds outside the world in order to see cunning and crafty people.
Lift up your eyes, disciple, and look at those who are coming to you and running lovingly to your door.
For they run to see those born of the Spirit, not people trained and knowledgeable in the affairs of the world.
For whenever they want to see clever and cunning people, practiced and polished in the wisdom of the world, they enter cities and towns.
But when they go outside the world, they run to see the childlike and simple, the children of Christ.
Do not let someone come and find you a snake instead of a dove, a hawk instead of an innocent bird, and your speech directed toward evil instead of being wise toward good.
Let him come and see you, disciple, as he longs to see you. For he has taken off his cunning and put on simplicity,
and in it he has approached you. But you have hurried to put on what he took off, and you have wanted to acquire what he rejected.
He did not carry and bring with him thoughts of cleverness, but the simplicity of faith.
He has come into your dwelling. Do not let him come and find, in the place of spiritual people, what he left behind in the world.
Listen to the prophet, who in his simple teaching also proclaims our Lord and compares him to a lamb and a ewe,
an animal that is purer than all other animals. He says, “Like a lamb he was led to slaughter.”
“And like a ewe before the shearer, he was silent.” The lion, the wolf, and the bear are cunning, along with all the other fanged animals,
whose makeup combines cunning with their viciousness. But innocent and unskilled in their behavior and movements are
sheep, lambs, and ewes. Our Lord was compared to them, and believers were called by their names.
For our Lord did not compare himself to a lion when he was being led to suffering and death.
Nor did he call his flocks by the names of animals that are cunning in doing evil by their created nature.
Instead, he was called a lamb and a ewe, because he was being led to suffering and death quietly, like them.
He says, “Like a ewe before the shearer, he was silent, and so he did not open his mouth in his humiliation.”
And to confirm the prophetic word by his actions, he was quiet when they led him away, and silent when they judged him.
When they flogged him, he did not protest. When they condemned him, he did not argue. When they bound him, he did not become angry.
When they struck his cheeks, he did not grumble. When he was stripped of his clothes, like a ewe of its fleece, he did not cry out.
When they gave him vinegar and bitter gall, he did not curse them. When they nailed him to the wood, he did not complain against them.
And when Simon wanted to take off his sheep-like innocence and take up a sword to avenge the insult to his master, he rebuked him,
telling him to keep the sword in its place. He said, “Put your sword back in its place. I do not need your help.”
He stands before the judge and is questioned—he who is the scholar and teacher of all wisdom—and gives no answer.
He kept the law of simplicity, to fulfill the saying that he was led like a lamb to the slaughter.
They lead him as though he were unable to speak, and take him around from one place to another.
They drag him from place to place and haul him from one judge to another.
He stood before Annas in silence and did not speak until Annas put him under oath. He was questioned by Pilate and remained quiet.
He gave him no answer until he heard him say, “Are you the king of the Jews?”—words indicating that he regarded him as a rebel against Caesar.
They took him to Herod, who questioned him to put him to the test, hoping to see and hear great things from him.
There too he stood silent and did not speak. He gave no answer to the man questioning him.
He was considered a fool who knew nothing, an ignorant man who had no answer to give.
The Jews and the priests thought whatever they pleased, but he did not abandon the innocence of a lamb.
Nor did he let go of the law of simplicity. Paul the apostle saw that those who crucified him considered him a fool without understanding.
His enemies counted him as someone without knowledge or understanding, and Paul spoke against them on Jesus’ behalf:
“The foolishness of God is wiser than human beings.” For, so that it would not be hard for you
to be considered a fool by people because of your simplicity, God himself presented himself as a fool,
by standing before those questioning him without giving an answer. They considered him ignorant because he gave no answer.
This was so that you too would persevere with strength of soul and not transgress the law of simplicity,
even if everyone considers you ignorant and regards you as having neither knowledge nor education.
For anyone who is troubled at being considered simple and uneducated by people has his mind bound by a passionate love for the empty knowledge of the world.
And if he is regarded in a way contrary to his wishes, distress and sorrow rule over his life.
For you ought to endure everything, so that you may complete your path and bring your journey to its end.
For look: even David the prophet, as a means of saving his life from death, presented himself to the Philistines as mad and senseless.
He let his saliva run down onto his beard, like a man out of his mind, to save his life from being killed.
If, then, David appeared in the guise of madness so as not to lose his temporary life,
and as someone without reason or discernment, how much more ought you to persist in your simplicity for the sake of eternal life.
Do not be overcome by the clamor of mockers and turn away from the goal set before you.
Our Lord also called the faithful of his flocks by names that express simplicity.
“If you love me,” he says to Simon, the chief of the disciples, “tend my sheep, my lambs, and my ewes.”
And just as he was wondrously called a lamb and a ewe in the prophetic word, and John also called him
“the Lamb of God,” so he also named the disciples who resemble him with these names that signify innocence.
Thus, when all the faithful hear what names the Shepherd has given them,
they should strive to remain entirely innocent, like sheep, lambs, and ewes,
and not depart from the rule of simplicity. And like these innocent animals, which are led away to be killed,
driven to slaughter, bound for shearing, and attacked by wild beasts, yet do not cry out or complain,
but remain quiet in their natural innocence, so too the Lord’s disciple ought,
in the face of every trial in deeds and words, of afflictions and insults, of confinement and oppression,
of mistreatment and imprisonment, of the shouts of oppressors and the accusations of liars,
to persevere in the innocence of his heart, not abandon his rule of quietness, and not cast off his innocence.
He must not abandon his simplicity and devise schemes to harm his enemies. For this is their own work:
evil intrigues and wicked schemes. Throughout their lives they have ample time to carry them out.
But you have a task hidden from their knowledge, which the serenity of your mind can accomplish.
You take delight in it secretly, while they are unaware of this delight, because they have not been found worthy of the comforts that you yourself experience.
For simplicity is free from anxiety, and therefore its joy is also constant at all times.
For just as children’s joy is constant and their laughter abundant because of their simplicity,
since worldly concerns do not suppress the joy that stirs with childlike freedom in their minds,
so joy is always constant in a simple heart, because it has no scheme that will fill it with distress if it is not carried out.
For someone who wants to harm his enemy but cannot, or schemes to become rich but does not become rich,
or runs to reach a goal but does not arrive—because of these things, sadness and distress rule his life.
And all that joy which is born of simplicity is taken away from him. For a simple person is regarded as being of no use to the world.
And if you are regarded as being of no use to the world, disciple, do not be saddened by this.
For this is a Christian’s glory: to be unpracticed in worldly affairs and of no use in anything belonging to a fleshly way of life.
For if someone tells you that you do not know carpentry, or that you do not know how to practice the trade of tanners,
Or if you do not know one of the world's lowly trades, this is no reason for you to be ridiculed.
For even a king is not dishonored by not knowing how to practice one of the world's trades.
Rather, this very thing brings him praise: because his authority is above these things, he does not stoop to learn them.
Thus, not knowing them proves to be grounds for praising him, while knowing them is grounds for reproaching him.
We also see this among many people who hold one of the world's positions of honor:
although they know trades and understand other matters beneath their rank, they deny knowing them.
They regard this very lack of knowledge as something praiseworthy.
They take refuge in it as though pursuing praise, saying that they have no knowledge of trades.
In the same way, then, for a disciple of Christ, ignorance of worldly matters is also praiseworthy.
It is to his credit that he is neither crafty nor deceitful, and it gives him a good name that he is unfamiliar with evil intrigues.
He considers knowledge of these things a disgrace. And even more than it is considered a disgrace for an earthly king,
knowledge of the world's trades is a reproach for the disciple who is enrolled in the kingdom above:
that he should know these things, which are foreign to his calling and far removed from the conduct of his discipleship.
For his life has no time free from communion with God for him to turn to learning these lowly things,
to occupy himself with these fleshly matters, and to devise ways to harm and injure his enemies, or ways to become rich and acquire possessions,
or how to exchange arguments with those who wrong him, where to find profit, and by what means to obtain these things.
For the simple person's communion with God does not allow him to turn to these things and occupy himself with them.
He does not descend from the height of the knowledge of Christ's kingdom to the schemes and thoughts of these sickly passions.
Those who are stirred by thoughts of these things are always in a state of sickness.
For it is not fitting for a mind in whose simplicity faith in Christ shines
to turn and dwell on these intrigues of the flesh and these destructive tricks.
So do not consider it a disgrace that you are unfamiliar with the world's tricks.
Rather, let this itself be an even greater honor for you: that, in your likeness to spiritual beings, you are high and exalted above these fleshly things.
For among spiritual beings there are no schemes or tricks concerning the affairs of the world.
For if their way of life is above everything bodily, it is clear that their mind too is exalted above these passions.
And their entire concern is solely with the praises of the Godhead.
As they grow in spiritual knowledge, in things higher than their understanding, they do not stoop to look at what is beneath them.
For they do not wish to descend from their ranks, but long to rise higher,
and always to reach forward into the mysteries of the divine Being.
Minds that are not stirred by bodily things are therefore patterned after these powers.
And this is the rank of spiritual people: that the things above the world
alone should be their study, and that their thoughts should not descend to investigating and learning things foreign to their way of life.
For just as the instruction belonging to each craft is distinct and well known, and whoever becomes an apprentice in a craft
is eager to learn that craft, and not another, at the place of instruction, so too a disciple's entire study and concern
should be with learning his craft, without letting anything else interrupt the reflection of his thoughts.
For our craft is the study of spiritual things, and that our thoughts and deeds
should be above the world, and that we should always reach forward in spiritual things.
For an apprentice who does not advance in learning his craft among the craftsmen is rebuked by his teachers,
and is laughed at and mocked by his peers. Just like him, and even more than he, deserving of rebuke is
the disciple of this spiritual craft, unless he grows day by day and advances in bodily labor and spiritual thoughts.
The loss that each of them suffers is also clear and well known.
For someone who does not receive instruction in a worldly craft loses the benefits available in that craft.
But someone who does not receive Christ's teaching and grow in goodness loses
the kingdom of heaven, and the blessings sealed up and kept for God's chosen ones,
and what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived,
and the fellowship that the perfect have with Christ, for the sake of which Christ himself came down from heaven to earth.
In short, this person's loss is his very self, together with the rest of the blessings that transcend nature.
For the mind capable of receiving these things is clear and simple.
And just as a child's mind is clearer and more agile than a fully grown man's in receiving instruction in anything,
so a simple mind learns spiritual things much more readily than shrewd and crafty thoughts.
For simplicity is good soil, and it readily receives the seeds and plants of this teaching.
And just as there are qualities in natural soils that receive trees and plants,
and make them yield fruit more quickly than other soils, so too the soils of the minds of the simple-hearted
simply receive the plants of this teaching of the Spirit, and it quickly takes root in them and produces fruit.
The soil of cunning, however, cheats this teaching. Either it does not receive it at all,
or, if it takes root and is received in it, its growth within it is choked by thorns and thistles
of doubts and thoughts that are constantly tearing down and building up, which are the adversaries of faith and simplicity.
Therefore rejoice in simplicity, O disciple, for it not only makes you dear to God,
but also makes you beloved in people's eyes. Look closely and see, if you wish, from practical experience,
that the simple-hearted are more beloved in people's eyes than the cunning and crafty.
For everyone loves simplicity, just as everyone loves childhood.
For the simple-hearted and children are both beloved. Cunning and wickedness, however, are hated by everyone.
Everyone is on guard against them, because they are full of tricks and ambushes, and habitually overturn the proper order of everything.
Simplicity, however, besides being beloved, is also trustworthy. No one is on guard against a simple-hearted person in anything he does,
because he is confident in simplicity's innocence, that it does not devise evil things. And just as no one is on guard against a child
when he wants to do wrong secretly inside the house, because the child is too young to recognize his wrongdoing,
so too no one is on guard against a simple-hearted person in whatever he wants to do, because the simple-hearted person bears the likeness of a child in his thoughts.
For who does not long to be loved by God and cherished by people? And both these things are found in simplicity.
Why, then, O disciple, do you flee from being loved by God and cherished by people,
and from obtaining, without toil, freely given love from the Creator and all his creation?
“But,” you say, “they mock me and consider me foolish and uneducated, without intelligence or discernment.”
And what good thing is there that has no opposition, O disciple?
But if you are afraid of the opposition to good things, you will do no good at all,
because opposition is found to all of them, and toil is mixed into the practice of them all.
Besides, envy and jealousy are also stirred up in people against the other virtues.
This virtue of simplicity, however, is freer from opposition than all the vices.
For neither envy nor jealousy continually opposes it, and neither hatred nor hostility fights against it.
Even if it has this disadvantage, that it is easily scorned and despised, love is nevertheless found alongside this.
The very people who look down on a simple person love him. It is not because of hatred that he is contemptible in their eyes.
Rather, because they trust him, or because he is of no use in the matters that concern them, they consider him ignorant
of worldly affairs, inexperienced in dealings among people, and without knowledge of cunning and evil.
You should therefore rejoice in these things: you are considered to be what you are, and you are called what you ought to be.
If someone tells you that you do not know how to lie, commit adultery, or steal, do you consider it an insult?
Or that you do not know how to stand on a chariot as a charioteer, or that you are unfamiliar with the skill of athletes,
or that you do not know singing and the movements of dancers, or that you cannot make jokes and laugh
and display the routines and entertainment of mime actors—do you really consider ignorance of these things an insult? I think not.
Nor does anyone blame you for being unfamiliar with these skills.
Likewise, you should not consider it an insult that you are without skill in evil or the defilement of shameful deeds.
For blessed David also said that the innocent and upright accompanied him. And it is well known that innocence is born of simplicity.
My discussion now concerns clarity of spirit, which comes about within the soul through the uprooting of every evil.
For natural simplicity belongs to one order, and clarity of spirit is a different degree. Natural simplicity
is the beginning of the path of Christ’s teaching, while clarity of spirit is the completion of the path of righteousness.
The person who begins in simplicity ends in clarity. Thus the blessed apostles, too, were simple when they were first chosen,
but at the completion of the divine plan, after they had received the Holy Spirit, they were shown to be clear. For clarity consists in this:
through toil, weariness, and battle against every evil impulse, a person separates out the sediment of evil and casts it out of himself.
There remain within him the clarity and transparency of pure thoughts and of the growth stirred in the spirit, beyond all doubt.
Simplicity, however, consists in this: by its nature it is not stirred by these thoughts.
It has not itself separated them out through its [?], or overcome them in battle,
or through wisdom rolled them away, brought them out, and cast them beyond the place of its purity.
For clarity does these things, while simplicity is the beginning of the path.
And land cleared of thorns, ready to receive good seed. For it is one thing for someone to uproot thorns and remove thistles,
and to clear the land, prepare it, and make it ready to receive good seed and fine plants.
It is another thing for the field to be sown and planted, bearing fruit, awaiting the hand that gathers its crops,
and for the crop it bears to be gathered and stored in granaries. This, then, is the measure of purity:
land fully sown with seed and completely planted, bearing fruits of various kinds that have reached maturity
and become ripe. Simplicity, however, is a field that has been cultivated and cleared of thorns,
prepared and fit to receive whatever is put into it. Malice and cunning, however,
are land full of thorns, thistles, and weeds. Even if good seed falls into it, it chokes its shoots
and stunts its growth. Disciple, be a cultivated field, prepared for Jesus, so that he may sow in you the good seed of his word
and plant within your soul the new plant of his teaching. If you possess simplicity by nature, rejoice in it,
and strive also to increase it. But if you have not acquired it as though from a natural seed, pursue it by your own choice and acquire it,
because it is a discovery that benefits your life in God.
It enables you to live without anxiety, with confidence in the dwelling where you live.
For a simple person does not think evil of anyone, nor is he afraid of the evil done by others.
Since he himself does not scheme to do harm, he does not even imagine that others are harming him.
For simplicity supposes that everyone resembles itself. And whatever a person is in himself,
it supposes that he is the same toward it, that he is like itself, and that everyone is alike.
For it is a mirror of its own soul and a reflection of its own being. As things are within it, so it sees them in everyone.
And just as it is without deceit, so it supposes others to be. Although those whom it observes differ among themselves in the various forms of their wickedness,
to it they are all the same. For this reason it remains at all times
without storms. No waves or tempests rise within it to disturb its purity,
because the wind of malice does not blow within it—the wind that stirs up all the waves of suspicion.
For just as storms arise in the natural sea through the action of the wind striking its surface,
so too the confused thoughts of malice are born from it, and meditation on evil things rises from within it
through the blast of cunning that strikes within it. But a simple mind is a calm in which there are no storms.
Just as the sea rests from its waves when there are no winds, so a simple mind is also at rest,
in freedom from all the anxieties that beat against it like waves.
For simplicity is a harbor that shelters within itself ships fleeing the storms of recklessness.
Whatever enters it, it settles into rest, and it transforms all turmoil into its own peaceful order.
For a simple person is not merely simple himself; he also brings whatever comes to him into his own order.
For obedience also accompanies simplicity, as does refraining from judging what is said to it.
It does not argue with those who give it orders. For the simple person's way of life brings ease to those around him.
All who know him delight in him. There is no strife in his neighborhood and no quarreling in his company.
There is no dispute in his companionship, no resistance in his obedience, and no opposition to what is said to him.
Everyone eagerly claims him. Even when people are selected and tasks are assigned, many choose him.
For whoever receives him considers him a good portion. He does not know how to disobey,
and he does not allow himself to argue with anyone. For all his knowledge concerns good things, not evil things.
He devises ways to please those who give him orders, not ways to resist their will.
Simplicity, then, befits the way of life of solitaries, and innocence is fitting for a life of mourning.
Serenity suits the monastic life, and gentleness befits a life of abstinence.
Lack of learning is also fitting for the ascetic life. For the chief priests of the Jews marveled at the apostles,
because, although they were uneducated and had no knowledge of books, they answered like wise men about the life to come.
In their very lack of learning, they became advocates for Christ.
For Christ chose unlearned advocates to speak on his behalf, so that through them he might proclaim all the more the triumph of his wisdom,
and so that everyone might recognize that it is not they who speak, but he who speaks through them.
“They realized,” it says, “that they had no learning and were ordinary men. They remembered that they had been with Jesus, and they marveled at them.”
So this too—that simplicity should keep the commandments—is astonishing. And that ordinary people should do what the wise do not do is marvelous.
For if the priests had known beforehand that the apostles were wise,
and they had spoken wisely, they would not have marveled greatly at them, since they would have been hearing from them what suited their education.
But they marveled at them all the more because they heard from them what they had not expected.
And they gave them an answer beyond the capacity of all the wise.
And through their simplicity Jesus triumphed, and his wisdom was proclaimed before everyone.
Indeed, this is also why our Lord chose the simple and rejected the wise and educated:
to teach everyone who becomes his disciple to adopt this starting point and advance toward him by it.
We should not pursue cunning because the world considers it wisdom,
or shrink from acquiring simplicity because people despise it.
For look: even in his choice, our Lord showed us both things, since he chose fishermen and chose tax collectors.
That is, the uneducated and the unjust, the ignorant and the wicked, those opposed to knowledge
and those opposed to righteousness. For that is what fishermen and tax collectors are:
the fisherman lacks knowledge, and the tax collector lacks righteousness. Thus, when they acquired both these things,
though they were strangers to both, Jesus would be revealed to everyone as the one who makes people wise and righteous.
For Matthew and Zacchaeus, who followed Christ, possessed worldly training.
But in their disposition they were found to be simple, and their obedience bears witness to their simplicity.
For until they had risen above worldly training and become strangers to the human cunning they had acquired,
and had attained the fishermen’s degree of simplicity, Christ did not bring them near to receive his teaching.
Nor did he give them authority over the treasures of his knowledge.
And perhaps, when he everywhere commanded simplicity and becoming like little children, he was also giving this advice to them.
He spoke for the sake of those disciples, while also restraining others from learning cunning.
For he taught the simple to remain in their simplicity, and urged those brought up in the teaching of cunning
to strip off this stained garment, so that both groups would come to the same level
and begin running along the path of good deeds as though from the same starting point.
For some, without training, are children of simplicity, like Simon and Andrew, James and John.
Others, through their worldly upbringing, had been confined in the womb of cunning, like Matthew, Zacchaeus, and Philip,
along with the rest of the others. And those who had not been born, he brought to birth out of craftiness into the state of childhood.
He wrapped them all in the swaddling band of simplicity, and then began to raise them to maturity through his teaching.
And let us bring them to the measure of spiritual strength. And if, there among the apostles, simplicity was shown to be so excellent,
how much more should it be found among us and cherished in communities of monks,
where our very way of life demands it, and those who come to us expect to see us living this way?
An unruly disciple, then, makes no progress. He is an example of evil to all his fellow disciples.
For he is a teacher of evil things, not good things, and a model of loss, not a model of gain.
He is a teacher of disobedience, an example of stubbornness, distracted by worthless things.
He speaks needless words, a distracted prisoner, bound by necessity, driven by force to something he does not want.
A worker full of grumbling, a hired worker who falls short, who does not work enough to earn the bread he eats, who keeps a diligent worker's place unproductive,
occupying his place but doing none of his work; a stumbling stone for those who run, a guide to unfamiliar paths.
He leads astray those who walk properly. He twists the road before those who run straight ahead.
He looks for others' failings, covets positions of authority, is a friend of the rich, an associate of the prominent, a companion of the proud.
He fasts out of necessity, kept from food by the compulsion of the rule. He labors without goodwill, a disciple in appearance
but not in thought; a nurturer of deceit, a soul that desires evil things, a mocking tongue, arrogant, empty,
conceited though he has nothing in him, an opponent of all good order, a figure portrayed in images of failure,
a body assembled from divided limbs, complaining about every matter, finding fault with every action,
pursuing those who pay him no attention, slow to do good, quick to run toward evil, a child of sleep,
a son of laziness, an enemy of wakefulness, a hater of prayer, a companion of a well-prepared table.
He waits for delicacies and looks for luxuries, the right hand of the slanderer, the hidden arm of the enemy.
These things and others like them are found in an unruly disciple. What has been said is only a sprinkling of his shameful qualities.
Anyone who is like this deserves to be despised by everyone, so that his wickedness may be beaten down through the contempt shown him.
For God's prophet rebukes those who are children when it comes to good things but wise when it comes to evil things.
He says, “Ephraim became like a foolish dove without understanding. He came to Egypt and went to Assyria, but he did not walk toward me on the path of repentance.”
For the prophet condemns childishness of this kind because it is not simplicity but foolishness.
This is also the condemnation of their childishness concerning good things: instead of the one Savior, they chose other helpers for themselves.
They abandoned the road that leads to God and ran after the Egyptians and Assyrians, asking them to come to their aid.
And although they had experienced many times that they could not rescue them from the evils in which they were caught,
they did not learn wisdom from the experience of these events and run to God’s place of refuge. And he compared them to doves,
whose offspring others took, and whose young were made servants of others.
And he considered them senseless, because they had not acquired the discernment by which they could draw near to God.
Solomon too, in his words, rebukes the person who is led like a child after his desire
and lacks the knowledge that fights against his passions. “He was going after her,” he says, “like a child,
and like an ox going to the slaughterer, and like a dog to its bonds, and like a deer with an arrow flying into its liver.”
For this childishness deserves condemnation, because it was not devoted to good things but served evil things.
And by any fair judgment it should not be called childlikeness, even if Scripture gave it that name
in keeping with the purpose it had in view. Rather, it is foolishness, loss of understanding, lack of discernment, and the destruction of proper conduct.
For our discourse does not encourage this kind of simplicity: that a person should ignorantly be swept along by every voice
and be persuaded by the deceit of every teaching. For God’s apostle also warns us against this.
“Do not,” he says, “be children who are shaken and shifted by every wind of deceitful human teachings.”
For see: in the apostle’s words, this way of thinking was called instability,
since it is led by every voice and teaching, and exchanges its uprightness for hateful conduct and a shameful life.
Rather, the simplicity whose entire concern is with good things is the simplicity that the words of our discourse also encourage.
Consider, then, the simplicity of all the faithful, and see the childlikeness of mind of Christ’s disciples.
Although they do not understand the deceit in the devices of heretics and do not know the bitterness of their evil teaching, they are careful not to share in it.
They hold to the truth without changing, because of their wise simplicity and because the fear of God accompanies their simplicity.
Although they do not know the thinking behind those teachings, they understand the thoughts of their own teaching. And like a child who knows only one teacher,
and is ruled by fear of him, trembling at his command and dreading his rod alone,
but is not even aware that other teachers exist, so too the childlike believer:
fear of Christ’s authority as teacher alone rules his life, and other teachers of doctrines count for nothing to him.
He is not persuaded to seek another instructor for himself, nor does he listen to any teacher except the one.
Nor does he tremble and recoil in fear of those whose authority as teachers he does not acknowledge.
But like a child by nature, whose reverence is carefully directed toward one teacher and one scribe.
And if another teacher wishes to give him another teaching, beyond the one he holds to, he does not accept it.
For his childlikeness is natural simplicity, not the corrupting error of thoughts.
Let us therefore run, as disciples of Christ, along the path he has shown us, and walk on the road he has opened for us.
Let the attainment of simplicity be precious in our eyes, and let us become little children in receiving good teaching.
And let us be shrewd as serpents against the enemy who schemes to harm us.
And let us always remember what Christ our Lord said in his word to all the disciples:
“Whoever does not receive the kingdom of God like a child will not enter it.”
May we all, by his grace, be found worthy of it and become heirs together with all the saints,
through the mercy of Christ himself, who is God, to whom be glory forever. Amen.
The second discourse on simplicity is finished.
Notes on the Syriac text:
The sixth discourse, in which he explains that after the faith that is born from natural simplicity, fear of God is stirred within a person.
And how this fear is born, and by what things it is established and strengthened within us.
Let us therefore approach the teaching of the discourse on the fear of God with a mind that fears God.
And as far as lies within our power and ability—that is, as the grace of God grants—
let us make use of this discourse to help our own souls and to benefit others.
For we do not write to appear knowledgeable; rather, because we desire our own benefit, we speak to others.
And we should not keep silent and refrain from speaking merely because many before us have spoken and written.
For those before us spoke and wrote as teachers, while we, as their disciples,
should repeat their teaching after them, like a child who practices and constantly repeats the teaching he receives from his teacher so that he will not forget it.
In the same way, we too repeat the things we have heard, so that by repeating them
we may remember them, and our thoughts may be kept from wandering after empty, unprofitable things.
For as long as the mind is not occupied with helpful meditation, it wanders outside itself
and moves about in a place beyond the help of God. And just as, when it meditates on good things, it dwells in the light of the remembrance of God,
Thus, when he broods and dwells on empty and idle thoughts, his whole way of life is in darkness.
And whoever stands in darkness neither sees nor is seen, neither distinguishes nor is distinguished, neither knows nor is known.
Instead, he is deprived of the beauty of seeing created things, and all who see are likewise deprived of seeing him.
He neither recognizes the road nor understands the path, nor does he see the course his steps are taking.
But so that this does not happen to us, let us occupy ourselves at all times with the word of God.
Not merely by having the tongue repeat it, but also by having the heart reflect and meditate on it in thought.
Thus our mouth will speak at all times from the abundance of our heart.
For whatever the mind ponders secretly, the tongue speaks openly, however careful a person may be.
And if the tongue is deliberately kept from speaking, then through gestures and movements of the other senses,
the heart's secrets are revealed to those who watch, and the face, through its changing expressions, gives evidence
of the hidden mind concealed within the soul. For whoever continually drinks in divine teaching,
the plant of his own being bears divine fruit at all times, provided that he does not listen to the teaching merely out of habit,
and does not attend to the helpful word of God for amusement, nor receive it to advance in human knowledge through it.
Nor does he listen to it in order to learn it as material for the art of winning empty praise.
For teaching that is spoken with knowledge and heard with discernment produces spiritual fruit on both sides:
in the tongue of the one who sows it and in the ear of the one who receives it. For the teacher, along with the learner,
joyfully listens to his own words, if he is a genuine teacher and not merely a channel for the teaching of others.
For constant practice of a craft increases knowledge of it and trains all the senses in carrying it out.
Likewise, continual reflection on the word of instruction awakens the thoughts to knowledge, sharpens the tongue for speech, and binds the mind to meditation on God.
And whoever reflects on God at all times and continually maintains this remembrance secretly within his soul:
the fear of God also grows within him, becoming a protective wall for him against all evils.
For just as a city's wall shields its inhabitants from the harm caused by the coming of enemies,
so the fear of God shields a person from the coming of the captors and enemies of our souls.
It restrains the body from acting on its lusts and guards the soul against ugly thoughts.
For whoever truly learns to fear God guards not only his body against lusts, but also his heart against ugly impulses.
For to what order the fear of God belongs, and at what rank a person who fears God stands,
and how this fear is acquired, and through what things it grows, we ought to explain,
as we learned from those before us who were witnesses of knowledge and servants of the word of instruction.
For they taught me that true fear of God is born from true faith.
And whoever truly believes also truly fears the one in whom he believes.
And just as his faith does not rest on contrivances, so his fear does not come about through artifice.
For when a person believes that God exists, he begins to receive instruction in his commandments.
For faith itself is born from the simplicity of human nature, and it is also established and preserved by that very simplicity.
But the commandments that faith hears and accepts are kept by the fear of God.
For just as simplicity preserves faith, so fear of God also preserves God's commandments.
But by fear I do not mean someone merely saying in words, “I fear God,”
or being considered God-fearing through habitual practice, as many are, but the fear that is genuinely stirred within the soul.
And when the soul trembles and quakes within, it also sets all the body's limbs trembling with it.
For the body fears whatever harms it, while the soul trembles before the one who has power to destroy it.
For just as the body's fear is of external dangers, whether wild animals or fire, or swords and iron combs,
or drowning in water, or falling from high cliffs, or news of raiders, or the sight of judges,
or agonizing scourges, or shackles and imprisonment, so the soul too has its natural fear,
of the unseen judge, who can torment it together with its body through spiritual afflictions suited to its nature.
And just as the body naturally fears all these things we have listed, so the soul too naturally fears
the remembrance of God's judgment, the torments reserved for those who provoke him to anger, and Gehenna, which is threatened against evildoers,
and hearing of the outer darkness, and the report of the fire that is not quenched and the worm that does not die.
For when the body sees the things that harm it, it fears them. And when the soul looks closely at the things that torment it,
it is terrified by them. For it is not through contrivances that the body is stirred by things that cause it harm.
Rather, as soon as it sees them or reflects on their memory, it naturally trembles and fears them.
So too, when the soul looks closely with the eye of faith at the threats of things to come,
And when it inwardly sees the terrible things revealed by the Judge’s word, it is immediately filled with fear.
And all its thoughts tremble; these are its spiritual members.
And in its trembling it makes the body tremble with it. Through the fear of its thoughts, the members of its body are also afraid.
And just as it shares in the body’s fear, so the body also shares in its own fear.
Although the soul’s nature is not harmed by the things that harm the body, nevertheless, because it is joined to the body, it is afraid along with it.
And although the afflictions and torments to come are not visible to the body’s eyes,
nevertheless, because the soul sees them inwardly and trembles and is terrified by them, it makes the body tremble with it as well.
And it brings dread and terror upon all the body’s members. For this is how it is in actual experience.
Those who have experienced this and have personally put it to the test know it:
the moment the soul remembers God’s judgment and trembles at the thought of it, it makes all the body’s members share in its trembling.
For the moment a person remembers God, if his soul and body are not clean from sins, his whole being is immediately filled with fear.
And all his members tremble, just as the body trembles when it suddenly sees something that destroys and harms it.
And if someone has not experienced this personally—since not everyone has reached the measure of the natural fear that comes from God—
from the fact that the body trembles and makes the soul tremble with it, something evident and known to everyone,
let him also understand how the soul is afraid and pours its fear upon the body, something that only a few have experienced.
These are those whose souls are not dead through the death of sin.
For sin committed contemptuously, without remembering God, is the complete death of the soul.
As Holy Scripture also calls the sinner who does not repent a dead person.
For repentance comes from remembering God. Therefore, whoever sins, and within whom the remembrance of God’s judgment is not stirred,
either during the sin itself or after committing it, is dead in his soul, even though he appears alive in his body.
But a soul is known to be alive by its constant remembrance of God.
And if it sins and repents, it is sick. But if it sins contemptuously, without repentance or remembrance of God,
this reveals that it has been killed by sin. For knowledge of God is the soul’s spiritual life.
For just as the body’s life consists in the soul’s remaining within it,
and its life is recognized by its awareness of everything that comes near it, or that it itself approaches,
Likewise, the life of the soul is knowledge of God. It is known to be alive by this: that it is conscious of God.
For a dead body does not feel injuries, nor does a slain soul feel anything at the remembrance of God's judgment.
Even if you inflict every affliction and torment on a corpse, it feels no pain.
And even if a soul that has once died to God takes part in every evil, it feels nothing.
For a dead body is struck and feels nothing; it is cut apart and pierced and feels no pain. Likewise, a soul that has died to God sins and feels nothing.
It acts wickedly and does not know it. It transgresses and takes no thought. It incurs guilt, but its conscience does not prod it. It does wrong and feels no pain.
And just as a person's conscience does not prod him to make distinctions when he properly satisfies the needs of nature,
so too a soul that has been corrupted by sin and has once died to God is not condemned by its conscience
for the things it does. Thus, remembrance of God
is the life of the soul. And just as all the pulses of a living body are constant,
and the whole body, all together, as long as it shares in life, pulses and moves in all its arteries and limbs,
so too, in a soul that has awareness of God, remembrance of God constantly pulses and moves.
And as long as it remembers God, it does not sin. But if it should happen, through the fumes of desire,
that the light of its knowledge is obscured for a time [?], remembrance of God immediately stirs within it.
And fear of him drives the person toward repentance. For fear of God does these two things within the soul:
it keeps a person from sinning, or, if he sins, it urges him to heal his sin through repentance.
For this is the habit of all those who have fear of God or of other people:
either they do not offend at all, or, when they have offended, they correct their transgressions.
The fear of God, then, is a barrier against every evil.
It protects the person within it from being harmed, and it is a wall that shelters him from every hateful thing.
Sometimes it also becomes a healer of evils, so that both functions may be seen in this fear:
it is both a physician and a protector. For it is a protective wall against evils, keeping them from coming,
and a wise healer of the evils committed through negligence.
For one person is terrified at the sight of the judge, while another trembles merely at the report of him.
For someone who is careful not to sin is restrained from evil by the sight of the judge.
But someone who turns to repentance after sinning is frightened by the report of the Judge.
Merely hearing about his judgment makes him tremble, for while committing his sin he cannot see him.
For sin is the blindness of the soul. When sin is practiced and carried out in a person's own being, as though from thick smoke,
the soul's sight is obscured by the fumes produced by desire, and it cannot see the Judge.
But it hears the sound of his threats from the mouths of others—that is, from the Holy Scriptures—and trembles at the report of him.
It is afraid of what it hears. This happens when the soul has not died completely to the knowledge and awareness of God.
