For even someone who is physically blind by nature does not tremble or become afraid of dangers from seeing them,
but from the report of them that he hears from others. For he does not see the lion coming to destroy him, or the snake crawling toward him to bite him.
But if he hears a report of them from someone else, he trembles. Nor does he see a precipice or a pit lying ahead of his steps.
But if someone else tells him about the danger ahead of him, he becomes afraid before reaching it and immediately holds himself back.
But someone whose sight is naturally sound does not need to learn about these things from others, because his own sight teaches him about danger to his body.
Through this comparison, let us also understand the person who is watchful and does not sin, and the other person who, after sinning, repents of his wrongdoing.
For the soul is not afraid at the sight of dangers to the body, even though it seems to be afraid because of its union with it.
Whenever the soul is afraid of these things, its fear is outside its own nature.
That is, the fumes of the body's fear rise over it and darken its understanding, and it becomes afraid along with the body of things that do not harm it.
But if the soul fears God, its fear is natural.
For this is the fear proper to the soul's nature: to fear God alone.
For the body does not naturally fear God, nor does the soul naturally fear wild animals
or other dangers. Consider livestock, wild animals, and birds:
because they are bodies alone, and no living soul shares their existence, fear of God is not in their nature,
but rather fear of one another or of other hostile things. In the same way, the body too, in its own sphere,
fears only dangers to itself. But if the soul raises it to share in its thoughts,
it too experiences fear of God along with the soul, just as the soul too lives with the body in fear of wild animals.
For God alone is the Judge who punishes the soul, because only one who is subtler than the soul can be its judge.
But human beings too can be judges of the body, and they can even kill it.
Yet in their judgments they have no authority over the soul, as the words of Christ testify when he says:
“Do not be afraid of those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul.”
The authority of judges is over the body alone. It is the body that they judge, torture, and kill.
But the soul’s nature is beyond the harm that killers can inflict, and it is not burned by their fire,
nor do their lashes fall upon its spiritual nature. It is not cut apart by their swords, nor is its being scraped away by their iron combs.
For the one who judges is bodily, and he proclaims with a bodily tongue the sentence he passes on offenders,
even though the soul secretly stirs his thoughts concerning the sentence. And all the instruments prepared for torture are bodily,
and through bodily tortures the body alone suffers harm. But as for the soul, because of its spirituality,
its nature is high above and beyond these things. However deeply the tortures dig, they dig into the sides of the body.
However far inward they penetrate and enter, the soul is farther within than they are, and the death they inflict has no dominion over its life.
Judges cannot kill the soul, and therefore people should not fear their judgment.
“But fear the one who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna.” The Lord alone is the soul’s judge.
And the one who made it alive is able to bring death upon its life.
And by a spiritual sentence he will torment its spiritual nature; he will torment its spiritual nature.
And because the soul recognizes that the Lord alone is its judge, it naturally fears him.
And just as the remembrance of worldly judgment restrains from their offenses those who are alive in the body but dead in their souls,
so too the remembrance of God’s judgment restrains from evil the person whose soul is alive.
And whenever he remembers his judgment, he restrains himself from sins. For it is not the judgment close at hand that is pictured before the eyes of the discerning person,
but he contemplates that distant judgment, and trembles and is terrified by it. And because, just as visible things are plain to the bodily eye,
so hidden things are plain to the eye of faith, and just as a living body perceives all the bodily things of this world,
so too a living soul senses all the spiritual things of that world and gazes upon them spiritually.
The remembrance of God, then, is a light that reveals things to come. And where there are sins, the remembrance of his name brings terror.
For unless a person’s conscience troubles him over sins, fear of the coming judgment does not trouble him.
For the remembrance of God affects each person according to that person’s inward condition.
For if he stands among offenders, God appears to him as a judge.
But if he ascends to another degree, that of the repentant, God reveals himself before him as forgiving.
If, again, he stands in the rank of mercy, he contemplates the wealth of God’s mercy.
But if he is clothed in humility and gentleness, God’s kindness appears before him.
But if he possesses an understanding mind, he contemplates the incomprehensible wealth of God’s wisdom.
And if he is free from anger and liberated from resentment, and peace and harmony are always stirring within him, he is raised up to see God’s untroubled serenity.
And if the stirrings of faith remain continually awake within his soul, he always gazes upon the incomprehensibility of God’s works.
And he affirms that even those things thought to be easy to understand are beyond knowledge.
But if a person stands at the exalted level of spiritual love, God appears to him according to the level at which he stands.
For he is wholly and entirely love. And this is the wonder: although God is simple in his nature, and there are no limbs or parts in him,
he reveals himself to everyone in many forms. And to anyone who seeks him, he appears in whatever aspects that person desires.
And although in himself he is one, without forms, he appears to minds in forms corresponding to the feelings present in the soul.
For whoever wishes to see that God is good must himself become good, and behold, the Good One has appeared to him.
Do not presume to see God as good while you remain in the realm of evil deeds.
For this vision produces laxity in you, and you have seen God in a way in which he does not wish to appear to you.
That is to say, you have not actually seen him, because you wished to see him contrary to his will.
For to the extent that you become like him in each of the good things he commanded you to observe, he appears to you as he is.
And if you think you see him, you are seeing your own imagining, not the reality of the vision of him.
Therefore, anyone who remains in the realm of sins and is aware that evil passions are present within his soul,
and whose conscience rebukes him for his wrongdoing, must see God as a judge and must not dare to regard him otherwise,
so that fear may increase within him through this and restrain him from evil deeds.
But if you wish to see him as forgiving, abandon your evil deeds and turn to repentance.
Forgive also the wrongs that others have committed against you, and then you will lift up the eye of your mind and see him as forgiving.
For someone who continually sins and does wrong, while supposing that God is forgiving, heaps evil deeds upon evil deeds for himself.
“Do not rely on forgiveness,” it says, “lest you add sin to sin.” For, trusting in forgiveness, many continually sin without repentance.
Yet they have not experienced forgiveness; they have only heard the report of forgiveness. For it is the one who forgives others who can experience God’s forgiveness.
And the same is true of each of God's good qualities. Until we ourselves practice goodness, we do not perceive it,
which is in God. For everyone has learned by hearsay that God is good.
But only good people perceive his goodness through their own soul's knowledge. And from what is said about him, everyone acknowledges that he is merciful,
and patient, and kind, and wholly and entirely full of love. But through the perception of their souls,
those who have preserved these qualities in themselves taste them in God.
Therefore, as long as you stand in the realm of sins, you must remember God's judgment, so that by remembering his judgment you may restrain your evil deeds.
And do not presume to think of him in any other way as long as you stand in the realm of fear.
For there is a realm of fear and a realm of joy. The realm of fear belongs to those who repent,
and to those who are aware of their faults, and to people who have not yet been freed from the passions.
But the realm of joy is above love. After victory over desires, a person is deemed worthy to attain joy.
And when he has subdued all his passions under the power of his thoughts, then he enters to rejoice in the realm of joys, where there is no anxiety or fear.
For fear is the opposite of joy, and where there is fear, joy is not born.
And where there is joy, fear does not enter, because fear accompanies evil deeds, and joy accompanies good deeds.
And just as good deeds are opposed to evil deeds, so joy is the opposite of fear.
Someone who is engaged in evil deeds does not experience the joy of the spirit that is born of good deeds,
nor does someone who lives in joy experience the fear that accompanies evil deeds.
For someone who wishes to live in joy while still standing in the realm of fear is like someone who thinks he is good,
though he is evil and fully accomplished in every shameful deed, or like someone who thinks he is rich though he is poorer than everyone else.
Therefore, everyone who is aware of faults and transgressions within himself must always cultivate the fear of God within him.
When he comes in and goes out, he should reflect on it. When he sits down and rises, he should meditate on it, and in all his conduct,
his thoughts should be filled with the fear of God. He should not set aside a particular time for this fear,
but every moment should be for him a time of fearing God.
For whenever this fear is not awake within a person, contempt for God's commandments is found in him.
His thoughts are submerged in the sleep of forgetfulness, and like a senseless tool, he thinks evil thoughts and commits shameful deeds,
sinning without knowing that he is sinning. But if he does know, it is knowledge from hearsay, not true knowledge.
For a true knowledge of evil immediately produces fear in a person.
Just as light shines within the pupils when the eyes are opened, so, through the remembrance of God,
the fear of God immediately shines within the mind and raises a person up, startled, as though from deep sleep.
It is like someone roused from deep sleep: although he had been ready to rise early,
the light comes and finds him on his bed. When he opens his eyes and sees it, he is immediately startled and shaken,
and his sudden alarm quickly shakes off all the heaviness of the sleep in which he had been sunk.
So too, if someone becomes negligent, and the wakefulness of remembering God is taken from him, and he sinks into the sleep of contempt and the stupor of negligence,
if it happens, through some circumstance or by his own choice, that the light of remembering God shines within his soul,
he is immediately startled and casts off his former contempt. He is filled with fear, and trembling grows strong within him as he remembers the Judge’s justice.
When contempt departs, regret for it immediately enters in its place.
He is filled with alarm over the things he has done, or over the times he spent without remembering God.
For consider someone who lives continually in this remembrance: even if a mere impulse of desire should spring upon his soul,
he is immediately filled with fear. He is shaken and startled by the thought of desire that has come to him.
This evil thought immediately flees and vanishes before the soul’s fear,
like a bird that takes flight before someone who suddenly startles it out of its stillness.
For fear of other people and shame before them guard the body against lusts.
But the fear and shame that a person feels before God guard the very impulses of the soul against evil thoughts.
Because he sees that God sees him at every moment, he constantly watches himself so that he does not sin.
He guards his hidden self against hidden blemishes, which the hidden eye of God examines.
Surround yourself, then, discerning person, with the fence of the fear of God, and evil things will not dare to enter the city of your soul.
Feel shame before God in secret, and your soul will be preserved in its purity. Stir up fear of him within yourself at all times,
and you will be kept from sins of thought. Let constant remembrance of him dwell within you, and the remembrance of evil will not dwell alongside it.
For as long as you remember God, you cannot remember evil, because light and darkness do not dwell together within the eye.
Nor do the remembrance of God and the remembrance of evil remain together within the soul. For until you have forgotten God,
you do not remember evil; and until you have forgotten evil, the remembrance of God does not stir within you.
For forgetting one thing is remembering the other, and the entrance of one is the departure of the other.
For remembering evil things is error, while remembering God is true knowledge.
Error is darkness, but knowledge is light. And just as modesty is close to someone standing in the light,
so too the soul in which the remembrance of God shines is constantly ashamed at all times
of the nakedness of its evil deeds. And just as the sight of other people makes someone hurry to cover his nakedness,
so, when the remembrance of God looks into the soul, it startles and astonishes it into becoming modest,
and suddenly spreads a garment of modesty over it. If any limb of its thought is exposed, it covers it.
If it is holding anything unbecoming to it, it immediately takes fright and throws it away. If it is disordered, it becomes orderly.
If it is agitated, it becomes calm. If it is sinful, it becomes righteous. If it is stained, it is made white. If it is dirty, it is washed.
If it is unclean, it is made holy. If it is defiled, it is purified. If it is shameless, it becomes modest. If it is frivolous, it becomes restrained.
If it is foolish, it becomes wise. If it is scattered, it is gathered together. If it is distracted by things outside itself, it returns to itself. If it is poor, it becomes rich.
If it has lost its life, it runs and searches for it. If it is sick, it becomes well. If it is weak, it is strengthened.
If it is wasting away, it is healed. If it has fractures, it binds them up. If it is full of wounds, it bandages them.
And if it has grown old and worn out in sin, the remembrance of God, together with fear of him, immediately renews it.
The experience of the fear of God, then, belongs to the soul. Only the person himself can know whether he fears God or not.
For each of us must acquire this good thing for himself.
If you remembered God and were shaken, and called him to mind and were immediately filled with fear, and your thoughts trembled along with your limbs,
and your soul was shaken along with your body, and your understanding bowed its head, and your mind inwardly felt shame before God—
if these things happen to you, know that the fear of God is within you, and that the remembrance of the Lord is truly close to you.
For it is not the person who says, “I am afraid,” who fears God.
Rather, the person who senses in his own soul the experience of these things I have described is the one who truly fears God.
For good deeds that are outwardly visible do not show that the person doing them truly fears God,
because there are many motives that cause people to do good deeds.
There is also that other manner of observing the commandments. For the person who keeps God's commandments out of fear of him—
this is a true servant and a worker for God, who fears the lawgiver and fulfills his law.
For the divine law is not kept completely unless it is kept in both body and soul.
For there are many who openly bear the burden of hard labors.
Yet in secret they practice every kind of evil. Some have bound their limbs with the chains of hardship.
Yet they have let their thoughts run loose, wandering among shameful things. Some are clothed in chastity on the outside, but wrapped in depravity within.
Some fast outwardly, but inwardly they are dissolute and gluttonous.
Some appear righteous outwardly, but secretly practice every kind of evil.
Some fast and yet are gluttons. Some appear to have renounced possessions, yet love money.
Some display their patience openly, yet bear grudges. Their endurance is visible outwardly, but anger secretly dwells within them.
Some publicly refuse comforts, but secretly ask for them.
Some will not stoop to listen to an obscene word, but inwardly they are constantly putting it into practice.
Some pray openly, and some pray in secret. Some sing psalms with their tongues.
And some sing psalms in their thoughts. Some have crucified only their bodies, and some their souls as well as their bodies.
Some keep themselves from sins so that people will not reproach them, while others refrain from them out of love for righteousness.
Some shrink back before the face of God, while others feel shame before the faces of other people.
Some shun sinning because they know that sin is hateful to God, while others are careful not to do wrong.
Because they see that evil is disgraceful in people's eyes.
Some do not act wickedly out of fear of the judgment in the world beyond, while others do not transgress out of fear of judgment close at hand.
Some, by remembering the fire close at hand, cool the desire of their bodily members and quiet its stirrings.
And some, by remembering distant Gehenna, restrain their desire and banish it.
Visible labors alone, then, are not enough to show that a person fears God.
But you, discerning person, examine yourself. Let your testimony come from yourself and within yourself as to whether the fear of God is within your soul.
For righteousness that begins within is brought about by the fear of God.
But righteousness that begins outside, and whose course of action remains there on the outside—
It is being seen by other people that spurs it on. Its activity is outward, not inward.
It is visible only to human eyes, and is not practiced in secret before the gaze of God.
Outward afflictions are good, because they bring the bodily members into submission so that they obey the thoughts,
and subdue the tyranny of the body so that it submits to the soul’s will. But they do not cleanse the mind of sinful impulses,
nor do they make the soul fear God, unless the soul itself is inwardly taught to fear God.
For hidden spiritual work belongs to the soul, and outward toil belongs to the body. Bodily toil without the soul’s spiritual work is not justified.
The soul’s spiritual work, however, can be justified even without bodily labors,
provided that a person does not withdraw from those labors out of contempt and flee from afflictions as a lover of ease.
For being watched by other people does not keep a person from sin both outwardly and inwardly.
But keeping the fear of God in view restrains both body and soul from sins.
Just as someone standing before a judge to be questioned about his offenses has no opportunity to commit an offense in the judge’s presence,
but is even eager to conceal his previous offenses, so also a person who keeps God the Judge before his eyes,
and whose thoughts are continually chastened by fear of him, cannot sin. Instead, by day and by night,
he always clothes his inner self in humility and chastity, and every sinful impulse that arises within him
he drives away through the fear of God. For the fear of God makes the inner person beautiful.
Fear of other people, however, adorns the outward person with good deeds.
For the one who is the judge of your deeds should also be the examiner of your struggle.
Keep the fear of him continually before your eyes. For if the fear of masters is kept before the eyes of their servants,
and those subject and obedient to kings, judges, and military commanders are always clothed in fear of them,
and fear of scribes and teachers likewise continually upholds and preserves the innocence of childhood,
how much more is someone who has become God’s disciple, and is by nature a servant of that heavenly King,
a worker for the eternal King, and a subject of the true Judge of the law,
obliged to make the fear of him continually rule over all his conduct: over his thoughts in secret and over his bodily members in public.
For the fear of God is a bridle that turns back a person’s impetuous rush in pursuit of evil
and checks him, drawing him back from running after hateful desires—not merely his outward self,
but especially his inward self. And it is not merely as servants fear their masters,
or subjects fear kings and judges, that the spiritual worker should fear God.
For fear of those people takes on outward forms and is visible externally in the parts of the body.
Even when people secretly hate them and despise them in their thoughts, they outwardly show them an appearance of fear.
But your fear of God must not be like this. Rather, display your fear from the very place into which he looks.
Where he secretly sees the movements of your soul, there let the fear of him take hold of you.
Fear God fully, with your whole being, both in secret and in public—
him who is the judge of your secret and public deeds. Let your soul feel shame before him and not sin.
Let your mind feel shame and do no wrong. For if shame before other people restrains us from sins,
how much more will shame before God keep us from evil! Always remember that God is looking at you.
You too must look inwardly toward him who sees you in secret, and sin will not linger in your thoughts.
For just as darkness does not remain in a place on which the sun looks, so neither does there remain in a soul upon which God looks—and which itself is aware that he sees it—
the gloom of evil. “The eyes of the Lord are ten thousand times brighter than the sun,”
says Holy Scripture, “and he sees all the deeds of human beings.” And again, in another place, it says:
“All the deeds of human beings lie before him like the sun, and he examines and knows their ways.”
By his words, God's prophet also rebukes the wickedness of the man who, without fear of God, was acting shamefully on the covers of his bed.
Reproaching his foolish mind, which did not see that God saw him, he presented him with this demonstration: “The eyes of the Lord are brighter
than the sun by ten thousand times.” Through this he would teach everyone that God sees our hidden things,
and that everyone should guard with all diligence against sins committed in secret. For you must not sin in your thoughts,
nor must you stumble secretly inside your house, because it is especially in these hidden things that God sees you.
For as soon as people's gaze turns away from you, God's gaze meets you.
When your fellow human beings do not see you, the Lord of creation looks at you all the more.
For as long as people are looking at you, he knows that you are careful to avoid shameful deeds in their presence,
and that fear and shame before them restrain you from sinful actions.
But when you are alone, and the walls and roof of the house conceal you on every side,
then you need the armor of the fear of God, because sin is easily committed in darkness.
Then you must awaken your soul to remember God and strengthen the parts of your body so that they are not overcome by desire.
And stand like a warrior against the sin that fights against you to overcome you, and against the hidden enemy,
who, through the stirrings of your desire, fights against your life. The thoughts of the soul are also hidden within the members of the body.
Just as the body is hidden inside a house, so the thoughts of the soul are concealed beneath the covering of the body.
And because the inner person cannot easily be seen physically, he sins readily and does wrong whenever he wishes.
Sin in thought is easier and simpler than sin through the bodily members, because the members are restrained and hindered by many things.
But as soon as a thought desires sin, the sinful act is accomplished within it.
It needs no time, place, or material means for sin, because the ease with which it sins matches the speed of its movement.
To counter this swiftness of thought, constant remembrance of God is also needed,
and a constant fear of the Judge of hidden things must dwell within it. And, so to speak, even faster than the movement of thought,
the movement of the fear of God must be within it, so that when a sinful thought stirs, the remembrance of God may immediately strike it down.
For the soul in which this bridle has been placed is held silent, restrained from the stirrings of evil thoughts.
And if it happens to be suddenly carried away, this remembrance rebukes it and turns it back,
so that it examines itself. There is, then, not a single virtue that is preserved without the fear of God.
And if someone calls the fear of God the guardhouse of virtues, he is not mistaken. For faith is strengthened by it.
It safeguards fasting. Through remembrance of it, our prayers become constant. It urges us to give alms.
It stills the evil impulses in the soul. It quenches the desire that burns in the bodily members. It cleanses filthy thoughts.
It uproots reflection on evil things from the soul. It clears thoughts, anger, and hostility
from the mind. It restrains anyone from daring to covet what is not his. It is the guardian that keeps the laws from being trampled.
It counsels people not to transgress the divine commandments. For it is a boundary against every evil.
It stands like a barrier in the face of every wicked thing. For it stands against the left side,
and urges us toward good deeds on the right side. It puts an end to evil deeds and encourages the practice of good ones.
For the fear of God is a hindrance that prevents evil deeds from being done.
It keeps a person from the path of wrongdoing. For it is a good helper in both directions:
it keeps a person from the path of evil deeds and admonishes him to walk in the path of good deeds.
It urges him to gather good things, and then safeguards what has been gathered through it.
For if there were no fear, corruption would rule over everything. Fear accompanies judges,
and because of this their orders are carried out. It surrounds kings, and therefore their laws are not transgressed.
It accompanies military commanders, and therefore their authority is feared by those under their command.
It holds all people in faith in God.
For although fear is born of faith, it is also the guardian of faith.
For whoever fears God is careful not to cross the boundary of his faith in God.
And whoever believes in God draws near to the fear of God.
And whoever has the fear of God dwelling in his soul becomes a watchful keeper of all the commandments.
Adam believed in God but did not fear God. He believed that he existed and received from him the law that he entrusted to him.
And because he cast the fear of God out of his mind, he abandoned faith. [?] bound the commandment upon him:
“On the day you eat from the tree, you will surely die.” And because Adam cast that fear away from himself,
he believed the deceiver instead of God and trampled on the law laid down by the Judge.
And it was not only around Adam that God placed fear, to serve as a fence so that he would keep his commandments:
rather, in every generation he attached fear to all the commandments he laid down. But Cain, who did not fear God of his own free will,
was ruled by fear imposed by necessity, and he trembled and wandered on the earth.
For because he did not fear the one who deserved to be feared, he was filled with terror at everything he saw.
And because of the torment of that fear, he pleaded with God and begged him
that whoever found him would kill him, so that he might find relief from a life full of dread and fear.
For God also gave the Law through Moses, full of many different commandments.
And he attached fear to all the commandments, because without fear the commandments are not kept.
“You shall not murder,” he said, “and whoever murders shall be put to death.” For he applied the medicine of fear to the disease, so that it would not grow and gain strength through wrongdoing.
“You shall not commit adultery,” he said, “and whoever commits adultery shall be put to death.” Fear guarded the commandment so that it would not be treated with contempt.
For through fear he restrained them from doing evil to one another.
Because he saw that they loved evil deeds, he restrained them from doing them through fear of judgment.
For where there is no love, fear keeps the commandments. For there are three things through which all the commandments are kept.
Either out of fear, or for a reward, or out of love. The first of all these is fear.
The second is the assurance of promised rewards, and the third is true love. The first belongs to slaves.
The second belongs to hired workers, and the third belongs to spiritual people and friends.
For fear accompanies the beginning of the path of Christ’s way of life.
For everyone who begins this instruction has the mind of a child, and fear is appropriate to childhood.
It urges childhood to accept instruction, for childhood cannot taste the sweetness of knowledge.
For this reason, fear ought to accompany it. Once the knowledge of Christ has been tasted,
and a person has experienced the power of his commandments, the very pleasure of what he tastes leads him to keep the commandments.
For as long as a person has not reached this point, fear is needed to nurture him,
to instruct him and remind him of all the commandments. For just as children in the natural course of life receive instruction from teachers,
and a tutor takes charge of them from the teacher, to remind them at all times of what they have heard,
so a person receives instruction in the commandments from God, who is the true teacher and instructor.
But fear is needed immediately, so that, like a tutor, it may remind a person of what he has received.
If he forgets, it reminds him; if he is negligent, it urges him on; if he falls asleep, it wakes him; and if he loves play, it rebukes him.
If he wanders astray, it brings him back onto the path; if he shows contempt, it reminds him of authority; and if he is scornful, it reminds him of the one who disciplines.
For a life unaccompanied by fear wanders among all kinds of evil.
Everyone who needs to learn needs fear to remind him of his instruction. For without fear, instruction is not imparted.
Even if it is imparted, without fear it is not accepted; and even if it is accepted, without fear it is not kept.
For God’s prophet rebukes those who broke the yoke and cut the bonds of the fear of God.
Again, in another place, he rebukes Israel for pulling its shoulder out from under the yoke of the divine commandments:
“Like a cow that rebels against the yoke,” he says, “so the children of Israel rebelled—they, their kings, and their rulers.”
But rebellion arose because there was no fear.
They trampled the commandments because they did not remember the threat, and they despised the law because they did not recall the sentence of the one who established it.
For the lawgiver himself, in his wisdom, because he knew to whom he was giving the law, multiplied his threats alongside his commandments,
so that even if the will should despise the law, the fear accompanying it would urge it to keep the law.
And because the one who received the law was a rebellious slave, he made him serve as a slave through fear of suffering.
For all forms of torment were [?] before him, facing him, so that whenever he looked at them, he would heed the commandments and keep the law.
Let us therefore strive to fix the fear of God in our minds, and night and day
let us meditate on it. If the fire of desire takes hold of us, let us set the fire of hell against it.
And if gluttony seizes us, let us remember the worm that does not die.
And if beauty of face entices us, let us remember the outer darkness.
And if the love of money fights against us, let us bring to mind the loss of our own selves.
And if worldly gains entice us, let us fear that we may lose the eternal kingdom.
And if anger seizes us with its violence, let us consider God's threat against those who are prone to anger.
And if empty glory disturbs us, let us bring to mind the disgrace and humiliation before our Judge.
For let us put an end to fear through fear, and overcome death through death.
Along with these things, anyone who wishes to guard his life carefully against sins also needs constant remembrance of death.
For someone who constantly remembers the day of his departure and always reflects on the hour of his death does not readily turn to wrongdoing.
Nor does he dare approach a sinful deed. For the remembrance of death quenches all desires.
For contemplating the remembrance of death scatters the evils that gather against the soul and the desires that marshal themselves against the body.
For before the death of hell, let impending death be our teacher, and let us guard our lives carefully in every respect.
Let us remember our God, fear his judgment, and keep his commandments, so that, being clean of evil
and adorned with every good thing, we may be worthy to enjoy the heavenly blessings with all the saints.
And together with them, let us give thanks to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit forever. Amen.
Here ends the discourse on the fear of God.
Notes on the Syriac text:
Another discourse, the seventh, in which he explains that all the righteous people of old also fulfilled God's commandments through fear of God.
Through contemplation of the righteous people of old, the path of Christ's way of life is well trodden and easy for anyone who wishes to walk it uprightly.
And the sight of the footprints of those who walked along this path before us draws us too to travel it without difficulty.
For they are like landmarks and milestones placed beside the road of nature to keep travelers' journeys within their bounds,
Thus the examples and images of the ancients, together with the divine commandment and law, surround this road on which we travel,
and the course of our steps is bounded within them, so that no one may dare to turn aside from the road to the right or to the left.
For just as we must not turn aside to either side from the clear path of truth, lest we wander into error and stumble in our faith,
so we must not depart to either side from the lawful road of godly conduct handed down to us.
Rather, just as on that road of faith, we should also walk straight in this good conduct.
We should know the beginning, the end, and the middle, and consider the many steps arranged in order, one after another, on this ladder that leads up to heaven.
The one who dwells in heaven showed this beforehand, as a symbolic revelation, to blessed Jacob, the chosen one among the patriarchs.
And those who ascend and descend on it are angels.
For that ladder was not for heavenly angels alone.
Rather, the words of Scripture indicate this to us by saying that the angels of God were ascending and descending on it:
that every human being who approaches its foot and begins to climb it step by step serves in the ranks of the angels,
is numbered among the company of spiritual beings, and enrolls himself to become a heavenly servant.
And just as people who receive human ranks
and serve in one of the world's orders have their former designation as civilians changed,
and are called servicemen instead, so too a person who willingly enrolls himself in this way in Christ's company
and serves in this order of spiritual beings is called an angel rather than a human being by the words of Scripture.
And rightly so. For because he has begun to perform the service of angels, he must also receive their name.
He is called an angel instead of a human being because of his service and conduct, not because of his nature.
For this reason, blameless Jacob also saw angels descending and ascending on that ladder,
although the ascending belonged to human beings, since it belongs to human beings to ascend from earth to heaven.
Those who were descending, however, were angels, because heaven is their home.
They were descending from the height, their home, to the earth. Thus angels and human beings mingled together on that ladder,
so that Holy Scripture might teach us that good conduct is common to spiritual beings and bodily beings alike.
Both groups are obliged to keep the commandments. For human beings keep the commandments in this way:
when they are raised from the depths to the heights by the steps of the commandments. Angels, however, do so in this way:
They carry out the wishes of the Majesty when they are sent down from above for the sake of those who are to inherit life.
For those who are earthly and bodily by nature, the practice of the commandments makes heavenly and spiritual.
And as for those who are heavenly and spiritual by their creation,
the Creator's command urges them to descend to the realm of earthly beings and to occupy themselves with bodily beings,
so that from orders of beings that differ from one another, one church may be gathered in the harmony of love,
singing holy praises of God's purposes and moving together as a whole,
with one living, spiritual movement, like a natural body that moves in its entirety through the life of the soul.
Now, then, since the words of Scripture have shown us that this ladder leading up to heaven is made up of many steps, let us climb,
and ascend these steps in order, as those who ascended this ladder before us have handed down to us.
For we have shown that the first step is faith, and the second is simplicity, which is an untroubled movement of nature.
Although faith is born from it, it also guards faith in turn.
For just as craftiness destroys faith,
so simplicity and childlikeness sustain faith. From simplicity, too, the fear of God is born.
For fear naturally accompanies childlikeness. Children are afraid, but the cunning despise us.
The simple tremble at the news of punishment, but the crafty prepare a refuge for themselves.
For just as fear accompanies natural childhood, urges it toward every kind of learning, and encourages it to accept books and instruction,
so the fear of God also accompanies the soul's childlikeness and urges it to keep the commandments and fulfill the laws,
and not to despise or scorn the things handed down to it from the word of God.
For fear guides a person until discernment comes. And until the justice of the Judge is revealed within him
and teaches him that he is obliged to keep the commandments, terror and dread of the lawgiver hold the disciple fast,
so that he vigilantly keeps the laws given to him. For when the justice within him is revealed,
and this goodness naturally placed within his soul shines forth, it demands that he repay his debt like a debtor,
by keeping the commandments. For just as creditors in this world approach debtors
and pressure and compel them to pay what they owe, so also the justice within our soul
presses us to pay God the debt of his commandments. For it is to this point that the fear accompanying childlikeness brings us.
Through this fear, all those of old found favor. For whoever still stands in the position of a slave
is required to be afraid. For fear accompanies slavery in all its forms.
But there is also fear in love that is not perfect. For Holy Scripture
said that there is no fear in perfect love. Therefore, fear accompanies someone who is beginning to love but has not yet become perfect.
Some fear being beaten: this is the fear of slaves. Others fear losing their wages:
this is the fear of hired workers. Others fear causing distress: this is the fear of friends.
Others fear being disinherited: this is the fear of children. For although fear has a single name,
many distinctions are found within it. For there was fear of God
both among the holy prophets and among the Jewish people at various times. But their forms of fear were different.
The prophets feared as friends, lest they distress God, whom they loved.
The Jews, however, feared the rod of his discipline as slaves. And so that this fear would increase in them,
the rod of his discipline appeared immediately upon their transgression.
The one disciplining them allowed no interval after their wrongdoing, because their slavery did not deserve patience.
For the rod of justice hung constantly over their heads. The moment they did wrong, they were disciplined.
They were flogged as soon as they transgressed, and at the very outset of their sins they immediately received correction.
For patience teaches a foolish slave contempt. And so that those foolish people would not become contemptuous,
living as they did in God's house in the role of a disobedient slave, the one disciplining them removed patience from there.
This was especially so at the time when they came out of Egypt. Let us also understand in another way the purpose of that severe discipline,
and why there was no patient delay in disciplining them for their transgressions.
For God, the teacher, took the people like a child from Egypt, their nurse, to impart to them instruction in the knowledge of himself
and teach them the book of his wisdom. But in their childishness, whenever instruction was imparted to them, the people would forget it,
and they did not retain the study of God's commandments in their memory at all. He took pains with them through repeated punishments,
so that, even if only through fear of punishment, they would retain the memory of the instruction. For the man who gathered wood on the Sabbath day
was stoned by the whole congregation. And others who were summoned by Moses
but treated his summons with contempt and did not come—the earth opened and swallowed them. And others who despised his priesthood,
And they sought to seize honor for themselves; suddenly fire came out and scorched their bodies.
And others, who under the pretense of giving honor carried and brought unauthorized fire at the wrong time, were scorched and destroyed by a tongue of fire that came out from the tabernacle.
And others, because they wanted meat and rejected the bread of angels, were tormented by the indigestion that came upon them.
And others, who went astray through the calf, were struck down by the swords of the Levites.
And others, who caused turmoil, were singled out by the waters of testing to lose their lives.
And others, who grumbled against the Lord, were killed by deadly snakes.
And all of them together, because they stubbornly refused to enter the promised land, perished and were destroyed in the wilderness.
These punishments, then, followed these offenses.
And alongside each transgression, punishment immediately sprang up.
This was so that transgressions might be checked by punishments, and offenses by penalties.
And so that the people, like a child, might fear the teacher who instructed them, and, like an offending slave, tremble before the judge who flogged them.
For this reason Moses too, the people's guardian, commanded them everywhere to fear their God.
He said, “Do this and that. Keep the commandments. Fulfill the laws. Love your neighbor.
Care for the poor among your people. Do not treat your brother with violence. Do not covet anything your neighbor has.
Honor your father and your mother. Do not swear falsely in the Lord's name.
Do not encroach on your neighbor's land. Do not plunder or oppress. Do not treat anyone weaker than you with violence.”
And at the end of each commandment he reminded them, “Fear your God.”
For Moses, their teacher, urged them to have the fear of God within them.
For he knew that the commandments are kept through fear, and that the fear of God restrains a person from wrongdoing.
For loving their God was beyond them, and for this reason he urged them to fear their God. He said, “Love the Lord your God
with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind.” This was the commandment for the righteous among them.
But those who were like slaves, and who, like slaves, were constantly committing offenses, he commanded, “Fear your God.”
For fear restrains evil deeds, while love brings good deeds to completion.
Fear cuts short the course of wrongdoing, while love encourages progress in good deeds.
“Fear your God,” and “Love the Lord your God”: both are laid down in the law given to the people.
For whoever rises beyond the commandment of fear will find before him the commandment of love, which is more perfect than it.
For this reason Paul too, when showing the difference between us and them, said to those being taught by Christ:
“You did not receive a spirit of slavery leading back to fear.” That is, you were not called to be slaves, so that slavery should give rise to fear in you.
Instead, you were invited to adoption as children, which is brought to perfection in love through every good thing.
Fear, then, is a fitting companion to childhood, and it is rightly required at the beginning of instruction.
For as long as fear remains with the learner, it reminds him not to forget what he has been taught.
For just as Moses commanded those who had newly begun on the path of learning from God to have fear,
so here too, fear should accompany every disciple who begins on the path of righteousness.
For someone who fears does not act contemptuously, neglectfully, or dismissively. Fear prompts him to keep the commandments.
And if he happens to become contemptuous, the remembrance of fear suddenly startles him.
For the moment a person remembers God, if the remembrance of him takes definite shape within his soul, he becomes shaken and troubled.
He is filled with fear and dread, and alarm suddenly comes over him because of his earlier contempt.
As that holy prophet said, who knew how to fear God and understood what the fear of God does within the soul:
“I remembered God,” he said, “and was troubled.” But surely the remembrance of God is not itself a source of trouble, holy prophet!
Why were you troubled at the remembrance of him? Why did his beloved memory clothe you in dread?
“Because,” he says, “I had sinned against him. I remembered my offenses and called the Judge to mind, and I was filled with fear.
I looked at my sins and at his punishments, and the remembrance of him troubled me.” For it says, “His heart is prepared, trusting in God.
His heart is firm, and he does not fear.” For a heart established in good deeds finds joy in the remembrance of God.
And whoever possesses spiritual health in his hidden inner self is gladdened by the remembrance of God.
For where the conscience is troubled by sins, there the remembrance of the Judge brings fear. An offender is troubled when he remembers the Judge.
And a wrongdoer is filled with dread at the remembrance of punishment. This is why the prophet said, “I was troubled at the remembrance of God.”
“I reflected,” he says, “and my spirit grew faint. Anguish seized my eyes. I became speechless and did not speak.
I considered my days of old and remembered the years of long ago.
I reflected in the night, and I reflected in my heart. I searched my spirit and said, ‘Can it be? Has the Lord forgotten me forever,
and will he never again take pleasure in me?’” With these thoughts the prophet of God kept watch.
And he prayed on his bed as though he were in the assembly of the saints.
He remembered what he was obliged to repay to God, and considered the days and generations that had passed.
He considered each of the righteous: how he had pleased God in his own time, and by what means and manner of life he had distinguished himself before him.
The prophet recalled these things so that all who came after him might remember,
and to teach everyone to fear God by following this example, and to take account of himself,
and also to consider others who came before him, and how carefully they conducted their lives.
For this prophet also said that he practiced both things.
He said, “I considered my days of old, and remembered the years of ages past, in which those who came before us pleased God.
And through remembering both, I was filled with fear: how greatly the righteous pleased him, and how greatly I provoked him to anger.
For I brought my times into account and counted my hours. I reflected on the days that had passed and the years I had lived in the world.
I considered how I had provoked him to anger, what offenses I had committed, and what sins I had committed in my actions,
and what sins in my thoughts, what sins through hearing, and what sins with my tongue. And as I reflected on these things, I said,
‘Do not bring your servant into judgment, because no one living is innocent before you.’” The prophet’s words call us to follow this example.
He handed down this pattern of instruction to us: to take account of our hours and our times, of how we have provoked God to anger, and of the things we think about.
For if those who go out to conduct worldly business calculate each day’s income and expenses, and what they gain and lose,
how much more is the spiritual merchant, who goes out in search of heavenly wealth, obliged to do this.
For taking account of these things brings him two benefits. One is that he gathers his mind together in order to take account,
and the other is that he becomes diligent in gathering his wealth. It is therefore a fearful thing for a person to provoke God to anger,
especially when he considers that greatness, and God’s immeasurable love and mercy,
and the good things he has poured out upon our race. And what we were not worthy to receive on the basis of our deeds,
his grace gave us. And when a person considers himself—what he is—and how great the things bestowed upon him are,
and who the giver of these things is, he ought to remember God and tremble, as the prophet taught him.
For we ought to fear God for two reasons: either because we have sinned, or so that we may not sin.
For whoever remembers the offenses committed before now and considers his former sins
should fear being called to account for his transgressions. And whoever supposes that he is pure and has no past offenses,
that he should think about them and be troubled by their memory; let him fear lest he grieve God by those that are to come.
In this way the righteous, too, used to guard their lives against sins and heal the wounds that occurred.
And they guarded against those that had not occurred. For the first blow a person receives becomes his teacher,
so that he will not be struck again. The suffering caused by the first pain urges him to guard against another suffering.
For what person, with an alert mind, would contemplate God, gaze upon his greatness, and consider his hiddenness,
and see him with the eye of his mind—that pure and holy nature, the one who needs nothing,
whose dwelling is high and whose abode is exalted, in whom all riches, blessings, and treasures are gathered,
who is entirely and wholly light, life, and delight, who is forgiving,
merciful, and good, compassionate, gracious, and full of love, glorious, desirable, and beautiful,
who pleads, entreats, and urges everyone to live, who is deeply concerned for our lives and seeks our prosperity,
and takes more delight in our rest than we do ourselves, who constantly urges us to take from his riches and plunder his treasury,
and become rich from his treasures rather than remain poor, who does not rejoice in his own life as much as in ours,
who, because our poverty could not rise to his wealth, himself brought his wealth down to our poverty,
who, because he saw that we did not want to become rich, himself became poor to make us rich,
whose name is beloved, whose title is desirable, and whose remembrance is sweet, who gives the soul that perceives him a taste of spiritual sweetness,
who is exalted in the abundant riches of his being, whom no human being has seen,
or is even able to see, whose nature cannot be expressed and whose riches cannot be explained,
whose gifts themselves resemble him and, like him, are beyond the limits of knowledge,
who is as good as we are evil—and indeed, his grace abounds even beyond our wickedness,
whose own nature alone is the measure of his grace, and by whom alone his love is measured,
whose grace is far-reaching and whose justice is restrained, whose love is enduring and whose retribution is slight,
who is rich in forgiveness and slow to rebuke, whose chastisements are few and whose gifts are many,
who, even when he disciplines us, bears compassion for us, and because he wants us to gain, chastises us for that very reason,
who suffers no loss except our destruction, and whom no sorrow overtakes except on our account,
who clothed himself in our sufferings to strip us of our sufferings, and wrapped himself in our sickness to put an end to our diseases,
He who suffered distress to make us glad, and was grieved so that we might be filled with joy.
He who came to need everything so that we might not be in need of anything.
He who, although he knew that we would provoke him to anger, created our nature as beloved children whom he desired.
He who, although he knew that we would enroll ourselves as slaves of demons, enrolled us as heirs of both his worlds.
He who, although he foresaw our image with the image of Satan’s desires stamped upon it, marked and fashioned us in his own lovely image.
He who, although he knew that we would not preserve the first things, prepared beforehand other things for us, greater than those.
That rich giver, whose loss is our failure to receive from him. He who, when he gives to us, thanks us in return.
And when we take from his treasury, he regards it as though we were depositing something in his treasury. He who loves humanity,
and is always good and does good. That serene one who cannot be disturbed, who labors over us through his teaching to make us serene like himself.
That rich one who cannot become poor, who devises ways to persuade us to receive from his wealth and become rich.
He who, when he possesses something, acts as though he were poor; and when we possess something, acts as though he too had become rich through us.
He who does not wish to possess anything apart from us, and if he possesses something without us, seems to take no joy in it.
He whose joy is our joy, and who considers our distress his own.
And he counts all our losses as his own. He who gave us every good thing and was not satisfied,
and poured out every kind of wealth upon us, yet was not fulfilled until he himself, in his love, was given to us.
Before this one, then, who is rich and good, generous and giving, kind and gracious, our sustainer and provider,
compassionate and forgiving, merciful and full of love, rich and enriching, good and doing good, patient and making peace,
who loves our race and cherishes our nature, our healer and teacher, our Father in his grace and the one who nurtures us in his compassion—
who would not be afraid to grieve him? Who would not tremble to provoke him to anger? And what human being is there
who could look at all these good things given to us, and consider the greatness of their giver, without his mind being shaken whenever he remembers him?
And what soul has received all these gifts without feeling shame before their giver?
For it is a fearful thing that a human being should not fear this God, and that mortals should feel no shame before all this love,
and that those who receive all this wealth of good things should feel no remorse. For the prophet remembered these things and others like them,
and therefore he was shaken. And everyone who possesses the watchfulness of that holy soul is likewise shaken, as the prophet was,
at the remembrance of this God. In his coming in and his going out, and in all his conduct, he is moved by the remembrance of him.
For the person who is afraid does not sleep; in his dreams he sees the cause of his fear. He neither eats nor drinks.
And if the demands of nature compel him, fear is mixed into his food and drink.
For everything that comes upon a person who is filled with the fear of God stays outside him.
For the region of his mind and all the entrances and exits of the city of his soul—
fear holds them. For just like guards standing at the gates of a city,
so the fear of God holds the entrances and exits of the soul, and does not allow any deed or thought to enter or leave without examining it.
For it does not allow any thought whatsoever to go from inside to outside, nor any improper deed to enter from outside.
This same prophet also makes known in other places his fear of God.
He says, “My flesh shudders from fear of you, and I am afraid of your judgments.” And again he said:
“I have become like a wineskin in the frost, yet I have not forgotten your commandments.” And again he said, “Sorrow is in my heart every day.
How long will you turn your face away from me? How long will you forget me, Lord? Forever?
And how long will you place grief in my soul?” And again he said, “Heal me, Lord, for my bones tremble.
My soul is deeply shaken. I am weary with my groaning, and every night I soak my bed; with my tears I drench my couch.
My eye aches because of your anger.” It is clear that all these things are because of the fear of God. And again he said:
“I groaned because of the roaring of my heart.” And again he said, “In the fear of you, Lord, lead me, and in your righteousness.”
And again he said, “There is no peace for my flesh because of your wrath, and there is no peace for my bones because of my sins.
For my wrongdoings have risen above my head, and like a heavy load they weigh upon me.
My wounds stink and fester. Because of my wrongdoings I tremble greatly. All day long I walk about in mourning.
For my hips are filled with trembling. I tremble and suffer greatly.” And again he said, “My heart is in turmoil, and my strength has left me.
The light of my eyes is no longer with me.” And again he said, “I became silent and sorrowful, and I suffered for lack of good.
My pain was stirred up. My heart grew hot within me, and fire took hold of my body.” And again he said:
“I became silent and did not open my mouth, because you did it. I wasted away under the rebuke for my sins.”
And again, in another place, he pronounces a blessing on the man who fears God.
He makes known the good things that the fear of God does in the person who fears him. He says, “Blessed is the man who fears the Lord.”
Here the blessing was given to the person who fears God. And while our Lord assigned the blessings to other deeds, the prophet David—
He pronounces a blessing on the one who fears the Lord. He says, “Blessed is the man who has not walked in the way of the wicked.”
It is clear that because he fears God, he does not travel the way of the wicked.
Again he said, “Blessed is the person whom you discipline, Lord, and whom you teach from your law.”
It is evident that fear of God teaches the laws, and the person who fears him accepts his discipline.
Again he said, “Blessed are those who are blameless in their way and walk in the law of the Lord.”
Here too, fear of God guards against faults and urges a person to walk in the way of the law.
Again he said, “Blessed is the one whose wrongdoing has been forgiven and whose sins have been covered.”
It is clear that here too, fear of God leads to repentance, through which forgiveness of sins is given.
Through the sorrow and tears born of the fear of God, the image of a person's sins is hidden from his eyes.
Again he said, “Blessed is everyone who fears the Lord and walks in his paths.” Here too,
the prophet David showed that it is through fear of God that a person walks in the path of the commandments.
In another place, he said of the one who fears the Lord that he carefully observes the commandments given by the Lord.
Again, this prophet counsels everyone to approach God with fear, and urges all creation to fear the Lord who made it.
He says, “Let all the earth fear the Lord, and let all the inhabitants of the world tremble before him.”
For the prophetic word laid fear and trembling upon all the inhabitants of the world.
It taught all created beings to come to God by this way.
For whoever is aware of his servitude is bound to fear the authority to which he is subject.
Therefore it is right for everything that is created and possesses the discernment to be aware of its Maker,
to approach him with fear and trembling, because fearing God is fitting for our nature.
But that we should love him is given to us by his grace. For a human being is not worthy to love God.
Rather, God himself stoops down to be loved by a human being. For creation is bound by its nature to fear God.
But if it is raised to the rank of love, its own nature cannot raise it there.
Rather, grace descends to seek it, raises it, and sets it on the height of divine love, so that through grace it may love God,
whom it is rightly bound to fear. For look: even toward the kings and rulers of the world,
not everyone is permitted to show love or to reveal before them freely expressed and confident feelings of affection.
But all the ranks under their authority show fear and servitude before them, not the confidence of affection and love.
For according to the arrogant custom found among the rulers of the world, they consider the love of the poor an insult.
And so, like masters, they demand fear from everyone, not love, as fathers do.
For God, by graciously making himself our Father, has also given us permission to love him.
Yet we should not presumptuously raise ourselves to this by our own will, but should remain all our lives in submission to the fear of him.
And whenever he wishes, his grace will raise us to the level of love for him.
For loving God is not within the capacity of our mind, but fearing God is within the capacity of our created nature.
For this reason, everywhere the Holy Scriptures require fear from human beings more than love.
For vigilance accompanies fear, and confidence accompanies love. Moreover, love itself is a cause of fear.
For until a person works, toils, and sows in fear, he does not come to reap love.
For just as the harvests of this world's farmers lie in God's hands, while cultivation and sowing depend on their own will,
so too the toil and work of fear depend on our own will.
But reaching the full measure of love and gathering its harvest depend on God's will.
For until the revelation of Christ, who brought love into the world, fear was at work in the world among all human beings.
And until Christ is revealed to a person within the realm of his soul, his life should be devoted to the work of fear.
For although our Maker has graciously called us children in order to honor and exalt us, nevertheless, in humility,
we ought to remain in the fear of servants. For it was not through anything of our own that we were called children,
but through the grace of the one who called us. Nor is it our place to demand a reward impudently.
Rather, our part is to work in fear, while giving the reward of love is God's part.
And no one is mistaken if he calls love the reward of fear. For just as a person receives a reward after his toil,
so, after the work of fear, Jesus gives us a taste of the sweetness of his love. From this we receive joy, and we stand with the confidence of children.
Our hidden inner self finds boldness before God, and our mind continually produces joy of spirit.
Our understanding secretly soars in the vision of heavenly light, and contempt for everything visible is born within the soul.
It is as though our dwelling were already in the kingdom prepared for the saints.
For these things, and others like them, belong to the soul that has tasted divine love.
For a person who stands firm in perfect love is in God.
What delight compares with this, or what rest and pleasure equals it—that a person should be in God?
For standing firm in perfect love is purity from every evil,
and the fulfillment of every good thing. For Jesus does not consent to give this wealth of love
except to a person whom he knows to be worthy of it. For confidence is born of love, and carelessness follows confidence.
For there is not a single good thing without a breach nearby through which it can be snatched away. But in fear there is no carelessness,
only vigilance, caution, and constant watchfulness that guards good things from the plunderer.
For fear of God urges a person to gather virtues.
And once they have been gathered, fear grows and increases in the person who gathers them. For he in turn adds to his fear,
and guards his good things carefully so that they will not be snatched away. For he cries out because he is afraid, and he also watches over his possessions because he fears being robbed.
In every respect, fearing God is fitting and necessary for a person's life in this world.
For the realm of fear is the realm of mortal life,
while the realm of love is the other world, the world of life that does not die. Let us therefore consider our own realm and cultivate fear within ourselves.
Let us reflect on the dwelling in which we live, and increase within ourselves trembling before God and remembrance of what we have heard of him,
so that we may come to our senses as though emerging from the stupor of deep sleep, and wake fully to keep all his commandments.
For this is the nature of the fear of God: it does not urge us toward one thing
and not another, but awakens us to carry out all the commandments.
For this reason, the Spirit of God chose to teach us the fear of God through all the prophets.
For the prophet David himself also said, “Let all the ends of the earth fear the Lord,
and let all who go down to the dust kneel before him.” He also said, “Lead me, Lord, in the fear of you and in your righteousness.”
Because he knew the benefit of fearing God, he asked God for it as a gift.
For when the fear of God guides a soul, its whole way of life is grounded in righteousness.
And when he pleaded with God not to remember against him the sins of his youth,
it was his fear of God that moved him to make this petition. He also said, “The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord.”
For the goal of the path of good deeds is spiritual love, and from love itself divine wisdom is born,
Blessed David taught us well that the beginning of this path of wisdom is the fear of God.
For just as every undertaking in the world has a beginning and an end,
and the roads properly laid out for travelers to walk on also have a beginning and an end,
so the path of good deeds also has a beginning and an end. Its beginning is the fear of God.
Its end, however, is the wisdom born of love. And it is right for everyone who wishes to begin the Christian way of life
to begin with the fear of God, according to the teaching of blessed David. Another prophet also said,
“The fear of the Lord will open my ears.” And again it is written about Jonah that he feared the Lord and fled to Joppa.
For although his fear was born of simplicity, he nevertheless fled as a man who feared God,
so that he would not undertake a task that he thought was beyond his strength.
And again, when the sailors asked him where he was from and which God he served, he said, “I fear the Lord, the God of heaven.”
And those who were with him in the ship, when they saw the wonders that God performed in the sea—
how the sea rose up like a discerning being to demand the runaway servant from them, and once he was handed over to it,
it rested and its waves grew still—and through these events saw the power of God, it is written of them
that the men feared the Lord, offered sacrifices to the Lord, and made vows.
Again, through Jeremiah, God demanded that the Jews fear him, rebuking them through the testimony of the speechless elements of nature:
while those silent things tremble at his word, they themselves despise his commandments.
“Will you not fear me?” says the Lord. “Will you not tremble before me, who set the sand as a boundary for the sea, an everlasting decree that it does not cross?”
Here again, the Maker asks fear and trembling of the things he has made. And because they abandoned the fear of him,
they were rebuked through the speechless elements of nature, which fear and tremble before the greatness of the Maker, while human beings despise his commandments.
For this reason, God everywhere reveals the greatness of his nature through the prophet, to instill fear of it in those who hear.
For to those who would have despised his humility if it had been revealed to them, he revealed the greatness of his nature, so that they would tremble before him.
But to others, whose love increased when they heard of his condescension, he displayed his gentleness and humility.
For a fool habitually despises someone who humbles himself before him, but a wise person loves him all the more because of his humility.
For a fool has no eye that can see the love within humility. And for this reason,
greatness is revealed to him, anger is portrayed for him, and severity and fearsomeness are depicted before him.
so that through these things we may revere and fear the one who is revealed in them.
As this testimony has revealed God's intention, it shows why he uses such words when addressing human beings.
“The sea obeys me,” he says, “and confines its terrifying waves within the lowly boundary of sand.
Its waves rise up, but they do not cross the humble barrier that surrounds them.
Yet you willingly despise this fearsome God.” And again, in another place, he makes known
that he used every means of helping them and brought before them every reason for fear and love.
But they neither feared him nor loved him. “If I am a master,” he says, “where is your fear of me?
And if I am a father, why do you not honor me?” So either fear him as a master or honor him as a father.
For this reason God also recounts before the people, in one place, the kindnesses he showed them: the awe-inspiring departure from Egypt,
the abundant gifts in the wilderness, the entry into the promised land, the subjugation of foreign nations,
and the kindnesses poured out upon their lives every day, so that by reminding them of these things he might awaken them to love the giver.
In another place, however, he recounts the great things he has done and the works he established by a gesture of his will,
all the creatures that depend on the power of his word, and the natural orders that keep within their boundaries,
and creation, which is yoked beneath the governance of his will; how the mountains are weighed by him on a balance and the hills on scales;
how he measured the heavens with his span and measured out the dust of the earth in his hand; and how the nations and peoples of the world are counted as nothing before him.
He spoke these things through the prophet, making his greatness known through them, so that hearing of his greatness might produce fear in his hearers.
For whenever God speaks to those who stand in the rank of servants, he recounts before them the great and fearsome things of his nature.
But when he imparts teaching to those who have been found worthy of the rank of love, he lowers himself to speak of condescension, affection, and humility,
and tells them these things because they do not despise him in his lowliness, but through this very thing revere and love him all the more.
For where God does not trust human beings because of their narrow understanding and childish knowledge, there he speaks dreadful and terrifying things.
He does not give them the freedom to draw near with confidence in his love, lest, when they become aware of him and his compassion
and realize that love and goodness are found in him above all else, they should for this reason despise his kindness
and throw themselves contemptuously into the practice of every kind of evil. For this is revealed only to people who have inherited the name of children,
not only through grace but also through the work of their own labors. For the more they taste love,
the more they love; and the more they perceive the goodness of God's nature, the better they become.
And the more his condescension and kindness are revealed to them, the more they too strive to resemble their Father.
In things like these. For this reason, all God's earlier revelations inspired fear.
But this last revelation is one of intimacy and love. For in the first he revealed himself to teach us
that he is our God. But in this last revelation he appeared and showed us that he is our Father.
For at that time he brought human beings near as servants, but today he has called them to the inheritance of children.
And when he revealed himself to gather servants for himself, he carried whips and chains, blows and chastisements,
torments and punishments, fear and terror, anger and severity, penalties for minor offenses,
a rod continually raised over the heads of offenders, an open court, and a judge ready to act.
Over there a stake is set up for a blasphemer to be crucified on it. Over there stones are gathered for stoning. Over there a fire is kindled for burning.
Over there whips are ready for offenses. Over there instruments are prepared to exact a tooth for a tooth.
Over there eyes are gouged out. Over there branding irons are ready to repay wounds. Over there jaws are struck.
Over there sentences are written down for transgressions: these lashes for these servants.
This is so that the offending servant will not raise his head and exalt himself above the lawgiver.
He breaks his legs so that he will not kick. He cuts off his hands so that he will not strike. He pulls out his teeth so that he will not bite.
He blinds his eyes so that he will not see and covet what is not his. He imposes losses on him so that he will not cause losses to others.
Through fear of torments he restrained the wickedness of that people, because they would not agree, out of fear of him,
to refrain from their vile deeds. For where there is fear of God,
a person has no need to fear these things or others like them, because fear of the unseen Judge
is enough to restrain him from all his wicked deeds. So hold this fear within your soul, disciple,
and fear nothing else. For fear of God does not fear the world,
and fear of the world does not fear God. Let us always be afraid of this:
that we might anger God. For this is why the capacity for fear has been placed within you: so that through it you may fear God.
For there is nothing in the world that is frightening to the soul that has experienced the fear of God.
Nor does the terror of afflictions count for anything to a person who has within him the trembling fear of God's justice.
Our Lord abolished one fear and established another. He removed from us the fear of temporal death.
And he placed upon us the fear of eternal death. “Do not fear death,” he says, “but fear death.”
Do not let those who kill the body frighten you. Rather, tremble before the one who destroys both soul and body.
Those who kill are not to be feared, since another raises the dead. Rather, the one to be feared is he who puts to death and no one raises the dead,
and who kills and no one restores to life. For whatever passes away, the fear of it also passes away with it.
But to the one who neither passes away nor changes belongs a fear that never ends. “He looks at the earth,” it says, “and it trembles.”
“He rebukes the mountains, and they smoke.” And again he said, “At your rebuke they flee, and at the sound of your thunder they are terrified.”
See, even upon silent created things, according to the prophet’s words, the fear of the Maker rests.
For everything is bound by its nature to fear him. And if things without speech fear him, how can rational beings not fear him?
For temporal fire is terrifying to human beings as long as the thought of eternal fire remains far from their minds.
Even the sight of visible tortures shakes and astonishes us as long as the torments to come remain far from the soul’s sight.
Even death here is full of terror as long as the image of eternal death is not set before our eyes.
For the moment the remembrance of these written things enters, the memory of the things here disappears from the heart.
And as long as our mind is not stirred by the constant fear of God, every fearful thing we encounter frightens us.
For as long as the king is far away, the judge is feared. When the king appears in his authority, fear of the judges disappears.
And not only that, but the judge himself, together with all the ranks beneath him, submits to the fear of royal authority.
And those who were feared become fearful themselves. For all fears are gathered together
and swallowed up in one fear. And all the leaders and officials from whom fear used to flow
upon the ranks beneath them obey and submit to one fear, the mistress of all fears,
so that only one may be feared, and through fear of him the authority of everything feared may be dissolved,
and the terror arising from all authorities may cease, and every leader may bow his head before the one head of the kingdom who reigns over them all.
So, in the same way, when the fear of God is far from the soul, it fears everything:
authorities, judges, rulers, ranks of officials, military commanders,
the rich, officials, lowly and ordinary people, the insignificant and the despised.
And along with these, it also fears afflictions and losses, injuries and torments, illnesses and pains, deprivation and poverty,
separation from relatives, distance from family, being deprived of friends, and expulsion from one’s homeland.
All these things, then, and others like them are a source of fear to the person who does not fear God.
For if the fear of God enters and settles within the soul’s dwelling, and takes possession of every part of its thoughts,
the soul has no room from then on to receive another fear.
Instead, every fear that enters to settle in it, when it sees that the fear of God dwells there in the soul,
leaves and goes away, because its house has no room to receive another inhabitant.
For just as a vessel filled with something cannot receive anything else put into it unless it is emptied of the first thing that filled it,
so too a soul filled with the fear of God cannot receive fear of the world,
or of anything in the world, because it is wholly gathered around that one true fear of God.
Let us all, then, strive to acquire this fear, and disregard everything else.
Let us be free from every concern, so that we may devote ourselves to the one task alone of fearing God.
And by remembering his awesome and hidden name, let us guard our lives with all vigilance.
And let us offer him glory at all times—to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, forever. Amen.
Here ends the seventh discourse, on the fear of God among the righteous people of old.
Notes on the Syriac text:
Next, the eighth discourse, in which he teaches that no one can become a perfect disciple of Christ unless he first strips himself
of all human possessions and openly leaves the world, both inwardly and outwardly.
Anyone who wishes to walk the clear path of perfection must, in a proper order befitting the path,
begin his journey. He must not begin this discipleship according to whatever rule seems good to him,
but according to the prescribed rule that was handed down to his disciples through the word of Christ our God.
For he himself also walked this path of perfection and became a rule for us in his own person,
and gave us a fine example, so that we might follow in his footsteps.
