For Jesus became our teacher not through words alone, but also through the deeds of perfection that he himself accomplished.
And therefore he is truly the good teacher, who taught and acted: his teaching is action, and his action is instruction.
For our Lord himself also illustrated and showed us this through his own ministry:
after he had fulfilled all the righteousness of justice and observed the law of the commandments that are fulfilled in the world, he then left the world and went out.
Outside it, to teach perfection. For I am not saying that even those who are in the world cannot be justified.
Rather, I am saying that they cannot attain perfection, because the world is opposed to perfection.
That is, it is opposed even to the righteousness and justice practiced within it.
A person cannot undertake two kinds of labor and become perfect in both kinds of goodness while living in the world.
For this reason, commandments were defined and set apart for those who live in the world, so that through them they might gain their lives.
And another path was opened up, the path of perfection, which is above the world. For this is the will of Christ, the lawgiver:
He wanted all human beings to walk in the way of the angels, and no one to fall short of the goal he set before everyone.
But because not everyone is capable of this, while he desires everyone to live,
he gives different commandments to each person, so that each may live by them, and he established measures and degrees in his teaching.
This is not because these distinctions exist in him, but because of those who receive his teaching,
and because of those who were in need and could not live without them.
For just conduct accompanies the worldly path, while perfection accompanies the path outside the world.
And the culmination of the path of righteousness and justice is complete renunciation of possessions.
For as long as a person possesses earthly wealth, whether little or much, he cannot walk the path of perfection.
For all wealth, in proportion to its amount, is a bond upon the mind and a fetter upon the understanding’s swift wings,
preventing them from flying along the path of heaven. For anyone who has wealth must give thought to it.
And whoever gives thought to wealth does not give thought to God. Even if remembrance of God does arise within him, it is not at all times.
For it is impossible to remember God at the very time one is thinking about possessions. Even if he seems to remember him, this remembrance is borrowed, not genuine.
For these two kinds of remembrance cannot dwell together within the soul.
And if they do dwell in it, then necessarily one of them is borrowed and the other genuine.
And even if someone sincerely believes that he is thinking about God while concern for wealth remains within his mind,
he is not doing so with the whole strength of his soul, which we ought to give entirely to God.
For we are not obliged to serve God with one part of ourselves,
and the world with another part, thinking about him at one time and about wealth at another.
Rather, we ought to devote all our strength to carrying out his commandments, and every moment should help us to remember him.
so that we may be temples for him alone, free from every thought and concern about anything apart from him.
And that a person cannot serve God as he should while living in the world, owning possessions and holding wealth,
our Savior’s own words testify: “You cannot serve God and mammon.”
Perhaps the listener thinks that here the door of righteousness has been shut before all people,
because they cannot free themselves completely from concern about wealth.
And according to the judgment expressed in Christ’s words, whoever concerns himself with it does not concern himself with God.
We must understand the saying as it was spoken. For at the level of the perfect, a person who concerns himself with wealth cannot concern himself with God.
For at that other level of righteousness practiced in the world, a person can be righteous
while possessing wealth, provided that he is not a slave serving his wealth, but is himself the master of his possessions.
For there are people who are slaves to their possessions, and there are others who are masters of their wealth.
There is a person whose possessions serve him, and there is another who serves his possessions.
Our Lord’s saying, then, was spoken about someone who is a slave to his possessions: he cannot be a slave to God.
“You cannot,” he says, “serve two masters.” You see that he pointed to two masters in his saying.
And in explaining who they are, he said, “You cannot serve God and mammon.”
So then, whoever has made mammon his master cannot serve God. Instead, he serves the master he has freely chosen for himself,
deeply cherishing his service to it and loving its mastery over him, because he has willingly enslaved himself to it.
For people are accustomed to love what they freely choose
much more than what rules over them by compulsion and by nature. For if there are a few who have pleased God or who please him,
it is because they were masters of their wealth and sent it out like a slave and a servant to perform every task:
sometimes to feed the hungry, sometimes to clothe the naked, sometimes to ransom captives,
sometimes for vows and offerings to God, sometimes to free those enslaved by debts.
And wherever the will of the one who ruled over it wished, there he sent it like a slave.
This was also the case with Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Job, Joseph, David, and Hezekiah.
For among these, too, some were wealthy and some were rulers,
and some were kings. Taken together, they were all owners of wealth and abundant possessions.
Rather, they were masters of their wealth, and their wealth was not their master.
It served them in all the good things they wanted, rather than their serving it in all the evil things that Mammon demands.
There are, then, distinctions among the commandments, and it is clear to whom each of them was addressed.
For this commandment, “You cannot serve two masters, God and Mammon,”
as the meaning of the passage indicates, was spoken to those who want to be righteous while remaining in the world.
He counsels and admonishes them that, just because they have fallen short of the path of perfection,
they should not become slaves to Mammon altogether and abandon God's lordship, which by nature is established over their lives.
“Do not,” he says, “store up treasures for yourselves on earth, where moth and rust destroy, and where thieves break in and steal.
Instead, store up treasures for yourselves in heaven, where neither moth nor rust destroys,
and where thieves do not break in or steal.” It is clear that this commandment does not apply to solitaries and the perfect.
For how could “Do not store up treasure for yourself on earth” be said to someone who has been commanded, “Do not worry about tomorrow”?
And how does the saying, “Store up treasures for yourselves in heaven through your charitable gifts,” apply
to someone who has been told, “Do not acquire two tunics, or a purse, or a traveling bag, or even copper coins in a purse”?
And what would there be for a thief to take or a moth to destroy belonging to someone commanded to have nothing apart from his own person?
Therefore, the saying, “You cannot serve God and Mammon,” is a commandment addressed to those who own possessions.
Because the Teacher saw that they were not rising to the level of perfection,
he lowered himself to their level in his speech and laid down for them a law suited to the position in which they stood, saying:
“Since you cannot now be without possessions, do not become a slave to your wealth and serve it as one enslaved.
Instead, be its master by using it in the service of every good deed. For when it is your master, it sends you wherever it wants:
sometimes to fraud, sometimes to theft, sometimes to false testimony, sometimes to oppress and plunder, sometimes to swear false oaths,
and sometimes even to murder. There are also occasions when it sends you into fellowship with demons.
It leaves out no evil deed that it does not command you to do,
as long as it is your master and you are its slave. And just as, if you are its master, you send it to do every kind of good,
so, if it is your master, it sends you to do every kind of evil. For this is the rule for a master: to give orders,
and for a slave: to receive orders. As long as someone is a master, he gives orders, and as long as he is a slave, he receives orders.”
And wherever there are people who give orders and people who receive them, actions are carried out according to the wishes of those who give the orders.
For Jesus the Teacher did not lay a burdensome command on those with possessions when he commanded them to be masters of their wealth.
Rather, through this arrangement he taught them how to acquire the very thing they desired but did not know how to acquire.
For it is like someone who wants to be wise but does not know how to gather knowledge, and someone else is found who becomes his teacher,
teaching him how to gather and acquire it; or like another person who loves wealth but does not understand how it is accumulated;
or like someone who loves ornate buildings but does not know how they are built and decorated.
In the same way, people desire to be masters of wealth, but through lack of knowledge their wealth turns out to be their master.
And the Teacher, having compassion on those with possessions, taught them: “Be masters of your wealth, as you desire.”
Along with this, he also showed them how to become its masters. For loving things is one thing,
and knowing them is another. Someone may love something yet not know how to obtain what he loves.
And someone else may know how to obtain and acquire it, yet not love it. But as for those who wanted to be masters of wealth,
yet found that once they acquired it, it became their master instead, Jesus taught them the knowledge of what they desired.
Jesus therefore commanded these people to be masters of wealth and not its slaves.
But those who are perfect he commands not even to be its masters.
And he counsels them not to lower themselves to lordship over mute things. For those with possessions,
he freed from slavery to lifeless things, so that by serving them they would not become worshipers of idols,
those of which it is written: “There is no breath in their mouths.”
And although they have eyes, ears, and hands, they do not see, hear, or act.
For this reason Paul called the love of money idolatry. For just as pagans worship lifeless things,
which have neither life nor sensation, so lovers of wealth serve silent gold
and mute silver, along with all the rest of their possessions, which have neither life nor knowledge.
Thus Jesus commands one person, “Do not be a slave to wealth,” and lays down a law for another:
“Do not even be a master of wealth.” To one he says, “It is an insult to your freedom to be enslaved to gold,” and to another he says,
“It demeans your lordship, which rules over created things, to lower yourself to possessions, which are the husks of created things.”
For to the man who abandoned lordship over everything and became caught up in the love of a small possession, he said:
that he possesses—provided that you are the owner of your possessions, and your possessions are not your owner.
But the other man, whom he saw had risen above being a slave to wealth, he raises to a still higher level and says:
“Do not even be its master.” For just as it is a disgrace for someone who wishes to be the master of his possessions to become their slave,
so too it is a disgrace for someone who has been freed from slavery to wealth to be found even exercising mastery over wealth.
For the poor man possesses the things of poverty, and the rich man possesses the great and celebrated things of wealth.
Therefore, because those who own possessions are poor, they possess poverty: wealth and temporal possessions.
But those who strip themselves of possessions are rich. It is a disgrace to that noble name to own the things of poverty: gold, silver, and clothing,
and to exchange eternal wealth for temporal poverty, and heavenly possessions for human wealth.
He said to the lover of wealth, “Do not serve wealth. Instead, be its master, and let it be your slave and servant.”
It is clear, then, that Jesus gave this commandment to the rich of this world.
But to the others, who wish to walk on the higher path of perfection, he said:
“Do not acquire gold or silver, or copper in their purses, or two tunics, or sandals, or a staff.
For the worker deserves his food.” That is, this freedom is fitting for this work.
He therefore stripped them of the whole world, and then led them out of the world.
“Go out,” he says, “and leave everything in its place within the world. Do not take dead things with you into the land of life.
You are called to wear purple robes. First take off the world's filthy rags, and then you will put on the purple robes of the kingdom.
Whoever wishes to put on everlasting glory must first take off clothes that wear out, and then put on that glory which never wears out.
Anyone who seeks to be registered in the Jerusalem above must have no dwelling on earth, and he will become an inhabitant of that city.
Whoever wishes not to be received there as a favor should be received here as a favor by everyone.
Whoever wishes to dwell in the bridal chamber must not own a purse or a traveling bag here.
Whoever seeks to possess God must not possess copper in his purse. For it is an immeasurable disgrace to possess copper along with God.
For someone who possesses temporal things along with eternal things does not recognize the greatness of his possession, and therefore runs to acquire poverty along with wealth.
For these two treasures cannot even be contained in a single vessel.
For no one ever puts thistles together with gold in one vessel, or places straw and wood together with precious stones.”
This commandment, then, was given by the Teacher to the disciples when he sent them to become fishers of people for life.
For he first cut all the world's fetters away from them and released them from all human bonds,
and then sent them to free others. For someone who is himself fettered could not free another who is bound.
For possessing worldly things binds all the limbs and fetters all the senses.
The whole person, in both his hidden and his outward life, is fettered and bound by it.
Our Lord therefore rightly released his disciples from the world's bonds first, and then sent them to free others who were bound,
so that those being freed might see that those who loosened their bonds
bore the sign of freedom and the emblem of the kingdom, so that they might have confidence in their release,
especially when they saw that those cutting away the world's bonds from them were themselves free people.
Our Lord therefore established this pattern here in these commandments that he entrusted to the apostles, when he commanded them, “Acquire nothing.”
He therefore stripped them of everything, and then sent them to serve his will by teaching others.
From this, everyone who wishes to become a servant of God should learn to renounce all his worldly possessions
and strip himself of everything, following the apostles' example. Then he should go out and become a servant of God's perfect will.
For as long as the apostles were with Jesus and traveled with him from place to place,
they had not attained the state of perfection. For this reason our Lord also refrained from giving them these commandments
as long as the apostles were with him, and allowed them to do other things,
things that went along with their constant attendance on him and were also useful to those who approached him:
whether serving the crowds reclining at meals in the wilderness, or being sent by him on errands needed for outward daily life.
For example, he sent Simon to the sea to catch a fish and pay the poll tax; and they were also invited, together with him in person, to banquets.
They went about and traveled with him from town to town, showing him outward honor
before the crowds, keeping the throng of people from pressing upon him and preventing just anyone from approaching him freely.
For example, it is written that some people wanted to bring children to him for him to bless them, and the disciples stopped them.
Everywhere they offered him honor of this kind, according to the measure of their understanding at that time.
But he accommodated himself to them and accepted these very things from them from time to time, because he knew
that they were capable of only this much: offering him outward service.
And because, even though their service was deficient, it was nevertheless in keeping with the measure of their understanding.
He looked at a person’s willingness and accepted his service accordingly. For this is Jesus’ custom.
Both at that time and today, he asks for service in proportion to the strength of a person’s willingness. He does not want the deed to exceed the willingness of the one doing it.
For if a deed appears to exceed deliberate choice, then either law, habit, or preoccupation brings it about.
Jesus does not want such things: to receive service from a rational human being as though from a mindless instrument.
For when he stoops to accept the choices made at every level and the services offered to him,
he nurtures them through his teaching so that they may rise to the service of the perfect,
from that initial service, so that the first form of service may become a path to the one that follows it,
and the first good deed may become training and preparation for another good deed more perfect than itself.
Alongside the deed, the teacher provides instruction, not only through the deed itself but also through his word,
as he did with Mary and Martha. While both of them were offering him service,
Mary’s service was more perfect than Martha’s. Both of them were serving him,
one bodily and the other spiritually. Our Lord accepted both forms of service,
and pronounced a blessing on the service that surpassed the other: “Mary has chosen the good portion for herself, which will not be taken away from her.”
It is as though someone were saying, “You too, Martha, leave behind what is lesser, and rise in your service to a higher rank.”
For Jesus did not reject even Martha’s service, because the measure of her knowledge and love
was also the measure of her service. For he wanted her to advance,
from lesser things to greater things, and from bodily service to spiritual service.
The service of Mary and Martha resembles, as a pattern, the service of the holy apostles, both earlier and later.
For in various places they too offered bodily service corresponding to Martha’s.
But that other service which he taught them to offer him,
through the command, “Do not acquire anything,” resembled the service of blessed Mary.
For there are many who are justified like Martha and like Zacchaeus,
and like those women who followed him and served him from their possessions.
And there are others whose service, like that of Mary and the apostles, is entirely spiritual.
Jesus desires and longs for this service, so that all human beings may attain perfection.
And this was also why he came into the world: to hand on this way of life of spiritual beings to human beings.
As the holy apostle also taught, the person who belongs to God ought to possess complete perfection.
“So that,” he says, “the person who belongs to God may be perfect, equipped for every good work.”
Jesus therefore handed on this perfection to his disciples through the commandments he gave them about renouncing possessions.
In doing so, he set them apart from the whole world and everything in it.
And not them alone, but through them and with them, everyone who pursues perfection.
For when he laid down a law addressed to the apostles, he was handing on instruction for everyone.
And he was urging the whole human race toward this good thing—everyone who was willing to obey him.
Moreover, at the very beginning of their selection, when he called them to follow him, this is what is written about them:
As soon as he called them, they left everything and followed him. “They were casting nets into the sea,” it says.
And he saw them and called them, and, it says, they left their nets and their boat and followed him.
He also saw James and John in the boat with their father Zebedee, and he called them too.
Immediately they left the fishing net along with their father Zebedee and followed him.
Here is the law for setting out after God. Here is the sound rule recorded for us in the holy Scriptures.
From now on, everyone who wishes to set out after God ought to emulate this departure of the apostles.
He must despise and reject everything visible and renounce the whole world. But Christ said
that anyone who wishes to be his perfect disciple must renounce even himself.
And if a person renounces his own life, according to the saying of our Savior, and only then becomes a disciple,
and if there is no way to attain perfection without this, how can someone who does not renounce worldly possessions
and despise all visible wealth and bodily comforts attain the perfection
that Jesus handed on? I am not saying these things on my own authority; rather, I am following the intent of the Scriptures.
And I stand by the law laid down by the King. For the apostles are the beginning of Christian discipleship.
And this is how their calling took place, as it is written about them: as soon as they were called, they left everything and followed him.
Anyone who longs to become a disciple should consider this example and keep this goal in view in all his thoughts:
to empty himself of everything, both inwardly and outwardly, and then begin to walk [?] along this heavenly path.
For he is not filled unless he has first been emptied, nor does he lay his hand on heavenly wealth unless he lets go of the poverty he holds.
For it is impossible to hold on to one unless he lets go of the other, especially since they are opposed to each other.
And each one, when it draws near, does away with the other.
And if, when we have emptied ourselves of everything and devoted ourselves solely to keeping his commandments,
our service is still not worthy of God, how, when the strength of our soul is divided and plundered,
and taken from it through love of worldly things, can it offer to God
the service of love? For this commandment is burdensome to anyone bound by the love of wealth.
And although it is indeed freedom from the world, it is difficult and hard for those who cling to enslavement to the world.
These are people who are bound and find it pleasant, who are shackled and enjoy their shackles.
These are people who have willingly placed the bonds of anxiety on all their limbs,
and have agreed to be enslaved to the world rather than be servants of Christ. For Jesus calls you to freedom,
but the world prepares slavery for you. And if slavery to the world is pleasant to you, it is not because its nature is like that,
but because your own desire has become corrupted and desires wrongly. Whenever a person desires anything from the world, his desire is not healthy.
Rather, like a sick person, he desires something that does him no good—a desire that is entirely harmful.
For this is generally the rule with sick people: they desire what harms them
rather than what benefits them, and what opposes their health rather than what heals their ailments.
For because the health within them turns into sickness, the power of natural desire within them also
departs from its natural order. For the health of desire is preserved through a balanced constitution and a healthy body.
And when the body's constitution is disturbed, the bodily desires are disturbed along with it.
Someone burning with fever craves cold drinks.
Although they are harmful to him, he asks to drink them and becomes angry with those who do not give them to him. But a wise physician does not comply with him,
because he knows that the blind desire within him is asking for something opposed to his health.
In the same way, the world's wealth is pleasant, and possessing it desirable, to those whose souls are sick
and who lack the health that comes from divine knowledge. They ask for everything that harms them.
But our heavenly physician, through his beneficial provisions, keeps us from harmful things and commands us to do.
Not what is pleasant to us and gives us comfort, but what helps us, even when we find no comfort in doing it.
For a wise physician does not follow the wishes of the sick,
nor does he give in to their desires, which are harmful to their health.
Instead, he leads them according to the beneficial rule of medicine and teaches them to struggle against their desires
for the sake of their health. Let us therefore accept the yoke of renunciation, as our Savior commands us, even if it is burdensome to us.
Yet it is not burdensome to a will that submits to Christ’s commandments. For there is no one who does not desire to be free
and to be freed from the yoke of slavery. Moreover, everyone cherishes the name of a free person more than that of a slave.
And by commanding us to detach ourselves from the world, our Lord gave us true freedom,
the freedom by which he himself lived while he was in the world. For although he is free by nature, since he is God,
he also lived in freedom when he took on the form of a slave, and he was above all the cares of the world.
For it is written that Jesus took on the form of a slave and became like human beings, and in appearance he was found to be a human being.
He truly became what we are. But he did not share in what is external to us,
that is, acquiring wealth, property, money, possessions, and buildings on earth,
or fields and vineyards. For Jesus did not acquire these things, so that he might teach his own followers not to acquire them.
And he, the free one, did not concern himself with them, so that he might free us too from concern about them.
He did not submit to the yoke of slavery to the world, so that he might remove from us too the heavy yoke of slavery to the world.
He was not bound by human affairs, so that he might loosen their bonds from us too. Destructive anxiety did not imprison him,
so that he might lift his disciples too above anxiety and distress over all visible things.
For as a free person he lived freely in creation, so that he might teach us too, by his actions, to live freely in it.
Therefore, whoever wishes to become a disciple of that Master should look at his Master’s way of life in the world
and live like him in creation. The Lord of the world was a stranger and a foreigner in the world.
His servants too ought to be like their Master. And see how stripped of human affairs he was,
he in whom all fullness was gathered: he did not even have a nest or a burrow in creation, such as birds and animals have.
“Foxes,” he says, “have burrows, and the birds of the sky have shelter,
but the Son of Man has nowhere to rest his head.” Here is your way of life, O disciple.
Be marked by your Master's word. What he did not have, you must not have; and what he did not possess,
you must not possess either. For disciples are not recognized by their outward appearance,
but by the likeness and agreement of their deeds, by following in their Master's footsteps, and by walking along the path he has opened for them.
For if the road had not been opened and our God's footsteps were not visible on it,
there might perhaps have been an excuse for the lazy, who love the world's bonds.
But look: the path is clear and the road is known, and the tracks along it are visible to everyone in the light of truth.
But if someone does not see them and place his own footsteps upon them, it is clear that this is because he lacks the illuminating light of faith.
And although he thinks he is traveling along the road, his journey is outside it, in error.
For Jesus told you that he had nowhere to lay his head in order to teach you that you too should have nowhere.
For he said, “Foxes have holes, and the birds of heaven have shelters.” Therefore, if you possess a house, you are making yourself like these.
And if you have a dwelling in the world, you are on a level with the animals and birds, because this is what that saying plainly taught.
But if you are emptied of everything in the world and have nowhere on earth to lay your head, you are making yourself like God.
For whatever the Master wanted his disciples to become, he himself portrayed and showed them in his own person.
And he confirmed his teaching for us through his deeds, as it is written about him:
that he began, from John's baptism, to do and to teach, until the day on which he was taken up.
For these were the good deeds: the virtuous ways of life that he displayed in his own person.
And although raising the dead, cleansing lepers, opening the eyes of the blind, making the lame run,
restoring those with withered limbs, straightening those who were bent over, driving out demons, walking on the waves,
and stilling the winds are indeed deeds, since they are signs and wonders, nevertheless the writer
calls the spiritual way of life that was visible in Christ's own person the deed that accompanied his teaching.
For if his coming was for good deeds alone, and not for the performance of signs, his teaching too concerned the spiritual way of life.
And he also accompanied this teaching with action, to show us in himself an example of complete perfection.
For immediately after John's baptism, he left the world and all human society and went out into the wilderness.
For until his baptism he had been fulfilling a different way of life and observing all the requirements of the former law,
to repay the debt on account of which our entire race had been subjected to slavery to sin, the law, and death.
And everything that those who live righteously in the world ought to do, Jesus himself observed in his own person.
For it is written about him that he used to go up to the temple and present offerings,
and submit to the priests, and fulfill everything written in the law. He did these things for two reasons.
One was to pay the debt, and the other was to teach everyone who is in the world to concern himself with this righteousness of the law,
and to serve God as a servant by keeping the observances of the law. He did not neglect even one of the law’s smallest requirements, but observed them all,
to teach the person who is still in the world to observe everything commanded him, as one under authority.
For everyone who is still bound up in the way of life of this world and in the dealings of human affairs is under the law.
But whoever empties himself and leaves the world comes to be above the world, and necessarily above the law as well.
For the law has no authority to subject those who are above the world.
For someone who occupies the position of a slave is governed by the compulsion of the law.
But someone who occupies the position of freedom conducts himself in every respect as a free person.
He does good willingly, as a free person with authority over himself, and not as someone bound under the yoke of the law.
In short, wherever evil deeds are committed, there the law also has authority to rebuke and restrain them,
as Paul the teacher testifies when he says that the law is not laid down for the righteous, but for the wicked and rebellious,
for the impure, for those who strike their fathers, for murderers, adulterers, and the sexually immoral, and the rest.
The law, then, has authority over these people. And now, while our discussion intended to show that the perfect, who are guided by the Spirit,
alone are above the law, Paul has been found teaching that even the righteous, who are below the perfect,
are freed from the law. For they too do good not out of fear of the law, but in agreement with the law.

For someone who refrains from killing so that he will not be put to death, while being ready in his mind to kill, is a murderer. And someone who refrains from adultery, though he desires to commit it,
out of fear that he might be condemned by the judge and handed over to the law, is an adulterer. And everyone who plans to cause harm,
but is restrained and does no harm because he fears the penalties prescribed by the laws, is, as far as his own will is concerned, a doer of every evil.
The righteous, however, refrain from doing evil, not because they are afraid that evils might befall them,
but so that they will not anger God by an action that displeases him. Thus, some refrain from evil because they fear evil consequences,
while others refrain from it so that they may do good. For unless a person puts an end to evil deeds, he cannot do good deeds.
Until baptism, then, our Lord handed on to humanity a righteous way of life: to do the good things written in the law.
And let them offer offerings to God from their possessions, and make vows and fulfill them.
And let them attend God's temple regularly and receive blessings from the priests in faith.
And let children submit to their fathers and serve them, and also seek the word of life.
And let them ask and learn from teachers everything they need for instruction in good things. And let them obey and submit to the prophets.
These things, then, and others like them, and all the righteousness that is fitting for believers who own possessions,
which they are to gather from their possessions while living in the world, our Lord fulfilled through the way of life shown in his gospel, from the beginning up to his baptism.
And everything he did was to teach us to act as he did. For he underwent purification according to the commandment of the Law,
to teach believers to purify themselves from wrongdoing. He was circumcised so that they too might circumcise themselves,
and cast away the uncircumcision of the heart, and cut off from themselves the service of all desires.
He went up to the temple carrying offerings, to lay out for them a path by which they might run to God's house, carrying their vowed gifts and offerings.
He approached the priest so that he might bless him and pray over him, even though that priest, through the Spirit, spoke other great things to him,
to show believers also that they should ask for the prayers of priests and bow their heads and those of their children to receive their blessing.
He used to go up to the temple every year, as it is written about him, to teach believers to run to God's temple at every opportunity.
He used to celebrate the festivals with their proper observances, to encourage you to celebrate the Church's festivals with discernment,
and to fulfill all their proper observances during those festivals. He used to sit among the teachers, listening to them, asking them questions, inclining his ear, and receiving instruction,
so that you too might listen and ask questions, and continually incline your ear to hear the divine commandments,
and ask about and learn the things that help your life, even from those who have less knowledge than you,
just as our Lord himself used to question those who had less knowledge than he did,
and receive instruction from those who had gathered their learning from the Law that he himself had given.
And again, at the end, when he saw all the sinners running to the baptism of John, God's prophet, he too went with them,
and bowed his head before the hand of the herald, and agreed to be baptized by him as one in need—by the very man who needed him.
And he left the places where people lived and ran with all the crowds into the wilderness to John.
And why did he do these things, except to teach property owners and those who live in the world
to go to the holy ones, to run to the solitaries, and to honor the prophets and the righteous,
and to obey the admonition of their words with the discernment of their faith? This, then, is the righteousness that our Savior fulfilled.
He showed believers this way of life during the time leading up to baptism, and he urged those who owned possessions to acquire these virtues.
For he did not give this way of life to solitaries, nor did he hand it down to the perfect.
For what temple does the spiritual person need to go to, when he himself is God's temple?
And from what dwelling does he need to hurry to God's house, when he does not even have a shelter in the world to live in?
And from what resources can he present offerings and fulfill vows, when he owns nothing in all creation?
And where can he find the means to clothe the naked and welcome strangers, when he himself is a stranger and naked?
And what evils is he to cut off and cast away from himself, when he is perfect and complete in every virtue?
And whom is he to ask, and from whom is he to learn, when he has no dealings whatsoever with other people?
And if he needs to learn, God's Spirit teaches him instead of a human being. Therefore this teaching,
which applies to the time leading up to baptism, was handed down to upright believers and given to righteous people who owned possessions,
and to those who had not left the world entirely, so that they would not be deprived of the virtues appropriate to the place in which they were.
And because Christ is everything—he in whom everything exists, through whom everything exists, and for whom everything exists—this way of life too,
Christ himself demonstrated in person. And although it is less than the way of perfection, he nevertheless fulfilled it too,
so that he might give everyone teaching according to their capacity, and lead them toward a good way of life according to their rank and order.
For there is no way for anyone to live without virtues. The virtues themselves differ from one another.
And the commandments given concerning them also differ from one another, just as the virtues do.
For it is written that before his baptism he was subject to his parents.
“He returned with them to Nazareth and was subject to them.” But notice that after baptism,
when he was handing down to people a way of life more perfect than this, he would not even agree to acknowledge earthly parents.
“Who is my mother, and who are my brothers?” he said to the person who called him.
And although before baptism he obeyed his parents and was subject to them, afterward, when he was handing down a way of life for spiritual people, he said
that he did not know them. They called him to come out to them, but he would not agree. His mother spoke to him, but he did not listen to her.
For now he was carrying out the will of the Father who sent him, and was not fulfilling the lesser commandments.
If our Lord had done this before baptism, while he was observing the law—if his mother had called him and he had not obeyed—he would have been breaking the law.
But now this was not so. Rather, it was to show that he obeyed his Father by nature more than his parents by grace.
And he would teach even the perfect to obey their father by grace more than their natural fathers.
“I do not seek my own will,” he says, “but the will of the one who sent me. And I came down from heaven not to do my own will,
but the will of the one who sent me.” These things were spoken at the time when he was bringing perfection to fulfillment,
so that spiritual people, those who are outside the world, might understand from this
that they should not obey and submit to their natural fathers, nor even to their own will.
Nor should they yield in anything to their own needs and comforts, but they should deny themselves.
As the Savior himself said, “Whoever does not deny himself cannot be my disciple.”
Now, three days after our Lord returned from the wilderness, it is written that Jesus was invited to a wedding feast,
he and his mother and his brothers and his disciples. And when the hosts ran out of wine, his mother said to Jesus,
“They have no wine.” Here too she began to speak to him with authority, as a mother, following her former custom.
But Jesus, regarding all this boldness, [?] while teaching that he had paid her the debt of honor owed to parents,
and was no longer subject to them as before. And see with what a rebuke he takes that former authority away from her.
“What have I to do with you, woman?” These words are full of rebuke and entirely stern.
And rightly so, because through these words he was giving the perfect an example, so that they would not be governed by the law of natural parents
once they had come to be outside the world in which their parents live.
For Mary followed one way of life, while Jesus followed another.
That is, hers was a life under the law, and his was a spiritual life. And it was not right for someone to be commanded,
when he follows the way of life of the Spirit, by someone who still lives according to the law.
For Mary gave an order as someone in authority, and Jesus answered her as a free man. “They have no wine,” she said.
These are words of authority, and she speaks as a mother giving an order. “What have I to do with you, woman?”
He gave his answer as someone who was not subject to her. He spoke as though to a stranger who was not his mother.
For he did not say, “What have I to do with you, my mother?” but, “What have I to do with you, woman?” You became my mother by grace.
And for the sake of the divine plan I was born from you, subjected myself to you, and obeyed you—not because I owe you a debt by nature.
My origin is not from you, so that I should thank you for having come into existence through you.
You did not conceive me in pain, nor did you give birth to me with labor pains.
You did not raise me as someone in need, so that I should pay you for meeting my needs. Everything you gave me, I myself gave you.
And if you carried me, conceived me, gave birth to me, took me up, and raised me, these things happened through the power that came from me to you.
And I obeyed you and submitted to you, not to repay you a debt on my own behalf—a debt I do not owe you—
but to repay the debt on behalf of all the children who disobeyed their parents, and to fulfill the Law.
But now that the debt has been repaid and I have completed the order prescribed by the Law, what have I to do with you, woman?
For this saying resembles the saying, “Who is my mother?” and what he said to John: “Here is your mother,”
and to Mary: “Here is your son.” It also resembles that other occasion when they wanted to take him
with them to the festival as they were going up to Jerusalem, according to the former custom before his baptism.
When Jesus broke with them in that custom, he said to them, “You go up to the festival, but I am not going up to the festival.”
After he had sent them off and had not gone up with them, he then went up himself in the middle of the festival.
His going up does not contradict his saying, “I am not going up.” For he said, “I am not going up
as someone under obligation.” For they were going up as people subject to the Law, to carry out the observances of the Law.
Jesus, however, was going up as one with authority, to gather guests for himself for the new festival.
For by saying, “I am not going up,” he showed two things: that he was subject neither to his parents nor to the Law.
For someone subject to his parents does what they command him. And someone who is under the Law
and keeps its observances along with all its commandments is obliged to go up at the beginning of the festival.
For at this festival they used to go up to the temple, as did all the Jews.
They would also arrive a few days early, in order to purify themselves
and reach the first day of the festival in a state of purity. Jesus, however, did none of these things.
He did not go up with them, to show that he was not subject to them; nor did he go up at the beginning of the festival, to teach that he had not gone up to observe the festival.
Instead, he went up in the middle of the festival, going up of his own will. And he went up after telling his parents, “I am not going up.”
This was like what he did at the wedding feast in Cana, when, after saying to Mary, “What have I to do with you, woman?”—
words indicating that he would not obey her in what she had said—
he then did what she had said, not because she had commanded it, but because of his own authority,
and because it was now time for him to begin performing signs, so that through them it would be seen who he was, and so that he might make his glory known and gather disciples for himself.
And again, to show that from then on he does everything freely and with authority, and not according to the weakness of human nature,
nor in submission to parents, nor according to the commandment of the Law. And these things that we have said,
we have demonstrated their force from Holy Scripture itself. The reader, too, ought, while reading our account,
to examine Holy Scripture and see that these words are understood in this way in their respective places.
And so that this meaning may be impressed upon us, the sayings are distinguished from one another,
and one way of life differs from another. Jesus, then, handed down this mystery to us through his way of life:
that which lasted until baptism, and that which lasted from baptism to the cross. For all righteousness is contained within these two orders:
either a person works with his own self, or he works with his possessions. Work with his possessions is righteousness external to him,
while work with his own self is the perfection of his person. For the righteousness of the Law is one thing, and that which Christ gave is another.
The righteousness of the Law extends until baptism, while his own extends from baptism to the cross.
And from there onward there are delights and life above the world.
Jesus, then, reached the full measure of the righteousness of the Law by the time of his baptism.
And from there until the cross, he stood at the full measure of spiritual perfection, in the goodness that brings perfection,
which he himself brought to creation. From this we ought to understand that all people who, while they are in the world,
do good deeds are like the righteous people of old. That is,
like Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, together with all the other righteous people and prophets of old.
And this is called the righteousness of the Law, which a person practices while living in the world:
whether he clothes the naked, gives relief to the distressed, or welcomes strangers into his dwelling;
whether he visits the sick or hastens to the holy people, solitaries, and monks;
whether he sets aside times for prayer or regularly attends the temple of God;
whether he refrains from lending at interest and usury, refrains from coveting anything belonging to his neighbor, or submits to his parents;
whether he obeys and honors priests and teachers, or does good to everyone.
That is, he should treat other people as he wants them to treat him.
This is the righteousness that the former Law taught, and our Lord fulfilled it up to his baptism.
And all believers who have not yet divested themselves of their possessions are obliged to practice it.
But Jesus handed down to us the spiritual way of life and perfection, from baptism to the cross.
May we all be found worthy of it through his grace. To him be glory forever. Amen.
Here ends the eighth discourse, on renunciation, composed by the blessed Mar Philoxenus, bishop of Mabbug.
Notes on the Syriac text:
The ninth discourse. On the same first theme, renunciation, drawing on the testimonies of the Holy Scriptures
and on the example of the first disciples. In it he teaches that unless a person strips off the world completely,
he cannot become a perfect disciple of Christ or share in the mystery of divine knowledge.
Let the departure of Christ our Lord into the wilderness be an excellent model for us in learning renunciation.
And following the pattern by which he moved from living among human beings to combat with the opposing power,
let us too go out from the world into battle against Satan.
Let us take nothing from the world out with us except our spiritual armor alone, which is not of the world.
Jesus, then, went out immediately after baptism and left the world and everything in it, and the dwelling place of humanity
and everything within it. He went out alone, in the strength of his own soul, to wage war against the devil.
It is written, however, that the Holy Spirit was also in him, and that it was the Spirit who led him out into the wilderness.
This was not because he needed the Spirit's power, since he is the Spirit's equal and himself gives the Spirit to others
so that they may conquer through the Spirit. Rather, it was to encourage those who leave the world in pursuit of perfection, so that they might learn beforehand
that the strengthening power of the Spirit accompanies their departure, helps them in their struggle, and crowns the combat in which they are engaged.
For those disciples who abandon the companionship of the world are immediately accompanied by the support of the Spirit.
When they disdain human assistance, they find heavenly assistance; and as soon as they reject bodily strength, spiritual strength immediately accompanies them.
Here, then, at baptism, our Lord completed the path of righteousness under the Law, and from the Jordan itself
he began the path of his own way of life. For until the Jordan there was servitude.
That is, he was subject to the Law like a servant. But from that point onward,
his way of life was the freedom found in his own teaching, and not in the commandments of the Law.
For Jesus was born anew through baptism, and from the womb of the Law the spiritual realm received him.
As he himself also said, unless a person is born anew, he cannot see the kingdom of God.
And for this reason, after his baptism, he began to proclaim the kingdom of heaven.
Again, in this same order, everyone who wishes to become a perfect disciple of Christ is born anew when he leaves the world and goes outside it.
From the world of the body to the world of the spirit, from wealth to poverty, and from comforts to afflictions.
And from family to separation from kin, from many attachments to solitude, and from pleasures to hardships.
From a bodily way of life to a spiritual way of life, from fellowship with people to fellowship with God.
From one kind of knowledge to another, from one course to another. In short, a person is born from one condition into another,
when he passes from the world's way of life to discipleship to Christ, and from owning possessions to the renunciation that God commands.
And just as, while a person is in the world, the world requires him to do everything belonging to the way of life in which he stands,
so, when a person leaves the world and goes out after Jesus, he is required to do everything belonging to the spiritual way of life, according to the order of the place to which he has come.
For it is one thing for a person to put off the world, and another to put off the old self;
and it is another thing to put off merely natural thoughts, another to put off error, and another to put off ignorance.
For a person is said to put off the world when he withdraws from everything in it and distributes his wealth and possessions
entirely to those in need, leaves the world, and goes out naked and alone, just as he came out of the womb.
For life in the world is to a person what the natural womb is to the child conceived within it.
And just as the child is in darkness inside the womb, in a dim and moist place, perceiving none of the things of this world,
and the things that exist in creation and in the realm of the world outside the womb do not enter its mind,
so too a person confined within the bodily way of life of the world, as though in a womb, whose discernment is also covered by the darkness of its concerns,
and whose mind is veiled by the gloom of human anxiety, cannot perceive the blessings and riches that exist in Christ's way of life.
Nor are spiritual things visible to him as long as his discernment is covered by the darkness of bodily things.
And just as a child in the natural order does not enter the created world unless it is born from the womb,
so it is here as well: unless a person leaves the world completely, he does not come to the spiritual way of life.
And just as there the child leaves the womb and comes outside it, so here too a person must leave the world and go outside it.
For the world is like a womb. And just as a child puts off the womb, a person puts off the world.
And just as a child, when it is born, is complete and fully formed in its natural constitution, with all its senses and limbs,
yet does not use them for their natural functions, because they have not yet grown and become strong,
But when he is born into the world, his body grows in the world, together with all its senses and members.
And as he grows and advances, he receives sensations through his members and senses, and gains experience of everything in the world.
All his senses function soundly in their natural roles: the eye in seeing;
the ear in hearing; the palate in tasting; the nostrils in smelling; the tongue in speaking; the hands in working;
the feet in walking; the whole body in touching; the heart in discernment; the liver in anger;
the gallbladder in clarity; the kidneys in understanding; the spleen in fear; and the brain in thought and comprehension.
Together with all the other members in him, they gradually grow in the world until they reach the measure of full stature.
They attain their full capacity to function in everything, and the human being becomes physically mature in the world,
into which he is born from the womb, and he acquires and attains the fullness of his knowledge.
In this same way, then, it also happens with the spiritual human being, who begins in the form of infancy,
and little by little becomes complete and grows into a mature man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ,
as it is written. At first, however, his beginning takes place in conception, like a natural infant.
For just as the natural infant is formed from seed and blood within the womb, so this one too is formed from fire and from the Spirit through baptism.
And just as the natural infant is born, passing from not existing into existence,
so this spiritual infant too is born, passing from not being a son to being a son of God and spiritual.
And just as, in the former case, once he has taken shape out of nonexistence and has gradually been formed, all his members grow,
according to the measure appointed for their growth within the womb, so also this human being who is born through baptism,
a son of God, after having been a slave and fleshly, begins to grow little by little within the world as though within a womb,
in all those good deeds that believers living in the world ought to do.
And when he has grown and developed fully according to the measure of his infancy within the world, as though within a womb,
he undergoes another birth, from the world to outside the world, in the same way that an infant is born from the womb into the world.
And when he has been born and stands in the realm of Christ's way of life, as though in another world, from there he begins to undergo another growth and become complete.
This is not in the body of righteousness, which underwent its growth within the world, but in the spiritual being, in which he reaches the perfection
of the fullness of Christ. Picture baptism, then, as a womb,
and the one who through it becomes a son of God, after not having been a son, as a natural infant.
that he is created out of nonexistence to exist. And as for baptism giving birth to an infant of the Spirit,
so that from being bodily he becomes spiritual: just as an infant takes bodily form from seed and blood
and receives the formation of all its limbs, in this same way there is born here
this infant too, from baptism, with all the spiritual limbs and senses created and formed within him.
And just as there, after being created and taking shape, he grows little by little in all his limbs and senses,
until he completes the measure of his infancy appointed for him while he is inside the womb,
and then comes to birth from the womb, so here too the infant of the Spirit grows within the world,
after being born from baptism, until he reaches the measure appointed for these spiritual infants.
And just as an infant cannot receive inside the womb the growth that takes place outside the womb, and become a fully grown man inside the womb—
for this is granted to him in the world after he is born—so a person cannot be brought to spiritual perfection
and attain the stature of a fully grown man while he still lives in the world as though in a womb.
Instead, he must first be born and cast off the whole world as an infant casts off the womb,
and then begin to receive another kind of growth, which leads to spirituality and perfection.
Therefore, all a person's righteousness, which he practices within the world,
and all the limbs of good deeds that develop in him, are like the infancy of an infant inside the womb.
And however much he grows and becomes strong in this righteousness while he is within the world, he still remains at the stage of infancy,
because he is confined within the world like an infant in the womb. And just as an infant cannot become a man inside the womb,
so a person cannot become perfect within the world.
And just as, however much an infant grows inside the womb, the measure of his growth there is limited
by the space in the womb, so within the womb of our nature, however righteous a person becomes within the world,
the measure of his righteousness is limited by the womb of the world in which he lives.
And just as one conceived inside the natural womb is called an infant and a fetus as long as he is inside it, but once he is born from the womb,
he begins to receive other names: newborn, child, boy, young man, and fully grown man.
So, in this same way, this infant of the Spirit too, as long as he is within the world and all the limbs of righteousness are growing in him,
however strong he becomes, however firmly knit together, established, and grown, is called by these names: righteous and upright.
And merciful, and generous, along with the other names appropriate to good conduct in the world.
But when he has been born out of the world, after his features have been fully formed through those initial members that we have listed,
and has come out into another realm, that of the way of life of Christ, like an infant born from the womb,
these titles are bestowed on him, and he is called by these other names,
which are appropriate to the realm into which he has come. He is named as follows: one stripped of possessions, a free person,
an ascetic, a toiler, a bearer of burdens, one crucified to the world, one who endures, one who is patient, a spiritual person,
one in the likeness of Christ, a mature man, a man of God, a beloved son, an heir to his Father's possessions,
a companion of Jesus, one carrying a cross on his shoulder, one dead to the world, one alive to God, one clothed in Christ,
a person of the Spirit, an angel in flesh, one who knows the mysteries of Christ, one wise in divine things.
These names and others like them are appropriate for a person who is born out of the world to be called by, so that he may grow up in the realm of the knowledge of Christ.
Just as a natural infant, when it is born from the womb, leaves the womb behind, yet the birth membrane in which it was clothed inside the womb accompanies it and comes out with it,
but once it has been born, the membrane is cut away and cast off from it, along with the other superfluous things attached to it,
and the human being himself is seen on his own, freed from everything that is not part of him,
and he exists in and for himself, so too, when a person comes out of the world, although he leaves the world behind as though it were a womb,
he is still clothed in the passions of his own self and the desires of his body, and he comes out like an infant clothed in its birth membrane.
For just as the birth membrane is not removed from an infant while it is inside the womb,
so a person cannot strip off the old passions in which he is clothed as though in a birth membrane,
while he is inside the womb of the world. And just as, in that case, it is only after the infant is born that they strip its birth membrane from it,
so here too, it is only after a person is born out of the bodily way of life of the world and comes to be in another, spiritual world, outside the world,
that he can strip off and cast away from himself the ugly passions of the old person, as though they were a birth membrane.
For just as an infant cannot grow to adulthood as long as it is wrapped in its birth membrane,
but when the membrane has been peeled away from it and it appears freely as its own individual self, it then begins to grow toward its natural stature,
in the same way, a person who is still clothed in ugly passions cannot grow in spiritual stature.
But when he has stripped them off and cast them away from himself, and has cut off all the members of the body of sin, which are the ugly passions,
then his stature begins to grow, and other, new members sprout for him,
of the new spiritual person, in place of the old members that were cut off from him.
For in place of these former members that are cut off, other, new and spiritual ones grow.
And as the old person comes to an end and disappears, so the new person is found and brought to light.
For although in baptism we took off the old person,
according to Paul's teaching, and put on the new one in his place, we were not aware of it,
either when we took off the old or when we put on the new. For grace accomplished both: it stripped us of the old person and clothed us with the new.
At that time we received the working of the mystery only in the name of faith. But when we willingly, through our own toil and effort,
take off the old person, then we take him off with awareness—not merely through hearing in faith,
but also through the experience of deeds, and through sufferings and tears, love of God, pure prayers,
unceasing petitions, wonder at the greatness of God's glory, constant amazement at him,
and the continual running of the hidden person toward the Lord. By diligently practicing these things and others like them, we put on the new person,
not through what the ear hears, but through our soul's awareness and the genuine experience of spiritual knowledge.
And from then on, at this very stage, a person begins to grow in the knowledge that is above the world,
where there is room for his stature to grow and for him to stretch it toward the appointed height of greatness.
For as long as ugly passions wrap around a person like a membrane and bind the members of his new person within them, growth is hindered.
And a person cannot reach that measure of stature given by Christ, of which Paul spoke:
that we should all grow and become one in the knowledge of the Son of God, and one mature man, in the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ.
But a person cannot reach this measure unless he leaves the world.
And unless he first takes off the entire bodily way of life, he cannot attain this knowledge:
to perceive the greatness of the things that are given by Christ in a mystery.
For these are the ways in which we take off and put on:
in baptism we take off the old person and put on the new;
and slavery, and we put on freedom; and bodily existence, and we put on spiritual existence; and sin,
and we put on righteousness; and other things like these. But all of them come through hearing in faith.
And although all these things truly happen to us in the very birth of baptism, they are all foreign to our awareness.
But when we reach the stage of bodily maturity that can distinguish good things from evil,
with good will and diligence of soul, we begin to take off evil and put on good, to take off injustice
and put on righteousness, to take off oppression and become generous, to take off mercilessness
and become merciful, to take off harshness and become gentle, to take off rapacity and become compassionate, and many other things like these.
All these things happen through the will of someone who fears God and struggles against the world,
for through these things a person grows little by little, until he takes off the whole world completely
and empties himself of everything in it, and stands free in his own person,
and appears in another world, that of Christ’s way of life, just as an infant leaves the natural womb behind and comes outside it.
And when a person has taken off the world in this manner that I have described, and has become completely emptied of everything visible,
then he begins to take off the evil passions within him: love of adultery, sexual immorality, gluttony,
debauchery, greed, and drunkenness. These are desires that destroy virtue.
And when he has taken off all these in practice, from his bodily members, he begins again to take them off also from the movements of his thoughts.
And just as he has banished them from the body, he also cuts them off from the movements of the soul,
so that they are not merely left unpracticed and unstirred in the outward members, but also in the inward thoughts of the soul.
And after he has also taken off from the soul the passions of hateful thoughts,
he then begins, from this point onward, to take off ignorance, error, and conceit as well.
These arise from indulging desires—that is, when the heart becomes dulled through luxuries and pride.
For whenever a person takes off the desires of the body, with his gaze directed purely toward God,
he hastens to reduce even his bodily necessities, because it is not only through indulging desires that the heart becomes dulled.
Rather, dullness of heart also occurs whenever the body receives all that it needs in full.
And the mind is not polished and purified of its bodily character. For meeting bodily needs in moderation preserves a balance.
And as long as the body remains in a balanced state of health, it does not submit completely to the wishes of the soul.
For balance indicates equality between both sides.
For just as the suspension cord placed at the center of a scale indicates that the two pans are equal in weight,
so, when the body remains in a balanced state of health, it stands at an equal weight against the soul.
And as long as it stands against her on an equal footing, it does not submit to the higher worth of her desires.
It is therefore necessary to break the body's strength by eating less, so that it will become subject and obedient to the soul.
But I will leave this subject of eating less, because I intend to speak about it in the discourse that follows this one.
But this is what we should understand here: unless a person takes off his clothes, he cannot put others on.
Let us all strive to strip ourselves of the bodily way of life, so that we may put on the spiritual way of life.
Let us strip off the world and all its cares, so that we may travel the road of perfection without hindrance. Renunciation, then, carries a light load of possessions.
And if someone calls poverty for God's sake wealth, he names it rightly and according to what it truly is.
For this reason our Lord also removed a heavy yoke from his disciples by making them free of the world's wealth.
He said, “Come to me, all of you who are weary and carry heavy burdens, and I will give you rest.”
And who are these, if not those who weary themselves with excessive wealth and carry the heavy yoke of the world's cares and anxieties?
For what toil is as exhausting as this, in which, when you come to rest, you become still more weary?
For concern over human wealth is a road that has no end in this life.
However far a person travels, it stretches out before his steps, and nothing brings it to an end except death.
And when someone gathers wealth and money so that he may rest, live in splendor, and enjoy luxury,
his very rest is toil. And if the world's rest is toil, what should its toil itself be called?
And if its pleasures and luxuries are heavy labors, what should its labor itself be named?
For the world is burdensome in all its dealings, but those who carry its burdens do not feel it because of their love for it.
They stumble in it like blind people and do not recognize it. They carry heavy burdens, yet these seem light to them.
They weary and exhaust themselves pursuing a trade that brings losses, and they do not know it.
And when our Lord saw them engaged in this futile exertion, he called them: “Come to me, so that I may give you rest. In your toil,” he said, “there is no rest.
Rather, toil itself gives birth to toil, and labor produces labor. Your wealth, too, gathers poverty.
Your rest is turmoil, and your pleasure is distress.
Your refreshment is exhaustion. For the road of desire for wealth, which you have traveled of your own will, has no end.
But if you come to me, my road does have an end. For just as you have tasted the world's way, taste mine as well.
And if it does not taste good to you, spit it out. You have carried the world's heavy burdens,
And you have felt how heavy they are. Be persuaded and take my yoke upon you, and learn by experience how easy and pleasant it is.
I do not make you rich so that you need many things, but truly rich, needing nothing.
For the rich person is not the one who possesses many things, but the one who needs nothing.
For in the world, however much you acquire, you remain needy. But with me, if you empty yourselves of everything, you will be rich.
But when the first need is satisfied, room is prepared within it for a second need.
And when the thing a person seeks to obtain has been acquired, it in turn pursues the acquisition of another possession.
And when the first desire has been fulfilled, a spacious place opens within it for another desire greater than itself.
For satisfying desires produces hunger, and the more desire eats, the hungrier it becomes.
And the richer a rich person becomes, the poorer he becomes. And the more wealth is gathered, the more it pursues further wealth.
And the more a person acquires and prospers, the more he longs for yet another possession.
Even if a person should acquire half the world, his desire is not satisfied by this possession.
Instead, he still desires to acquire all of it, if he can.
And even when he has acquired all of it—which is impossible—his desire is not restrained within the limits of his possession of the whole world.
Instead, he still desires to acquire another world like it, one that does not exist.
And he begins to torment himself by seeking something that has not yet been made. Who would not weep over such a way of thinking?
That is, rather than laugh at him, since he is bound by a love of seeking things that do not exist.
Come to me, then, all of you who are weary from wealth, and find rest in poverty.
Come, owners of property and possessions, and find delight in having nothing.
Come, lovers of the passing world, and taste the world that lasts forever. You have tried what is yours; come and try what is mine as well.
You have experienced your wealth; come and test my poverty as well. In your case, your wealth is wealth.
But in my case, my poverty is wealth. It is no very great thing for wealth to be called wealth.
But it is perfect and great when poverty is wealth, for greatness is proclaimed through its opposite.
And when you have tried these things of mine as well, if they are not more pleasant and lighter than yours, go back and take up your former burdens.
See, through this testimony too, our Lord has shown us that unless a person throws off his worldly burden, he cannot bear the yoke of Christ.
For the two yokes are opposed to one another. Righteousness, however, can also be acquired amid wealth.
Perfection, however, is found in giving up possessions. And all those who pursued perfection,
whether in the New Covenant or the Old, gave up their wealth and then began on the path of perfection.
When the apostles were called by our Lord, they gave up the whole world, and then went out after the one who called them.
Our Lord himself also portrayed and showed us in his own person the end of one path and the beginning of another. At the Jordan he set the boundary between the two.
For there he completed the path of the Law along which he had been walking, because he had kept the Law.
And from there he began on the path of perfection, which he demonstrated in his own person to teach those who love perfection.
For after he had conquered the world and scorned and rejected everything in it, he then went out to fight against the god of the world.
And just as he had subdued the enemy's stronghold, he would also subdue the enemy himself.
For the Jordan became for him a crossing from one world to another: from the bodily world to the spiritual world,
and from the way of life under the Law to the way of life of the New Covenant. For just as the sea served the Hebrews,
where they brought their slavery under Egypt to an end, and where their fear of the Egyptians who ruled over them was taken away, and from which they went out into a land of freedom,
where the lordship of others would not rule over them, and they would not do the will of others, but only that of God,
so Jesus too brought his subjection to the Law to an end at the Jordan, and from there began to live in freedom.
And just as the wilderness received the Jews from the sea, the desert also received him from the Jordan.
He was no longer fulfilling the weak will of the Law, but the perfect and complete will of his Father,
to give sound commandments and demonstrate a spiritual and perfect way of life, the one that he desires.
And understand that when Jesus went out into the desert, he went out alone, without company and without help,
without friends in his company or loved ones, without wealth, possessions, clothes, or finery.
Nor is anything from the world recorded as having gone out with him, but only he himself, with the Holy Spirit also accompanying him.
So take this departure of your Lord as a model for your own departure from the world, and go out yourself as he did,
carrying nothing belonging to the world, so that the Holy Spirit may accompany you in this way. Look, then, at the freedom
with which Jesus went out, and go out yourself as he did. Consider how far the human way of life accompanied him,
and where he left it behind. You too must leave behind the world's way of life where your Lord left behind the way of life under the Law.
And go out with him to battle against the powers of error, that is, also to the struggle against the world.
For when you have left the world, since it is its habit to pursue those who leave it and depart,
Turn to the struggle against it, and stand upright against it, remembering what Paul said: “I am crucified to the world, and the world is crucified to me.”
So lay aside the world's weight, so that the battle you are preparing to fight against it may be easier for you.
Instead of the Jordan, bathe in the waters of knowledge, and after your bathing, follow a spiritual way of life.
See that what happened among the Jews is also a pattern of these things taking place with you.
For just as all the evils of the Egyptians were removed from the Hebrews,
so here too all the world's evils will disappear and be removed from you, along with its excesses and its weight,
its anxiety and its worries. For until they reached the sea, the Hebrews were serving the Egyptians.
But from the sea onward, they were set apart by the word of God for the service of God.
For the slavery of the Jews in Egypt is a pattern of your slavery in the world.
And the freedom they received in the wilderness is likewise an image of the freedom you receive after your departure from the world.
Egypt put the Hebrews to work with mud and bricks, with drudgery and hard labor.
The world likewise puts you to work with worries, anxiety, distress, and sighing.
The Jews were washed clean of Egypt's mud when they passed through the sea. You too have two baptisms:
one is that of grace, which takes place through water, and the other is that of your own will, when you immerse yourself in the love of God, away from the world,
and emerge outside it. And just as, after the Hebrews came out of the sea, another way of life received them,
and they were deemed worthy of different food, and fresh waters were opened up for them to drink,
and other commandments and a law were entrusted to them to observe, and they received heavenly revelations,
and were deemed worthy of spiritual visions, and heard God's voice close at hand as he spoke with them,
and angels also mingled with them, and they attained the companionship and fellowship of spiritual powers,
and the Tent of Meeting was fashioned among them, and they were shown the distinct forms of service within it,
and an uplifted serpent was set up for them in the wilderness to cure and heal the bites of venomous snakes,
and their entire life was already as though in another world, removed from all the customary ways of this world,
so you too, in the same way, when you leave the world as though leaving Egypt, pass through a sea of afflictions.
And you experience fear and suffering, because they too were full of fear beside the sea and within the sea,
and terror of the Egyptians and dread of the sea tormented them.
And until they had gone down into the sea, turned back and come up out of it, and seen the corpses of their enemies floating among the waves,
they were not filled with joy. So too, when a disciple leaves the world and wishes to be freed from its slavery,
joy does not welcome him immediately, nor is he immediately granted a taste of spiritual delights,
just as joy did not welcome those people immediately when they left Egypt, nor were they immediately granted spiritual delight.
Instead, disciple, what first confronts you after your departure from the world
is fear of afflictions, the turmoil of thoughts, and regret over your departure from the world,
and over having given away what you owned, or abandoned your inheritance and moved away from your ancestral home.
For demons secretly gather against you like the Egyptians, and Satan their chief is like Pharaoh.
They stir up thoughts like these within you and bury you in anxious reflections,
which habitually darken the soul and deprive you of the vision of the light of the knowledge of Christ.
They begin to stir up things like these among your thoughts: “Why did you leave the world, where it would have been easy for you to become righteous?
Why did you go and scatter your wealth, through which, while you still had it, you were seen to be so merciful?
For now, because you distributed it hastily, it may even have been given to those who do not deserve it.
But if it had remained with you and been managed wisely by you, you would have used it to relieve those in distress.
With it you would have welcomed strangers; from it you would have clothed the naked.
Even solitaries and monks would have been cared for through your gifts.
You would have supported widows and orphans. Your home would have become a haven for every good thing.
With patience, as long as your wealth remained with you, you would have enjoyed relief from it yourself and provided relief for many others.
Your righteousness would have been like that of Abraham and Job and the other faithful people who became righteous as they did.
Did you perhaps want your righteousness to grow greater than theirs? Moreover, through this very mercy you would have resembled God himself, according to the word of your Lord.
You would also have gained a good name among people, and everyone would have called you a father to orphans.
