Everyone who saw and heard would have called you blessed because of your good deeds.
And just as your righteousness would have shone before God, so it would also have been revealed for people to see.
You would also have been a good example for others to emulate. For whenever wealthy people like you saw you
distributing your possessions to the needy, they too would have been inspired by your example and become generous givers.
And from this you would have gathered a double measure of righteousness for yourself: one from your own gift, and another because you had prompted others to show mercy,
so that they too became givers like you. And if you had wanted to fast, that too would have been easy for you,
while you were living in the world, just as you have seen many others in the world who also fast.
And in this way the triumph of your fasting would have been all the greater, the closer the foods were to you,
and the more the things your stomach craved were laid out before your eyes, while you overcame them all through the strength of your endurance.
For in this you would even have surpassed the solitaries,
because someone who overcomes things close at hand, which he could use if he wished,
has a much greater triumph than someone who endures simply because he has nothing,
for even if he wants to rest and enjoy himself, the things that would give him comfort are not available to him.
But if you had loved prayer, this too would have been easy for you: to pray secretly within your house,
and to go at every opportunity to the temple of God and bring others with you as well.
And there was not a single good thing you wanted to do that would not have been easier for you in the world,
to accomplish. For who rejects comforts together with the kingdom?
And who would ask not to enjoy himself here too, if he is certain that the delight to come is also prepared for him?
This was available to you personally because of your mercy and your alms to the poor.
And after these things, those same evil demons, together with their chief, Satan, gather and heap still other things upon your soul,
depicting before your eyes the labors of asceticism and the severe pains that befall those who fast,
and the bitter illnesses caused by lack of food, which are not easy to cure,
nor is it easy for you to treat them, because you cannot use the things that cure and heal them.
And if you venture to apply human remedies to them because of the distress of your pains, you become a stumbling block to others who see you.
And again, the road of this way of life is long, and it does not end except in death.
And if you want to bring it to an end while you are still alive and cease your labors, then you have made yourself an object of laughter and mockery to everyone who knows you.
But if you do not stop, then you are carrying a burden of afflictions, and your torment increases for many reasons:
first, because of the weight of your labors; another, because of their length; and again, because of the pains and illnesses caused by those labors;
and again, because it is not easy for you to provide remedies for them; and again, if you want relief from your afflictions.
Through the sources of support to which you turn, you have become a laughingstock to those who see you. And again:
You have become a stranger to your family and your friends, and the rule governing your way of life does not even allow you to approach them for conversation and companionship.
And now you have become dependent on receiving kindness from others—you who used to show kindness to others.
And if you happen to receive something, you become bound to please those from whom you receive it.
But if you no longer receive anything, you are tormented by the pressures of poverty.
The demons gather these things and others like them and bring them into the disciple’s mind as soon as he leaves the world.
They throw him into fear and terror, disturb the order of his thoughts, and reduce him to helplessness,
so that he does not know what to do. And they sink his soul into sorrow.
They set him between the intermediate things and the final things, so that he remembers what he has left behind and recalls what lies ahead.
And in his mind he considers their counsels as though they were convincing, especially since even the thoughts
that they first stir up in you are not thoughts of frivolity, corruption, or evil conduct,
but of compassion and love of almsgiving, along with all the other good things that a person can do while living in the world.
They stir these things up within your soul not because they love what is good, but to bring you down from the high degree of righteousness to another lower than it.
And when you listen to them and descend with them, they bring you down even from that one
to another degree lower still. Little by little they lead you, drag you, and bring you down,
until they overthrow you and drown you in the depths of evil, for they are cunning in their counsels.
Whatever they see you attached to, they use that very thing to nurture your passions.
For they do not immediately take something you hate and offer it to you in their counsels, but rather the very thing that is dear to you.
Then they try to persuade you, seeking only to ease you a little away from the strictness of your way of life.
And so, through all these things, the distress caused by your thoughts grows stronger within you.
Sorrow and cries of distress arise anew within your mind, while joy remains far away from you:
the joy of the world, because you have abandoned it, and the joy of Christ, because you have not attained it.
Your soul is left amid these storms like a ship whose helmsman is asleep, battered this way and that,
wandering and being dashed about in every direction, driven against every reef and battered by every sea.
The mind’s journey along its path is thrown into confusion, and the signs marking the paths you travel are lost from your sight.
And a weight presses heavily upon you, and drowsiness seizes you in both body and soul.
And you are plunged, as though at night, into the heavy sleep of despondency. And just as fear is great at nighttime
for those who are in it, so fear grows great within you, because your soul has become dark, deprived of the light of knowledge.
For knowledge within the soul takes the place of light in the world, and from it joy is also born.
And just as darkness arises within creation when the light departs, so, in the absence of spiritual knowledge,
the darkness of distress and the gloom of sadness spread throughout the realm of the soul.
From this, fear begins to arise within it concerning what has passed and what is to come, along with distress, terror, dread, weakness,
faintheartedness, oppressive thoughts, and constant agitation that continually renews itself within the soul and springs from the soul itself.
It happens that the soul is distressed even when there is no distress to fear, and its mind is troubled without understanding the cause of its trouble.
Not a single one of its impulses gives it any pleasure at all. Through this place, then, you must pass,
O disciple who leaves the world. For like the people who came out of Egypt, you too have been called and have gone out after God.
And just as the sea stood as a barrier before the Hebrews while the Egyptians pursued them, so there lies before you
a terrifying depth of afflictions, sufferings, toils, troubles, and torments,
privation and poverty, pains and illnesses, and deprivation of friends,
distance from your family, separation from your parents, silence and solitude, and oppressive confinement,
humble clothing, meager food, abstinence and ascetic discipline, and reproaches and insults
if you grow slack, and toils and hardships if you strive diligently, exhausting vigils, tormenting thirst, and debilitating hunger.
All these things, then, and others like them, stand like a terrifying sea as a barrier before your departure,
while demons pursue you from behind like the Egyptians. But do not be afraid or alarmed, because instead of Moses,
Jesus is with you. For just as Moses accompanied the congregation as a foreshadowing, so Christ also accompanies your soul invisibly.
And to your oppressed and weary thoughts he also says what Moses said to the Jews:
“The Lord will fight for you, while you remain still.” But do not be afraid as the people were.
Instead, rouse yourself and keep vigil like Moses, and cry out to the Lord as he cried out. For this is what is written:
Moses prayed all night with loud cries and suffering. Then, during the morning watch, the Lord said to him,
“Why are you crying out before me? Stretch out your hand over the sea and divide it, and let the Hebrews pass through it.”
And the Egyptians will drown in it. For everything that happened there is a pattern of what happens to you.
So your enemies, the evil demons, gather and press against your soul,
just as the Egyptians who were pursuing the Jews gathered and pressed against their souls.
But just as Moses set aside his fear of the Egyptians and turned to prayer and crying out to God,
you too must set aside the worries and thoughts that your wretched enemies stir up within you. Stand in earnest prayer and cry out with heartfelt anguish.
Let the sound of your cry rise from the depths of your soul’s thoughts. And immediately the word spoken in answer to Moses is spoken to you as well:
“Why are you crying out before me? Stretch out your hand over the sea and divide it.”
For immediately your troubles give way, and the covering of sorrow that lay before your face is rolled away.
The dreadful depth of afflictions gives way. You tread through and cross the depths of those things you thought could not be crossed on foot.
Difficult things become easy for you. And that wall which had been built, which you thought could not be breached, immediately collapses before you,
as your prayer pierces and passes through the abyss of all the evils that had gathered and stood before you.
And just as the pillar there was behind the Hebrews and came to be before them, and darkness came between them and the Egyptians,
so here too the light of salvation shines before you, and darkness is placed between you and the demons who are your enemies.
And in the very place through which you passed, they are drowned.
The afflictions from which you were freed turn back and become those of the demons who are your enemies.
Your sorrow and distress are turned back upon them. And the joy they had, represented by that pillar,
while they thought they were fighting and defeating you, is taken away from before them and placed before you,
like the pillar of light that was taken away from the Egyptians and came before the Hebrews.
And just as Pharaoh and the Egyptians were drowned in the sea, so Satan, together with all his demons,
is drowned in the depths of the troubles in which you were drowning. And now you repeat to your thoughts the words of Moses:
“The Lord will fight for you while you remain still.” And like the Hebrews with Moses, all your victories cross over with you.
For it was during the night that fear ruled over the Hebrews, to serve as a pattern for you:
as long as fear is with you, your life is as though it were in the night.
And just as there, when morning appeared, the night passed and fear was taken away, so here too, as soon as the light of salvation dawns upon you,
at the end of your prayer your troubles are wiped away, and your thoughts become light, like limbs in the morning.
And the gloomy cloud is scattered, bright, clear skies dawn within your soul, and the sea of your afflictions is crossed on foot.
And the wall of troubles built before you is breached. You walk confidently through a frightening land and cross a depth that you could not cross before.
And you tread a land that the old nature has never trodden. You escape the yoke of slavery and enter the land of freedom.
And you leave Egypt with all its turmoil, and the wilderness, full of heavenly blessings, welcomes you.
And you are conceived and born anew into the new world of spiritual life.
And within the land that conceives and gives birth to you, there the wheels of your enemies are bound.
And the force of their onrush is halted, and the advance of their chariots stops.
And the uproar of their voices subsides and falls silent. Afflictions turn back upon them like waves, and they are covered in the depths of the abyss—
those who wanted to cover you. But you stand on the shore, above the sea of affliction and troubles,
after the glorious crossing, and turn to see your enemies being battered within it,
and the passions together with the demons being drowned in it, and the entire way of life of the old self being submerged within it.
And when you have seen this, and your soul has found rest in the destruction of those who hate you, and you have gained fresh confidence through the death of your enemies,
you turn to look toward the holy mountain of God and begin to walk through a land you have never crossed.
And your journey takes place in the world of the Spirit, which is spiritual life, as even here you are found worthy to see
the things above the world, and to eat spiritual manna that your ancestors did not eat,
and to drink sweet and pleasant waters, which flow for you from the rock, Christ.
And you will dwell within a cloud of light, and the pillar of the Spirit will shine upon you, and you will see what you have never seen.
And you will hear voices you have never heard, and as you journey day by day, you will draw near to Zion, the holy mountain,
where the presence of the hidden Being dwells, and you will share in the knowledge of the angels.
And you will perceive spiritual realities above the world, while your clothing and footwear grow along with your stature.
That is, as your new self grows day by day, the adornments of your clothing are also revealed to you,
which is Christ. And your footwear also grows with you, which is readiness for the gospel of peace.
And you enter into the mysteries of the Spirit and share in the fullness of the knowledge of Christ,
as you are continually awakened by living impulses, and wonder at the inexpressible greatness of God carries you away,
while you are withdrawn from the whole visible world, and your dwelling is entirely in the world of the Spirit.
And you appear to those who see you as though only in the outward form of the body.
Yet all the activity of your hidden self dwells in the highest heavens.
And you are exalted in realms without boundaries or number, where there is no bodily form,
nor any material composition; where there is no change of natures, nor any movement of the elements;
where there is only stillness and tranquility, and all the inhabitants of that realm are spiritual beings.
With voices not composed of parts, they cry out praises of holiness to the Being who is worshiped.
There you taste something that cannot be tasted with the body's palate, and you perceive something that does not reach the bodily senses.
You know only that you are enjoying delight, but you cannot explain what your delight is like.
There, instead of communion with human beings, you have spiritual communion with Jesus Christ.
You bear hardships without feeling their distress, because your awareness of Christ does not allow you to feel your afflictions.
And the rapture of your mind toward God deprives you of all awareness of bodily things.
There you see and hear and taste and smell, and with all the senses of your hidden self you receive a taste of God's world.
And in keeping with the nature of that world, your senses themselves taste it spiritually.
There, face to face, divine revelations are imparted to you as they were to Moses.
And within the Holy of Holies, which God established and not a human being, visions and wonders welcome you.
The hidden glory of God overwhelms your thoughts, and you move among the spiritual powers with a spiritual mind.
There, what is set in place is not, as in a symbol, an ark of spiritual signs
and divine knowledge; rather, your knowledge encounters knowledge in its reality, without anything mediating.
There, it is not a golden altar that is prepared, from which material incense rises,
but another altar, a spiritual one, which receives the pure incense of all holy and rational thoughts.
There, it is not a jar of manna that is set in place, as in the symbolic pattern,
nor is food given through the mediation of angels kept there; rather, a table of life is prepared, which is the very person of Christ.
From him all his spiritual members receive spiritual nourishment, like limbs drawing nourishment from a body.
There, it is not the staff that is the sign of Aaron's election
that is kept as a memorial, but the very person of the high priest, Jesus Christ.
He offers living and rational persons as a priest before his Father, where you are wholly immersed, beyond awareness of these visible things.
And you hear nothing of the things expressed and perceived in composite form.
All the members of the old self within you have died, and you have put on the new self, which is renewed in knowledge according to the likeness of its Creator.
In this way of life, then, is your dwelling, O disciple, after you have departed from the way of life of the bodily world,
provided that, when you entered this place according to its rule, you labored in it as the requirements of the place demand,
and did not bring dead portions from the dead world with you into the land of the living.
For leaving the world in outward appearance is not what constitutes departure from the world,
but rather stripping off the world and its entire way of life, inwardly as well as outwardly, and becoming completely estranged from every remembrance of it.
And just as a person has cut off and cast away bodily practices, so he must also cut off and cast away dead thoughts: those that dwell on dead things.
For the mind necessarily becomes, in its reflections, like the nature of the body to which it is bound.
For when it dwells on the things of the world, all its activity is dead.
But if its meditation concerns the things of the spirit, it moves as something living among living and spiritual things.
Take the likeness of your body as an illustration also of the spiritual mind in which your thoughts move.
For just as the body, as long as it dwells in the bodily world,
is bodily in all its movements and actions, but when the time comes for it to pass into the world of the spirit,
it is renewed and becomes spiritual, and then enters the world of spiritual beings, so too thought, as long as it dwells in the world,
and its meditation and reflection are concerned with that world, is itself bodily, in keeping with the nature of the world in which it dwells.
But if its dwelling is in that world of the spirit, and in all its reflections it moves as though in that place,
then thought becomes spiritual, according to the order of that place in which its movements are engaged in meditation.
It is this portion, then, that every disciple who leaves the world must pursue.
For this is our inheritance, and in this place is our way of life as well, according to the teaching of Paul, who said,
“Our citizenship is in heaven, and from there we await our Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ, who will transform our lowly body,
to make it like his glorious body, according to his great power, by which everything has been subjected to him.”
But as I said, as long as a person is still confined in the womb of the world, he has no awareness of this way of life.
Nor, again, can he become aware of it if he leaves the world outwardly but does not leave it inwardly.
For this way of life is not tasted through the body. Rather, the mind tastes it spiritually when it is purified of thoughts
and bodily concerns. Therefore, as I said, the beginning of this path is the end of the world's path.
For until a person completes that bodily path, he does not walk on this spiritual one.
Now the end of this world's path is this: complete emptying of oneself of everything that is in the world.
One must not empty oneself of one thing but not another, abandoning one thing while holding on to another.
Rather, one must free and release the members of one's being from all the world's bodily things, which hold a person bound to them.
Some people are held fast in the world by all their members, and some by two parts of them.
Some are half enslaved and half free. Some have one part standing in freedom and two parts in slavery.
Some have only a little of themselves enslaved, while all the rest of their members are released and free.
Some are held and fettered by only one of their members, and all their members move,
while they themselves still remain in place. Yet even someone bound by one member has his whole being attached to the world.
He is like a bird caught in a snare by its claw alone: its whole being is held in the snare by its claw.
Although its wings are entirely free from bonds, and it flaps and moves them as though to fly,
the bond and fetter around its claw do not allow it to rise into the heights of the clear air.
Instead, it lies where it is and flutters on the ground, burdening its wings and its whole being with the weight of the dust.
So it is also with a person whose members are all released from the world's fetters, but who is bound by one of them.
For that one member by which he is bound binds all of him. Although only a little of him is fettered, strong bonds are laid completely over his whole being.
Therefore, those who long to be released from the world's bonds must free themselves completely,
take off and throw away the old garment, and put on the new one, which is Christ's way of life.
This garment, then, is the garment of the kingdom, and all the adornments of virtuous conduct must be found in it.
For anyone who wishes to change his garment must take it off entirely and put on the other completely. And consider these examples
of what I am advising you about, and from bodily things understand spiritual things as well.
For look: someone who wants to put something into a vessel, until he empties it of what is in it,
does not put into it what he wants to put there. But if those substances—
the one emptied out of the vessel and the one put into it—are incompatible with one another, even if he washes and scrubs the vessel,
from the smell and taste of the former, so that the sweetness of another flavor that enters the vessel will not be altered.
Again, whenever a farmer wants to sow good seed in his land and sees that there are thorns and thistles in it,
he first uproots and removes them. Then he sows good seed in his field.
Again, anyone who wants to put on a new garment first takes off the old one that is on his body.
Then he puts on the new one. Likewise, in the case of an ulcer, a doctor
skillfully removes the foul matter on it by means of corrosive and strong medicines.
Then he applies a plaster that builds up new flesh. Many other things like these are also done in nature.
For unless the former things are cut off and thrown away, people do not introduce other things,
especially when those things are opposed to one another.
So too, in this case, a disciple of Christ must act this way if he desires to approach Christ’s perfect way of life:
he must cut off and cast away from himself the entire way of life of the old world, and then approach the new way of life.
He must take off ignorance and then put on spiritual knowledge. For attachment to things that do not last
comes from ignorance, while release from them comes from knowledge. Whoever takes off the world takes off ignorance.
And whoever puts on the world puts on foolishness. For this is true knowledge:
not to be deceived by something that does not exist and imagine that it exists. Ignorance, however, is recognized by this:
it attaches itself to something that does not endure and regards it as though it were real.
Therefore, those who have clothed themselves in the world have clothed themselves in it as though it were something lasting.
They are rightly called ignorant, because they have mistaken a shadow for a solid body. And rightly called wise
are those who separate themselves from the world, because they have taken off the worn-out garment before it strips them.
For someone whom the world itself strips receives no credit for his action, because the world itself has fled from him
and rejected and cast him away as something superfluous. But worthy of blessing and praise
are those who, of their own good will, separate themselves from the world and go out from it,
so that it will not hinder their journey. For like a covering in front of one’s sight,
so is concern for the world in front of divine contemplation.
And just as our sight cannot pierce and pass through the solid objects before it, whether a mountain, a building, or anything else like these,
And until a person is above it or steps past it, he cannot see the things placed above him.
Likewise, our mind cannot gaze at the things outside the world as long as the world's wall stands before our sight,
and its heavy roofs cover us overhead, along with the mountains and heights of its cares and concerns.
But if someone wishes to see the spiritual way of life outside the world, or to contemplate the heavenly things above him,
let him go outside the world or rise above it. Then, behold, both will become visible to him:
the spiritual way of life sustained by the movement of living thoughts, and the kingdom of heaven, which is above the world.
For when a person is freed from the world's passions, it is as though his dwelling were in the kingdom of heaven.
For what is the delight of the kingdom of heaven? Is it not the end of all troubles,
and the enjoyment of every joy? Is it not that sorrow and sighing dissolve and flee, as it is written,
and that we delight in the varied spiritual beings, in the splendor and pleasures of the blessings sealed and kept safe?
We have no expectation of troubles, nor any fear or dread of losses yet to come.
For that world is entirely a world of joys, whose inhabitants constantly delight in joys.
And these very things—joy kept safe and lasting delight—
are found even in this life by the soul that is freed from passions and clears away from itself the shadows of illusions.
One of the spiritual teachers also spoke well when he said that the kingdom of heaven is a soul free from passions,
together with knowledge of the things that truly exist, which are words and movements without a body.
For when the soul is freed from evil passions, from which arise fear and distress,
worry and lack of confidence, it is immediately filled with their opposites: hope and courage,
joy and blessedness of thought. For what does a person have to be distressed about,
or whom does he have to fear, if he has cut off and cast away from himself all the causes of distress and fear?
For distress comes from the prospect of being deprived of the world, its comforts, and its pleasures,
and fear from the prospect of being separated from this temporary bodily life.
And when someone, through the philosophy of Christ, puts off both love of the world and love of life, he is freed from distress and fear.
Even before the Gehenna to come and the judgment that has been prepared, these are themselves a tormenting Gehenna.
For if freedom from passions is the kingdom of heaven, according to the saying of that spiritually wise man,
Therefore slavery to the passions, too, is a tormenting hell and outer darkness,
and the worm that gnaws at the heart and thoughts. For a taste of both these things
is given here. Mastery over thoughts is a sign of that kingdom which is to come,
and the tormenting hell of fear and distress is a pledge of that eternal hell.
For even a pledge given for something has a kinship with the thing for which it is given.
Just as in this world, too, whatever is given beforehand as a pledge for something is akin to the thing of which it becomes a pledge,
so too the spiritual mysteries, which have been handed down to us here as a pledge,
have a great kinship with the true bodily reality of Christ.
For here we receive the body and blood of Christ as a pledge to us of how, there, by Christ himself,
we are spiritually sustained, and receive strength and support from him as limbs do from the body.
And this pledge, through a spiritual transformation, has a kinship with his very person.
Thus it too is called the body and blood belonging to that very person.
Again, we receive the Holy Spirit through baptism, to be for us the firstfruits of the complete communion
that we are to have in the mysteries of the Spirit. As for how closely this pledge is akin to that fulfillment,
the very name, which is one and the same, bears witness: both are called “Spirit” in the words of Scripture.
Again, it is also written about Christ that he became for us the firstfruits of these good things to come. Christ, the firstfruits, has a kinship with us
and with the good things that are to come to us: with us because he became human, and with these things
that are prepared and made ready for us beforehand in the Father's foreknowledge, because he is God, and he too, together with the Father,
with a will that nothing precedes, prepared these good things for us beforehand. In this same way, then, there is a kinship
between the joy born here from freedom from the passions and that joy which is to be given to those worthy of it.
Again, the hell of distress and sorrow that is born here from serving evil passions
is related by kinship to that hell which is to come. Let us therefore strive to cast off the world,
so that along with it we may also cast off the passions that spring up in us from it. And let us also cast off the evil passions,
so that afterward we may put on the living impulses of joy and love. And if you wish to know, disciple,
that without leaving the world you cannot approach the way of life of perfection, learn this from what is written in the Holy Scriptures.
Remember also the ways of life of spiritual people, which are recorded in the holy Scriptures.
For which of all those of old was deemed worthy of such an exalted and marvelous gift as John the Baptist,
according to Christ’s testimony about him, when he said that he was greater than all the prophets? And again he said, “Truly I tell you,
among those born of women none has arisen greater than John the Baptist.” ... And this remarkable man, who attained all this greatness—
let us examine and see how and where he lived, and why he was deemed worthy of so great a gift,
with what upbringing, with how much toil, after what ascetic discipline, and after how long a time spent apart from human company.
And when we have seen and understood these things about him, let us consider the greatness of what was bestowed on him.
Let us first examine the things that belong to the will, and then afterward those that belong to grace. For until the will had shown its fruits,
the Spirit did not give her gifts. Look, then, at the way of life of this remarkable man.
From childhood he separated himself from life in the world and from human company.
He was not first stained and soiled, and then washed and cleansed.
Rather, he went out while his childhood was still pure, before reaching the natural impulses by which good and evil are distinguished.
He grew up in the wilderness, with none of the world’s preoccupations in him at all.
It was not as though he had tasted human wickedness through experience and then spat it out,
or had first been disturbed by desires and passions and then, through the labors of his free will, attained peace of mind.
For even this—departing from the world’s evils before tasting them—
contributes greatly to the serenity of the soul in those who are deemed worthy of it.
Thus a person who follows this way of life may stand only a little below the purity of Adam’s soul before he transgressed the commandment.
For since John was destined to be set apart for the service of the divine mysteries,
and a gift not given to other human beings was destined to come to him, it was fitting that he separated himself from childhood and went out into the wilderness,
so that, without experiencing evil, and without his mind receiving the imprint of images from bodily memories,
and without being disturbed and troubled by the world’s preoccupations and cares,
he might receive spiritual revelations and teachings about the divine mysteries in the serenity of his soul, and perceive something
beyond the reach of the whole mortal race. For this reason he also received the Holy Spirit while he was in his mother’s womb,
so that the very thoughts of his soul might be moved spiritually by the prompting of the Spirit.
For it was not fitting for him to be born without sexual union, because this belonged to Jesus, God, alone.
But he was destined to receive visions and revelations surpassing the old nature, so he received the Spirit while still in the womb, after being conceived through sexual union.
For there is no doubt that it would have been easy to create him anew, as Adam and Eve were created.
But through this he would have become a stranger to the old creation.
The Creator did not wish to do this, lest he be thought to despise the first creation.
As for being conceived from that very same old nature without sexual union, it has been said that this was fitting for Christ alone.
And again, while growing up in the world and experiencing its evils, he might suddenly be deemed worthy of the grace that is above the world.
Through election, as with the apostles, this was destined to be given after the cross,
when the old nature died, and sin and all evil passions died along with it.
But because John was destined to be deemed worthy of the apostles’ knowledge before the lifting of the curse, the abolition of sin, and the event of the cross,
it was fitting that he both received the Spirit from the womb and was brought up outside the world, so that by these means
he might attain the natural purity of the first human being before he transgressed the commandment, and in this very purity of soul
receive knowledge of the divine mysteries. For where these wonders took place through grace,
these purposes and means were [?]. But where, through the inexpressible depth of God’s love,
this salvation was being accomplished, God himself, exercising his authority freely, stood in the midst.
In him and through him he abolished the old things and began the new, and the old human being died on the cross, as Paul wrote:
“Our old human being was crucified with him.” And the new human being was revealed, made known, and seen—not merely one worthy to live in paradise,
after the pattern of the first Adam, but one fit to dwell even in heaven and move among spiritual beings
and be like them in everything. And from then on, even people experienced in every evil, tax collectors,
the sexually immoral, murderers, bandits, and worshipers of created things—
grace suddenly snatches them up and, without means or preparations, makes them worthy of the wealth of its mysteries, and, as in a new nature,
acts in whomever it wishes, because the old human being has been crucified and has died, according to Paul’s words.
And again the apostle himself spoke on behalf of the whole of human nature: “Wretched human being that I am!
Who will rescue me from this body of death?” And after asking, as a question, who could rescue him,
he revealed, giving thanks and teaching through his words, who it was that had rescued him from the old and mortal nature.
“I thank God,” he says, “through our Lord Jesus Christ, who rescued me from this body of death” ... After these things, then, which have become known to us,
in which the death, dissolution, abolition, and destruction of the old person take place, and the resurrection and renewal,
and the appearance and revelation of the new person—all operations, all powers, and all knowledge,
and all mysteries and revelations, and every activity of the Spirit, and works beyond nature—
grace accomplishes sovereignly in whomever it chooses. These things, however, have been spoken by us briefly,
so that I might explain the reason for John the herald’s departure into the wilderness,
and why he received the Spirit from the womb, and why he was brought up in the wilderness from his infancy.
But you, disciple, on hearing these things, make every effort to cast off the world and draw near to the freedom of a pure way of life.
Love constant communion with God, and diligently flee from all human conversation.
See the benefits of this way of life from what happened to John the Baptist.
For if, long before the cross—through which the old things were dissolved and abolished and the new things appeared—
the solitary way of life, and freedom and estrangement from the world, were able
to give John the Baptist the knowledge of the apostles, and through these things he attained wisdom beyond human nature,
how much more will this spiritual way of life now establish you in the knowledge of Christ’s mysteries,
and give you inexpressible delight in the perception of spiritual revelations. Take, then, this righteous man’s way of life as your example.
Learn also from him that a person cannot become a perfect disciple of Christ unless he becomes a stranger to the whole world,
just like this righteous man, as Christ’s own word has also clearly taught us:
“Unless someone renounces the whole world, his brothers, his relatives, his family, his father and mother, and everything he has,
and, greatest of all, even his own life, he cannot be my disciple.”
Again, in another place, to the man who wanted to fulfill both things together—honoring his parents
and being his disciple—he forbade this and told him that two opposing things cannot exist together.
“Teacher,” he said, “allow me to go and bury my father and mother, and then follow you.”
That is, “Let me keep the former law, which commands me, ‘Honor and obey your parents,’ and then I will follow you and serve you.”
But what answer did Jesus give to this? “Leave the dead,” he said, “to bury their dead.
But you, go and proclaim the kingdom of God. You are not required to keep the law, because it has been observed and set aside.”
Nor are you to serve your natural parents, because I obeyed [?] and served bodily parents on behalf of everyone.
The yoke of the law and of nature has therefore been lifted from you, and you have been left free to govern yourself.
There is no compulsion from the world that enslaves you, because the world is dead to you, and you to it.
For corpses do not serve; they are only wrapped and buried.
So leave the dead to bury their own dead, and go proclaim the kingdom of God.
Look, from this testimony too we learn that someone who becomes a disciple of Jesus is not permitted to serve even his natural parents.
For he has a true Father, who by his grace enrolled him as his son and set him apart to serve his will.
Now listen to another example, which also offers you teaching of this kind.
Through the pattern of this testimony, it urges you to estrange yourself from everything and go out after Jesus.
One of his disciples, it says, approached Jesus and said to him, “Allow me to go and say farewell to my household, and then come after you.”
Here too, listen to what the Teacher answered the disciple, and regard it as something said to you through that disciple.
Accept it: “No one,” he says, “who puts his hand to the plowshare and looks behind him is fit for the kingdom of God.”
Someone, he says, who carries out this natural work and drives a plow with oxen, as people customarily do,
does not stop looking ahead and look behind him, because the work cannot be accomplished in this way.
He cannot move forward, nor are his furrows cut straight,
nor do the oxen advance. And this is so even though the work is bodily
and visible, and he remains in that very place. Merely looking behind him throws his work into confusion.
But here, in discipleship to me, the one kind of work differs from the other as one world differs from the other,
and one life from the other, and the immortal from the mortal, and God from human beings.
Therefore, if you have taken the yoke of discipleship to me upon your soul and body, carry out the work of my commandments.
Do not turn back toward the world, and do not concern yourself with bidding farewell to your relatives.
Do not be anxious to repay them the debt of bodily honor and fulfill for them the world's rules of farewell,
and only then come after me. For if you pay what is due to the world, what is due to me remains unpaid.
And if you are eager not to distress the world in anything, then you have resolved to anger me. Do not be at peace with the world,
so that you may have true peace with me. You have neither a home nor a household. Why are you hurrying to bid them farewell?
For hostility has been set between you and them. Why are you so concerned to be their friend?
For I did not come to bring peace on earth. Why do you hurry to have peace with the people of the earth?
For I call for the sword, while you hurry toward peace. I proclaim division,
while you hurry and press for harmony. I came to divide a man against his father and a daughter against her mother,
and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law. Yet you hurry to greet your household
and, in your foolishness, to stitch up the tear that I made in the world. For I tore this garment of harmony
because it was woven entirely in error, and in its place I laid the warp for another garment, one of heavenly peace.
Weave this garment yourself as well, and do not hurry to sew up the old garment.
For I abolished the peace that fostered evil in everyone, and I scattered that fellowship which had gathered to amass sins.
Do not hurry to become a companion of evildoers. He says, “Let me go and say farewell to my household.”
He told him, “You have no peace with them.” And he says, “Do not greet anyone on the road.”
This is also the meaning of this saying, through which Christ likewise estranged his disciples from the peace of the world.
These things are spoken to everyone in the person of a single disciple—that is, to those who profess discipleship.
For it is fitting that no one should be God's disciple in name but the world's in reality, hiring himself out to one and working for another.
For the world is not required to attain perfection, since neither its outward appearance nor its conduct professes perfection.
But a disciple, through the signs of his outward appearance, proclaims perfection for himself.
And through the things in which he appears openly before people, he pledges that he will also appear in the same way before God in secret.
For the marks of discipleship impressed on you outwardly urge you to have every good thing inscribed within your soul.
And you are required to appear before God in your hidden life in the same way that you appear before people in your outward life.
For you have cast off concern for the world's clothing. Cast off from your soul, in secret, the love of adornment as well.
You keep away from outward sexual union. Keep away also from the hidden desire of your thoughts. You abstain from eating meat
and from visible comforts and rewards. Abstain in your soul also from the desire that longs for those foods.
You have removed from your head the hair of worldly youth. This is a sign that you should not become entangled in the world's cares
or bound by its concerns, or caught by any of its passions, which are many and beyond counting.
You have left the world and become a stranger to it in your outward appearance. Leave it and become a stranger to it in your hidden thoughts as well.
You have stripped yourself of wealth in your outward appearance; strip your hidden thoughts of the love of wealth as well.
You have rejected the sounds of music and the pleasures of the world. Take delight with your whole soul, without growing weary,
in the sounds of the songs of the Spirit of God. Let your discipleship be evident inwardly more than outwardly.
And just as people recognize from your outward actions that you are a disciple of Christ,
so let Christ himself recognize from your hidden actions that you are his disciple. Take care not to make your discipleship a trade for profit.
Do not put on the honorable garb of discipleship for the sake of empty glory and passing comforts.
Do not buy bodily things with spiritual things. Do not exchange heavenly things for perishable treasures stored in the earth.
Be a disciple of him alone to whom you have pledged your allegiance.
For he has already taught you and removed from your sight this rust of presumption: a servant cannot serve two masters.
And again, through another testimony, he warns you that if you are not going to be a perfect disciple, remain in the world's way of life; that is better for you.
Otherwise, when you begin to build and do not finish, everyone will mock you. For, he says, what person begins to build a tower
without first sitting down and calculating its expenses, to see whether he has enough to finish it? Otherwise, when he begins to build and does not finish,
everyone who passes by and sees it will jeer and mock him, saying, 'This man began but could not finish.'
And what king goes to war to fight another king and to confront with ten thousand the one coming against him with twenty thousand,
without sending envoys and asking for peace if he cannot confront the multitude of the other king's forces in battle?
See, through these things, the one who called you to be his disciple has taught you not to begin this journey unless you are resolved to complete it.
Do not lay foundations to build a tower if you do not intend to finish it.
And do not go out to battle against Satan unless you have gathered armies of powerful thoughts.
Otherwise, when you go out to battle, the enemy may defeat you, and discipleship will be maligned.
For someone who makes no promise is not required by the principle of justice to do what he has not promised. Until the promise is made, it is a matter of choice.
But from the promise onward, it is a matter of law. For as long as the yoke of commitment has not been placed upon your soul's freedom,
your service is a matter of your own choice. But if you take on the sign of discipleship and the pledge of Christ's covenant,
your conduct is no longer a matter of your own choice, but must follow the demands of the law that you willingly imposed upon yourself.
If, while you are in the world, you do what a disciple does, this is to your credit. But if, within discipleship itself, you do the things that befit it,
you are thereby paying a debt and fulfilling what has been laid upon you.
For consider how high the tower is to rise, and what stones and courses of masonry its structure is to be made of,
and only then lay its foundation. Do not begin a building that will expose you to the laughter of those who see it.
Do not make yourself an object of contempt and mockery in the sight of many. Do not give passersby a reason to speak against you.
If you are determined to be a disciple, act as your master's will requires; otherwise, remain in the world.
Do not strive to be honored with a title you do not deserve. Do not hold a pure pearl in filthy hands.
Do not put on the purple robes of discipleship when you do not possess the knowledge that safeguards them.
Consider within yourself what discipleship requires you to do, and only then place its yoke upon yourself.
For many become disciples so that they may be honored through the name of Christ, and not so that they may honor Christ.
They enter his service to enjoy bodily comforts, not to bear the hardships of his commandments.
Others, out of a desire for wealth, approach this way of life that requires renunciation,
so that they may go out and acquire outside the world what they could not acquire from the world.
Through that one lax disciple described in our Savior's Gospel, Jesus exposed this wicked intention in all such spies.
It says that someone came forward and said to him, “Teacher, I will follow you wherever you go.” Jesus said to him,
“Foxes have holes, and the birds of the sky have shelters, but the Son of Man
has nowhere to rest his head.” That is to say, “Go away from me, wicked disciple.
I do not have what you desire to give you, and you are unwilling to receive what I give. I know what your will is seeking,
and I do not give what you are looking for. For it was your love of the thought of riches that made you wish to follow me.
You have come out to seek darkness amid light, poverty amid true possessions, and death amid life.
The things you tell everyone to leave behind and follow me—you wish to acquire those very things by coming to me.
Through the very door by which I wish to lead you out, you have struggled to enter and come to me. That is why I do not accept you.
For in my outward condition I am poor, and therefore I have no outward possessions to give in the world into which I have come.
I appear as a stranger, having neither a house nor a shelter. Whoever wishes to be my disciple
inherits poverty from me. Why do you wish to acquire from me the very thing whose possession I am stripping you of?”
Since, then, many go out after Jesus with thoughts of the love of wealth, and put on the honored garb of his discipleship
as though taking up a trade, he exposed this deceitful intention beforehand by his words.
And through that one man he exposed all the false disciples and kept them from becoming his disciples by saying:
“I have nothing to give you of what you desire, and I do not even have a house or a shelter.”
But those who begin and then grow weary and slack, either through love of comfort or because of the labor of building, he held back by saying:
“If you have sufficient funds for the tower; otherwise, it is wiser not to begin than to begin and not finish.”
For Jesus showed us here that he requires perfection from all the disciples who follow him.
For this tower, which rises to heaven, is completed through perfection and finished by bringing together every good thing.
And Jesus himself said, “If you will finish it, begin; otherwise, do not begin it.”
It is as though someone were to say, “If you will be a perfect disciple, complete in every victory; otherwise, remain in the world,
and practice that other righteousness, the righteousness of justice, which is below spirituality.”
Thus he held back each of these people whose requests were improper, giving them an answer suited to them.
To the one who was reluctant to distress his relatives and wanted to repay them with human affection,
and asked him for permission to go and say farewell to his household and then follow him,
he said, “No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God.”
And to the one who wanted to honor his earthly parents while they were alive and then become a disciple after their death, he said:
“Let the dead bury their dead.” And to another, who, through the perfection of Christ’s own teaching,
wanted to satisfy his greedy desire, he answered, “Who appointed me judge and divider over you?”
And to another, who wanted to gather wealth in his name and, through the mighty deeds, signs, and wonders that he performed by his authority,
was scheming to become an owner of property, he said, “I am poor, and I have nowhere to lay my head.”
And to another, who wanted to enter this service merely because he was drawn by its outward appearance, he said:
“Do not begin the tower if you do not have the funds to finish it.”
And again, to another who was weak and had little strength, and had not yet gained mastery over purity of thought and serenity of soul,
but wanted to fight against the opposing powers, he said, “No king goes out to war against another king
unless he gathers enough troops to meet the enemy who opposes him.”
Through these things, then, Jesus exposed all diseased thoughts.
And he gave the disciple the true soundness of discipleship and the very substance of spiritual conduct.
For even in worldly affairs, unless a person frees himself from doing other things,
and devotes himself solely to the work he wants to do, he cannot complete it properly. How much more, then, is this true of spiritual work:
a person cannot accomplish it unless he frees himself from work involving everything visible.
As blessed Paul also said, everyone who competes restrains his mind from everything.
And what contest was he speaking of, if not the bodily athletic competition of this world?
And if work involving bodily things is an obstacle to bodily competition, how much more will it oppose spiritual competition!
For there, in worldly competition, all these things are of one nature and belong to the same realm:
the contest, its struggle and its victory, and also the affairs that hinder its triumph.
And although all these things are closely related to one another, the world, with its cares and concerns, becomes an obstacle to those who compete.
Here, then, where the contest and the work are spiritual, and the way of life is above the world,
how can a person accomplish it if he is entangled in and held fast by worldly affairs?
And Paul himself also said that no one who serves as a soldier and is entangled in worldly affairs can please the one who chose him.
And if someone competes, he is not crowned unless he competes according to the rules. Now, if soldiers of an earthly kingdom free themselves from everything,
so that they may learn the skills of their service and thereby please the king who chose them,
what disciple chosen for this spiritual service can excel in it while entangled in worldly affairs?
Let us also consider Simon’s words to our Lord, and learn from him, that first disciple,
how we ought to be disciples. “Look,” he said, “we have left everything and followed you.
What, then, will we have?” Have you heard what this disciple said, and how he revealed to you the reality of their complete renunciation,
and that they possessed nothing else besides Jesus? “We have left everything,” he said, “and followed you.”
Here is the clearly defined rule of discipleship. For they did not give up one thing and keep another, leaving something behind and holding on to something else.
Rather, they left everything and went after Jesus. You too must leave everything and go after him,
and see how he immediately clothes you with the power of the apostles. Try it in practice and learn
that this saying is not false. For you must not demand that he make you worthy to behold his hidden, spiritual riches
when you have not stripped yourself of everything visible. For as long as you hold on to what is yours, he does not show you what is his.
Give everything you have solely out of love for him, taking care over the gift you give.
also from the thought that seeks human praise; and go out and travel lightly along the way,
bearing afflictions and hardships while keeping your thoughts pure.
And see how his glory immediately dawns within your soul, and he mingles you with it in spirit, so that you are wholly absorbed in his love,
and you forget even the weight of your afflictions, and he suddenly makes you a different person from the one you were.
That is, he makes you new instead of old. Otherwise, what benefit is it to you
that, while your purse is full—and perhaps you even collect fixed charges and interest—and you keep your own possessions and live off his generosity,
you want to become his disciple and have him give you authority over the treasures of his wealth? Far be it from him, however, to make the knowledge of his revelations dwell
within a soul unworthy of him. Indeed, if those occupied with trade and the cares of human wealth
are greatly hindered from acquiring worldly knowledge, do you want to acquire spiritual knowledge while occupied with the cares of wealth?
Did you want him to pour the new wine of the wisdom of his mysteries into the worn-out vessel of your being, riddled with passions and desires,
without your spilling this knowledge onto the ground if it came into you? That is, even your old vessel itself would not have been able to receive it.
Our Savior himself explained this beforehand in his clear teaching:
“No one pours new wine into worn-out wineskins, lest the wine burst the wineskins, and the wine be spilled and the wineskins ruined.
Instead, they pour new wine into new wineskins, and both are preserved.”
For as long as sin, in deed or thought, lives and works within you, and worldly concern for the body stirs within you,
you are still an old vessel and cannot receive the new wine of Christ’s wisdom.
Renew yourself, then, by stripping off your passions, and immediately you will be able to hold within yourself the new wine of Christ’s teaching.
Leave everything, as the apostles did, and then you may boldly ask
to be given authority over the treasures of the Spirit. Do not turn back, and see that the furrows ahead of you are straight.
For your hand rests on the plow of carrying out the difficult and demanding commandments.
Do not turn back to look at comforts. If you have renounced something, do not again acknowledge what you renounced.
And do not look forward at one moment and backward at another. Instead, keep your gaze fixed straight ahead.
For someone who looks backward and forward is like a person who walks back and forth,
and returns again and again to the same spot, never moving away from the place where he stands.
No one says that such a person is traveling along a road or completing a path by his steps. So it is also with a disciple.
At one time he looks ahead, and at another he turns back; at one time he is full of sorrow,
and at another, laughter. At one time he purifies his thoughts, and at another they are defiled by wicked reflections.
At one time he bears the weight of affliction, and at another he enjoys comforts; at one time he engages in prolonged fasting,
and at another in undisciplined eating; at one time he occupies himself with prayer, and at another with talk that pours out empty words.
For at one time the remembrance of God is within him, and at another his soul is dead to that remembrance.
At one time he longs to cast off his life and be with Christ, and at another he clothes himself in bodily comforts and finds them pleasant.
At one time his entire mind is stirred by the Spirit, and at another it drifts among empty reflections.
At one time he is filled with wonder at God, and at another his mind is clouded by bodily concerns; at one time he purifies his mind of the stirring of lust,
and at another he even longs to commit adultery. At one time he fasts without measure, and at another he eats without discipline.
At one time he gives away his possessions out of love for God, and at another he is gripped by distress over having given them away; at one time he is full of love for other people,
and at another he burns because he cannot take revenge on his enemies. At one time the light of knowledge shines within him,
and at another his mind is darkened by the world's errors; at one time he advances steadily,
and at another he walks backward. At one time he is wholly and completely immersed in the Spirit, and at another he is wholly and completely immersed in the flesh.
If, then, amid these things a person goes and comes, advances and turns back, walks onward and retreats, ascends and descends, becomes refined and becomes coarse,
is polished and is stained, becomes radiant and becomes filthy, is cleansed and is defiled, becomes modest and becomes shameless, empties himself and becomes greedy,
denies and confesses, practices restraint and indulges desire—with these things and others like them, the path of discipleship is not brought to completion.
Rather, the person who is in this condition stands in the same place and does not advance beyond the place where he stands.
For this reason he does not attain what he is pursuing. But how can he attain it when he is not running?
If, then, this person who set out on the journey, advancing and walking forward,
and who spent, so to speak, half his life in the practice of discipleship, because he served both sides,
could not hold on to the one, how will someone who has not sought goodness with his whole being, except in name, find it?
And how will someone who has not experienced the ardor of love for Christ even for a short time gain mastery at the summit of love?
But if the person who walked as though alive was found to be dead, what will become of someone who is truly dead?
You have set out, then, after Jesus: walk after him and do not turn back. Remember Lot's wife,
who, compelled by love for her relatives and the sound of her loved ones' cries of lamentation, turned and looked behind her.
She became a pillar of salt, as it is written about her. And because her soul had not been salted with the fear of the Most High,
she became a perishable mass of salt. Remember, then, this woman who wavered and perished, and do not waver as she did.
Do not turn back, lest you remain fixed where you are. For this will happen to you, even if not in your body, then in your soul.
For whoever turns and looks back after setting out on this journey—his soul becomes a pillar without feeling.
And just as Lot’s wife lost her bodily awareness and thus became a pillar of salt,
so here too, the mind that constantly looks back becomes inactive and numb, losing its awareness of spiritual things,
as it looks at perishable things. For remembering the world makes our hearts dull,
and stains the soul’s clarity and purity; and that clear sight which it used to give the mind through constant contemplation directed toward God—
this bodily preoccupation dims and darkens it. And if thinking about bodily things deprives us of the vision of spiritual things,
how much more will actually possessing them deprive us! And if, when we look at these things
in other people’s hands, they bind us to themselves, how much more will they bind us when they are in our own hands!
Leave the world, then, disciple, in the same way that the apostles left it: in deed, not in name;
in thought, not merely figuratively; in will, not in outward appearance; in desire, not in occupation; through discernment, not through tradition;
in freedom, not under compulsion of law. Renew within yourself, day by day, the desire for this spiritual way of life.
Taste life by putting to death within yourself everything that is dead. Take courage and cross this frightening region that lies between.
For it is frightening and deep. It is a [?] full of vicious beasts and harmful, deadly creeping creatures.
And if you resolve in your mind to cross this frightening region, and your will is fully prepared, grace immediately welcomes you and becomes your companion.
Do not focus on the fact that soul and body are joined to one another and naturally mingled with each other.
Rather, there is a vast region between them, a frightening depth into which not everyone can venture and cross.
But if you restrain the body in its desires, with sorrow, prayer, and compassion accompanying you, you will be able to cross this frightening region.
But since our discussion now concerns leaving the world, and not leaving the passions within,
let us speak only about this. “We have left everything,” they said, “and followed you.”
Here is a saying that provides instruction common to all disciples. Keep it constantly in your soul’s remembrance.
At the beginning of your discipleship, let it be your meditation, and, remembering its encouragement, leave the world.
And as you travel the road of departure, let it be your companion. Reflect on it at all times.
And if any of your wealth urges you to keep it with you, or love for friends and family binds you to it,
remember the words of Simon, who left everything, and leave everything yourself, as he did.
For Jesus is as near to you as he was to Simon—and perhaps even nearer than he was to him when he spoke those words.
For they had not yet received the power to be spiritually united with the love of Jesus.
Rather, in the simplicity of their faith, they went out after him upon seeing his deeds and experiencing the sweetness of his words.
And while he drew them after himself with a word, they followed him with resolute action.
For “Come after me” was a word, and as soon as they heard the word, they began to act.
But your own attachment to Jesus today is an accomplished act, since he has united you with the life of the Spirit through baptism.
While he brought the apostles near to himself with a word at that time, today he has actually united you with his own person,
by making you a spiritual member of himself through baptism. However much you follow him through your deeds, his deed precedes you.
If you run toward him, he already dwells in you. If you go toward him by your own choice, he comes toward you first.
However much you strive and run, even if your love and service were to surpass those of the apostles—which is impossible—you are still far below them,
and you do not reach the measure of their loving union with Jesus.
Yet even though your deeds fall far short, he brings you to that point through his grace. For the apostles’ love was a marvel:
at a time when the Holy Spirit had not yet been united with their nature, they accompanied Jesus with all that fervor.
And this was not because he stirred them up or coaxed them, as he coaxes you today with every kind of persuasion.
Rather, he spoke to them from above and, to all appearances, openly drove them away from himself.
“If you want to go, go,” he told them at that time,
when many left him and went away because of the harshness of his words. Simon said to him, “To whom shall we go?
For we have gone out after you once and for all, and we have nowhere to go away from you. For you have the words of eternal life.
That is, your words are life. How can we leave life and go after death?
For we have left everything and come after you, because we have believed and know that you are the Christ, the Son of the living God.”
So you too, disciple, if you have believed as Simon believed, go out as Simon went out.
Leave everything and follow your rich Master. For he lacks nothing that would require you to take provisions of wealth from a foreign land.
His wealth is not limited, so that you must support him from the surplus of your own wealth to keep him from being in need.
For your part, strive to leave everything behind. For giving you everything is his part.
This is what he promised you through Simon. Could Simon have become a disciple of one teacher,
and you of another, so that you do not go out after your teacher as he went out? But if you do not go out as he did,
it is clear that you have become a disciple of another teacher, however much you may think you are a disciple of Jesus.
For both are set out for you in the same place: the manner of your departure and the reward for your departure.
For you learn how you should go out from the words, “Look, we have left everything and followed you.”
And our Lord’s words show you what the reward for this departure is.
He says, “Truly I tell you, in the new world, when the Son of Man sits on his glorious throne,
you too will sit on twelve thrones and judge the twelve tribes of Israel.”
Look at the reward for this departure: sharing with Jesus in exalted honor.
For he prepared thrones for the disciples opposite his own throne. And what is impossible by nature, he showed by his word would come to pass.
For he did not promise to honor the disciples who loved his word as slaves or as subjects.
Rather, as friends and equals in his honor, he made them worthy of the greatness of thrones. And this is the wonder of love beyond words.
For it is written of the angels, “A thousand thousands stand before him, and ten thousand times ten thousand serve him.”
And of the seraphim, that they stand above him and fly, calling to one another and saying, “Holy, holy, holy.”
And again it is written of the cherubim that they are yoked to the chariot, and while their faces gaze downward, the impulses of their spirits attend to the bidding of the Most High.
They too cry out, “Blessed is the glory of the Lord from his place.”
The spiritual beings stand in this service, and the heavenly hosts and orders are obedient to the word of Jesus.
As Paul said, they are ministering spirits sent out to serve for the sake of those who are to inherit life.
But of the apostles it is written that they will sit on thrones. For the greatness of their honor and their equality with him in the inheritance,
he made known to us through this. As Paul himself also said, “If we suffer with him, we will also be glorified with him.” And again he said,
“Heirs of God and fellow heirs with Jesus Christ.” And again he said, “If we endure, we will also reign with him.” And again he said,
“He will transform our lowly body and make it like his glorious body, according to his great power, by which everything has been subjected to him.”
The disciple, then, attains this greatness if he follows perfectly in his teacher’s footsteps.
And so that you will not think this share of honor came to the apostles alone, Paul said:
For if we suffer with him, we will also be glorified with him; and if we endure, we will also reign with him.
And our Lord himself said to the apostles, “Not only you, but everyone who leaves houses or family,
or brothers or sisters, or parents or children, for my sake and for the sake of my gospel, will receive a hundredfold in this world,
and eternal life in the world to come.” What sleeper would not awaken at the sound of these promises?
And what dead person would not come to life through these bellows of spiritual life?
And who would not become swift instead of sluggish when shown this road that leads up to heaven?
And who would not wish to be despised and dishonored on hearing his incomparable promise?
And who would not renounce the whole world, even if he happened to possess it,
so that he might sit with God on the throne? And who would not wish to exchange temporal things for eternal things?
For even if the things we leave behind were equal to the things given to us,
we ought to leave them because God commanded it. How much more now that they are contemptible and worthless!
Even if we do not abandon them because of Christ’s word, nature itself requires us to detach ourselves from them
and rise above them. These things are of no use: we are exchanging nothing for something.
Who would not run to a fair where such an exchange takes place? For look: rags are exchanged for purple robes,
and worthless pebbles for pearls, and ordinary stones for beryl stones; boundless poverty
for immeasurable wealth; worthless counterfeit metal for pure gold; darkness for light;
death for life; bitterness for sweetness; sickness for health; dishonor for authority;
lowly status for leadership; things that decay for things beyond decay;
what dissolves for what does not pass away; shadows for substance; hunger for fullness; error for knowledge;
the way of life of beasts for the way of life of angels; bodily existence for spiritual existence; boundless misery
for immeasurable blessedness. And still more than this, if we had the words
to speak of these things as they deserve! Who would not exchange these things for those?
And who would not give up all this deprivation for all that kingdom? But because the word of the Spirit,
even when spoken plainly, is higher than all the wisdom of the world,
Paul revealed to us in one brief statement the greatness of this exchange, and how inferior the things we have are.
And he showed us how great the things of God are in one short saying: “The things that are seen are temporary, but the things that are not seen are eternal.”
Who, then, would not exchange these temporary things for those eternal things, except us and fools like us?
But you who renounce the things that are seen, do not ask what the wealth you receive in exchange for your poverty is like.
Instead, strive for this: to leave your poverty behind and run to acquire that wealth.
As for what it is like and what it resembles, Paul explains to you—not what it is like,
but that it has no likeness; and not how much it amounts to, but that it cannot be measured. He says, “What no eye has seen,
and no ear has heard, and what has not entered the human heart—what God has prepared for those who love him.”
For the greatness of the rewards is revealed through these words and others like them.
But listen to the divine words that urge you to set out after Jesus and to be completely stripped of possessions.
Then you will be a perfect disciple. For he says, “Whoever does not renounce everything he has
cannot be my disciple.” After this, what do you have to say or offer in reply?
For look, with a single saying all your suppositions and excuses are nullified.
The word of truth is a lofty path for you to walk on. And again, in another place he said,
“Whoever does not leave everything he has, take up his cross, and come after me cannot be my disciple.”
And again, teaching that we should not only leave our possessions for his glory and renounce the world to confess our faith in him,
but also renounce our passing lives, he said, “Unless someone renounces himself, he cannot be my disciple.”
And again he said, “Whoever wants to save his life will lose it, and whoever loses his life for my sake will save it.”
And again he said, “Whoever loses his life will preserve it for eternal life.
And whoever serves me, the Father will honor.” And again he said to his disciples, “Get up, let us go from here.”
By this he showed that this was not his place—neither his nor his disciples’. Where shall we go, our Lord?
He says, “Where I am, my servant will also be.” If Jesus calls to us, “Get up, let us go from here,”
what fool would agree to live with corpses inside tombs and make his home among the dead?
So whenever the world wants to hold you close to itself, or your relatives, your family, or your friends do,
remember the words of Christ, who said, “Get up, let us go from here.” This call is enough to startle you, if you are alive.
For whenever you want to settle down so that you can rest, or your soul looks with affection on the place where you are,
Remember this urging voice, and say to yourself, “Get up, let us go from here.”
For you must go in any case, but go as Jesus goes.
Go because he told you to, and not because nature itself carries you away against your will.
For whether you wish it or not, you stand on the road of travelers. But make your journey because of your Lord’s word, and not from unavoidable necessity.
“Get up, let us go from here.” This is a voice that awakens those sunk in sleep. It is a horn whose blast drives away the sleep of laziness.
It is power, not merely a word, for it suddenly clothes anyone who perceives it with new strength.
And it carries him from one thing to another as swiftly as the blink of an eye.
And so that the disciple does not linger in the ease that keeps him seated, this word of God makes him spring up.
“Get up, let us go from here.” Look, he himself is going with you! Why are you lingering? For he did not tell you, “Get up and go.”
Instead, he said, “Get up, let us go, you and I together.” God is calling you to go in his company.
Who would not become eager and hurry, so as not to fall behind the company of God who called him?
For on this road there is neither anxiety nor fear, neither loss nor deceit, neither bandits nor thieves.
And even if people stand along it to block your way, as long as the Lord is with you, they all flee before you.
For what bandit would dare to appear in his robber’s guise on a road along which the king is passing?
Instead, when evildoers hear news of him, they either flee or hide.
Look, from this too you learn to leave behind the world’s way of life, if you understand and listen discerningly to the force of the saying.
But to another man who, out of a desire for a perfect way of life, wanted to follow Jesus,
Jesus showed this same road of perfection—to this teacher too—in a manner suited to him.
It says that someone approached him while he was teaching in the temple and said to him, “Good teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?”
And what did Jesus say to this man? “Why do you call me good? No one is good except God alone.”
“You know the commandments: Do not murder. Do not commit adultery. Do not steal. Do not give false testimony.”
“See, I have taught you to refrain from evil and to turn your desire away from the paths of sin.”
“But if you also want to advance beyond this, and to move from not doing evil to doing good,
and to keep the commandments of the law, honor your father and your mother, and keep all the commandments that belong with this.”
“But if you also want to rise above the compulsion of the law through the freedom of your righteousness,
And by your own free choice, conduct yourself in good deeds, beyond fear of the sentence of judgment. Love the Lord your God with all your soul,
and with all your strength, and with all your mind. And do not do to your neighbor what is hateful to you.
This is the way of life of the righteous, which is above the compulsion of the law. Moses and the prophets taught this righteousness.
Over anyone who observes this, the law has no authority to threaten his righteousness. Go, observe these things that are written,
and rise beyond them also to love for God and for your neighbor, a love that is above fear of the law.
For it is love. And when you observe these things, you will inherit eternal life. These are the things Jesus taught that arrogant teacher to do,
although he was unwilling to stop at them, and with an arrogant mind was seeking things greater than these.
But what he did not teach that man ought to be sound instruction for us disciples,
so that we may learn from this saying how to turn away from evil deeds and, little by little, advance and grow in the practice of good deeds.
For what he said to him—“Do not murder, do not commit adultery, do not steal, and do not bear false witness”—agrees with what David said:
“Turn away from evil and do good,” and with what Paul said: “Do not let evil overcome you.”
But the saying, “Honor your father and your mother, and do not do to your neighbor what is hateful to you,”
is like the saying, “Do good, and overcome evil with good.”
And the saying, “Love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul,
and with all your mind, and your neighbor as yourself,” is like the saying, “The law is not laid down for the righteous.”
For these commandments are above fear of the law.
Thus Jesus established these levels of conduct in these commandments.
First, a person should turn away from evil deeds and refrain from practicing anything hateful.
Second, he should do those things that are prescribed under fear of the law.
Third, the practice of good deeds that is above fear of the law.
Fourth, the beginning of the path of discipleship to Christ, which is a complete departure from the world.
Fifth, the labors and afflictions by which we weaken our old self.
Sixth, we should carry the cross on our shoulders and attain the fullness of Christ’s perfection.
Thus, in these things two ways of life have been distinguished for us, and we have learned two forms of righteousness.
Each of them consists of three stages: to refrain from evil deeds; to obey and fear the law.
And let us do good things, so that we may be above the law by willingly practicing good deeds, concerning which Paul taught us:
“The law is not laid down for the righteous.” For this reason he raised those who practice these deeds above the authority of the law.
These three orders of righteousness, then, are practiced in the world.
