Those who practice them are upright and righteous, but they are neither spiritual nor perfect. Two of these orders
are placed above the fear of the law. But the third order is above both the compulsion and the fear of the law,
because it is fulfilled within the heart and the hidden mind, where the law cannot look and see.
For the eye of the law sees outward actions, not hidden thoughts.
But the love of someone who loves God with all his heart, mind, and soul is hidden.
More particularly, he said, “Love your God”—something that is above the law—
and not, “Fear God,” because the law has authority over fear, not over love.
For love is above the commandment of the law, and the law has no authority over those who are guided by love.
The third order, then, occupies the middle position: it is higher than the law but lower than Christ’s way of life.
See from this how perfect the teaching of our Life-giver is: what is above the law is only the lowest step of his own teaching.
Our Lord therefore taught these three things for righteous people living in the world to practice.
In them are gathered all the good deeds that are done out of compassion
and are performed for the needy by those who have possessions, through their wealth.
In them lies the entire force of this commandment: “Do not do to your neighbor what is hateful to you.”
As the Teacher himself also explained, “This is the Law and the Prophets.” But concerning his own righteousness, which is above the law,
he said, “Enter through the narrow gate.” For over there, under the law, you are sometimes confined and sometimes given room,
and sometimes you labor and sometimes you rest. Your whole life of righteousness is woven from these things and others like them.
But here, concerning Christ’s way of life, it is written, “Enter through the narrow gate.”
For our Lord, acting well and as a wise and good teacher, guided his disciples and brought them forward step by step through the things of the old and the things of the new:
first, to show that he himself is the giver of both the former things and the latter;
and second, to lead the disciples step by step from lesser things to greater things,
and from “Love as you love yourself” to loving more than you love yourself.
And from “Give some of what you have” to “Distribute everything you have.”
And from “A little of your property” to “Give away all your property.”
For he put first what is easiest of all: that a person should not do evil.
For someone who was restrained from practicing evil by the punishments prescribed by the law
could easily advance to doing the good things that the law commands, because of his fear of the law itself.
And someone who was disciplining his outward actions and doing good
would also advance to being obligated to God and his neighbor with all his heart—not for show, nor to win approval,
nor out of fear, but because it is fitting for a human being to love God and his fellow human being. And after he had set these boundaries for us
and explained to us these ranks in the righteousness of the just, he went further in his teaching to teach us perfection.
And he said to the scribe who was questioning him—while through him teaching all the disciples—
“If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all your property and give to the poor,
and you will have treasure in heaven.” Yet even here we have not yet begun on the path of righteousness.
For taking up one's cross and going after Jesus is another way of life.
For just as living in the womb is one thing, and the child's coming out of the womb is another,
and a person's being in the world after birth from the womb is yet another, so it is one thing to take shape and develop limbs
and acquire a human body within the womb, with all its senses and limbs, and another thing to be born,
and yet another to be in the world. For righteousness within the world is like the formation of an infant within the womb.
And the saying, “Sell all your property and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven,”
is the womb through which a person is born from the old womb into the new creation. It is the gate through which a person goes out from one world into another.
But the saying, “Take up your cross and come after me,” concerns the way of life of perfection and the path of spiritual life.
For it seems a great thing for a person to sell everything he has and give to the poor, and to leave the world stripped of everything.
Yet this is still natural, and it is the condition in which we enter creation at our first birth. The first human being, too,
was created this way. That is why righteous Job also, when everything he had was taken away
and he was deprived of possessions and heirs, because it seemed that something unprecedented had happened to him,
something beyond nature, eases the severity of his suffering with his words and says:
“For I came naked from my mother’s womb, and naked I will return.” What, he says, was new for me, apart from the very state in which I came out of the womb?
For a person to renounce everything he has and appear in the world with nothing but his own self
is still a natural thing. But it becomes something above nature if it is done willingly for God’s sake.
Just as dying is natural, but dying for God’s sake is martyrdom,
in the same way, for a person to appear alone in the world, possessing nothing, is also a natural thing.
For Adam was created this way, and Eve was formed this way.
They lacked not only the world’s wealth but also the world’s clothing and coverings.
They were like a baby that comes naked out of the womb into the outside world.
As Job also said, “I came out naked, and naked I will return.”
And as Paul also said, “We brought nothing into the world, and it is clear that we cannot take anything out of it either.”
And just as the placenta in the womb, after the baby is formed and takes shape,
then wraps around him to preserve his life, and when he is born from the womb,
it is cut off and thrown away from him, because it is not part of his own being and is not counted as part of the person,
so too wealth and possessions, together with all other human things, attach themselves to a person after he is born, like a placenta.
And when he comes to be born again from this world into another world through death, his possessions are cut off and thrown away from him,
like a placenta cut off from the body. And just as the baby appears as his own self, apart from the placenta, so a person leaves life
stripped of all his possessions. And just as being born wrapped in one’s placenta,
and having it stripped off upon entering the world, is natural, so too for a person to leave the world naked,
or to renounce his possessions while he is still in the world, is natural.
But a person gains favor when he takes the initiative in stripping himself of his wealth,
before nature strips him, and by his own free choice anticipates the time of his departure.
What difficulty, then, is there in this commandment, that a person should renounce all his possessions?
For this is a natural commandment. Let a person look at his beginning and his end, and conduct himself in the same way during the time between them.
Just as he entered naked and leaves naked, so let him be stripped of his wealth
throughout his stay in the world, and let him give thanks to the one who brings that stay to an end.
for what belongs to nature to become a matter of choice. Our Lord therefore rightly did not make it the beginning of the path of discipleship:
renunciation of wealth, because it belongs to nature, whereas his way of life is above nature.
For just as our human death is not the beginning of the path of the world to come, but our death is the end of the path of this world,
and our resurrection from the dead is the beginning of the path of the kingdom of heaven, so too renunciation of wealth and visible possessions
is the end of the path of this world and the removal of the foreign garment which, after entering the world,
we put on within the world. And if it seems difficult, it is not because it is above nature.
For look: it is easy for those who stand in the freedom of nature.
But this is difficult for those who are subject to the passions and serve desires as slaves.
Those who serve Mammon as a master are afraid to renounce it,
because they have already willingly made it their god. And it is not only this passion that people fear—
those who are subject to it—but every passion under whose authority freedom is yoked is its master,
and the constraint of fear of it lies upon that freedom, which cannot easily cast it off.
Take this as evidence that the passions do not enslave us by force, but our freedom has subjected itself to the passions,
and they have become its masters. For look at those who stand in the freedom of their souls
and cast off this garment of concern for possessions: if someone tries to force them to become enslaved to wealth,
they are more afraid of becoming its owners than the wealthy are afraid of abandoning it.
And if renunciation of possessions were naturally frightening or difficult, everyone would be afraid of it,
and its authority would naturally rule over everyone. But look: free people are above subjection to it,
and their sovereign freedom regards it as bitter slavery.
Therefore all the commandments of righteousness and mercy that a person carries out while living in the world
are still on this side of the boundary of nature. For this reason, the whole ancient Law and its commandments
were placed under nature, because it was not possible for the Law to be above nature.
But when our Lord was asked by Nicodemus, the scribe of the Law, “What is your teaching?”
he said, “I proclaim rebirth to human beings.”
And although in this saying he also alludes to baptism, it also points still more strongly to this:
That a person is born from one world into another through the power of God's grace and also through the power of his own will.
And complete renunciation of everything the eye sees becomes the womb that gives him birth.
Thus, the person who belongs to God is seen to undergo three births. The first birth is from the womb into the world.
The second is from slavery into freedom, and from being a human being to becoming a child of God.
This happens by grace, through baptism. And the third birth is:
When the person himself is born, by his own will, from a bodily way of life into a spiritual one, and the womb that gives him birth becomes
renunciation of everything, together with the other births that follow this birth of renunciation, through which a person is born when he leaves the world behind.
Such are the passage from bodily existence into spiritual existence, and from passions into freedom from passions,
and the complete transition from all the impulses that stir the old person to the living movements of the spiritual person.
For these stages, measures, and births exist within this way of life.
And however far a person wishes to advance, there is room for his steps.
For the realm of spiritual existence is a spacious place without limit.
Now, if even within this bodily world there is room for a person's steps however far he travels,
and if a person were to travel throughout his entire lifetime, he could not reach the world's limit by his journeys,
how much further may we travel in that spiritual world, where our journey has no end!
And the further a person goes inward, rises, and enters, a place deeper within than the last and a stage higher than the last receive him.
For it is a world without limit. This world, however great it may be, is subject to limits and boundaries.
But that world is above boundaries and beyond limits. Blessed is the one who has been found worthy and has entered it,
through the change from the old person into the new, putting to death within himself every bodily stirring,
and awakening to other movements, living and spiritual. And he rightly said,
"Unless a person is born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God."
For unless a person empties himself of everything in the world and strips off the entire bodily way of life, in both its hidden and its outward aspects,
just as an infant leaves its natural womb and is born into this world, he cannot see the kingdom of God.
That is, he cannot perceive the living movements of the spirit, which lie deeper within than bodily perception.
Let this, then, be an illustration for you: just as an infant is enclosed within the womb, so a person who is in the world is enclosed.
In the bodily way of life of the world, with all its heaviness and darkness, its coarseness, its anxiety and its concerns.
And just as an infant is born from the womb through the opening of the womb into this light of creation,
and, once born, sees all things in the light that it finds before it,
and the beauty of the world, all the diversity of created works, and the intermingling of the natures in this composite creation,
and receives this sight and experiences these tastes through the gradual growth of its bodily stature,
so too the person who is born anew out of the world's way of life and passes into another, spiritual world through the gate of renunciation,
as soon as he is born and that world receives him, the light of knowledge begins to appear to him.
And just as the things of this world are seen in natural light, and everything is distinguished from everything else by it,
so too, through that spiritual knowledge which a person begins to receive, he sees all spiritual things,
and boundaries and regions, orders and ranks, and everything that lies beyond bodily perception.
For just as the body perceives the things belonging to its nature, because the perceptions of its senses are [?] in relation to the things of the world,
so too the soul, through the mediation of the Spirit, perceives all those things that are akin to its nature and are above the world.
This, then, is also the rebirth, alongside that of baptism, of which our Lord spoke to Nicodemus.
Now let us examine our Lord's reply to that young man who approached him and asked to learn the teaching of perfection,
so that we too may receive perfect knowledge from it and be born from one way of life into another.
When he asked to learn, saying, “What must I do to inherit eternal life?” Jesus said to him, “Do not murder.
Do not commit adultery. Do not steal. Do not give false testimony.” These things consist in keeping away from evil.
And after them comes the practice of good deeds, through the words he spoke: “Honor your father and your mother,
and do not do to your neighbor what is hateful to you.” And he said that anyone who observes these things inherits eternal life.
For the inheritance of eternal life belongs to all the righteous, the just, the merciful, and those who do good,
while they live in the world. These are also called blessed by the living word of our Lord,
when he said to them, “Come, you who are blessed by my Father, and inherit the kingdom that was prepared for you before the foundations of the world.
For I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink,” along with the rest of what our Lord said to them.
All these things apply to the righteous people of old who lived in the world, and to the just who also possess wealth.
For the person who clothes the naked, welcomes strangers, and prepares a table for the hungry,
And he provides those in need with everything required for the body; clearly, this is because he owns possessions.
For these things cannot be done without wealth.
But those who have renounced possessions have no wealth with which to do these good deeds—much less the spiritual and the perfect.
Thus this promise given here by our Lord is not only inapplicable to the perfect and the spiritual,
but also to those who have renounced possessions, because they too have no wealth with which to do these good deeds.
But how much higher the rank of those who have renounced possessions is than that of the righteous is clear
from the fact that everyone acknowledges that the person who owns absolutely nothing is higher—
having completely stripped himself of his wealth out of love for God—than the person who keeps his wealth
and does good deeds with it. Again, the spiritual are higher than those who have renounced possessions, and the perfect are higher than the spiritual.
For spirituality is a likeness to the spiritual powers, while perfection is an image of the fullness of Christ.
Through it, all who attain the stature of the knowledge of the fullness of Christ are made perfect in the Spirit, as Paul said.
As for how much higher this rank of the perfect and the spiritual is than that of the righteous and merciful who are in the world,
our Savior’s own words, spoken to those who possess worldly wealth, are sufficient:
“Make an effort,” he said, “and make friends for yourselves with unrighteous wealth, so that when it runs out, they may receive you into their eternal dwellings.”
See, then: the perfect, like owners of the place and citizens of the city, receive the righteous strangers who enter their world.
For they are coheirs with Christ and heirs of the Father in heaven.
As Paul said of them, “Heirs of God and coheirs with Jesus Christ.”
And to make known that they attained this measure because they carry Christ’s cross, he said:
“If we suffer with him, we will also be glorified with him.” For sharing in Christ’s sufferings
does not come about through giving alms and showing mercy to those in need,
but through dying completely to the world, to the body, to desires, and to passions, and crucifying the old self
with all its desires, just as Paul also said of himself
that he was crucified to the world, and all awareness of the world had ceased in him, just as it has ceased in those who have died a natural death.
For just as a corpse feels nothing at all that is brought near it, so neither in the person who has been crucified with Christ
and has put the entire old self to death in him is there any awareness of the things of this world.
For this reason Paul too calls those who follow this way of perfection dead.
For the righteous person who lives in the world and has a wife, children, wealth, and possessions cannot be called dead.
For his whole way of life is that of a living person. A dead person neither marries nor fathers children,
whereas among those people there are marriage and childbearing, along with everything else that accompanies these things.
“You have died,” Paul cries out to the perfect, “and your life is hidden with Christ in God.”
And again he said, “You are dead to the world, but alive to God in our Lord Jesus Christ.”
And again he said, “If you have died with Christ to the elements of the world,
why do you accept regulations as though you were living in the world?”
A person reaches this way of life after divesting himself of possessions and beginning to do good works with the members of his own body.
For as long as he has wealth, he practices righteousness through his wealth, and his concern for wealth leaves him no time to work on himself.
Even if he seems to practice these things while still possessing wealth, his work is confused.
That is, he moves forward and then turns back.
Besides this, even if this person engages in the [?] of the body, he cannot remain in purity of thought.
This is the soul’s freedom from passions, through which a person enters into spiritual love, from which is born knowledge
that contemplates everything. From there the mind advances by stages and ascends to divine discourse.
This, then, is why those who long for perfection divest themselves of wealth: so that they may have time to work on themselves.
And, freed from everything in the world, they may wage war against the desires of the body.
A person should work on himself, not on things outside himself. Once he has uprooted the desires of the body and crushed the passions of the soul,
he begins to sow within himself the seed of living knowledge.
Whoever, then, wishes to approach this way of life must be stripped of wealth and be born anew; only then does he enter it.
For otherwise a person cannot enter it, according to Christ’s own testimony.
“If you wish to be perfect,” he says, “go, sell your possessions and give to the poor,
and you will have treasure in heaven. Take up your cross and follow me.” See, then, how perfect Christ’s teaching is:
even when someone has divested himself of everything he has, he has still not begun on the path of his teaching.
For renunciation is the end of the path of righteousness practiced in the world.
But the saying, “Take up your cross and come after me,” is the beginning of the path of spiritual conduct.
Jesus placed the reward in the middle, between the righteous and the perfect: “Go, sell your possessions and give to the poor.”
“And you will have treasure in heaven.” Here is the reward for righteousness, for he calls this recompense “treasure.”
For those who pursue righteousness in the world do good deeds on condition of receiving recompense.
And Jesus fittingly placed the treasure in his saying at the end of the path of righteousness within the world.
Thus, with their reward set before them, they may run straight toward his promise.
They are like those who compete in a contest, with the crown of their victory set before their eyes. But into the realm of the perfect,
our Lord did not introduce recompense, because it is a disgrace for the perfect to practice spiritual conduct for the sake of a reward.
For the very spirituality in which the perfect stand is the reward of the righteous and the just.
For when these people do good deeds within the world, they do so on condition that they will be transformed and become spiritual,
and be freed from all the world's bodily existence, its passions, and its bondage. But for the perfect, this is their way of life.
For they are moved by the Spirit and work by the Spirit, and they have already been transformed from bodily existence to spiritual existence while still in this visible world.
How, then, can they expect to receive as a reward the very thing that is their work here?
For just as an angel does not expect the spirituality of his nature to be a reward for him,
or the very fact that he is sent out and serves the wishes of the divine Being—because he exists in that spirituality and acts in it by nature—
so neither does the perfect person expect a reward in spiritual transformation, because he already stands in that spiritual transformation.
All his activity is like that of the powers of heaven, and his entire way of life resembles theirs.
Like them, he offers praise of holiness in the Spirit and sings in the Spirit, and he serves God in spirit and in truth.
As the Word of God has said concerning the perfect: “God is spirit, and those who worship him
worship him in spirit and in truth.” God, he says, is spirit, and the service of the perfect is spiritual.
So, then, they serve in a divine manner, and they have been raised even above the order of spiritual beings,
so that they too may act in the likeness of God, with authority and freedom,
a freedom that is not enslaved, that rises above laws and commandments, in that likeness which belongs also to God.
We cannot describe in our words the working of the living impulses of the perfect.
For unless someone has reached their stature, he cannot speak about the perfection of their work.
For even they themselves, if they wished, could not describe their living inner movements and their divine service.
For this service does not take place in the body, so that it could be described with a bodily tongue.
Rather, they only perceive it and perform this divine service in their hidden inner self.
Their service cannot be put into words, nor can their inner movements, their perception, or their continual wonder,
nor the visions and revelations that come to them. This is the goal of Christ’s way, O disciples.
At this vision your journey comes to rest, if you run. This is the way of life handed down to us by Christ. Go out, then, from the world,
and empty yourself, in body and soul, of everything in it, so that you may find these things that are beyond words,
and delight in them with all the ranks of light, in the world of truth, in Jesus Christ.
To him be glory from all generations, forever and ever. Amen.
The second discourse, on renunciation and the practice of the spiritual commandments, is finished.
Notes on the Syriac text:
The tenth discourse, against the appetite of the belly, in which he condemns gluttony,
exposing and revealing all its forms, and also rebuking those who enslave their lives to this passion,
and making known that it is impossible to approach the knowledge and practice of any of the achievements of virtue
for people who serve as slaves to their desires.
Although all evil passions and the service of desires are condemned and rejected by the teaching of divine knowledge,
this detestable passion of love for the belly is rejected and condemned more than all of them.
It habitually makes those people who are enslaved to it resemble animals,
because it takes away from them the movements of understanding appropriate to rational beings, and weighs down and darkens their minds with the heaviness of food.
For this foul and detestable passion is the gateway to all evils,
and wherever it gains control, it opens like a great, wide gate to let in every hateful thing.
For it destroys all virtue and hinders all righteousness,
and in every way it opposes all godly labors.
For a person brought low beneath this hateful desire cannot take up the yoke of discipleship to Christ.
For once the belly becomes mistress over the body, it commands it and subjects it to all its wishes.
And instead of the path that leads up to heaven, it shows him this other path that leads down into Sheol.
It hangs on him the weight of food and an excess of provisions, and fills him with moisture and weighs him down through excessive drinking.
So that, when he bears the weight of the food, his lightness is dragged downward, and another body of desire is piled upon his body,
he will easily slip and descend along the downward path that leads into Sheol.
For this passion of gluttony is more loathsome than all the passions. And anyone who has once become its slave
and borne its heavy yoke on his shoulder is no longer given any rest from serving it.
Instead, it makes him work night and day, and sends him wherever it wishes, like a wretched slave.
Not along smooth paths, but along roads full of stumbling blocks, and to a place where losses are found.
For the lover of pleasures has no eyes that see the light.
For even if he has them, they are darkened by the weight of food. Day is night to him, and night is a second death.
His mind is submerged in the heaviness of sleep. His thoughts are scattered by the stupor caused by the moisture of his body.
Even the natural fire within him is cold, because excessive moisture weakens it.
His thoughts are darkened and deprived of knowledge, because the eye of his soul, which perceives through knowledge, has been extinguished.
An excessive weight hangs on him at all times, because another body of food is joined to his body.
Gluttony, then, opposes everything, and is the enemy of every struggle requiring diligence.
It destroys a good name and obstructs every victory.
Not only spiritual victories, but bodily victories as well.
For the appetite of the belly also opposes those things accomplished in the world through diligence and strength.
For everything that brings renown and praise calls for diligence,
and requires sound health, and depends on nimble limbs and vigorous strength.
The love of gluttony opposes all these things. For when strength grows weak from an abundance of food,
and the limbs have lost their vigor, they are no longer ready for action or agile in performing works of righteousness.
And, as I said, if anyone examines the matter with the eye of knowledge, the weight of food opposes everything:
the strength of the body, the knowledge of the soul, the labors of righteousness, acts of mercy, and gifts of alms.
For anyone enslaved to his belly is a beast without discernment, and his entire way of life resembles that of animals.
And while his whole constitution is stirred by bodily passions, he is completely inactive in matters of the soul.
Consider these practices and recognize that gluttony opposes all these achievements that I have mentioned:
learning, knowledge, diligence in worldly affairs, the labors of righteousness, compassion toward other people, love,
and knowledge of God. That it opposes learning is attested even by the world itself, through the tradition it follows concerning learning.
For children who are set apart to receive instruction are kept by their parents from excessive eating.
For greed is a barrier to learning, because when the limbs are burdened with the weight of food,
they cannot bear the lightness of learning, since lightness is the opposite of heaviness.
Children who receive instruction therefore take food in moderation, so that their minds may be [?], their thoughts ready,
and their memories clear enough to receive and retain, because food hinders both.
And it is not only children receiving instruction from books who are restrained from excessive eating.
Rather, along with those who receive instruction and are trained to be diligent in worldly affairs,
those others who possess worldly knowledge also need this.
For no one who has approached knowledge, composition, or discourse fails to recognize that excessive eating opposes these things.
For when the thick vapor from food increases and is not cleared away, it clouds the heart and darkens the mind.
It confuses discernment and closes the door to the production of speech.
It spreads like a covering over all the faculties of perception, hindering and disabling their power to act.
For an eloquent person cannot speak when weighed down with food, nor can a knowledgeable person know, nor an intelligent person understand.
And, so to speak, the entire inner person is darkened by the vapor from the heaviness of food.
For the spiritual and light nature mingled within us seeks spirituality and lightness.
And the more the body is made lean through abstinence, the more it comes to share in that spiritual nature.
And the less excessive weight is laid upon it, the more it acquires lightness, through which it shares in the lightness of the soul.
Thus, through a wise arrangement, the portion belonging to the spirit was placed within the portion belonging to the body.
And the more the body grows heavy through food, the more it draws the soul toward itself and drags it down, attaching its own heaviness to it.
It binds and shackles the wings of the soul’s thoughts. But if its life is sustained by a consistently small amount of food,
it becomes light, clear, and pure, the heaviness of its nature diminishes, and it enlightens and gladdens the soul within it.
And it, in turn, readily obeys her will. Because it becomes light and thin, the soul draws it toward everything she desires.
It does not resist her, nor does its bulk prevent her from placing it wherever she wishes.
For each of them, whether soul or body, draws the other toward its own desires.
For they oppose one another both in their natures and in their desires, according to the words of the apostle, who said:
“The body desires what harms the spirit, and the spirit desires what harms the body, and the two oppose one another.”
But if all the body's desires, according to the words of the wise apostle, oppose the soul,
then this desire, the love of the belly, does so more than all the others. For it is the gateway to all desires, and none of them is as burdensome as it.
For just as a weight is hung on something naturally light and capable of flight and drags it downward,
so it is with this appetite of the belly, for its existence depends on moisture and heaviness.
Although the body itself is naturally heavy, because that is its nature, an additional weight is added to it by an abundance of food.
And when weight is added to weight and body is doubled upon body—that is, the body of food upon the natural body—
the weight bears heavily upon the soul, and the mistress becomes an enslaved servant. The soul no longer governs the body as a free woman,
but carries its weight like a slave. The appetite of the belly also opposes compassion.
For everything that is distributed as a gift of compassion, it diverts to itself and makes its own.
And if it happens to show mercy—which it is incapable of doing—no thought of compassion stirs within it unless it has had its fill.
Thus even when a glutton gives gifts, his gift is seen to come from the fullness of his belly.
This is not compassion, but a likeness to wild animals and livestock. For even a beast, when it has filled its belly,
leaves its manger and lies down. So too the glutton, until he has filled his belly from the table of the things he craves,
cannot be persuaded to look at another with an eye of compassion.
Nor does he give any of what is set before him to someone in need. For, enslaved to his appetite, he imagines
that no one is as needy as he is. And truly, no one is as needy as someone enslaved to his appetite.
For however much a person gives his appetite what it needs, it remains in its state of need.
It is never satisfied by an accumulation of foods. Rather, the more he eats, the more he longs for other foods.
And the more he drinks, the more he craves clear wines.
Thus his food becomes his hunger rather than his satisfaction, and his drink becomes his thirst rather than his relief.
For however much a glutton eats, he is still hungry, and however much he drinks, he is still thirsty.
There is no end to the love of the belly. For when he has filled himself with the first dish,
since his aim is not to satisfy his need but his craving, he seeks another dish better than the first.
And again, when he has taken some of this to gratify his craving, he looks toward another that is more pleasing and tastier than it.
Thus, step by step, his gluttony passes through all the dishes, yet is not satisfied by any of them.
And if he seems to have had enough and withdraws his hand from the food, it is not his craving that has been satisfied, but his belly that has been filled.
It can hold no more. Yet he wishes his belly were as spacious as his craving,
and his stomach were like his eye, so that he could gather everything he craves and put it into his storehouse, open at both ends.
For the glutton is a foolish lover of possessions, who gathers and stores up treasures of the things he craves
in a breached house that retains nothing that enters it. For the Creator too, in order to restrain the craving of gluttons,
made the belly a measure with fixed limits, so that even by necessity, against their will, they would be held back from the things they crave.
But when the will wants to take in great quantities, the cavity of the belly will not receive them.
Has he not, then, been forcibly prevented from pursuing his craving? While his will still craves, that small cavity, unable to hold any more, restrains him.
For if the cavity that receives the things gluttons crave were also as large as their will, sea and dry land would not suffice for them.
Mountains and hills would not be enough for them, and the air and the sun, together with everything in nature, would not satisfy their cravings.
But if even now, when a small vessel has been given to their boundless will, sea and dry land do not suffice for them, and they gather every kind of food without being filled,
and every delicacy without having enough, and they ask and inquire about all the foods that are far away from them,
then if they had a belly to match their will, what would they not do? The glutton, then, is worse even than the animals.
For when an animal has filled its belly, it leaves the rest of its food in the manger,
and does not know how to save it for itself for another time or another day. But it is not so with the glutton.
Rather, because his craving is not satisfied when his belly is filled, once he has filled the measure within it that is naturally appointed to receive food,
his craving takes the remainder and saves it for another day—that is, for days and months.
The glutton sits at the table to meet his needs and thinks about the times yet to come.
He is not concerned merely to sustain himself with what is available, but thinks about what he will eat tomorrow. His hand is on the basket nearby,
but his mind is at a distant table. He carries food in his right hand and his left, yet neither hand can supply enough fuel for the fire within him.
All his limbs serve the harsh mistress he has willingly set over himself, yet they cannot do enough.
His whole being serves her completely, yet he cannot satisfy her. His eyes, hands, and feet have become her slaves,
yet they cannot keep up. In his hidden thoughts he dwells on her; in his outward actions he runs about on her behalf. She receives their service like a mistress, yet she is never satisfied.
Like Sheol, she receives corruption yet is never filled. Like fire, she takes food as fuel
yet never says, “Enough!” Like the earth, she drinks yet is never satisfied. Like the eye, she desires everything, yet nothing can fill her.
For the glutton wishes he had other limbs that could provide enough service for the wicked mistress he has acquired.
The glutton's eye watches even the person sitting with him at the table. He looks at him with a hostile eye, afraid that he might eat more.
Perhaps he even counts the other man's mouthfuls in his mind, or wonders whether the portion set before him is larger than his own.
For his belly receives food, while his mind dwells on his companion sitting beside him.
Because the wickedness of gluttony spills over onto everyone, it looks with envy even on the person close to it.
How, then, could it fail to look with envy on someone who shares its table?
Indeed, if it keeps watch for days and months, and envies others who are far away from it,
and asks about everyone—what he eats, what dishes are arranged on his table, and how much food he has—
and when it has inquired and compared its own desired foods with those of the person it hears about, if its own are more plentiful than his, it rejoices;
but if his are more plentiful than its own, it is immediately filled with grief over him, and with that grief comes envy,
and with envy comes a burning torment of mind: why has someone been found who surpasses it in food? Indeed,
if the greedy eater envies those who are far away, does his eye not watch the person at the table with him?
For it is not that he openly tells him, “Do not eat!” Shame prevents him from saying this.
But this is precisely what he longs for in his thoughts: “If only he would hold back his hand, so that what is on the table would suffice for my own gluttony alone!”
Gluttony, then, is more disgraceful and loathsome than all other desires, and it has no likeness among the other passions,
except in this alone: it is the mother and nurse of them all.
For just as a root supports a tree's branches together with everything on them, so greed for food is the root of all evils.
Like branches and shoots from roots, all the passions of desire spring from it.
It gives birth to them, raises them, nourishes them, and puts them to work; through it all evils reach their fulfillment.
For through it a person starts along the road to the left, and it becomes his first step outside the path of righteousness.
For just as asceticism—that is, fasting from all foods—is the beginning of the path of struggles for righteousness,
so too, love of the belly is the beginning of shameful deeds. And if you look with the eye of knowledge,
O disciple, you will see that all evils follow after it, one after another.
For first it darkens the intellect, keeping it from contemplating God, and clouds the mind, keeping it from remembering Christ.
And when the remembrance of God has been removed from the soul, there is no doubt about this: what evil will a person not think and do?
For just as the beginning of everything done in the world is our remembering it,
and until we bring things to mind, we do not proceed to do them,
so too, the beginning of all good things is the remembrance of God. When, therefore, a person remembers God,
he approaches the practice of good deeds. And if a person does something good without remembering God in doing it, his good deed does not belong to God,
but to whatever he had in mind when he did it.
Now, this good thing that is the beginning of all good things—I mean the remembrance of God—
has the appetite of the belly as its opponent, besides the fact that this appetite is itself the beginning of all evils.
Thus, just as the remembrance of God stands at the beginning of the path of good things, so the appetite of the belly stands at the beginning of the path of all evils.
And when these two beginnings oppose each other, and one of them defeats the other, along with that first one which is defeated,
all those that come after it are defeated as well. For just as a house cannot be built without foundations,
so good things cannot exist without the remembrance of God.
And just as a building that is not set on a firm foundation is inevitably close to collapse,
so too, good deeds that are not built on the remembrance of God are necessarily subject to imminent change,
and do not remain firm in their practice, because they have no solid foundation to support them.
Gluttony and a full belly, therefore, first remove the remembrance of God from the soul. And when the foundation is uprooted,
all good things are uprooted with it. Gluttony is also the opponent of fasting,
the nullifier of prayer, the stain on purity of thoughts, the clouding of the mind, the darkener of the intellect,
the defiler of understanding, the nullifier of learning, the destruction of knowledge,
the injury of wisdom, the forgetfulness of memory, the painter of images, the mother of fantasies, the intoxication of the soul,
the drowning of the mind, the producer of sleep, the multiplier of troubled dreams, the producer of sexual immorality.
The defiler of the body. It causes unnatural discharges. The fire of lust. It commands adultery.
It commits fornication in thoughts, even without the bodily members. An eye that desires everything. A relative of despair.
The mother of laziness. The cause of the love of money. It hates the wise. It despises teachers.
A passageway for every hateful thing. The nurturer of envy. The sickness of health. The weakness of strength.
The debaser of the body. The worm of the bodily members. The maggot of the body. It diminishes the strength of the senses.
It wanders amid empty thoughts. A relative of wild animals. A partnership with livestock. It hates the diligent.
It envies the industrious. The destroyer of labors. A stumbling block to good conduct. It loves empty conversations.
It seeks diversion at every hour. The silencing of holy song. Idle in everything good. Diligent in everything evil.
An image of destruction. A stone placed in the middle of the way for many to stumble over. A target for injuries.
It produces slackness in all who see it. The queen of evils. It flees from afflictions.
It loves comforts. It searches for banquets and dining tables. A sickness of soul and body alike.
A vessel of putrefaction. The smell of foulness. The fountain of the body's excess. It loves darkness.
A relative of gloom. It eats alone. The enemy of those who give it nothing.
A loathsome image. An ugly likeness that cannot be depicted. The enemy of God.
The uprooter of faith. The beginning of the road of error. The gate that leads to every hateful thing.
It demands tribute from everyone. It enslaves everyone. It nurtures fear. The destroyer of courage.
The cause of distress and sorrow. The nourishment of dullness of heart. The yoke-fellow of a greedy dog.
It returns to its vomit. Full of diseases. A nest of pains. It finds excuses to avoid toil.
The primary cause of straying from God. It worships idols. And there are countless thousands of names like these.
If someone were to gather them and apply them to gluttony, they would still fall short of it.
It has not been called by names that do it justice, for it is the mistress of opposition to God.
And just as, even if God were called by every glorious and exalted name,
they would still fall short of him and would not suffice to reveal the splendor and beauty of his nature,
so too, even if gluttony were called by every epithet, they would not suffice to reveal its loathsomeness and ugly appearance.
For what beautiful thing is there that this evil does not destroy?
And one rightly calls it the evil of evils, the injustice of injustices, and the sin of sins.
The glutton, then, has no time for anything else but eating.
For he considers every activity apart from this worthless.
He does not think that a human being was made for anything else but satisfying his desires.
For the glutton's entire concern is with his stomach, and all the sentiments expressed in his speech are directed toward it.
For whatever subject you put to him and question him about, he brings you around to talk about his stomach.
For even before eating, the very thought of food gives him pleasure.
Even when he is not sitting at the table, all his thoughts are at the table. And even when he has not actually eaten,
in his thoughts and speech he is entirely occupied with food. The beginning and end of his speech are drawn from his stomach.
For he begins with it and ends with it. It is the reason for everything he says.
If you recite teaching before him, he considers it pointless. And if you speak,
and if you read spiritual things before him, he thinks he is seeing a dream. And if he hears of the victories of the saints,
and the labors, ways of life, and diligence of righteous people, he does not believe they are true.
For he considers explanations of the Holy Scriptures to be so many unnecessary stories.
For a sermon puts him to sleep, and a word of admonition brings drowsiness upon him.
He considers those who read and teach to have nothing to do, because he thinks there is no work more excellent than his own.
He labels the search for truth a quarrel, and calls discussion of faith prying. And if someone occupies his thoughts with the Scriptures,
he considers him insolent and [?]. If he sees someone devoted to reading, he says to him, “You have nothing to do.”
If he sees another person going about asking questions and seeking to acquire [?] knowledge of Christ, he considers that person's life a life of futility.
He gives bad names to good things, so that by reviling them he may free himself from blame.
For, to avoid being reproached with the question, “Why have you not devoted yourself to excellent things?”
he portrays excellent things as inferior, so that his own disgraceful conduct will not be condemned by those who see it.
With his words he makes the beauty of good things look ugly, and he reviles praiseworthy deeds along with those who perform them.
He disparages divine teaching along with those who study it. He condemns the wisdom of Christ along with those who seek it.
He speaks ill of knowledge along with its disciples. But since it is not easy for him to speak openly against the things themselves,
Wisdom and knowledge, reading and learning, faith and the search for truth, constant study of the words of the Spirit,
spiritual engagement with the Holy Scriptures, hidden conversation with the mysteries of Being,
the word of God, which is nourishment for the soul—for since he cannot easily insult these things openly, he insults those who practice them.
By insulting these people, he pours contempt upon the praiseworthy things themselves. For he openly insults these things too.
For when he calls discussion of faith meddling, and the search for truth disputation,
and the study of the Holy Scriptures excessive investigation, is it not obvious that he calls good things evil
and gives beautiful things ugly names? For he regards zeal for God as contentiousness.
And he considers anyone who struggles for the truth a troublemaker.
And when someone refuses to show people favoritism for God's sake, he calls this insolence.
If someone advises him, “Stand up and show zeal for God,” he cries out, “I have not been appointed to this,
and matters like these are not my responsibility. For I consider these things pointless,
and I do not involve myself in sorting out pointless matters.” And if someone asks him, “What do you want?”
he answers without shame, “Let us eat what God provides for us and be quiet.” But this means, “Let us serve our bellies
and abandon the faith.” For this is the meaning of his statement, even if he dresses it in a humbler form than this.
He is not ashamed to seek God's bread while denying his truth, or to look to his grace while despising his faith.
He presents himself as someone who loves quietness and flees contention and disturbance, although this is not really so.
Rather, he is afraid of putting any strain on that mistress of evils whom he serves,
and of being deprived, for any reason, of the bodily comforts to which he has pledged himself once and for all.
For he considers abstaining from learning to be wisdom. And refraining from learning about the faith
seems to him to be faith itself. “We are not required,” he says, “to learn anything else.
It is enough for us to believe and be silent.” Although he is not a believer, he takes refuge in faith,
not because he loves it, but because he loves his belly and cherishes his life.
For he brings the course of faith to a halt so that the pursuit of his desires may run its course.
Openly, his words support the truth, but secretly he speaks against the truth.
His struggle is for himself. When he is called upon to show diligence, he puts forward quietness.
And where diligence and zeal on behalf of the faith are required, everyone is to keep quiet and teach and admonish only himself.
A helpful discussion arose, and he fell asleep. Harmful subjects came up, and he woke up.
If matters of interpretation are introduced, he dozes. If riddles and stories are brought up, along with the world's tasteless sayings,
and the foolish chatter of old women, there he is, ready and making himself first to repeat them, prepared and wide awake,
so that he himself may be the first to tell them. For, enslaved to his appetite, he knows nothing except worthless talk.
His soul is empty of fruit but full of a heap of leaves—frivolous stories.
He runs and takes refuge in simplicity whenever he hears truths being spoken.
Though he is skilled in evil and cunning in malice, he calls a person's failure to know the truth 'simplicity.'
And for someone to surrender his faith to those who go astray is, in his own estimation, faith.
He orders everyone to say nothing about spiritual matters, so that he may have room to repeat the empty things he loves.
From beginning to end, this is his story: the cravings of his belly and the comforts of his body.
For he neither knows nor perceives that anything else exists besides serving his belly.
The glutton has therefore taken on the likeness of animals in all his ways, while his soul is even lower and more degraded than theirs.
Animals were made by the Creator for these two purposes: that, while their lives are sustained by their food,
they should perform work and service for the human race. But the glutton eats and does not work.
Though he is diligent at the table, he is idle when it comes to every deed requiring diligence.
For the soul that serves the belly has no awareness of God, because it is asleep to all thoughts of knowledge
and to meditation on God. For the soul's knowledge flourishes through the lightness of the body's senses and limbs.
The body's lightness comes from eating little. But the glutton is known to be bound by both:
darkness of thought and heaviness of body. Even accounts of the labors of the diligent are burdensome to him,
because they are opposed to his way of life. And if he happens to hear that one of them relaxed his abstinence out of love for his brother,
or freely, because of the pressure of illness or the necessity imposed by weakness, to support his body, which bears such labors,
relaxed his ascetic discipline a little for a short time, he seizes on this and repeats it constantly: 'So-and-so was eating such-and-such.'
He speaks of it in front of everyone, so that it may provide an outlet for his laxity and so that he may use it to conceal his ugly cravings.
For things are not, glutton, as you imagine them to be.
The diligent do not nourish themselves with the same aim with which you eat. Nor do they satisfy their desires with their food.
They have not become slaves to their bellies as you have. Rather, as free people, they take only what they need.
They take nourishment. Do not take from their example only this: that they have stooped to eating because of necessity.
Rather, look also at their ascetic discipline, and consider the long duration of their abstinence.
And consider that when they eat, they satisfy not desire but need. For it is one thing for someone to eat to satisfy desire,
and another to take nourishment out of necessity. For someone who eats to meet his needs eats for his soul and not for his body,
in that he nourishes his body so that it may always be ready and prepared for the soul that needs it.
But someone who eats out of desire takes his food for his body and not for his soul.
For it does not even enter his mind that there is a spiritual nature within him. Rather, only as though from a distance,
he hears from the words of others that he has a soul. For the glutton’s soul is dead, and although it is within him, it is as though it were not.
For when it is not moved to any of its own activities, nor acts or does anything, but instead puts to death all the movements of knowledge,
and all activity and conduct belong to the body alone, is it not then as though the soul, though present, were absent, and though dwelling in the body,
seemed not to be within it? For the body is known in two ways: by its appearance and by its actions.
But the soul is known only by its actions, because its nature is hidden from sight. And for this reason,
although the glutton has a soul through the Creator’s action, by his own choice it is as though he had none,
because the actions by which its presence is known are not found in him.
The glutton’s soul therefore complains and grieves over him, even though he does not sense its grief, because he is dead to it.
For just as a living body is joined to a dead one that does not sense it, so the glutton’s soul is joined to his body, though he does not sense it.
For the soul carries a corpse around, one that is alive only to desires and not to the soul.
And although all the passions, as I have said, deserve blame by a just judgment, this passion rightly deserves more blame than all of them,
not only because it is opposed to knowledge, but also because it is an enemy of God.
For a person who has sunk into the idle life of devotion to his belly thinks nothing of either the world or God.
And neither of them accepts him, because diligence is required for the world.
God, in turn, requires toil, hardships, and purity of soul from human beings.
And if these are not in him, God does not accept him. For gluttony is opposed to these things and flees from toil and hardships.
I think it is impossible for anyone to describe in words this evil of gluttony.
Especially for someone who has not experienced its passions.
For fasting is its enemy, and the mention of asceticism and abstinence frightens and unsettles it.
For the glutton lives for nothing else but to conduct himself like the animals.
Yet although he is one in practice, if someone calls him by that name, he becomes angry.
The fool does not understand that what another person says about him in words is actually present in his own conduct.
It is not someone else who insults him; rather, he himself is an insult.
For when the insults against him are drawn from his own conduct, and he himself is the root of his disgraces,
whom can the wretched man blame, and how can he find fault with those who speak of this?
For he has placed himself in the midst of the crowd to become a subject of conversation for others. Everyone thinks about him,
and everyone talks about him. One curls his lip, another winks his eye, and another points his finger.
Others whisper and recount his self-indulgence. But the glutton [?] himself among those who endure.
Even though all these things happen to him, he endures them and rejoices, taking the satisfaction of his belly as his only consolation.
The senseless man does not realize that, since toil and hardship now meet him on every side,
he should undertake to bear the hardships of asceticism rather than the reproaches of gluttony.
Whether a person turns to self-indulgence or to asceticism, weariness meets him on every side.
For it is better to endure hardships accompanied by praise in asceticism than to endure weariness accompanied by reproaches and insults in gluttony.
Indeed, the glutton too [?] more than the ascetic—not to subdue his desires, but to serve them.
And not to acquire endurance, but to serve as a slave to his belly.
And not to persevere through afflictions fitting for a life of discipline, but to serve the desires of self-indulgence, exhausted and weary.
Sometimes he gathers and brings himself material for his desires, like kindling gathered for a fire;
at other times he bears the weight of the foods after eating them.
For food weighs more heavily on a voracious belly than lead does on a shoulder carrying it.
As soon as someone eats beyond proper measure, the foods heap weight upon his whole body, and all his limbs grow sluggish.
The strength of his senses weakens, and even his eyesight grows dim from the abundant flow of moisture.
The ear’s hearing also grows dull, the tongue’s speech falters, and the mind, the wellspring of words, grows clouded.
The intellect, the pilot of wisdom, becomes confused, and the flow of speech also becomes obstructed and falters.
The joints shift out of place, the knees shake, and the hands tremble.
The glutton’s entire bodily frame becomes weakened and wears out before its time, because of the excessive weight of food with which he burdens it.
Many, then, and beyond counting are the illnesses produced by excessive eating.
Ascetic discipline does not cause illness in the body as gluttony does.
For gluttons give themselves over to food on the pretext of not becoming ill, as they say.
The fools do not realize that the very thing they flee from overtakes them.
For in the place to which they run to obtain health, they find sickness waiting before them.
Where they seek relief from pain, diseases gather against them.
For who does not know that eating little and following a meager diet give health to the body?
Especially when these are also accompanied by moderate exertion. The teaching of physicians also bears witness to this:
They are the ones who, more than those in all other professions, are thoroughly acquainted with the body’s health and sickness.
That is, their learning is the art devised for maintaining the body.
If these very people are consulted, they always recommend eating little.
Along with this, they also recommend that a person’s diet be meager, and they warn emphatically against drinking much wine.
If, however, they permit someone to drink out of necessity, they dilute its strength with plenty of water and then give it to him
to drink. They also strongly instruct a person to guard against idleness, to love exertion, and to occupy himself with work.
In every way, through exercises involving exertion, they preserve the health of people’s bodies.
They do these things, as they themselves say, so that the body’s arteries will not become filled with undigested fluid produced by excessive eating
and become blocked, preventing the vital power of food, which strengthens the body, from passing through them continually.
They also state this in their writings: that the cause of all the body’s illnesses
is food. Even if illnesses happen to arise from other causes,
food itself, if consumed in excess, makes them worse and completely prevents medical treatment from helping them.
Along with the statement of the physicians, it is right that we too, as wise people, should understand from experience,
That overeating is the cause of all evils, pains, and diseases of the body.
If you wish, consider the rich and the poor, those who live at ease and those who struggle, the idle and those who labor.
See whose body is kept sound, and whose illnesses are many and frequent.
Besides being numerous, their illnesses are also difficult to cure. Are they not those of the rich? Are they not those of people whose bellies are stretched by so much food?
Are they not those of people who, before they have digested and emptied out their first meal, hurry to another because of their gluttony?
These are the people who have severe and troublesome diseases. This is the reward their gluttony gives them.
Indeed, they deserve to receive this repayment from that wicked mistress whom they serve.
Theirs are pains in the hands and pains in the feet. Theirs are swellings and boils that arise from the body's excess.
Theirs are trembling limbs, a shaking head, and disease of the internal organs, along with all the other afflictions
that spring up for them like thorns from this very soil. Theirs is a sinking into sleep at every moment.
Theirs is constant drowsiness at all hours. Theirs are heaviness of the whole body, sneezing, and frequent belching.
Even the glutton's speech plainly comes from heavy limbs
and is born from a mind submerged in the flesh. All these things happen to gluttons,
even though they very persistently supply their bodies with other aids:
purges, cleansings, and other means of helping the body, bloodletting, purgative medicines, and frequent bathing
at every hour. Overeating defeats all these remedial measures
and creates severe pains and troublesome diseases in their bodies, which even skilled physicians find difficult to cure.
But the poor person who lives a life of work and toil enjoys bodily health.
His body is light and ready for every task. No weight from excess hangs upon it.
Even if he happens, without realizing it, to eat more than the proper amount of his scanty food,
his hard work immediately counteracts the heaviness of his meal, for his labor serves him as a constant physician.
From it he receives health without resorting to medicines. What physician knows how to make the body healthy
as hard work makes it healthy—and, moreover, without expense and without medicines?
Labor does not, like a physician, obtain medicines from outside itself and supply remedies.
Rather, it is itself the physician and the medicine, the one who bandages and the bandage, the healer and the health.
Help comes from it and is found in it, and through it health is gathered for all the body's members.
Thus poverty finds health in the very thing that laziness shuns out of love for comfort.
I am not saying, however, that ailments do not also afflict the poor, or that illnesses do not also come upon those who work and toil.
Rather, the ailments of the rich are numerous and difficult to cure,
because they are idle throughout their lives and have become slaves to their pampered bodies,
whether by serving their bodies' desires, reducing their excess, or healing the ailments that arise from overeating.
For they spend their whole lives in the idle pursuit of these things, unaware that anything else exists beyond them.
The poor person's ailment, however, is easy to cure, and the excess in his body is slight and small.
He readily recovers his health through the medicines given to him,
because the causes that increase excess in the body are absent from him.
If these things are so, who would not love eating little,
which is the mother of health? Yet I am convinced that gluttons consider these things superfluous.
For the glutton's ear is blocked by his appetite, and he cannot hear sound teaching.
For it is as though food itself has become a door shut in front of all his senses, preventing them from performing their natural functions.
Who would not weep over this man, who in his baseness ruins God's beautiful handiwork? He indeed justly deserves punishment,
not only because he serves his desires and angers God through his appetite,
but also because through his gluttony he ruins healthy bodily members that the Maker fashioned well.
For someone who damages the members of his body through gluttony is an accomplice of a murderer and a companion of a destructive robber.
What is written in the Law also applies to him: every murderer shall be put to death, and whoever cuts off his neighbor's limb shall have his own limb cut off.
But the glutton damages his own bodily members, and little by little destroys and exhausts the strength of his body and its members.
He ruins God's beautiful creation and tears down the structure of his body, which the Architect's will had previously built.
On every ground he brings punishment upon himself, according to the verdict of justice:
first, because he has transgressed God's commandment, which commanded that no one should be a slave to his desires;
and again, because he is hindered from virtuous deeds and from practicing all the good things that the Holy Scriptures constantly urge us to do;
and again, because he willingly drives the remembrance of spiritual things away from himself; and again, because he is also deprived of compassion toward the poor.
And his gluttony further urges him to go on from it even to oppression.
And besides these things, with his own hands he disfigures his beautiful form and damages the lovely limbs fashioned by God,
which he created in his grace to serve his purposes. Consider, then, the purpose for which you were formed, you glutton, and tremble before God.
Do not disgrace yourself, for there is another hope that is unseen. Why is your hope tied to your belly?
There is another food, that of the spirit. Why do you run madly after worthless foods?
Christ has a table, the one he promised to those who love him.
Why does your own expectation hang in suspense, watching for mealtime? There is another world, with its heavenly blessings.
Why have you confined your hope for life within the visible world, and counted its losses as gains?
For the Creator did not create you to eat like animals, but to take nourishment as a rational being and praise him as a living being.
He did not give you life so that you could eat. Rather, he gave you food to take in moderation so that you could live.
Your life is not designed for eating, you wretched one, but to be sustained by a moderate amount of nourishment. Distinguish your life from the life of animals.
Do not become a slave to your belly and offer it the service of destructive desires, for you are a human being endowed with wisdom.
Do not willingly harness yourself under the yoke of animals. You are the beautiful image of your Creator.
Why have you stamped the likeness of animals upon yourself? The word of the one who called you has invited you to equality with spiritual beings.
Where are you tumbling and descending, to wallow with pigs in the mire of desires?
You are appointed to proclaim holiness with the seraphim. Why, in your degradation, do you make your life resemble that of a speechless beast?
You are lord of creation by the will of your Maker. Why have you become a slave to your belly by your own free choice?
Your Creator's will subjected all creation to you, yet a little belly has subjected you to itself.
All created natures are harnessed under the yoke of subjection to you, yet upon your own shoulder rests the yoke of a perishable mistress.
All species and created things obey your word, yet you have become a lowly slave to foul desire.
You have been made a god by the true God, yet your belly has become your god.
You are a glorious ruler over his handiwork, yet in your degradation you have lowered yourself to a desire for all this worthless stuff.
He created everything for your glory, yet you exchange his glory for your belly.
God calls you to converse with him, yet your thoughts are bound to the table.
You have been made a rational instrument for holy praises, yet you wear yourself out and, in your degradation, cut the strings of your lyre.
Your Lord loved you so much that he became food for you. Yet you have not abstained from worthless foods out of love for him.
The Living One died and was buried to give you life, yet you have made yourself a grave for food.
He did not spare his own life, but gave it over to death for your life. Yet you have not acquired even a little endurance in your life out of love for him.
Look at the life promised to you, you lowly person, and see what sort of life you have lived in the world. Be ashamed, even if only before yourself.
Therefore, do not become a grave for your soul while you are alive, destroying your own self before it decays in the grave appointed by nature.
Look, your soul is buried inside your body like a corpse inside a grave.
The Creator fashioned the body to be a glorious vessel for the soul and a partner in every good thing.
Why have you made it a grave for the soul, so that it is imprisoned inside it as though in a place of decay?
For the glutton's body is ruined by his eating before natural death ruins it.
It wastes away and falls apart little by little before its stay in Sheol wears it away. For the glutton's ailments come from his own choice,
not from nature. Although they spring up in his bodily constitution, his own choice is their cause.
They arise in him from his free choice, through excessive eating. Thus the life of someone who loves sensual pleasures is a stumbling block.
He not only sins against his own soul but also causes harm to those who see him. For he is a stone lying in the middle of the path,
and everyone who passes over it stumbles on it: the lax and the zealous, the dissolute and the chaste, the pampered
and the ascetic, gluttons and those who abstain. Some stumble, while others become still more lax.
For the glutton sees someone like himself and becomes still more lax.
The lax person looks at him and puts on still more laxity, like one garment over another.
Someone held captive by his stomach's appetite sees him and clings still more firmly to his love of it.
But those who are diligent and ascetic are harmed by him because he becomes a stumbling block to them.
His conduct draws them into talk they do not wish to engage in. For he stirs up a battle against them on every side:
either to keep from being brought low by the sight of his laxity and becoming like him, or to keep from being distracted by discussing his laxity
from communion with God, or to keep from becoming proud of their zeal when they compare their well-ordered lives with his laxity.
And just as the diligent and hardworking benefit both themselves and their companions,
in exactly the same way the lax and those who love sensual pleasures harm both themselves and those who see them.
Their lives in this world thus prove to be a cause of harm to other people in every way.
For the glutton’s childhood is hateful, his youth is laughable, and his old age is ridiculous. His childhood is idle.
His youth is dissolute; his old age is pampered. Play and amusement are enough for his childhood,
adultery and sexual immorality for his youth, and gluttony and empty conversations for his old age.
For he hates not only doing good deeds, but even hearing them spoken about.
Not only is practicing them burdensome to him, but even talk about them, if he happens to hear it.
And so, if someone tells him about the victories of the saints, sleepiness and yawning immediately seize him.
His whole body bears the weight of sluggishness, as he shows signs of his soul’s deadness by stretching his limbs
and shifting his body. If he can, he leaves and goes elsewhere; otherwise, he immediately falls asleep where he is.
For the glutton’s soul is like a dog, and he rightly deserves to be called by its name.
For just as a dog sleeps through every activity, and human conversation and speech are foreign to its hearing,
and only the sound of the table and the sight of food wake it, so too the glutton, like it, is sunk in the sleep of sluggishness.
He considers every beneficial subject superfluous, and divine words flow over his ear like water over rock.
But let someone tell him something about the belly or speak about foods, and immediately his soul wakes up and his thoughts are filled with wonder.
His body immediately becomes light, and he leaps toward the talk he loves, like a dog toward its crust of bread.
The glutton therefore deserves to be called by names like these, so that he may hear his names and be ashamed of his appetite.
For because he wallows like a pig in the mire of desires, he deserves to be called by its name.
And because talk about the belly awakens him, like a dog that leaps up at the sound of the table, he is appropriately called a dog as well.
And because he too runs swiftly toward the table, like an animal toward its feeding trough, he is rightly called by the name of an animal.
And because, like a wild beast, he is devoid of all concern with wisdom and knowledge
and lives only for his body, he is rightly called by the name that suits him because of his deeds.
And if there were still other names more disgraceful and repulsive than these, it would be fitting for him to be called by them.
Yet this discourse does not insult him by calling him names like these,
because his disgrace comes from himself. For just as names are taken from things, and those things are designated by the very names taken from them,
so the glutton’s names are rightly taken from himself, and he is appropriately called by names derived from himself.
For who will honor someone who dishonors himself? And who will praise someone who himself runs after his own degradation?
And as for someone who brings mockery and offensive talk upon himself, who should care more than he does about his good name?
Yet along with these things, although I have said much, I ought to speak again and describe the ways of gluttons,
so that through them they may be recognized by all discerning people, and rightly scorned and despised by everyone who sees them.
For these are the rules of someone enslaved to his belly: he has no genuine love for anyone.
If he happens to love someone, he loves the person who has become a slave to him and a servant of his appetite—and even this person only as long as he satisfies his pleasures.
But if that person happens to change for any reason, becomes neglectful, and reduces his attentions a little,
he too immediately changes in his love for him, and his praises of his friend turn into abuse.
For because his love is bound to his belly, whoever serves it is his friend.
But whoever treats him with contempt appears to him as an enemy. He also searches and seeks out friends who are useful to him,
those who can serve his appetite. He does not love upright people; he has no affection for the self-controlled.
He considers those who undertake hard labors to be boorish, and counts the righteous as fools.
He calls those who persevere in prayer idle. When he sees a stranger, he passes him by on the outside.
But when he hears news of someone whom he expects to provide for his appetite, there he goes, rushing off in his love for satisfying it,
with his belly carrying his feet, and he roams everywhere. He becomes a friend to the rich, and a slave and servant to the powerful.
He considers association with them something to boast about, and conversation with them a source of pride.
Hearing the Gospel is not as dear to him as conversation with someone he expects to have brought something to satisfy his appetite.
Perhaps even Abraham's feet were not so swift, when love carried them and he ran to the herd to bring a calf for the angels,
as the glutton's feet are swift when he runs toward someone who has brought him food.
For all his love is directed toward receiving. And if he happens to give, it is so that something greater will be returned to him.
For he does not even know how to gain a friend apart from the belly. For through the very thing he himself loves,
he also wants to show love to others. If someone is angry with him, he thinks that person can be pacified with a gift for the belly.
If he angers someone by his foolishness and envy, he runs to appease him with a gift of food.
On it his hope rests, and through it he thinks the knots created by his actions can be untied.
The madman imagines that everyone, like himself, is yoked in bondage to the god he worships,
and that his belly is his god, just as his own is. He waits and longs to see a friend.
But if he comes and brings nothing, the soul’s expectation changes, as does the expression on his face.
The greedy man’s hand is stretched out to receive, but closed against giving gifts. If he happens to give, it is to put out bait for himself, so that he may be repaid generously.
For when someone knows that a rule governs the gift, and that it is given to him as a matter of custom,
he does not bother to show honor there. For he knows that even if he makes no return, custom and the rule themselves govern the gift.
But he makes a return where he receives something in return, and lays a foundation of affection where none had been laid.
He also recounts stories of old friends in the presence of new admirers, and recalls the gifts he received from them.
“So-and-so,” he says, “[?] so-and-so sent me something. And so-and-so pressed me, and although I did not want it, he bound me by oaths, and I accepted.”
It is as though someone were saying, “Listen, learn, and act this way yourself.”
He teaches his new friends the deeds of his old admirers, and makes them disciples of the rules followed by their predecessors.
For he passes over every other subject and brings his own into the discussion. If any subject happens to be discussed,
whether an act of hard work or divine teaching, he skillfully draws it away and removes it,
so that he may bring the subject of the belly into the discussion. For he lives for nothing else—not in his conversation,
not in his speech, not in his conduct, not in his deeds, not in his reflections, and not in his thoughts.
For he considers love of the belly the greatest of blessings, and all his questions revolve around it.
For he knows the different kinds of food and is also familiar with the flavors of different places:
which orchard has delicious fruits, and which river has tasty fish,
and who knows how to season delicious dishes. These are his questions and his explanations.
Two buildings are dearer to him than the New and Old Testaments. The sound of [?] alarms him.
A long prayer is torture to him. If you prolong the kneeling, he grumbles. If you lengthen the prayer, he complains.
He constantly turns his gaze toward the windows. He watches the sun’s course, makes marks for himself, and notes the hours.
One day seems like two in his eyes. His prayer is short; his mealtime is long.
There is nothing he will undertake except to satisfy the cravings of his belly.
He considers everything superfluous: reading, learning, fasting, abstinence, prayer, and singing,
worship and kneeling. And if he happens to perform them because customary practice requires it, out of shame,
he performs them wearily and with grumbling. [?] excuses for him also to abandon prayer.
And he seeks out dealings with other people, along with all the other matters that arise in the meantime, so that he may be kept from worship and psalmody.
