For he does the things of God reluctantly, but the things he desires with complete eagerness and love.
If he has a little pimple on his body, he treats it as a severe ulcer.
And if he feels a little weakness, he considers it a serious and troublesome illness.
In everything beneficial he finds an excuse, simply to neglect what gives him life.
He is diligent in everything except serving God. Even when he has no illness, he contrives to make himself appear sick.
This is so that when he neglects worship and fasting, he will not be blamed too much. For he recounts his pains before everyone.
And although the cause of his illness is small and insignificant, he magnifies and exaggerates it, calling God as his witness,
so that he may thereby persuade those who hear him that he undertakes the monastery’s work only by forcing himself. The glutton devises ways to secure his bodily health.
And although the means of stopping the source of his pains is within his reach—to restrain his gluttony a little—he wanders about looking for help outside himself.
If you advise him, “Reduce your food a little, and keep yourself from oil and wine,” he considers you someone who hates his life.
“Pain is better for me,” he says, “than putting any restraint on my stomach. I accept prolonged illnesses, provided that I can satisfy my desires.
If the medicine is willing to heal me while I eat, so be it; otherwise, eating is better for me than getting well.”
So the glutton has many worldly friends, so that provisions to satisfy his desire may be gathered for him from every direction.
He is cunning and skilled in his schemes, and knows whom to choose and make his friends.
For he will not consent, even by mistake, to make friends with any of the blessed or those who have renounced their possessions,
or those who endure hardships, or lovers of virtue, or any of those who possess the knowledge of Christ.
For he will not consent to be a friend to these people, even through association or in name.
And not only this: he is also their secret enemy.
For their appearance, their speech, and their deeds rebuke his gluttony; therefore he is angry with them and hates them.
And if you see him honoring one of the wise or one of the righteous, he does this for appearance’s sake,
so that he will not be reproached by the faithful who love these good things, and also to silence the grumbling of the many against him
and hold back from himself the onrush of zeal from those who honor good things.
If he sees someone who is still young in his discipleship, distinguished by zeal for the faith, he quiets him as though concerned for him.
And as though having compassion on him, he advises him, “Keep quiet, and do not disgrace your kind. Otherwise, you will abandon your solitude.”
“You were silent,” he says, “and look, you have received mercy. Occupy yourself only with fasting and prayer, and do not concern yourself with anything that does not concern you.”
He gives this advice here to quiet the disciple’s zeal, not because he desires the practice of good deeds.
After bringing him down from this good practice—taking a stand in the struggle for God’s sake—he then begins to undermine the good practices that follow it as well.
That is, the burden of labors and afflictions endured for God’s sake,
the fasts of ascetic discipline, and prolonged prayers. “These things,” he says, “are not required.
Rather, a person should purify himself and acquire a good disposition.” For he uses inward things as a pretext to abolish outward things.
He justifies himself by things that are not required, because his laxity exposes his conduct in outward matters.
Where it is not easy for people to see, there he makes himself out to be righteous.
But where afflictions and labors are visible, he devises ways to undermine them, giving them other interpretations.
“God does not require this of us,” he habitually says, “that a person should kill himself and afflict his body beyond measure.
Rather, we should be righteous in our souls and cleanse our thoughts of evil.”
Although the wretched man’s conduct is beneath even the level of animals, he speaks about spiritual matters as though he were perfect.
His explanations in defense of his evasion are lengthy. If he hears a saying from Scripture that suits him, he holds on to it with the utmost care,
so that it may serve him when the occasion arises, when he fights with his words against those who rebuke his gluttony.
For when he wants to eat everything and not exercise endurance by abstaining from any food,
he begins repeating what is written as a saying of our Lord: “It is not what enters the stomach that defiles a person.”
For his ear is open only to hearing this sort of thing—things that seem to support his desire.
But he closes the door of his hearing against other sayings. For he does not wish to hear that other saying:
“Whoever wishes to be my disciple must deny even himself, take up his cross, and follow me.”
Nor that other saying: “Whoever wishes to save his life will lose it.” Nor, again, what he said to his disciples:
“In the world you will have afflictions.” Nor this: “When the bridegroom is taken away from the wedding guests, then they will fast.”
And perhaps also that meal of our Lord, where it is written of him that he celebrated the feast and ate the Passover,
or where it says that they set before him a portion of broiled fish and some honeycomb, or where it is written again
that they had fish with bread.
The glutton brings forward these passages and others like them as evidence when he wants to eat everything without restriction.
And the free conduct of Christ, who as God was above laws and commandments,
he makes into a stumbling block for his own life, without understanding the reason for that conduct.
He does not realize that other patterns were being outlined there. And again, when the Apostle is read and he hears him say,
“Everything God has created is holy, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving, for it is sanctified by the word of God and by prayer,”
or that other saying, “The stomach is for food, and food is for the stomach,” or again what he said, “Let the one who does not eat not judge the one who eats,”
and similar things recorded in Paul's teaching, he rejoices in them and welcomes them enthusiastically.
Yet the fool neither understands the reason for these words nor wishes to hear the other things Paul himself wrote about diligence and ascetic discipline,
or when he recounts his many fasts, or when he cries out to his disciples,
“You are dead to the world,” or when he writes that it is good not to eat meat or drink wine,
or where he warns that a person must enter the kingdom of God through many afflictions,
or where he says, “But God will do away with both the stomach and food.”
So the glutton passes superficially over the reading of these things and others like them.
He does not even want to hear them. These, then, are the patterns that shape the life of someone who loves pleasures.
And just as the remembrance of God is close to the perfect, so concern for his stomach is always close to him.
He sings psalms and thinks about it. In his prayer and his worship, he carries the memory of it at all times.
He thinks about it constantly, because he has no other life apart from it.
For remembering it cuts short his prayers, and constantly thinking about it keeps him from all his duties.
For the glutton has no set times for his meals; instead, he eats both night and day.
Even when he is not eating, he remains a glutton. For you should not look at the fact that he has one or two mealtimes.
Instead, consider that at every hour of the night and day, food is his concern.
And when his body is not eating, his mind eats. For he does not even have distinct times for eating as animals do.
For although an animal eats at any time, without restriction by night or day, it does not think about its food all the time.
But the glutton eats all the time, because he thinks about his stomach all the time. Perhaps even when he is asleep, he sees himself eating in his dreams.
Shame has been taken away from before the glutton's eyes, because he has made his face brazen so that he feels no shame. He hears the insults directed at him and disregards them,
and he does not take his disgrace to heart. For within him, love of his stomach overcomes all the storms that beat against him.
He neglects spiritual things; indeed, he does not even know that they exist. He selects fresh oils.
He seeks clear wines. He asks about tasty foods.
He has no other occupation in the world but this. However much we tell his story, the account of his laxity never ends.
For even in what we have said, we have given only a small taste of the forms his laxity takes, so that those who see him may recognize him by this.
But you, disciple of diligence, flee from resembling this man, and do not let the sight of him weaken the diligence of your conduct.
Know for yourself why you became a disciple, and let your discipleship itself be the motive for your course. Do not imitate the lazy.
Instead, compete with the diligent in their devotion. Do not take as your example a human being who resembles animals.
Do not consider it a good thing for someone to eat and drink and satisfy his desires, but an evil worse than all other evils.
Listen also to the prophetic word, to the woe pronounced upon the gluttonous.
It says, “Woe to those who rise early in the morning and run after strong drink, and linger into the evening while wine inflames them.
They drink wine with harps, lyres, flutes, and tambourines, but they do not consider the works of God.”
See, the Spirit too has taught you that someone who serves his desires cannot understand the works of God.
For just as we cannot, in our sleep, speak and act like people who are alive and awake,
so neither can a person sunk in the sleep of desires understand the living works of God,
or know how to contemplate his governance and marvel at the variety of his providential care,
or experience within himself wonder at the greatness of his glory, and be alert to knowing him and ready to respond to the word of his wisdom.
For someone sunk in desire is unaware of these things, because these thoughts belong to those who are awake and alive.
And a blessing is given to whoever considers these things. For if, upon those who eat and drink,
and do not consider the works of God, a woe has been pronounced, then, in contrast to them,
a blessing is given to ascetics and those who practice abstinence, who meditate at all times on the works of God.
But you, disciple, strive to be worthy of the blessing, and flee from the woe promised to the gluttonous.
Let your examples in goodness be the devoted, not the lazy; those who fast, not those who gorge themselves; ascetics, not the gluttonous;
those who practice abstinence, not those who indulge themselves; those who serve God, not those who serve their bellies; the diligent, not the lax;
and the good, not the wicked. For the world does not lack good people who can be examples of good deeds for you.
Let us imitate them, not the wicked. Therefore, do not fix your attention on those who stand below you.
Instead, lift your eyes upward and look at those who are greater than you, and rise to their level.
For just as everyone chooses greater things for himself in worldly matters, so also in these divine matters,
let us choose great and lofty things for ourselves. There is no one in the world who loves poverty more than wealth.
Instead, everyone shuns it and runs after wealth. Everyone flees from pain and runs after bodily health.
In the same way, here too, let us pursue the things of the spirit, and love the wealth of diligence, not the poverty of gluttony.
And let us love the health of our soul and our thoughts more than the sicknesses of sinful desires.
For the soul of someone who serves sinful desires is always sick.
And he has no control over his spiritual strength and health. For just as someone whose body is sick
has no command over his health so as to eat whatever he wants, nor over his strength so as to do whatever he wishes,
so too a person whose soul is sick with gluttony has no control over the strength and health of his soul.
He cannot conduct himself in everything he does as he wishes and desires.
For just as a sick person's limbs do not respond to him when he wants to move them to perform some action,
so too a glutton's thoughts do not respond to him when he wants to use them to accomplish something good.
For all good things are difficult for someone enslaved to his stomach, because he is a slave to every sinful desire.
For if a craving for food is stirred up within him, he cannot easily overcome it,
because he is enslaved to it. Nor can he overcome sexual desire if it stirs in his limbs, nor fury,
nor anger, nor envy, nor malice. None of the hateful passions is easy for him to overcome,
because he is a slave and subject to them all. For they are difficult to subdue, especially when they are many.
And if a single passion gains control over our lives and keeps us enslaved for a long time in its service,
it is hard for us to overcome it. How much more will we be overcome by many masters!
For, as I said, all the other passions enter along with gluttony, because it is the gateway for every sinful desire.
Our Savior said in his Gospel, “You cannot serve God and Mammon.”
And if, when we are enslaved to one master—that is, to Mammon alone—we cannot serve God alongside him,
how, when many masters enslave us and each forcibly leads us according to his own will,
can we serve God, who does not accept that a person should serve anything else alongside him?
Now, even if these sins are all alike opposed to God's righteousness,
each one of them is opposed to the others in its activity. How, then, could they not all hinder God's commandments by what they do?
For they differ from one another in their actions, but God's will is opposed to them all.
This is especially true of this appetite for gluttony, through which all the other desires are gradually brought in and gain entry.
So when a person becomes enslaved to serving his belly, it entangles him deeply in the world,
so that he gathers from every direction and brings it what it needs. For it does not merely want to eat, but is concerned with how it will eat.
For if its sole concern were to meet its need, the belly's need could be met with very little,
and with ordinary, humble things that are reasonably priced.
How often have many people met their needs with roots and herbs,
because they sought what they needed, not the satisfaction of their desires. For although God, as a generous Creator,
has abundantly given everything for our use, we ought to look to his will and conduct ourselves accordingly.
For this reason he has multiplied foods and varieties of flavors in the world, so that they might be a furnace for testing desire,
and so that through them people's minds might be tested, to show what they desire and what they pursue.
For where there are no things that arouse desire, desire cannot be tested.
But a disciple ought to know himself and not become enslaved to his body's appetite, nor open a gate that lets destructive beasts in upon him.
For just as a fortified gate is kept shut, and evil beasts and harmful creeping creatures are held outside it,
but if it happens to be opened for some reason, they all find their way inside, to the harm of the inhabitants of that place, so too, when it is shut,
the gate of the belly's appetite keeps outside all the deadly passions of desires that destroy the soul,
and they do not enter to harm and destroy the soul's spiritual nature.
But if through our laxity this gate is opened before them, and we indulge our belly in whatever it craves,
all evils immediately gather and enter our soul, destroying within it every thought of virtue.
For immediately, as soon as you open this gate, the destructive beast of sexual immorality enters,
which devours and destroys soul and body alike; and after it comes love of the belly,
on which both the belly's appetite and sexual immorality depend, and which in turn is born from them.
And from love of money comes distress, either over what we do not possess, or if we happen to lose something we have gathered.
Either all of it or a little of it. From this, too, the passion of anger is born in us.
When we become angry and enraged at those who will not let us mistreat them as we wish,
or at those who will not obey and provide the service we need for our lives—sometimes at slaves, sometimes at hired workers,
and sometimes at those who are lower and less important than we are—we become filled with anger and rage against them because of the circumstances we encounter.
We are also filled with envy toward those who are greater and richer than we are, and with plunder and oppression.
How often we are even driven to murder for this reason! Through wealth itself, pride also takes hold of us.
And through the display of wealth we crave empty praise from other people.
From this we also learn slander: to accept it from those who are beneath us.
And we ourselves also slander others before those who are greater than we are.
From these things we constantly proceed to lies and oaths, and to blasphemy against God.
And when the remembrance of judgment has completely vanished from the soul, it then commits every kind of evil without fear.
Greed, then, is the primary cause of these things and others like them.
For who does not know that sexual desire burns in a body that eats, drinks, and indulges itself?
Even when it is not acted on openly and is not seen by other people in actual deeds,
it nevertheless constantly inflames the thoughts, and a person devises and seeks an outlet for the fire within him.
He desires every kind of beauty and stumbles over every form that is attractive to look at.
For as long as the fire of desire is in his limbs, his thoughts fly toward every face, and he secretly commits sexual immorality with everything he sees.
Even when a person does not commit sexual immorality openly, he constantly commits it in secret.
And even when he is not an adulterer in his body, he commits adultery in his soul at every moment and every hour.
Food and drink, then, are fuel for the fire of desire.
Anyone who wishes to extinguish this fire hidden in his limbs should withhold this fuel from it, and there—it is extinguished.
For fasting, ascetic discipline, and abstinence are water that extinguishes the fire of desire.
For wine is to desire what oil is to fire. And just as manure stimulates the earth to produce fruit,
so the richness of foods also excites the limbs with shameful desires.
For an abundance of food is a veil over the mind.
Even before thoughts of sexual immorality arise, food itself darkens the mind on its own.
There is no doubt about how greatly the turmoil of desire disturbs clear thoughts.
Those who have experienced it know this especially well. But even before this desire arises,
gluttony weighs down the understanding, veils the discerning mind, and darkens thoughts that possess the light of knowledge.
For the aroma of food is darkness to the enlightened mind, and just as clouds and smoke disturb the pure, clear air,
so too the aroma of food disturbs the mind’s clarity. A disciple of Christ ought
not only to abstain from expensive foods, but also to eat inexpensive foods sparingly.
For food does not disturb the mind and darken the understanding because it is expensive,
but because of its quantity. This harm can be found in inexpensive foods as well as expensive ones.
The Holy Scriptures rightly warn people everywhere against gluttony,
as Paul teaches: those who occupied themselves with foods gained no benefit from them.
Not only were they deprived of benefits, but they also accumulated harm and suffering for themselves.
“Neither the dissolute nor drunkards,” he says, “will inherit the kingdom of God.” Read that passage, disciple,
and see with what evils the apostle ranks this evil: with sorcerers and those who corrupt others, and other things like these.
For although gluttony itself is not these things, it leads to them.
For when the heart grows fat from food, it immediately drives the remembrance of God out of itself.
And when the remembrance of God departs from a person, what evil will he not commit,
and what wrongdoing will he not eagerly pursue? This is also what the prophet Moses taught us:
that for this reason the people forgot their God, and from gluttony they went on to worship idols.
From food they were led into blasphemies, and from luxuries they came to every kind of evil.
“He settled him,” he says, “on the high places of the earth, fed him the produce of the field, and made him suck honey from the rock and oil from the flinty rock:
butter from cattle and milk from sheep, with the fat of fattened animals, rams from [?], and young goats,
with the fat and richness of wheat; and he gave him wine to drink, the blood of grapes.
Israel grew fat and kicked. He grew fat and strong and acquired possessions.” And what happened to him as a result of these things?
Where did he end up because of these desirable things, and where did he find himself because of the luxuries in which he reveled?
And into what illnesses gluttony and excessive eating cast it!
Moses himself explained and clearly showed us what the people gained from these possessions.
“It forgot,” he says, “God who made it, and insulted the Mighty One who redeemed it. It provoked him to jealousy with foreign gods and angered him with objects of worship.”
“They sacrificed to demons that were not gods, to gods they had not known.” These, he says, were what the people gained from luxurious living.
They inherited this legacy of demon worship from bodily excess and from a table rich in food.
They were drawn to the unclean tables of idols, and from luxurious living they went out to pour drink offerings before carved images.
And from the desire that draws its strength from nature, they came to unclean thoughts foreign to nature.
Look, disciple, and see where those people started and where they ended up, and patiently uproot from yourself the root that makes idol worship sprout.
It is a plant that begins with the belly and ends in demon worship. The prophet did not merely tell you that the people worshiped idols.
Rather, he first showed you the reason why they worshiped them. He did not simply tell you about their severe and grievous illness
without showing you where the cause of the illness came from. “They ate,” he says, “and drank and lived in luxury.”
And from this they forgot God who made them; and because error entered, it gave birth to insults and blasphemies.
“They insulted,” he says, “the Mighty One who redeemed them.” And this was not enough for them: they also made gods for themselves in opposition to God.
In place of the One, they fashioned many for themselves. “They provoked him to jealousy,” he says, “with foreign gods, and angered him with objects of worship.”
Along with the testimony of the word, let us also see from the deed itself how they came to offer praise before a calf in the wilderness.
“The people sat down,” he says, “to eat and drink, and rose to play.” Until food entered them, no blasphemies came out.
And until wine was poured into them, they did not clothe themselves in unfaithfulness toward God.
These, then, are the harms that eating caused. Who, therefore, would not flee from eating too much?
For someone who is determined to be dissolute becomes a glutton.
For the greedy person takes empty thoughts into his soul, and then approaches luxurious foods.
Love of the body leads a person to become a slave to his belly. And whoever loves desire is clearly an enemy of the glory of Christ.
For the desire of the body is opposed to the desire of the spirit. As long as one lives, the other cannot live.
For in anyone in whom the desire of the body is alive, the desire of the spirit is dead. And just as the body is deprived of everything it desires
when it is cut off from its own life, so the soul is cut off from all good things when it is deprived of the desire of the spirit.
For the desire of the spirit is the beginning of entry into all the virtues.
Bodily desire, however, is the gateway to every evil. For it would be right,
even if the appetite of the belly did not hinder us in any good deed,
to restrain ourselves from it for its own sake alone, so that it would not make us resemble animals.
How much more so, since it is the gateway to every evil and a field that regularly produces thorns and thistles.
For if those who compete in worldly contests
and want to become renowned for their bodily skill sustain their lives with little food,
how much more do spiritual athletes need this, so that through it they may gain vigor and run the course of their labors.
For if the body itself, whose natural life is sustained by food, when it wants to become renowned in one of the bodily contests,
adopts a rule of abstinence, how much more will the soul itself need abstinence,
which regularly reduces the body's weight and makes it light and obedient to the soul that dwells in it.
For the heavier the body becomes through an abundance of flesh, the harder it is for the soul to conduct its life.
But whenever the body becomes lighter and smaller through abstinence, the soul also easily carries out all its wishes through it,
because it gains strength through the body's lightness. For the heavier and thicker the body is, the more it opposes the soul, because the soul is subtle and rational.
And just as the soul loves the realm above, which suits its spiritual nature, so the body loves the density of the earth and the heaviness of dust.
And while the soul leaps to rise upward, the body, through its heaviness, drags it down,
so that it crawls with the body over the ground of desires like a creeping creature. For a gluttonous body makes the soul irrational
and strips it of all its impulses toward wisdom.
For since the heart is the instrument of the soul's discernment and thoughts, when it becomes thick through an abundance of food,
all the soul's thoughts, which arise from it, become thick along with it.
And because it becomes heavy and the fire naturally mingled within it grows cold, the warmth of the soul's knowledge also diminishes within it.
And the swift movement of its thoughts ceases. For although the gift of reason originates in the soul,
its activity is nevertheless manifested through the mediation of the body's members, and all the parts of the soul's nature
depend on all the parts of the body's members. For we see
that whenever the soul wants to examine the world, it looks through the body's eyes. And when it wants to hear a bodily sound,
it receives it through the sense of hearing. Or again, if it wants to send out a word belonging to its nature, it conveys it to us by means of the tongue, the bridge of words.
And, in short, whenever it wants to perceive anything from the world, it sends out or brings in through the mediation of these bodily senses.
But whenever it wants to see the realm of spiritual beings, or to hear the living words of their spiritual nature,
and seeks to contemplate a vision beyond nature, it has no need at all of these senses.
Instead, it even puts them aside and moves independently within its own faculties, with living movements beyond nature.
And now, just as we have learned that the soul needs the outward senses, so it also needs the inward organs,
so that through them it may act in all its faculties, whether in wisdom, understanding, or illumination,
whether in thoughts, discernment, intelligence and comprehension, or the fear of God.
In all these things, then, it functions through the mediation of these organs. And to the extent that they are light and not burdened with the weight of food,
and are not disturbed by excessive vapors from nourishment, it too works readily through them.
And just as light mingles with light, and through their mingling they shine with greater light,
so the luminous soul also mingles with luminous organs, whenever they are light and clear of the fumes of food.
But if they become thick and heavy, they become like a dense mass and a thick covering in front of its brightness.
And instead of its receiving help from them, they become impediments and obstacles to the ease of its activity.
These things and others like them are understood by those who perceive the knowledge of nature with keen insight.
But if you too, O disciple, desire to share in this knowledge of nature,
and through it to rise to the knowledge of the Spirit, guard yourself against the weight of food.
The natural density of your body is enough for you. Do not make it still denser and heavier with excessive food.
And if, moreover, you eat excessively under the pretext of health, whoever thinks this way is greatly mistaken in this too.
For much food does not produce health; rather, it breeds pains and diseases in the body.
It makes only the body of desire healthy. And to the extent that all the organs become diseased, grow weak, and lose their strength,
so the desire for sensual pleasures grows healthy and strong in soul and body. And along with desire, ignorance also grows stronger.
For gluttony increases this hateful passion of ignorance more than all the other desires do.
For ignorance is the darkness of the soul, just as knowledge is the light of its nature.
And just as a lamp is extinguished by winds and storms, or grows dim so that its light does not spread brightly through a house whose air is thick and damp,
so the light of the soul’s knowledge grows dim within a heart darkened by the weight and moisture of food.
For look: even the sun, whose light is inherent in its nature and is not gathered from external sources,
has its rays dimmed in disturbed and murky air, just like a lamp.
And although its light exists in abundant fullness in its own natural sphere, within the body of the world it is dark and dim.
Think of the soul in the same way. The light of knowledge is gathered within it, like the natural light in the sphere of the sun.
And when the heart is murky like the air, and all the internal organs are disturbed by the fumes of food,
the rays of the soul’s knowledge are obstructed, so that they cannot spread fully throughout all the parts of the body.
Then all a person’s movements, whether those of the outward senses or of the internal organs, take place foolishly and confusedly.
For the soul’s knowledge is a hidden pilot for the whole body.
It keeps the eye modest, the eye orderly, and the ear guarded;
the hand careful, the tongue properly restrained, and the feet walking gently.
And like a charioteer with unruly horses, so the soul itself holds and guides all the senses with the reins of knowledge.
Like a charioteer with horses, it too orders the senses and directs the internal organs.
And this good thing, which is the body’s light and the order of all its organs, is lost through gluttony
in someone who is not watchful and careful. Let us therefore flee from this foolish passion, and let Christ’s disciple not become a slave to his belly.
For if we cannot serve God and Mammon together,
according to Christ’s words, it is clear that neither can we serve the belly and God.
For the belly too has been called a god, like Mammon. And just as Jesus called Mammon a master,
so his apostle also called the belly a god: “Those whose god is their belly, and whose glory is their shame.”
For he is mocking those who make a trade of the word of God
and have hired themselves out to Christ for the sake of their bellies, not out of love for him.
Even today there are many who wear the honored garb of discipleship
and present themselves as teachers and good servants of God, not out of love, nor with discernment and fear,
but only to serve their bellies, which they have made their god and which they serve. But God’s apostle himself teaches plainly
that the heaviness of the belly turns the soul’s gaze downward, from heaven toward the earth.
“Those,” he says, “whose thoughts are entirely on earthly things.” For he first stated, “Their god is their belly, and their glory is their shame.”
Then he said that their whole mind is set on the earth, to show that the reason they are bound to the earth,
and their minds wallow in the dust, was their love of food.
Just as the love of it bound them within the earth, so it also binds everyone who serves it.
For how does someone who wallows in the cravings of his belly differ from worms crawling in filth, or from pigs rolling in mud?
Here too, this loathsome craving ought to be called filth, mud, and shame.
For if Paul called it this, how can we fail to call it the same, following his example?
We can all see that it is the beginning of all evils, also in the case of Adam’s fall.
For through it he transgressed God’s commandment. With his own hand he scorned and cast aside the law given to him.
The devil took it as his helper because he saw that it was far stronger than all the other desires,
and that through its doorway he could enter into all the other evils. For it was not through sexual immorality, or love of money, or empty glory,
or fine clothing, or envy and pride, or any of the other passions
that this enemy fought against those first parents of our race, but only through the craving of the belly.
For he saw that it was enough to serve him as a scout leading to all the other desires.
Because the tempter is crafty, he saw which passion was strong in us and came first in us, and he approached it.
He stirred it up and sowed weakness in its wake. After this craving, the passion of sexual immorality also entered.
“As soon as they ate,” it says, “the eyes of both of them were opened, and they knew that they were naked.”
Clearly, because the desire for sexual intercourse stirred in their sexual organs, they themselves became aware of it and were ashamed to look at one another.
For until food entered, desire was not aroused. And when desire was aroused, shame and fear did not reign.
See, then: love of food is the beginning of shame. The blessed apostle was right to call it shame.
“The woman saw,” it says, “that the tree was beautiful, a delight to the eyes, and desirable to gaze upon.
She took some of its fruit and ate, and she also gave some to her husband with her, and he ate.”
You see that the craving of the belly was the beginning both of the sin common to all and of the first transgression of the commandment,
and through it all sins and all punishments were brought upon us and entered our lives.
For just as envy was the beginning of evil for Satan, so also for Adam and his household,
the belly was the beginning of transgression of the commandment. Through it sins entered, and through it all punishments were brought upon us.
It was the beginning of pains and illnesses. Through it the pains of childbirth came in.
Because of it the earth was cursed and brought forth thorns and thistles. It estranged us from the delights of Paradise.
It cast us into the land of curses as into exile. Because of it we became slaves to demons.
Under its dominion over us, we served Satan as slaves. Because of it evil spirits made sport of us and mocked us.
It brought in death, which dissolves and scatters our bodily frame. Through it this glorious and beautiful image was disfigured and cast out.
It fed us the bread of pain. It gathered food for us by the sweat of our faces.
For gluttony is foolish and blind. It wanted to eat, but was deprived of food.
It desired comforts and lost the rest and bounty of Paradise. For when it wanted to eat, it did not know how to eat.
It did not hold to patience, because this is the nature of this desire: it is impulsive and impatient.
For it hurried and picked a single fruit, and was deprived of the table laden with all the splendors of Paradise.
Let that desire among Adam and his household serve as a pattern for this desire among us: just as there, because of eating a single fruit,
they were deprived of the food of all Paradise, so too a full table here deprives us of the table of the kingdom of heaven.
For as long as the belly is full and burns with an abundance of food, the remembrance of the blessings to come is absent from the soul.
And as long as the eye gazes at these foods and desires them, the mind’s eye is too dim to see spiritual delights.
Now, if Adam, because he desired a single fruit, lost [?] the enjoyment of all Paradise,
how much more will someone weighed down by desire for many foods be deprived of the table of the kingdom!
For Adam lost Paradise because of his eating, and inherited death together with all the curses.
And Esau, because of his eating, cast off his birthright together with the blessings. He became a slave to sin and subject to his brother’s authority.
And because of food the people forgot God, and instead of God they worshiped the likeness of a speechless animal.
And again, because of food, God’s anger rose against them.
And again, through food they were led into sexual immorality with Midianite women, because of which a sudden plague also took hold of them.
For it is written about them: while the meat was still between their teeth, God’s anger rose against them.
Again, through food and luxurious living, the Sodomites too defiled themselves with an unclean act.
Comforts and gluttony brought them to that boundless evil, as God’s prophet declares about them.
“This,” he says, “was the wrongdoing of your proud sister Sodom: she was filled with bread and sat at ease.”
For through an abundance of bread and ease, they defiled themselves with unnatural desire.
Let these things and others like them serve as reminders to you, you who wish to walk on the road to heaven.
Cut off and cast away your belly’s insatiable appetite, which sinks the soul into the depths of evil like a millstone in the sea.
Do not suppose that gluttony is reckoned only in terms of expensive foods.
For look: Esau’s gluttony was revealed in a meal of lentils.
It was not in an abundance of meat, nor in excessive wine, nor in other elaborate preparations of food.
Rather, solely because he greedily desired a meal of lentils, the word of God rejected him and cast him aside.
Whatever food is available to you, show your endurance in dealing with it. Struggle against what is close at hand.
Let your battle be against the cheap and humble foods set before you, so that you do not use them to fill your belly.
For no one leaves nearby opponents alone and fights against those who are far away.
And no one neglects an illness that is present and causing pain, while offering treatment for a disease that has not yet appeared.
For since luxurious foods are not available to you—the foods enjoyed by the wealthy and prominent people of the world—
restrain yourself from these little things set before you. And if you overcome these humble things,
you can be trusted to prevail against greater things as well, and to win victory over expensive foods too.
For a full belly does not bring forth pure prayer, and a stomach distended with too much food does not produce alert singing.
For if the only harm found in gluttony were its own inherent harm, then, although it is blameworthy, perhaps the charge against it would not be very grave.
But because of the other evils that spring from it, the disciple must guard against it.
For the glutton sleeps a great deal. His dreams are disturbed; his visions are confused.
His lust flows profusely. His sleep is a stupor, not healthy sleep. If he gets up to sing, consider him as though he had not got up.
For just as he was sunk in his dish, so he is sunk even while standing. He throws himself against the walls and grasps the hangings.
He leans on pieces of wood so that they may help him carry his heavy body—that is, so that they may help lighten the weight of the food he is carrying.
For he may begin and finish his service without being aware of where he is.
Many voices cry out in his ears, but he overcomes them all through the stupor of his sleep. His ear is blocked by the weight of the food.
His eye is shut with sleep. His whole body is tired and worn out because he did not restrain himself within proper limits.
The living stand beside him and look at him as though he were dead. Those who are awake see him and mock and ridicule his appearance.
He does not know which psalm is being sung. He is angry with anyone who wakes him.
He is full of anger and threats toward anyone who rouses him from his stupor. For he sometimes falls down while standing.
The noise of his fall disrupts the service, and at a time of quiet he creates a disturbance.
While the living and wakeful sing praises to God, he stands before him like a lifeless corpse.
As for saying that he feels no shame or embarrassment—how could someone be ashamed when he is not even aware of where he is?
By the way he stands, he shows contempt for God. He provokes indignation in those who see him. He also insults those who wake him.
He becomes a stumbling block and an obstacle to those standing beside him.
They stop their singing and talk about him, crying out at the sight of his stupor.
For if the glutton sleeps, he is sunk in sleep; if he wakes, he is still asleep; if he sings, he is mute; and if he stands, he lies on his side.
Consider these losses, then, you who love spiritual gains, and draw back from this evil,
so that through it you do not forget God and forget yourself as well, and your discernment does not grow dark to everything you ought to do.
Along with these things, remember also what Moses the prophet said to the Jews:
“Take care that you do not eat your fill and forget the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt.”
See, the Spirit of God has clearly taught you that forgetfulness is born from eating your fill.
When someone forgets God, he walks fearlessly into every evil and takes part in every wicked deed.
For just as the sight of a respected master puts unruly servants to shame, so remembrance of God puts the disorder of thoughts to shame.
As soon as the thought of him enters the mind, all its unruly impulses hurry into the order imposed by reverence.
Suddenly the soul becomes a peaceful house, a temple of order, a dwelling of purity, and a holy chamber of the Trinity.
Whoever wishes, then, to travel the road to heaven should loosen the shackle of desires from his feet
and remove the weight from the wings of his mind, so that, made light, he may travel to the meeting with the Majesty.
Let him listen to the counsel that Saint Paul gives us as he teaches and admonishes us:
“Take care,” he says, “that none of you is base and lax like Esau, who sold his birthright for a single meal.
For afterward, although he wanted to inherit the blessings, he was rejected. He found no opportunity for repentance, even though he earnestly sought it with tears.”
Let these things, then, be a reminder to us, and let testimonies like these be written within our hearts.
Let us be light so that we may be spiritual. Let us shut the door to the appetite of the belly, so that all evils may be kept outside.
Let us put bodily desire to death within us, so that spiritual desire may live within our souls.
Let us patiently cut back even on the necessities of our lives, so that by grace we may be counted worthy of the life of glory.
Let us renounce the foolish mistress, so that we may fully acknowledge the holy Being.
Let us free our limbs from their burden, so that our limbs may become light for pure prayer.
Let us drive out the smoke of desire, so that the eye of our soul may be polished for the vision of knowledge.
Let us not long for a table full of many foods, so that the table of the kingdom may welcome us as hungry people.
Let us despise and reject bodily health, so that we may be able to gain the health of our hidden inner person.
Let fear of pain not draw us toward food, lest wounds thereby multiply in our souls.
Let us thank the one who nourishes us for a little food, so that we may be seen to be children, not slaves hired for the sake of their bellies.
Let us overcome the first desire through patient endurance, so that through this we may gain strength to overcome all desires.
Let us say to one another what the apostle said to us all:
“The belly is for food, and food is for the belly, but God will do away with both.”
But the body is not for sexual immorality, but for our Lord, and our Lord is for the body. To him be glory from us all forever. Amen.
Here ends the first discourse on gluttony, by Saint Philoxenus, bishop of Mabbug.
Notes on the Syriac text:
The eleventh discourse, on asceticism and the subduing of the body,
in which he explains that through afflictions a person can enter the spiritual realm of the delights of knowing Christ.
“Enter through the narrow gate,” the word of our Savior proclaims to all the true disciples of his word.
For without this gate, no one can enter the kingdom of God.
For a person is not fully worthy to taste the way of life of Christ
until he puts an end within himself to all awareness of the tastes of the world; and he cannot cut off this sensation itself and cast it away from himself
unless, through the strength of patient endurance, he cuts off the pleasure of all desires.
For when a person cuts off evil things and casts them out of his soul, good and beautiful things spring up within him in their place.
That is, in the very place from which evil is cut off, goodness immediately springs up and takes its place.
And just as the whole strength of the soul had been directed toward watering and nurturing that plant of evil,
In this way the power of all thoughts is wholly redirected toward nurturing the tree of goodness planted within the soul,
after evil has been uprooted from it. For unless evils are uprooted, good things do not grow in their place.
And unless bad habits are cut off and thrown far away from us, the practice of good conduct does not take hold within us.
And unless we abandon laxity, we do not take hold of diligence. And unless greed dies, ascetic discipline does not live within us.
For death and life are at work within us in both cases: the death of the old self,
that is, ugly desires; and the life of the new self, that is, upright conduct.
For the death imposed by the sentence passed on humanity is brought about by a command.
But this death of the desires is summoned by the will of each one of us.
For in the beginning, too, the death brought by sin entered through the will, and afterward the death imposed by the sentence followed it, by the will of God.
So here too, before the dissolution of the body's nature, which is dissolved by the sentence,
the will of each one of us can break apart the structure of the old self made up of desires.
And when this death is undone, natural death too is no longer secure.
For since the death brought by sin introduced natural death, when the former is undone, the latter is also abolished.
And those who do not die beforehand are the ones who truly die.
But those who voluntarily put to death within themselves the self made up of desires—through its death, the death of their natural self is undone.
It is therefore good for us to die before our death, so that we may also live before our life.
For wherever voluntary death comes first, natural death too is undone.
And wherever natural death has already been undone through the power of free will, the one who dies is alive before he lives.
And since these processes of undoing and renewal take place beforehand within us in every form, it is fitting for us first to uproot evils,
and then to lay within ourselves a foundation for the building of good things, so that the rock may receive our foundation, as it is written,
and the firm stone may receive our building, as it is said. In this too we imitate doctors who treat the body:
until they have removed and cleansed the foul matter from a sore, they do not apply the dressing that builds up and promotes the growth of living flesh.
So we too, now that we have uprooted the foulness of gluttony and condemned its filthy and repulsive forms,
let us now show in our discourse the benefit of ascetic discipline, and through helpful teaching encourage the disciples
to embrace within themselves this endurance, which, though it is thought to involve difficult labors,
Rather, it is labor pain that brings us to birth into the taste of Christ’s blessings. And just as an infant is born into the world through its mother’s labor pains,
so a person is born into the world of the knowledge of Christ through the pains of affliction and the endurance of hardships.
And if someone calls ascetic discipline a cleansing of bodily desires, he is not mistaken.
For just as the body is washed by bathing, removing the things smeared over it that conceal its natural appearance and color,
so through ascetic discipline the blemishes of the old person are healed and polished away, and the beauty of the new person is revealed, clear and pure.
And when he is revealed and stands in his natural appearance, then it is easy for him to see and to be seen in the beauty of his soul.
For from this he receives the garment of knowledge. The beginning of ascetic discipline is bitter and hard,
but its end is pleasant and sweet. Its burden is heavy for those who have not experienced its lightness;
carrying it is difficult for those who have not gazed upon the spiritual riches within it. For it is the narrow gate
that leads into the spacious realm of spiritual beings. And just as renunciation of possessions is the end of the world’s road,
so ascetic discipline is the beginning of the road of life according to the gospel.
It was therefore fitting that we too, after the discourse on renunciation, entered into the teaching on ascetic discipline.
For as long as a person possesses something outside himself, he works with it and gathers a harvest from it.
And although goodness and compassion begin in his will, he nevertheless takes seed from outside himself and scatters it in the fields of those in distress.
One might say that he takes from the world itself and gives within it. And although the fruits of this righteousness
are gathered into the person’s own self, the labors lie outside his own person.
For what bodily hardship and affliction does someone experience whose righteous almsgiving is accomplished through wealth outside himself,
apart from this alone: that he restrains the thought of gluttony and subjects it to the will to show compassion?
But when he has stripped himself of everything and stands freely in the world with only his own self, his own person becomes the field he cultivates.
He himself cultivates it, and he himself sows it. His afflictions begin in himself and are completed in himself.
He no longer sows other people’s lands with the seed of almsgiving, but the rational field of his own person.
And in it he begins the work of the labors of righteousness.
Now the first practice in cultivating this field is the work of fasting and ascetic discipline.
For without this, all personal virtues are practiced feebly, and their strength within us is, as it were, diminished and limited.
For our prayer is not pure, nor indeed is our singing; our thoughts are not made holy, and our knowledge does not grow.
Our mind is not purified, nor does our understanding become clear, nor, in wonder at the greatness of God's glory,
is our hidden inner self renewed without the practice of fasting and the discipline of asceticism.
For through these things we enter into those things, and from this stage we rise to others greater than it.
For by persevering in abstinence from food, we come to resemble the angels.
Since the angels are entirely without food, let us voluntarily turn away from food that gratifies our cravings,
and reduce a little what the body requires. For by this we show that we have a longing to resemble spiritual beings.
For this reason our Lord, who came for our salvation, although he could, by his own authority,
have made us like the angels as soon as he appeared—the likeness he will give us at the end according to the riches of his grace—did not make us so.
Instead, he taught us how a person can resemble the angels, and left it to our own will to pursue their likeness.
Thus we ourselves, through the power of our freedom, may strip off our old bodily condition and put on the newness of the angels' likeness.
Let us exchange one food for another, one desire for another, one table for another, one nourishment for another,
one kind of food for another, and one flavor for another, because we too have one stomach and another,
which receive their different foods. When someone closes off one,
then he opens the other to receive the foods of the Spirit and to enjoy and delight in spiritual kinds of food that are beyond nature.
And because our nature was too weak to cut these things off and cast them away by its own power,
the gift of the Spirit came to our aid, so that what nature cannot do alone, we may accomplish with grace.
Therefore, disciple, struggle with all your soul against the cravings of your body, and cultivate good things in the field of your own self,
which is what remains to you of the world. For you yourself alone, out of everything in the world, will attain life.
For you the bridal chamber stands open, the kingdom is prepared, the reclining couch is spread, and the halls are made ready.
The table of delights is prepared at that living banquet, where God himself acts as the servant,
just as he himself proclaimed to you in his true word,
saying, "Truly I tell you, he will have his chosen ones recline at the table, fasten his belt around his waist, and come and serve them."
Therefore, keep this table in mind at all times, so that remembering it may give you strength and enable you to scorn the table of the natural life.
For no one exchanges the luxurious table of the kingdom for a poor, ordinary table of barley bread.
For this table of bodily foods is smaller and lower beside that spiritual table than even this comparison conveys.
Wake up, then, and keep watch over yourself when this desire begins to wage war against you.
Gather the whole army of your thoughts, with your watchful mind standing at their head as commander.
Confront the leader of the raiding bands, namely the passion of gluttony. For this desire knows
that it is too weak to fight against a thought sustained by endurance, so it brings hunger along as its helper.
It gives you the impression that you are not greatly to blame if hunger compels you.
That is, it presents you with arguments like these: necessity has been implanted in you by the Creator;
hunger naturally rules over your body; and your human life is sustained by food;
without these things you cannot remain in the world; and if you wish to live without them,
you are resisting the will of the Creator, who wills that your bodily life should be sustained in the world in this way;
and eating in moderation is not blameworthy, nor is drinking in a disciplined manner.
Once this desire has led you along by these enticements and brought you from not eating to eating,
it draws you further, from this to how you should eat and what you should eat.
For it does not advise you from the beginning to eat to satisfy your desire.
Instead, it persuades you to eat out of necessity, and then leads you from necessity to desire.
For a person stands firm through the strength of endurance when struggling to overcome natural hunger.
But if weakness gains control over him when he should be strong, he is easily defeated and brought into utter degradation,
once even a small measure of weakness has gained control over him. But examine carefully, with discerning understanding,
the fact that not all hunger is natural hunger, and not all eating is for the satisfaction of a need.
Examine the different kinds of hunger, and use your understanding to distinguish and identify your own hunger among them.
There is hunger that occurs in childhood, hunger that comes from weakness, and hunger that comes from illness.
Some comes from excessive depletion, some from habit, and some from the idleness of thoughts that have nothing to occupy them.
Some comes from the weakness of the thoughts themselves, and some from the midday exhaustion that overtakes the body.
Some is called for by the body's coldness, so that it may be warmed by food, and some is produced by excessive labor.
These and similar things are the causes of hunger, though there are also others
whose hunger is not healthy hunger. This is why you find many people who are hungry from the very beginning of the day.
Some become hungry after two hours, others after four hours, others after six, and others after nine.
Others become hungry in the evening. Some even overcome the hunger at the end of the day by fasting through the night, and some extend their fast even to the third day.
Once they have reached the length of a double overnight fast, natural hunger disappears from them completely.
For instead of food, the natural heat stirred up in the body becomes their nourishment.
Now that you understand from this the different kinds of hunger that arise in you, distinguish and single out from them all the hunger that comes from your actual need.
Yet from time to time you must resist even this hunger, so that your endurance of hardship may be revealed more fully,
and through it your love for God may be made known. But take care that the hunger of desire does not mislead you into thinking that it is natural hunger.
For true natural hunger is this: not the emptying of the stomach of food, but the depletion of the strength supplied by food from all the body's members.
For when the body's members have shed the strength derived from food and have clothed themselves in weakness instead,
and you call on them but they do not respond to perform the service you want, this is natural hunger.
At this point you need to take food carefully, to restore the strength of your body's members,
while guarding your mind so that it does not become entangled with the body in eating,
and putting the desire within you to sleep, lest it awaken and, instead of need, desire should impel you toward food.
For if this happens, your eating becomes blameworthy, even if you take only a little nourishment and eat plain food.
Let your mind, then, always watch over all your actions, whether they concern things in the world or things in your body,
or the rest of the things carried out in the soul. For a human being is not an animal, to eat whenever he becomes hungry.
Rather, as a rational being, he must ensure that even when the body displays its natural hunger, the soul also displays the endurance proper to it.
The soul too should exercise its own powers, just as the body exercises those belonging to its nature.
Let the body's hunger remind the soul of its own hunger, and let it take the body's need as testimony to the need of its own spiritual life.
For a manly soul ought not to be enslaved to the body's feminine passions.
Rather, it should rise up to fight against them, subdue and bind them, prevail and conquer, and produce riches and provisions within itself,
to counter these desires that rise from below to above, seeking to abase its greatness and defile the beauty of its splendor.
For whenever the body attacks you, at any time, through its needs or through the hunger of its desires,
overcome its attack at that moment through endurance, bringing forth within yourself another hunger to oppose that hunger,
and turning your mind away from dwelling on the body's hunger toward meditation and communion with God.
For in this way you can overcome the pleasure of his passionate hunger.
For if natural hunger ruled in each one of us, we would all grow hungry alike, a little sooner or a little later.
But because hunger also arises from the passion of desire, we grow hungry at different times.
For who does not know that the hunger that comes at the beginning of the day, or at the third hour, and perhaps even at the sixth, is not natural hunger?
For, as I said, natural hunger is the depletion of the nourishment supplied by food from the arteries.
Moreover, the fact that the passion is overcome by the strength of endurance shows that it is not natural hunger.
And even if it is natural, it must be overcome in this case too, because our way of life is above nature.
And our struggle is against nature. For the human life within us is not one of nature’s passions,
but is nature itself. Yet even though this is so, for the sake of the truth we struggle even against human life.
For the boundaries are clearly distinguished and established. For up to the boundary of death,
we have a struggle for righteousness against these desires.
But the battle for faith is against natural life itself.
For our Savior has not commanded us, in enduring the labors of righteousness,
to kill ourselves voluntarily. But for the sake of the truth we are commanded to die.
Therefore, even in practices below the level of faith, we must struggle against all the needs of nature,
but for the sake of the truth, against nature’s very life. Subdue, then, the passion of your hunger when this desire is stirred up within you,
and marshal all the forces of your thoughts for battle against it, so that if it is not overcome by one,
it will be overcome by many. For how could it fail to be overcome by the force of many thoughts,
when it is regularly overcome even by a single living impulse for God, provided that this impulse is sound within us, as though arising from a living and healthy nature?
For the force of the stone that is thrown corresponds to the strength of the hand that throws it.
And the force of the arrow that is shot corresponds to the strength of the arm that sends it.
Likewise, the strength of the impulse sent out by the soul to battle against desire corresponds to the soul’s strength and health.
And desire cannot hold out against it, even if it has held us through habit for a very long time.
That is, not even need can hold out. But notice that there are distinctions even among needs themselves.
For there is a need arising from desire, another arising from health, and another arising from strength.
And there is the need to sustain life. Let us therefore leave aside the earlier needs and attend to this last one.
When we are compelled to meet a need, let us meet neither the need of appetite, nor that of health, nor that of strength, but only the need to sustain life.
As we have also learned from the testimony of the righteous people of old, they were not speaking of a need for any of these three.
For some of them persevered for forty days, and others for three weeks, enduring fasting.
Is it not clear that they were meeting only the needs required to sustain life? And the duration of our Savior’s fast, too,
showed us this very thing. His reply to the devil also taught us this clearly.
“It is written,” he said, “that a person does not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God.”
He says “lives,” not “becomes healthy and strong,” or “has the needs of his appetite satisfied.”
Although this statement is brief when read, a great distinction can be seen in it.
For he taught us clearly through this statement: “A person does not live by bread alone.”
Let us eat only to live, not for appetite or for strength,
nor for health, since this kind of life is sustained even in sickness.
A person lives this life in the world even in weakness. For just as someone who has a severe illness in his body,
that is, in the organs that receive food—the food he takes
nourishes his illness rather than his strength—so too, when someone eats to satisfy the appetite within him, his food nourishes his appetite,
and not his human life. It is clear that someone who feeds himself to satisfy appetite produces desires.
For the flavor of trees that spring from the earth also corresponds to the nature of that earth.
Therefore, do not eat like a slave, but take your nourishment like a free person.
Let your food be for you, not for others. Instead of serving appetite as a slave, serve your own self.
For who is so foolish as to take food away from his own mouth and put it into the mouths of others?
If only it were the mouth of a helpful friend! But it is that of an enemy who opposes your true life.
For appetite has no power of its own to enslave your life. Rather, it draws power from your strength to enslave you.
Therefore, do not take your strength and give it to appetite, so that it can use it to fight against you.
Do not equip your enemy with the weapon you use to fight against him. Do not be divided against yourself.
That is, do not place yourself entirely on your enemy’s side and turn to wage war against yourself.
For this desire is weak, if you wish it to be. How could it not be weak, when it does not even exist without you?
But if you create it, you also give it strength.
And if its existence begins with you, it also receives from you the strength to gain power over you.
For just as God rules over created things, you are a god over your desires.
And just as created things exist by the will of their Maker, and do not exist if he so wishes,
so desires exist by your will, and by your will they sink into nothingness.
For it is said, “God calls things that do not exist as though they existed.”
In the same way, your will also creates desires that do not exist, bringing them into existence.
But God looks upon everything, and it becomes nothing.
In the same way, your will also looks upon all the passions, and immediately they disappear and sink into nothingness.
If you wish, your passions exist; and if you wish, they do not exist.
The growth of your desire springs from you, and its destruction is born from you. If you give it life, you put it to death [?].
And if desire lives in you, you put your life in God to death.
For there is no way for someone to live both with God and with desire, just as there is no way to live both with the devil and with Christ.
For bodily desire is hostile [?] to the spiritual person, just as the devil is an opponent of your whole being.
For good passions spring up in you from the soul, with the help of grace.
But evil desires have their origin in the body, with the enemy acting as their instigator.
Therefore, overcome what ought to be overcome, so that the one to whom victory belongs may be victorious in you.
Fight and overcome the first desire, so that victory over all of them may become easy for you through this.
For if one overcomes you, how much more will many overcome you!
For even when all the desires gather together, they are still weak.
But how much weaker they become when you overcome them one by one with steadfast endurance!
For you should also separate them from one another, so that victory over them may be easy for you.
For when the desires want to marshal themselves together against your endurance, do not give them what they seek,
or fight against all of them at once. Instead, divide them and separate them from one another.
Fight against each one of them individually, win the victory, and do not let them accomplish in you
their will. Do not merely keep them from overcoming you; also keep them from coming together.
For the very fact that they come in a band like this reveals their weakness.
And if their defeat has become apparent to you even when they gather together, how much more will their profound weakness become apparent when each one comes alone!
Be watchful, then, over the part of you that desires truth, which longs for life and yearns for good things.
And desire with a sound and incorruptible desire. For corruptible desire is subject to corruption,
and anyone who wishes to acquire the strength to endure can easily destroy it.
But incorruptible desire, even when its enemies think they are overcoming it,
is not loosened from the firm foundation of its nature. And if it seems to be overcome, it has not really been overcome.
Rather, it withdraws itself from a thought unworthy of it—a thought which, while holding on to it, struggles with hateful desire.
It is good, then, for us to overcome all desires, but especially this first desire.
If we overcome it, we will gain from it the strength to prevail against the other desires.
For whenever this evil desire is overcome within us, the others that follow it are defeated along with it.
And the more we see how great our achievement is, since by overcoming one we have overcome many, the more diligently we should pursue this work.
For if we are negligent, defeat will occur not only at that point, but also in the remaining battles that follow this one.
And just as, if we win, our first victory is a victory in all the contests, so too, if we are defeated,
it is a defeat in all the battles. We ought, then, to be victorious at all times,
because victory belongs to our nature. Defeat, however, is contrary to our nature and results from our own will and the enticements of our enemies.
Let us, then, willingly submit to the will of God our Maker, who has placed us in the contest so that we may be victorious.
Let the King who chose us not be ashamed of us or be reproached for choosing weak soldiers and bringing them into his army.
For our defeat suggests a lack of knowledge on the part of the one who chose us. Let us therefore be victorious, so that the wise one may not be thought ignorant because of us.
Observe, then, through the experience of your struggle, which thoughts overcome this desire of the belly whenever it harasses you.
And through this practice, whenever it draws up its forces against you, draw up these same thoughts against it.
And after victory, the delight of victory welcomes you. For as long as you are troubled by the incitement of desire,
you cannot taste the sweetness of victory. After a little while, when you are clothed in the armor of endurance,
And come out victorious from the contest of battle, and when the delight of victory comes to you.
For rest cannot come to you in this world; rather, rest is born from toil itself.
You cannot have a harvest spring up in your lap while you are still holding the seed in your hand.
Rather, harvests are gathered from the seed once it has been scattered. Nor, again, while you are still standing in the struggle of battle,
and it has not yet become clear which way victory is turning, is your triumph proclaimed in the cities.
Rather, after the battle ends and victory becomes evident, then the warrior’s triumph is proclaimed in the towns.
Take illustrations like these for this spiritual battle in which you are engaged.
And if you are troubled while you are fighting, know that this is to be expected.
And if you are toiling and sweating, this too goes along with your work. For if it is a struggle, there is toil in it.
And if it is a contest, those who enter it run with exhaustion and sweat. But do not look at these things that are close at hand.
Instead, look ahead to the rest that comes after afflictions. Do not let your mind be bound to your body.
Instead, let it run ahead and see what is to come, so that through the memory of victory you may strengthen the limbs engaged in battle.
You are spiritual, and you are fighting against the desire of the body. For it is ridiculous for a spiritual person to be overcome by the body.
And it is a disgrace for someone invited to heaven to have his belly fight against him and overcome him.
For if, against the principalities and spiritual authorities—that is, against the powers and armies of the enemy—
you have been appointed by grace to fight and conquer, how much more ought you to conquer your belly! For your very habit promises this.
And the appearance of your way of life proclaims that you are victorious over the opposing powers.
And who would not laugh at someone equipped for these things when he sees that his belly defeats him?
Especially when it is not the necessity of sustaining life that compels you to do this,
but a desire born from the weakness of your will, and an offspring of your own has risen in battle against you and brought you low.
If only it had done so when it was strong! But it is still an infant and a child, and it would be easy for you to put it beneath your heel.
See, then, how the Spirit also counsels you. It says, “Dash Babylon’s children against the rock while they are young.”
For the prophetic word rightly called these passions “children,”
to show their weakness and encourage you toward victory.
And it did not call them your children, so as not to disgrace you by showing that children like these had come from you.
But it called them the children of Babylon, that is, those born of slavery and not of freedom.
For slavery is the mother that gives birth to desires. The prophetic word represented her by Babylon the plunderer,
who violently plunders the strength of our spiritual self, as though taking spoil, and strips away its wealth.
Therefore, when desire and hunger join forces to fight against you, join your thoughts to grace and stand in prayer.
And, as someone who despises desire, do not even turn your thoughts toward it. I am speaking of the greater thing:
even when you fight and win, your victory still falls short, because you needed to fight
and only then conquered the belly, which you ought to have treated with contempt and regarded as beneath you,
without even letting your thoughts dwell on it. Instead, you should look down on it as a strong man looks down on a weak one,
and as a mighty, powerful man looks down on someone contemptible and lowly. For this is also the custom of valiant warriors:
when they see weak men coming to fight against them, they despise and scorn them and make light of their approach.
As it is also written about that blasphemous warrior, whose pride rested on bodily strength:
“When he saw David, he despised him.” If his confidence in the flesh filled him with such contempt for David,
how can you, with the strength of the spirit within you, fail to scorn and despise the appetite of the belly?
For whom does it usually overcome except infants and little children?
As soon as the appetite of the belly presses them with its need, they begin weeping and clamoring to their parents,
and demand that they supply their needs. This happens because they have not yet reached the stage
at which the strength to endure is born from the soul. But you have reached the stage of manhood,
and the strength of your soul has been revealed to you, if you wish to use it. Why are you overcome
by the belly like a little child, becoming a laughingstock as a childish passion mocks you?
For to the same extent that being overcome by the belly is natural to a child's stage of growth, victory over it is natural to you.
And just as his childhood is subject to defeat, so victory accompanies your full maturity.
Recognize the weakness of the appetite of the belly from this as well: its struggle is with those at the stage of childhood.
For we see that the other desires arise anew in our lives with the changes in our growth that come afterward.
But this appetite of the belly is stirred up in childhood itself. Know that it fights with a child because it is weak.
When it fights against you, however, it comes to put you to the test, not to win a victory.
Conquer it, then, by the strength of your endurance, even though conquering it is no very great achievement.
For it is a childish battle. Yet the help that arises from it is not as weak as it is itself.
For although it is small and insignificant, and conquering it is nothing remarkable,
it opens a door for us to victories against all the passions.
And when the other desires that follow it see this, they grow weak and do not come to fight.
Or if they approach to fight, they do so in fear and anxiety. For this very reason they come with half their strength, not with their full strength.
For fear tends to diminish and scatter strength. Fight, then, O disciple,
and conquer like a man, so that you may be worthily crowned as a mighty warrior. Do not be defeated, for this is not what you have set yourself apart for.
Do not fall, for this is not why you were chosen. Do not surrender, because a mighty hand is with you.
For the hand of Christ is with you in all these things whose battles you face,
if you are aware of the right hand that holds your right hand, and of the mighty arm that grasps your weak hand.
But since I must also teach you the first steps toward this victory, listen, and I will tell you.
Do not, then, count it a victory merely when you overcome the desire for lavish foods that cost a great deal.
Rather, when you also overcome the small and insignificant ones, count this all the more a victory.
For a disciple must abstain not only from eating meat and drinking wine, but from everything he craves.
Do not, then, fight against food, but against desire.
For if you wage war against food, when you have won the battle against one kind, another fights against you.
But if you fight against desire, in one battle you overcome many.
Besides this, there is another consideration: there are foods for which the blame is obvious whenever a solitary or a monk eats them.
Here, shame before other people helps you in the battle, and often embarrassment before those watching you restrains you from eating.
And because help comes to you from outside in this battle, its victory too is small.
But you, being wise in seeking benefit and skillful in finding help, struggle also with those foods that are permitted to be eaten.
Wage war against the desire for them. To put it briefly, I give you this sign:
Whatever is placed on your dining table, and your eye sees and desires, give it no thought.
Instead, say quietly to your stomach, “Because you craved it, you shall not taste it.”
And when it has received this rule from you, it attends to its needs and does not let the unrestrained eye of its appetite range over foods.
But I mean this—which perhaps not everyone accepts because it seems new.
Only a few understand it, and these are the ones capable of it:
It is better for you to eat meat without craving than lentils with craving.
Why? Because no passion arose in connection with eating the meat. But here, with this humble food,
the passion of craving preceded the eating. The food was condemned because of the craving for it, not because of its nature.
Or have you forgotten what Paul proclaims: everything God has created is holy, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving?
But take care here too, I ask you. Do not take this free statement as an opportunity for the flesh and use it
to serve your desires. For it is written for free people.
If you have experienced within yourself that you stand at the height of Christ’s freedom, and through the strength of your endurance have subdued
the slavery within you, make use of this statement—if you have realized that when you eat, it is as though you have not eaten,
and when you drink, you do not taste your drink. If, then, you eat like a dead person, eat.
But if you eat like a living person, take care not to taste. For awareness of the taste of what sustains you
itself testifies against you that you are still alive to craving, and that you ate in order to eat, not in order to live.
For holy Paul, standing at the height of this freedom, said: “Let the one who does not eat refrain from judging the one who eats.
And let the one who eats because of freedom not despise the one who does not eat because of slavery to the law.”
For someone governed by the law is still a slave and has not attained the perfect freedom of Christ.
So take care, then. Do not imagine that you stand in the realm of freedom while you are still serving in slavery,
