and eat everything when you have no permission to do so. For the blessed apostle also warned you against this: do not be enticed by thoughts of freedom
while you are still a slave. He says: “You were called to freedom, my brothers. Only do not let your freedom become an opportunity for the flesh.”
And if you are still a slave, let not only laws outside you govern you, but also the laws of your own discernment.
For external laws are observed for many reasons: to be seen, out of fear,
for praise, for love of honor, out of conceit, and to foster other passions,
and so that someone may humiliate his enemies, and so that he may show others to be lax in comparison with his own wickedness.
External law has many motives like these.
Let this be the rule for your discernment: if you crave something, restrain yourself from using it.
Moreover, recognize from this very craving that you are still a slave.
When you become aware of this slavery of yours, know that you need a rule.
Therefore you are obliged to surround every movement of your thoughts with a rule.
Restrain every thought that stirs within you with a craving for something, through fear of the rule.
At the same time, examine closely both the impulses of nature and the impulses of desire.
If the impulse comes from nature, check it; but if it comes from desire, uproot it.
For you have the power to uproot the impulses of desire, but those of nature you can check and quiet.
For desire itself receives its impulse from nature. It follows nature and watches for it to stir.
When it sees nature stir, it takes that impulse, makes it its own, and brings it out and hands it over to your will to carry it out in action.
But you, as an observer of your passions, must consider whether anything arising from desire is mixed into the impulse.
Say, “I accept the impulse that comes from nature, so that it may receive what it needs and subside.

But I separate out the impulse of desire, so that I do not incur condemnation by eating.” Conquer, then, the craving for vegetables, so that through this you may also conquer the craving for sexual immorality.
Do not let plain food entice you, so that a beautiful face may not excite you. Despise insignificant things,
so that cravings for stronger things do not gather against you. For desire presents you only with what weakens your way of life.
For because you keep far from the world's foods, from elaborate preparations of cooked dishes,
and from eating meat and drinking clear wines, desire does not bother presenting these things to you.
For it knows that they are very far removed from you, and that using them is incompatible with your vows.
They are cut off from you by habit, by the rule, by where you live, and by your way of life.
Where desire sees that something is fighting against it, it withdraws from the battle over these things,
and excites you with other things—your customary food—with a craving for [?],
with a craving for vegetables, with a craving for cold drinks instead of clear wines.
It uses these things, which seem to you not very blameworthy; that is, their very plainness serves as an excuse for them.
It advises you: “Eat, and you are not to blame; drink, and you incur no reproach. For these are necessities,
and you should not deny yourself necessities, especially since you come to taste food only in the evening, or once every two days.”
Eat everything set before you, and eat your fill as well, so that your body may grow strong and bear hardships.
For laxity counsels you under the guise of righteousness, because it often sees
that you recoil from openly lax advice. But do not let yourself be enticed even under these guises.
Do not look down on ordinary things, and do not think that food itself is blameworthy by nature,
but only when someone consumes it with craving. For whether someone eats meat or eats vegetables with craving,
the eating of both is the same. Both are blameworthy, because craving has consumed them.
For it was not the fruit that Eve ate that brought forth death; rather, craving for the fruit brought forth death.
For if she had kept the law and had not eaten with craving at that time, she could afterward have eaten from it many times
without being blamed, provided she approached it in an ordinary way, just as she approached all the other trees.
For it is written that she craved and then ate, and for this reason she was also condemned.
What, then, was the nature of this fruit, that it could bring forth death together with every evil?
For indeed, as many people say, and as Scripture itself also gives us a slight hint,
the fruit that Eve ate was a fig. And it is clear that the nature of a fig does not bring forth death.
So it was craving that brought forth death—the same craving that brings it forth in everyone in every generation.
For the root of death is craving, and the root of craving is sexual union. For this reason, all who are born from sexual union
are stirred by craving and subject to death, apart from the one who was not born from sexual union,
and for this reason was also free from the stirring of craving. Hence he was also shown to be above the death imposed by nature.
When he accepted death, it was a matter of choice, not of nature. The nature of food, then, is not blameworthy.
It is blameworthy, however, when craving consumes it. Even those foods that are distinguished in the law
were distinguished and prescribed for the Jews for a reason: to teach them to master their craving, even if only in certain things.
For if he had forbidden them all foods in the law, the commandment would have been too burdensome for them, and they would not have accepted it.
But if the commandment had not forbidden them even one food, they would have been driven like animals
indiscriminately toward everything desirable, and they would have had no way to learn that it is good for a rational being to overcome his craving.
For this reason, he allowed them to eat because of their weakness, but forbade them to eat many things,
so that the discernment belonging to their rational nature might be evident, and they might learn to struggle against cravings.
And because they would not willingly undertake the battle against desires, he declared foods unclean for them,
so that, if only because they were unclean, they would refrain from using them. But in your case he did not act this way.
Instead, he made everything clean and holy, as it is written: “Everything is made holy through the word of God and through prayer.”
This is so that the endurance arising from your discernment may be evident: you do not abstain from eating because the foods are unclean,
but because of what is said: “It is good not to eat meat or drink wine or anything that causes our brother to stumble.”
And also so that you may overcome desire by your own will, rather than under the constraint imposed by the uncleanness of foods.
For desire is not aroused toward things that are unclean by nature.
For this reason he made everything holy for you, so that, when things that arouse your desire appear on every side,
you may prevail over them all and overcome them through the love of God. Furthermore, for this reason too, it is fitting for you to show endurance.
For you, then, this is the distinction between foods: whatever you crave is to be unclean for you.
But whatever you approach out of need, without craving it, you are permitted to eat without blame.
The law that restrains and persuades you is not written outside you, as it was for them.
Rather, it is the law written on your heart, to which your conscience bears witness. It is read by you alone, and others outside you do not see it.
Nor is your freedom bound, as under the law, to abstain from eating lest it transgress the law
if you eat. For freedom is above the law, and for this reason it is the same for you
whether you eat or do not eat, as Paul also said about this freedom of the Spirit: “The one who observes a day observes it for his Lord,
and the one who does not observe a day refrains from observing it for his Lord. The one who does not eat abstains for God, and the one who eats eats for God
and gives thanks to the Lord.” In this freedom, then, we have the choice to eat or not to eat.
For this reason he does not distinguish foods for us by the law, so that, according to whether we crave them or not,
they may be distinguished for us, and we may refrain from eating whatever we crave as though it were unclean,
whether it is costly or cheap, and whether or not custom permits us to eat it.
But whatever we have no craving to eat, let us eat as something clean, provided that our conscience does not reproach us for eating it.
For the reproach of conscience is itself a transgression of the law, as the apostle also said:
“If anyone doubts and eats, he stands condemned.” For the Jews ate meat in the wilderness,
and it is written about them: “While the meat was still between their teeth, God's wrath came upon them.”
Not because they ate meat, but because they asked to eat it out of craving.
For if eating meat in itself brought wrath, they would have received such punishment wherever they ate it.
The priests too, who regularly ate meat inside the temple, would have deserved that very same condemnation.
But nowhere is it written that wrath came upon them because they ate meat, except in this one place, where they sought meat out of craving.
David testifies that they asked out of craving, saying, “They craved intensely in the wilderness and tested God in the desert.
He gave them what they asked for and sent satisfaction to their souls.”
And in the very passage where they asked for meat, it is written that the people said to Moses, “We were better off when we were in Egypt,
where we sat beside the pots of meat and ate our fill of everything we desired.”
And Moses too, when he saw that they had craved and had defiled themselves through their craving, said to them,
“Purify yourselves for tomorrow, so that you may eat meat.” As one might put it: since they had defiled themselves through their cravings,
and God's gift does not come near the unclean, “Purify yourselves from that craving, so that you may be worthy of the gift of meat.
You will eat it not for one day, nor ten, nor twenty. You will eat it for a whole month,
until it comes out of your nostrils and becomes loathsome to you, because you rejected the Lord who is among you and said, ‘Who will give us meat to eat?’”
See, then: according to Moses' words to the Jews, everyone who eats out of craving rejects the Lord who is within him and rests content with satisfying his craving.
It was fitting that loathing should become the limit of that eating which craving had demanded.
For need observes a limit, but craving has neither limit nor end.
Consider again, from another angle, that they were condemned because they craved, not because they ate meat.
For look: Elijah did not ask out of craving, yet the ravens fed him bread and meat in the evening and in the morning.
He drank water from the stream. And when meat was sent to the prophet by the Giver, he, exercising his freedom,
accepted it as he would a meal of vegetables. Consider again, in another way, that it is craving that is blamed.
For every day, morning after morning, the people gathered the manna that came down for them.
As long as they gathered it according to the commandment, they were neither blamed nor condemned.
But when they craved to gather more, it teemed with worms and rotted, to the shame of the craving that had gathered it.
Moreover, when they ate it, it changed in their mouths into the flavor of every kind of food.
Clearly, it also supplied them with the taste of meat, since it is written that it was like a honey cake.
And its taste was like that of something kneaded with oil. And although it was transformed into all these different flavors,
those who ate it were not condemned for this, because it was a gift of grace, not something sought by their craving.
But to understand that anything eaten with craving is blameworthy, even if it is plain, set these two examples before your eyes:
Esau’s meal and Elijah’s meal. Esau was condemned for eating lentils,
and because of this Paul calls him lax and sexually immoral, saying that he sold his birthright for a single meal.
But Elijah, though he ate meat, was pure, holy, and spiritual. And as a spiritual man, he was taken to the dwelling place of spiritual beings.
See, then, and understand from these examples of Elijah and Esau that craving brings condemnation, not food.
Do you therefore want to eat anything without being condemned? Rise above craving in everything, and eat anything.
But if you do not rise above craving, whatever you eat brings condemnation on you, even if it is plain,
just as Eve was condemned for eating fruit, and the Jews were accused over their gathering of manna,
and Esau too was condemned for eating lentils. The people also perished because they ate and drank with craving before the calf.
Let David, who was wise in the things of God, convince you that even drinking cold water is blameworthy when it is done with craving.
For when he longed to drink water from the great well in Bethlehem,
and those who heard him heard and brought it to him, he overcame his craving and poured it out before the Lord.
It was as though, through the water, he was pouring out the craving within him. It was not the nature of the water that would have caused him to sin
if he had made use of its refreshment, nor was it because the water was cold and pleasant.
Rather, because he recognized within himself that he had sought it out of craving, he overcame his craving and did not grant it what it asked.
He also meant to distress those who had served his craving, by rejecting the kindness they had shown him,
to teach everyone not to be enslaved to craving, and not to smile upon those who serve our craving.
God also permitted Noah to eat everything, just like green plants.
While Adam was accused for eating fruit, Noah was given authority over every kind of food, as though by a covenant of generosity.
But when he indulged his craving, he too was blamed. For when he enjoyed the pleasure of wine with a craving appetite,
and went beyond proper order and moderation in his drinking, he then fell into disgrace.
For God had permitted him to eat any meat his soul desired.
And that food, which is burdensome to the discerning, was given to Noah by a promise.
And it was sent to Elijah as a gift, and with it Abraham welcomed God and his angels.
And Isaac was pleased by it in his old age and poured out blessings upon Jacob; and Samuel, for Saul,
first presented this gift to him as to a king. And David and all the righteous kings
made use of food like this, and it was widely used among all the righteous.
And they are not blamed for it, because they were above desire. They did not eat with desire like slaves,
but like free people they used everything with authority. And while they are praised for eating lavish foods,
others are despised and reproached even while feeding on plain and humble foods.
And although Paul cries out to us, “Do not let your hearts be weighed down by eating meat and drinking wine,”
to teach us that this food weighs down the heart, they ate and were not weighed down.
And perhaps they ate it for this very reason: to show that their lightness was stronger than its heaviness.
And through the very thing that dulls the heart, their understanding was polished all the more.
And through what weighs down the body and darkens the thoughts, the lightness of their minds was illuminated.
For they did not consider it so great a thing to be clear, pure, and holy while abstaining,
as to be purified through things that dull the heart—that is, to gain clarity through things opposed to clarity.
Thus, like mighty warriors, they would conquer through opposition, and like people with authority and freedom, through things that cause harm
they would remain unharmed. But you have not reached this point, nor have you risen to this level.
For this reason you need to abstain from everything and take nourishment in moderation, so that you may gain clarity.
And you must eat and drink by weight and measure, so that you may become clear. For, as you profess,
you are pursuing clarity of soul, and you are striving to become like the angels.
But you cannot stand in the freedom of spiritual beings until you have completely cast off the slavery of bodily beings.
For once you have cast off this slavery, you are beyond reproach in whatever you eat, like a spiritual being and a free person,
provided that eating meat does not weigh down your heart and drinking wine does not darken your thoughts, just as it is also written of the angels
that they ate meat and drank wine in Abraham’s house, and their spiritual nature was not weighed down by this nourishment.
And likewise all the righteous recorded in the Scriptures ate without becoming weighed down or dulled,
because they did not take nourishment with passion. Be free from passion, and eat like the angels in Abraham’s house.
And like all the righteous people in the Old Testament, you are not blamed.
Yet even in this you are obliged to preserve chastity in your conduct, because this is fitting for your commitment.
And for the benefit of others. For not everything over which we have freedom and authority
is permitted for us to approach. For although freedom has authority over everything, it does not make use of everything,
so that it does not lose its freedom. For a free person demonstrates his freedom by not being bound by a desire for anything.
And by not making use of something even when he has the authority to do so, he further increases his freedom and preserves it from being undone.
As Paul also writes about this freedom: “Everything is permitted for me, but not everything builds up.”
And so that you may learn that, along with the other matters, especially in this matter of eating or not eating,
he was making known the authority of his freedom, he said immediately afterward: “Food is for the stomach,
and the stomach for food. But God will do away with both.”
Therefore, disciple, observe the rule of ascetic discipline, so that you may also attain the authority of freedom.
Subdue yourself and do not eat, so that you may approach the state in which, even when you eat, you feel nothing.
Abstain from food through your own self-control, so that the desires mingled into your bodily members may be beaten down.
Do not eat, so that you may not sin. Do not drink, so that you may not go astray. Train yourself in fasting, so that through it you may become worthy of purity in prayer.
Reduce your food at mealtimes, so that the wing of your mind may be light for its flight toward God.
Call your body to account even for the smallest things, so that through these your soul may gain command of the abundant riches of divine knowledge,
and the one who reveals to you the treasures of his wisdom and knowledge may not call you to account.
Close your eyes to desires for a little while, and look, you have crossed the difficult terrain.
For the time of being subject to passions is only a little, brief time, but the time of freedom from passions is endless.
Therefore, do not be defeated at the time of victory. Seize the battle against desire as an opportunity, so that your soul may find work to do.
For as long as desires carry out their work in you, your soul has no work to do in you.
Although it is within you, it is as though it were not, because it is empty and idle, not performing the activities proper to its nature.
But when the body begins to stir its desires within you, pause and stand firm, and marvel at the sight of your desire,
like an idle person who has found work. Say to your soul: “Why are you troubled, my soul, and why were you grieved
that you were deprived of benefits? Look, work has fallen into your hands. Apply yourself diligently to it.”
Look, desire is stripping for the contest to face you. Show your athletic skill and the strength of your arms.
Here is material for gain, since you love gains. Look, your enemies have gathered for the clash of battle.
Shout against them with your mighty voice; rebuke and scatter the armies of the passions.
Here the undisciplined trade in losses; but you, as a diligent worker, gather gains.
For your victory is proclaimed all the more through this: where others are defeated, you win the victory.
Desire is a cause of defeat for the slack, but for you, because you are diligent, let it become a cause of triumphs.
For just as a warrior who trusts in his strength and relies on his skill,
who rejoices at the sight of enemies, so you too should rejoice at the arrival of the passions.
For without them your triumphs come to nothing, and you have no material for the struggle from which victory is born.
Say these things to your own soul whenever the passions happen to rise up against you.
Especially say them against this foolish desire of gluttony, which habitually sprouts from childhood.
For, foolish as it is, it enters alone, because it likes to appear by itself, and lays a foundation of laxity from the beginning of bodily growth.
Thus, beginning from here, it is found to be a helper to all the desires that spring up at every age.
This, then, is the first desire that conquered the world, and because of it the first transgression of the commandment occurred. And perhaps Cain too,
when he turned toward it, resolved to kill his brother and inherit the earth alone. It placed a blemish on righteous Noah.
It stripped Esau of his birthright and his blessings. It also brought the Sodomites to the practice of impurity.
In its company the descendants of Seth also came to the passion of sexual immorality, because of which they were rejected from God's household.
It destroyed the people in the wilderness through punishments of every kind. They rose from desire's table and worshiped a lifeless calf.
At its urging they denied all the kindnesses shown to them. For Israel grew fat and kicked through this desire;
it is written of him that he forgot God his Maker. Because the priests indulged their cravings, drank, and became confused in the place of atonement, fire consumed their bodies.
The prophet also reproached the people for it, pronouncing woe on those who rise early in the morning and run after it.
Again, another prophet accused them of this very desire: 'They eat fattened animals from the flock,' he says, 'and calves from among the herds.'
Because of it the scribes and Pharisees received a pronouncement of woe from our Savior, for it taught them to take account even of [?], dill, and cumin.
It exacted levies through the priests, who took them unjustly from those presenting offerings.
It stripped the sons of Eli of their priesthood.
Through its excessive indulgences, even Solomon was led into the error of idolatry. Even today it corrupts everyone.
For its sake the world toils. For its comfort creation runs about. All human beings serve it as slaves.
It is as though, if it did not exist, the door would be shut against every evil.
Examine and consider with understanding the running about of every person, and the labor, exhaustion, and sweat of all who enter the world:
it is solely for its sake. On its behalf and because of its needs, merchants travel the roads.
Sailors voyage on fearful seas. Farmers and laborers endure toil and hardship.
Craftsmen work in the cities. Hired workers run about for wages. Slaves serve their masters.
Masters, in turn, buy and acquire their slaves for its sake. Treasures are gathered, and stores are kept for years.
Gold, silver, and produce of every kind are gathered and accumulated on its behalf.
Go up, then, and stand on the height of knowledge, and from there look out over the whole world,
and see its haste, its restlessness, its turmoil, and the rushing of its inhabitants in every direction.
See those who go up and others who come down, those who go away and others who come, one who shouts,
and another who quarrels, one who disputes and another who fights, one who seizes what is not his and another who plunders his fellow,
one who steals like a thief and another who snatches things along the roads like a bandit; battles
drawn up at the borders; kingdoms divided against themselves; army commanders rebelling against kings;
kings fighting for their dominions so that they will not be seized; judges accepting bribes;
advocates unjustly selling victory in court; students studying for its sake;
scribes teaching in exchange for it. And when you have seen all these things and many others like them,
and the various kinds of turmoil and tumult that fill the world, turn and seek the cause of all these things, and you will find
that it is nothing but love of the belly. If it were overcome, everything would be peaceful and at rest.
You would see nothing in the world that opposes the will of God or leads us to transgress the commandment and trample on the law.
If someone says that there are also other causes of the passions, of all those practiced in the world,
let the person who says this know that love of the belly is also the origin and cause of these other evils.
Although the passions are very numerous and intertwined, and are stirred up in different ways in all human beings,
and through this the world is thrown into turmoil and creation is disturbed, yet the great source,
That from which these muddy streams flow in every direction is this desire: gluttony.
If someone blocks up this spring through the strength of his endurance, he immediately sees all the streams of evil that gush from it drying up.
Stillness comes over everything, and peace reigns over all flesh.
Rest pours into troubled places, and all thoughts are filled with delight and joy.
And, so to speak, if it were not present, you would not see a single evil in the world.
For all evils gather around it, and all labors and struggles run their course because of it.
The fact that we must eat bread by the sweat of our faces arose from it.
It made thorns and thistles grow. Through its fall, the sentence of death came to reign over everyone.
For it is the commander of the left side, and all the forces of sin are bound to it.
And just as commanders go out to battle against their enemies at the head of their armies,
so it too goes out to battle against good things at the head of the army of all evils.
Thoughts and deeds of wickedness accompany it, along with sinful impulses and actions.
Every form of evil conduct follows in its crooked footsteps, and all the deeds of sin serve as its limbs.
From it they receive strength, and from it they are nourished. For just as the senses are bound to the head,
so error, idol worship, doubt, conceit, and falsehood are bound to gluttony.
And again, just as all the limbs of the body receive strength and support,
so all evils are strengthened by it itself, namely sexual immorality and adultery,
and other corrupting passions, elaborate clothing, and the empty pleasures belonging to gluttony,
and distress, empty glory, pride, anger, despondency, bitterness, and malice,
and hatred, hostility, resentment, arrogance, shouting, and irritability,
and envy, bitterness, troublemaking, deceitful appearances, and leadership,
and authority, slander, treachery, a tongue that constantly strikes in secret, and contempt,
and mockery, oppression, violence, murder, sorcery, drunkenness, and blows,
together with the rest of the hateful passions like these, all of which are bound together to gluttony.
But I leave aside speaking of the labors, afflictions, pains, and illnesses:
And other things like these that afflict us bodily, of all of which it is the cause.
Whoever fights with the strength of his endurance and overcomes this first evil can, by overcoming it, overcome every sin.
The godly men have also rightly handed down to us that whoever wishes to become perfect in the way of Christ must first fight against this passion.
So too, those who leave the world in pursuit of perfection, if they do not begin with abstinence,
do not begin the way of the commandments according to the rule, and perhaps cannot even complete it.
For the appetite of the belly steals them away, even if at first they exercise it in an orderly manner,
and brings them to the excitements of thoughts and the fantasies of the mind.
And it makes still thicker that veil which stands before the intellect and darkens it, keeping it from the vision of God.
Until that veil is torn away from before the mind,
a person cannot look into the Holy of Holies of the knowledge of Christ, even if he bears afflictions and hardships.
For unless he tears apart that veil of dullness of heart, the heavenly light is not visible to him.
Nor does he practice the way of life of Christ with conscious awareness in his soul.
For once this veil is torn apart, a person begins to perceive the renewal of his soul and to know, through the understanding of its mind,
that there is something else beyond what can be seen and touched, and also to receive awareness of the things above the world,
and wonders and living impulses toward God, so that a person may be moved toward him in a living way, like him, and not in a lifeless way, like the nature of his body.
In short, a person is found worthy of every spiritual vision after victory over this appetite.
For if those who are in the world and practice righteousness need fasting and abstinence,
how much more do those who have left it under a commitment to a spiritual way of life.
For this is the defining rule of this abstinence: to struggle against all foods that serve the belly,
not only through the endurance of the bodily members, but also through perseverance in one's thoughts.
And if a person is compelled by his need to take nourishment, let him take it from foods that are humble, looked down on, and ordinary,
and inexpensive and easy to obtain. But let him also guard against filling his belly.
For, as one of the spiritual teachers has said, a bloated belly cannot give birth to a subtle intellect.
For excessive fullness of the stomach undoubtedly darkens the intellect.
None of those who have gained knowledge through experience can doubt this, even if fools dispute it.
They doubt because they have not experienced it, or because, although they know it, they find it hard to turn away from their desires.
Conclusive testimony, then, will show you this: the more the body is nourished, the weaker the soul becomes.
And the more it grows fat and adds flesh upon flesh through nourishment, the more the soul dwindles and wastes away.
Although it is there, it seems as though it were not in the body.
And the more the body increases in strength and vigor of stature, the more the soul’s own stature bows down and its limbs diminish,
which are its thoughts. Its knowledge dwindles, and the light of instruction is withheld from it.
The more the body is found, the more the soul is lost; and the healthier it becomes, the sicker the soul becomes.
But anyone who wants to find his soul should surrender his body to destruction through every kind of affliction. And behold, he has found his soul,
through the destruction of his body. And the health of the spiritual person lies in the sickness of the bodily person,
as Paul also testifies: “When I am weak, then I am strong.”
For whenever two opposing sides are fighting one another, as long as they are equal in the number of their troops
and equal in the art of warfare, their fighting is continual: at every turn they conquer and are conquered, and they take
and give victory to one another, snatching triumphs from one another and driving one another back.
Their equality gives rise to continual warfare between them. This, then, is also how
the soul and the body stand toward one another. Just as their natures oppose one another, so do their wills. Concerning this Paul also said:
“The body desires what harms the spirit, and the spirit desires what harms the body, and the two oppose one another.”
As long as they remain at this level of equality, they are engaged in continual warfare without respite.
Sometimes the body defeats the soul, and sometimes the soul overcomes the body. Anyone who fights in this way stays where he is.
For even if he takes a small step to advance in the things of the soul, the body clings to it and turns it backward.
Then it drags the soul even from that place and brings it down into the depth of sin.
Through these ascents and descents, these comings and goings, a person does not move from his place.
He cannot grow in the stature given to him by God, through which he is to grow into spiritual life.
If, then, those whose vital impulses remain balanced between soul and body
cannot gain victory and reach the harbor on the journey of their way of life,
how can those who live in the body, continually nourish the body, and give it everything it needs,
They feed him to bursting, give him as much drink as he wants, and plunge him into the heaviness of sleep.
They can gain victory over the passions and complete this Christian path along which they are traveling.
For those who nourish themselves in this way and care for their bodies in this manner,
not only cannot overcome the sin within them, but their soul dies and is utterly lost.
Their bodies become tombs for their souls, and their souls are buried within them like corpses in tombs.
They are entirely unaware of their souls' own life. And if there is any stirring of life within them,
it is all on behalf of the body. For when the soul puts the body to death, the activity in everything belongs to the soul.
For if the body puts the soul to death, the body thinks, acts, and speaks like a living being, while the soul dwells within it like a dead person who feels nothing.
And if the soul seems to be alive, because its nature is immortal, it lives for the body and not for the soul.
Therefore, take away from the body and give to the soul. Do not take away from the soul and give to the body.
As your Creator has promised it will be for you, so you too should act toward yourself. For this hope has been given to you:
that at the resurrection your body will be raised to the level of your soul, not that the soul will be brought down to the body's mortality and decay.
For you have been told that one half of you will live together with the other half, not that the superior part within you will perish along with the inferior part.
Therefore, lift up the strength of your body to your soul; transform its life and blend it with the soul's life,
so that its mortal life may be preserved together with the soul's immortal life, and its feeble strength may be blended with the might of spiritual strength.
For instead of letting the grave consume your body and dismantle and scatter the structure of your limbs,
take the portions belonging to its limbs, through the inward labors of all the limbs, and lay them upon the soul.
Then, when the soul leaves you through the dissolution of death, it will not depart alone, but carrying with it everything belonging to the body:
its strength within the soul's strength, its life within the soul's life, its bodily nature within the soul's spiritual nature,
its limbs and senses, and all the activity of their service, within all the spiritual parts of the soul.
We need this struggle, especially to gain victory in it, from the beginning of our youth.
For from the first growth of people in infancy, this passion accompanies their lives,
and at every stage of growth it causes the passions suited to that stage to spring up.
For in infants and old people, in children and those advanced in years, this passion produces anger, shouting, constant pestering, and irritability.
But in the other, intermediate stages—youth, adulthood, and middle age—it produces sexual immorality and empty pleasures.
And love of money, and love of power, together with the rest of such things.
And corresponding to the order of these stages, the forms of struggle should also vary.
For at the stage of childhood, because it falls short of the knowledge needed to distinguish things,
they should be restrained by the compulsion of the law from indulging this desire, and trained by teachers and masters
to carry out this practice of asceticism. And even when it is burdensome to them and they find no comfort in it,
they should nevertheless compel themselves and complete it, so that they may acquire a good habit and be trained in endurance from their childhood.
And when they reach the stages that bring forth knowledge, they become aware of the taste of endurance itself and taste the sweetness of victory.
For a childhood that is taught good things from the beginning and trained in the practice of endurance
is like a field cultivated and sown in advance, so that at the proper time it may yield the fruits of knowledge.
And why do I speak of children, since even at every stage, including those of the mature and fully developed,
their knowledge of the contests is not apparent to them at times when their thoughts are disturbed by the struggle of those contests?
But when they have ceased from battle, then they become aware of that knowledge.
If, however, knowledge is found in them at the time when they are struggling, their knowledge concerns how they should struggle.
That is, it is the knowledge of the tradition of the law, which is established through hearing, through what is handed down, and through teaching and speech.
But this is not the knowledge of the Spirit, which dawns naturally in the soul and brings forth words without recalling what has been handed down.
For just as the eye, through its swiftness, receives the sight of light in its simplicity, so too the soul’s sight receives,
after victory over these bodily passions, the clarity and simplicity of the knowledge of the Spirit.
And just as the sun, itself undivided, falls upon distinct natures and bodies, and in them appears to be divided and separated,
although its nature is one and simple, with no division in it, so too the knowledge of the Spirit, when it dawns upon ways of life and labors,
appears to be distinguished and divided along with them, although in itself it is single and simple.
But the soul is not found worthy to receive the dawning of this light unless the person has first been born from bodily existence into spiritual existence.
This birth is brought to completion through labors and afflictions.
“Flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of heaven,” the blessed Paul teaches us.
It is as though someone were to say: As long as a person’s impulses arise from flesh and blood,
he cannot inherit the spiritual knowledge of Christ, which he calls, as in a riddle, the kingdom of heaven.
Although this expression has other meanings in other contexts, nevertheless, with reference to the subject before us,
it is fitting for us to use it in this sense as well, because the true kingdom is this:
knowledge that neither errs nor conjectures, but clearly sees everything in its proper place,
both the things of nature and those above nature, according to the measure granted to created beings.
A person whose life is sustained by the impulses of flesh and blood cannot become an heir to this knowledge.
Even if he should happen to receive it through instruction conveyed in words, he is hearing words from others,
and knowledge itself has not revealed itself within him. For this knowledge lies deeper than words,
and deeper than readings and names, as the example of those chaste young men who were brought up in Babylon also testifies to us.
While they were receiving human learning through spoken instruction,
they longed to receive divine knowledge beyond what spoken words could convey. This knowledge did indeed reveal itself within them
at the proper time. And this knowledge taught the young men what human learning could not discover.
It was revealed within them because they, too, had followed its own path toward it in accordance with its rule.
For although their provisions were supplied from the table of kings, and they were instructed to take food suitable for those receiving royal learning,
they rejected this table because they perceived that it fostered worldly knowledge.
Refined and purified foods are required for those receiving human learning,
so that their bodily senses may be sharpened and made nimble in proportion to the refinement of their food.
But knowledge of the spirit has no need of these things, because it does not take hold within the soul through the clarity of the bodily senses.
Rather, when all the parts of the soul have been purified and cleared of evil passions, then this knowledge dawns within it.
Pure foods help and provide no small benefit to the alertness of the senses of those receiving knowledge of the soul.
But spiritual people have no need of this at all. To know that this is so, take the testimony of these chaste young men themselves.
Instead of the refined and purified royal foods, they chose pulses for themselves and water to drink.
These give the body coarse and heavy nourishment.
The effect of this food of pulses is adverse to those receiving the knowledge of human learning.
But because they were purifying not their bodies but their souls, they chose a diet of pulses for themselves,
so that the body would be weakened, and the strength and natural vigor of its limbs would be brought low, and after these things there would be revealed
the living faculties of the soul, to the perception and vision of divine knowledge—which indeed came to pass:
After three years in which they ate seeds and drank water, knowledge was revealed to them.
Not the knowledge born of words, but the knowledge born of deeds.
For they performed deeds that give birth to spiritual knowledge, and learned words that give birth to human knowledge.
But because their own expectation was directed toward the revelation of the knowledge that comes from deeds,
and not toward the knowledge that comes from words, they saw where they were looking, and received from the source from which they expected to receive.
They became a passageway for words and vessels receptive to spiritual knowledge.
For you can understand from the account itself that they were not merely eating seeds
and drinking water, but were also taking this ascetic food after prolonged fasting.
For someone who eats seeds also trains himself in fasting.
And someone who drinks water also continually devotes himself to pure prayer, if that is the purpose of his ascetic discipline.
Understand this from the reading itself: when the time came for knowledge to reveal itself in them,
they devoted themselves to ascetic discipline, fasting, and prayer. Then the revelations they were asking for were shown to them.
It says that Daniel told his companions to ask the God of heaven that this mystery might be revealed to them,
so that Daniel and his companions would not perish with the rest of the wise men of Babylon.
Then the mystery was revealed to Daniel in a vision at night. This, then, was the gift that ascetic discipline gave the young men.
This was the harvest they gathered from those fields that were sown with seeds and watered with water.
Run, then, disciple, as they did, so that you may find as they did. Constrain yourself so that you may come out into a spacious place.
Make yourself small so that you may enter through the narrow gate. Drink water so that you may drink knowledge.
Feed on seeds so that you may become wise in mysteries. Eat in moderation so that you may love without measure.
Be one who fasts so that you may become one who sees. This is your food, for your very discipleship
promises such things. Luxurious food and a full belly are not for you,
but for those who live in wickedness in the world, who continually produce the thorns and thistles of sin.
For a person sown with luxuries and drinking wines habitually produces fruits like these.
But as for eating seeds and drinking water, their harvest is
Visions and heavenly revelations, knowledge of the Spirit, divine wisdom, and the interpretation of hidden things.
And what human knowledge does not perceive, the soul that practices such things does perceive.
Begin the life of spiritual labors while you are still young. Do not say, “I am only a child,” because the example of the young men takes away your excuse.
For those beloved ones, as the scriptural account indicates, were young in years when they began this divine work.
They discovered this without teachers. You, however, should practice it when you have teachers.
They were being urged to do the opposite—that is, to eat and drink.
But divine teaching advises you to do the opposite: to love the ascetic way of life and hold firmly to endurance.
Although they were under no obligation and were not required to do so, they chose this for themselves of their own free will.
But if you do as they did, you are paying a debt and fulfilling your pledge in accordance with the word of God addressed to you.
Rouse yourself, then, and look at these children of the old covenant.
Although they were born of one mother, they drank the milk of another.
For although the old covenant gave birth to them into faith in God, they fulfilled the spiritual way of life of the new covenant.
Their mother’s milk did not please them; instead, they longed to suck from the breasts that nurse you.
They desired your very own table. But when you do these things, you are doing what belongs to you.
You are being nourished from the same source from which you were born, and you are keeping the laws that you are obliged to keep.
For your calling proclaims this: labors, afflictions, ascetic discipline, and subduing the body.
After these things, the consolations born from them come to you: delight, joy, and confidence.
All these things are above the world, and before the kingdom comes, you inherit the kingdom.
For a person who, along with bodily afflictions and heavy labors,
also purifies and cleanses his soul of evil—this person inherits the kingdom before its time.
Before the revelation of glory to all, his glory is revealed to him from within his own soul, and he himself becomes the fountain of his knowledge.
For one person is destined to be found worthy of the kingdom in heaven, while another finds the kingdom within himself.
“Look,” he says, “the kingdom of God is within you.” And elsewhere he said, “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near.”
Both are true: that the kingdom of heaven, which the righteous are destined to inherit at the end of the world, is above in heaven,
and that the kingdom is within you—that is, the knowledge of the Spirit that is revealed to spiritual people.
And they are as though already in the kingdom of heaven, enjoying delight that cannot be expressed.
But not one of these things can be attained without afflictions and bodily toil.
For those who bear toil in their bodies are heirs of the kingdom of heaven.
And those who, along with toil, also possess purity of soul discover the kingdom within them.
They exult and delight in its blessings, in lasting joy over which sorrow has no power.
For they always rejoice with a joy born within them, as Paul also said: “Rejoice at all times.”
And again, in another place, he said: “Rejoice in your hope, and endure your afflictions.”
For through endurance of afflictions, hope for the things to come also grows within us.
As Paul himself said elsewhere: “Affliction develops endurance in us, and endurance, proven character;
and proven character, hope. And hope does not put us to shame.” For someone who does not bear afflictions with personal perseverance clearly does not even keep hope in mind.
For if he had hope, he would also suffer for the sake of his hope, just as all the righteous who came into the world suffered every kind of toil,
and through many afflictions traveled this road that leads to the kingdom of God.
And because they traveled in hope, the taste of afflictions was sweet to them.
For all of them, the beginning of the road of afflictions was ascetic discipline, just as the beginning of all evils
is the greed of the belly. For both roads begin from it, from that very same place:
from love of the belly comes the road to the left, and from hatred of the belly, the road to the right.
Anyone who wishes to begin the road of discipleship in good order must begin here.
By afflicting and disciplining his body, reducing its food and drink, and making it bear the toil of keeping vigil, hardships, and fasting,
its desires are cut off, and it becomes light and easy for the soul to direct in its activities.
But undergoing afflictions is not as difficult as hearing about them, because hearing of something from a distance tends to frighten everyone.
But once these things have been tested and experienced in practice, they become easy for those who do them.
But for you, who have renounced the world, there are things that help you greatly and lend you a hand in leading a good life.
For the very fact that you keep away from the things of the world, from seeing and hearing them, does much to preserve your life in holiness.
But those beloved young men whose example I have given you, though the royal table was set before their eyes,
despised its delicacies and chose afflictions for themselves instead of comforts.
Consider from this the strength of their endurance: although there was no teacher to admonish them, nor anyone to lend a hand and encourage them,
nor the example of others who had gone before them, nor fear of a law imposed on them, nor deprivation and need,
nor anxiety and fear to restrain them, nor the fact that they kept away from the sight of things—
which also helps endurance—although none of these things was present, they filled themselves with the strength of endurance.
But you, even with all these things helping you, persevere with the endurance appropriate to your discipleship,
and overcome the evil mistress, the mistress of every wrongdoing. Subdue your body and discipline your limbs.
As Paul also said: “I subdue my body and enslave it, lest, after I have preached to others,
I myself should be rejected.” And if Paul, although he had decisively overcome the passions through the power of grace,
still needed to subdue his body, how much more must those in whom the desires of the flesh are still alive
subdue their bodies through fasting and ascetic discipline, and fight and overcome!
But as for you, disciple, if you wish to excel in your discipleship, let the table, which is a place of rest for others,
be a place of combat for you. At it, draw up your battle line against every kind of food,
whether great or small, whether costly or ordinary.
Do not make light of desire because it has fastened on little things, and dismiss it as undeserving of blame.
Rather, you are more blameworthy if you are defeated by little things, even more than by great things.
For if desire defeats you through little things, how much more will it defeat you through great things!
And if it overpowers you through vegetables, how much more will it overpower you through eating meat!
Whoever is unjust in a little is also unjust in much. For whatever desire uses to wage war against you, defeat it in that very thing.
If it is through eating meat and through varied and tasty preparations, fight in these things and overcome gluttony.
But if it is through seeds, vegetables, fruits, and humble and ordinary kinds of food, establish your victory over it in the very thing through which it wages war.
Do not say, “It is no victory that I overcome these things.” Instead, consider how great the condemnation is if you are defeated by them.
Now, if desire itself, which is always accustomed to craving great things, has come down and craved little things
in order to enslave you, will you not lower yourself along with it and defeat it
where it wanted to defeat you? For wherever it calls you, you must follow it there,
and in the very thing it craves, draw up your battle line against its provocations. In this too, imitate Christ your Lord.
Wherever the tempter wanted to tempt him, he was there for him.
And wherever the tempter wished to begin the struggle, he too met him there.
He began first with the battle against gluttony, and he overcame this desire by enduring fasting.
He did this to give us too an example and establish a clear rule for us:
that if we too wish to begin a spiritual way of life, we should begin with fasting, and afterward, little by little,
be led on to every victory. For our Lord too first overcame the appetite of the belly,
and after it, the love of money, the empty pride of the world, and dominion and authority, which arise from it.
After these he overcame vainglory, the hateful passion that arises from good deeds.
Through these three victories, he overcame and put an end to all the passions associated with them.
Then he began to proclaim his Father's kingdom with authority and to impart the teaching of perfection to humanity.
Therefore, just as Christ our Lord, when he had fulfilled the observance of the Law and began the life of the Spirit, began with fasting,
so you too, following his example, must make fasting the beginning of your discipleship, which is above the world.
For what ascetic discipline was ever as perfect as that of Jesus?
He withdrew not only from the taste of foods, but also from their smell and their sight,
by leaving the inhabited land where these things were available and going out into the wilderness, deprived of everything,
so that he might cut off this hateful desire from all the senses and cast it away.
For unless a person leaves the world, he cannot travel the path of perfection.
Consider this too: how long our Savior extended his fast—to the limit that our nature can reach.
For our nature did indeed go as far as this number of days in Moses and Elijah.
And if our nature had been able to go further, our Savior would have fasted longer.
But if its strength had been insufficient to reach this number, he would have reduced the number of days he fasted,
and would have measured out the time according to the limit that human nature could reach.
For our Savior did not fast according to his own strength, but according to ours.
For if he had fasted according to his own strength, he would not have become hungry at all, since it is the nature of his spiritual being not to hunger.
Rather, he fasted bodily, according to the measure of strength of bodily beings. He lowered himself to our level and revealed to us the limits of our nature's endurance.
For an abundance of luxuries had weakened the power of endurance within us.
And we thought that our nature could not live without these things, and that if it lacked these luxuries and the support provided by food, it would perish.
Our Lord fasted for forty days and taught us that the power of endurance in our nature extends this far,
provided that the barriers of desire are not placed in the way, cutting off the path of endurance.
But our Savior broke through and passed beyond all the barriers of desires,
and the ordeals of illnesses and pains, and reached the end of forty days.
And therefore many others have also reached this point. But this limit that our Savior established,
no one has passed, because it belongs to nature. But if it has been heard or reported that someone has passed this limit,
this is beyond the power of human nature and has happened as an exceptional act of grace,
for many reasons, some of which are hidden from us and some of which are known to us.
This, then, is the example that the disciple should set before his eyes if he wishes to be diligent in the spiritual life.
And just as our Lord overcame all the other passions, so you too, after practicing ascetic discipline, will find it easy to overcome the remaining desires.
And just as Jesus, after all desires had been conquered, then began to teach with authority and to act with freedom:
to eat with everyone, to accept invitations from everyone, and to mingle and speak with people of every kind—these things are
a sign of freedom exercised with authority—so you too, when you have overcome gluttony and, through it, the remaining passions that follow it,
stand in the freedom of Christ, and with authority mingle with everyone and speak with everyone.
You eat and drink with tax collectors and prostitutes, and your dealings with women are without fear,
since your freedom makes no distinction between male and female, because you have cast off the way of thinking that perceives differences through the passions.
For when the mind is not disturbed by passion, a man's face is no different to it from a woman's, nor a beautiful appearance from an ugly one.
Instead, it encounters everyone and looks at everyone without passion. You enter every house [?] without fear, and you greet everyone.
You become all things to everyone, while remaining one and the same, unchanged, for everyone's benefit.
Examples of these things were seen in Christ himself and in his apostles.
But consider that our Savior came to these things and others like them through ascetic discipline. And not he alone,
but also the holy apostles and the divine prophets, and also the one who stood between the two covenants,
John the Baptist. And remember how Holy Scripture tells you about his way of life in ascetic discipline.
which was new and different from the way of life of all other people.
For his clothing was made of camel hair, and he bound leather around his waist, like the prophets.
His food was locusts and wild honey, and his dwelling was a desolate wilderness, cut off from inhabited places.
He lived among the wild animals. He had practiced all this profound asceticism fully from his infancy.
After these things, he was then found worthy to receive a revelation,
and to become a herald before the coming of the Most High, and, before the cross, to be found worthy of the things that come after the cross.
While human nature had not yet been born into spiritual life, he alone was to be born before the birth of everyone.
And this vision beyond words, this astonishing and marvelous transformation—
together with the power of grace, for which everything is easy—he was found worthy of it through his rigorous asceticism.
For this is the nature of this way of life whenever purity of soul accompanies it:
it gives a person birth into the world of the spirit, to become an equal of the angels while still dwelling within the bodily world.
Consider also that even the blessed apostles, although they were chosen by grace,
were not found worthy of the gift of the Spirit until the ascetic way of life had first appeared in them.
Indeed, while they were going about with Jesus in the world, it is not written of them that they lived according to the rules of asceticism.
For, through the abundance of grace, they were living according to the freedom of Christ,
which our Savior himself attained after his trial in the wilderness.
Although they themselves had not yet reached this through the testing of their own course of life, Christ himself, in his grace, gave them a share in his perfection.
And because the Pharisees and John's disciples did not understand the authority of this freedom,
they boldly reproached Christ: “Why do we fast often, but your disciples do not fast?”
Jesus answered with a saying whose meaning was beyond their capacity to understand.
He said, “The wedding guests cannot fast as long as the bridegroom is with them.”
But just as, at a wedding feast, it is not only the bridegroom who wears white garments and enjoys the festivities,
but also all those invited to the feast, so likewise it is not only I who, after victory and payment of the debt of all the sufferings,
have entered this freedom of the wedding feast and rejoice and enjoy myself. I also give my disciples, whom I have invited to the kingdom, a share with me.
But days are coming when I will be taken away from them, and then they will fast in those days.
That is, when the abundant light of free authority is gathered to me, then they too light the lamps of their endurance.
And so that there may be room for the Spirit, that he himself may shine within their hidden depths in place of the light of Jesus.
This also happened after the ascension into heaven. Although they had already advanced in the practice of freedom, as though receiving a pledge,
they did not receive this freedom in their own persons until they had first labored in ascetic practices.
So, immediately after our Savior ascended, it is written of them that they returned to the upper room where they had been staying, and devoted themselves to much fasting,
with anguished thoughts, pure prayers, and continual tears. Then they were found worthy to receive the Comforter.
And although the days of their ascetic practice were few, from Christ’s ascension to the descent of the Spirit,
let us learn that even after they received the Spirit, they continued in this same practice of fasting and ascetic discipline.
Everywhere it is written of them that they fasted and prayed. “While they were fasting and praying,” it says,
“the Holy Spirit said to them, ‘Set apart for me Saul and Barnabas for the work to which I have called them.’”
Again, when the apostles themselves wished to choose seven deacons, they said, “We will devote ourselves to prayer and the ministry of the word.”
Again, when Simon was confined in prison, it is written that the whole church was praying. And Paul too, before he was baptized
and received the Holy Spirit, had this written about him: for three days he neither ate nor drank,
nor did he rise from his place, where he lay face down and prayed. In this way he received the Holy Spirit.
For all the rest of his life after his calling, he was occupied with fasting and prayers,
as he himself everywhere mentions his fasting and prayer, and the many afflictions he endured for the gospel.
Along with all his other labors and afflictions, he also counted his frequent fasting. “In frequent fasting,” he says,
“in frequent sleeplessness, in great hunger, in lack of clothing and nakedness.” Again he said, “I am trained in everything,
both in being well fed and in being hungry, in abundance and in need.” How needy and poor he was
is shown by the fact that once, until he sold his clothing, they could not buy food for him and those with him,
despite his constant labor, working with his own hands at night so that he would not burden anyone.
Again, it is written of Simon that he went up onto the roof to pray at the ninth hour, and he became hungry and wanted to eat.
He told them to prepare food for him. From this he taught you that, along with constant teaching and prayers at every hour,
he also prayed regularly at the appointed times for communal worship.
Along with his prayer, his fasting too was constant. For the statement that at the ninth hour he became hungry and wanted to eat,
His hunger came from providence, not from habit, nor was it his rule to eat at that hour.
This is clear from the statement that he went up onto the roof to pray.
Suddenly hunger came upon him, and he left his prayer and told them to prepare food for him.
If that had been the hour when he usually ate, his hosts would have been preparing it as usual.
But the fact that he himself told them to prepare it for him makes it clear that he became hungry through providence,
so that, through the experience of his hunger, he might receive instruction in the things said to him.
His own fasting was constant. But suppose that the apostles did not fast.
Even so, it is not appropriate to cite their way of life as evidence for your position, because they were perfect once they had received the Spirit, the Comforter.
Just as our Lord did not fast after his temptations, so it was not fitting for them to fast either,
in view of the life of freedom in which they stood and the perfection in which they lived.
Yet although their life in the Spirit was far above arduous practices, they would descend to hardships and afflictions.
One reason was to give us a good example so that we might imitate them; another was that afflictions and hardships were their rest and delight.
And what was the food of these great men who had attained perfection, whenever food was available to them?
Was it not only bread, vegetables, and olives? And if the apostles needed ascetic practices,
and even at the stage of perfection lived like people filled with fear, who would not tremble and draw back from laxity,
and run to embrace a life of strenuous effort? You can also understand from the testimony of the prophets
that whenever they too were granted a vision of God or of angels, they practiced extensive fasting,
and then they were granted the sight of revelations, as it is written about Daniel, the greatly beloved man:
only after three weeks of fasting was he granted a vision of angels.
And if all this fasting was required of someone who was looking forward to the coming of an angel,
and only then was he granted spiritual revelations, how much more do you, who await a spiritual vision of Christ
and the reception within your soul of perception beyond nature, need extensive fasting,
ascetic discipline, and the subduing of the body, so that you may attain things greater than what Daniel saw?
Likewise Elijah, after fasting for forty days and forty nights,
then received a vision of God on Mount Horeb, while he was alone in the wilderness.
Along with prolonged fasting, he also bore the hardship of traveling on the road.
Along with these things came separation from other people and stillness, which purifies prayer.
After these things, he heard the voice of God speaking with him. And like this holy man,
blessed Moses too, on the two occasions when he was deemed worthy to enter the thick darkness and receive the law on tablets,
was purified by fasting like this, and then was deemed worthy of that awe-inspiring vision. So it was also with the prophet Ezekiel.
When he was about to receive a prophetic revelation concerning the uprooting of the city and the destruction of the temple,
the word of God brought him into severe afflictions: he was to eat bread by weight and drink water by measure,
and lie on his side in distress. Then he came to prophetic visions.
And so you find that all the righteous and the prophets, whether of their own will
or by God's command to them, were always bearing afflictions and hardships.
Blessed David likewise makes known that the very limbs of his body had grown weak from the severity of his fasting.
He says, “My knees have grown weak from fasting, and my flesh has wasted away for lack of oil.” And again he said:
“For I forgot to eat my bread, and from the sound of my groaning my flesh clung to my bones.”
For he had no respite from remembering God to turn his attention to the nourishment his body needed.
Rather, he completely forgot this perishable nourishment, because his mind was absorbed in spiritual nourishment.
From the severity of his hardships and afflictions, and from the sorrow and anguish of his groaning, his flesh clung to his bones.
Again, he also teaches you about the preparations he made for his food. He says, “For I ate ashes like bread.”
These were the seasonings and flavorings set on this righteous king's table at his mealtime.
But listen also to what he says about the clear wines he drank: “I mixed my drink with weeping.”
Here are the righteous king's food and drink: his food was ashes, and his drink was tears of sorrow.
What disciple could hear these things without his heart breaking in sorrow over his own lax life—if indeed he is a disciple?
Again he said, “I humbled myself with fasting, and I became an object of reproach to them. I made sackcloth my clothing, and I became a byword to them.”
By this he taught us that he endured not only the hardship of virtuous deeds, but also the reproaches and insults he heard because of them,
and bore them patiently. From this you too should learn that if your labors are despised by the lax,
and your afflictions are recounted mockingly by those who love comfort, you should remember this saying of the prophet and take comfort.
And it will be a resting place for your soul whenever an assault from evil people comes upon you.
And again, elsewhere, concerning the severity of the hardships he reached through patiently enduring his afflictions,
he said, “I have become like a wineskin in the frost, yet I have not forgotten your commandments.”
Through this he taught you that intense sorrow and thirst had exhausted and consumed even the moisture of his body.
And again, listen to him elsewhere teaching you that before someone enters into afflictions
and is tested in the furnace of patiently enduring hardships, he cannot emerge into the spacious relief of spiritual delights.
“You brought me into fire and water,” he says, “and brought me out into a spacious place.”
By fire and water he represents the afflictions, misfortunes, and hardships that surrounded him on every side,
whether they were afflictions he accepted willingly, or discipline from God that came to test him,
or troubles from evil people who envied his good qualities. Along with this righteous king, listen also to the words of Job, the spiritual athlete.
Consider what kind of dish the healing art of the Spirit taught him to place on his table before all his food.
“For my sighing came before my bread,” he says, “and my groans poured out like water.”
These were the fruits he took first: sighs and weeping. Only then did he approach the nourishment required by nature.
For he first fed on sufferings and drank the tears of his sighing, and only then received nourishment for his body.
As a result, even what he fed on was holiness, not mere food.
Listen again to him telling what afflictions he bore, while never departing from his love for God.
“Why,” he says, “do I carry my flesh in my teeth, with my life placed in my hands? Even if he kills me, I wait for him alone.”
It is as though someone were to say, “Even if he does not love me, I will not turn away from loving him.”
God disciplined him as an enemy, but he cried out, “I am receiving blows from a friend.” And he did not renounce his love for the one who disciplined him.
And wherever you look, disciple, you will find that none of the righteous pleased God in this world without afflictions and hardships.
For this is the road to the city of the kingdom above. “Narrow and constricted,” he says, “is the road that leads to life.”
Let us therefore travel along the narrow path that God has opened for us, and walk the road of afflictions that he has shown us.
Let us suffer distress here so that we may find relief there. Let us hunger here so that we may be satisfied there.
Let us reduce our food and drink so that spiritual nourishment may be poured out abundantly for us there.
Let us bring ourselves into the furnace of afflictions so that we may be offered to the kingdom as pure gold without blemish.
Let us not be troubled by the decay of our body, so that our inner self may be renewed day by day.
Let us not dwell on the pains and illnesses that befall us, but consider that without these the wounds of the soul are not healed.
Let us be filled with joy as we run, so that it may be known that we are running toward hope.
As children of grace, let us work in the house of the true Father, so that we may be worthy of that inheritance, full of blessings, which is promised to the children.
Let us always remember the apostle’s words: we must enter the kingdom of God through suffering.
And with the apostle, let us say to one another: if we suffer with Christ, we will be glorified with Christ.
And if we endure, we will also reign with him. To him be glory from us all, forever. Amen.
The end of Discourse Eleven, on the ascetic life.
Notes on the Syriac text:
Discourse Twelve, against the passions of sexual immorality. In it he explains that sexual immorality is not reckoned only as the enactment of desire,
when it is carried out in the body, but also when desire lingers in thought and makes the soul commit sexual immorality with a person far away.
Wise physicians who wish to apply their knowledge to healing the ailments that befall human bodies
first learn the causes of the ailments and remove them, and then provide treatment for the illnesses without difficulty.
For when the cause from which the pains and illnesses sprang is removed, the illnesses it produced are also uprooted along with it,
because shoots or fruits cannot survive when the root that nourishes them is removed from the ground.
And even if the plants happen to survive for a short time because of their natural moisture,
they are nevertheless bound to dry up once their roots have been loosened and removed from the ground.
So too with the pains and illnesses that befall human bodies:
when physicians first remove the causes from which the ailments arise,
the ailment gradually comes to an end and disappears, once the cause that produced it is cut off from the body.
For we should act in this same way toward the sinful passions that arise either from the soul or from the body:
first we must remove the causes that give rise to these passions,
so that through this our lives may be kept free from evils, and our conduct may be free from wrongdoing.
For anyone who wishes to be free in God
must first be freed from the desires that stir within him, and then approach the way of life that belongs to the freedom of Christ.
For that place of free people will not even admit him as long as the disgraceful mark of slavery is visible in his person.
And now, as we consider this—what we were and what we are becoming, and from where to where we have been called—
and what life we have exchanged for what, let us always remain mindful of ourselves,
and constantly take account of our conduct. Let us first learn the causes of sinful passions,
which continually afflict our lives with their inflammations, so that we may obtain health for our souls without difficulty.
Let the medicine of the natural world, which heals human bodies, serve us as a model for healing our souls.
Like physicians, let us first examine the causes from which the inflammations of sin arise in our lives, so that we may attain spiritual health.
Since we rebuked the craving of gluttony in the preceding discourse, it is fitting that our discourse should now also
advance in order against the evil passion of sexual immorality, whose cause, mother, and nurse is the craving of the belly.
It is easily overcome once a person overcomes its primary cause.
For this passion of sexual immorality grows strong and flares up in our bodily members through food and drink.
Besides this, it also arises from lax associations, from human conversation, and from the memory of beautiful-looking people whose images are formed within our souls,
and from the recounting of stories about lust, whenever they are told and listened to with pleasure,
and from constantly looking at people whose appearance has already taken captive the souls of the lax through passion.
For once gluttony has fed the fire of sexual immorality within the body, corrupt associations come and stir it up.
For this desire has been naturally placed by the Creator in the members of our bodies for procreation through marriage and the continuation of the world.
But in disciples it is preserved not for this use, but to become for them a means of gaining spiritual crowns
and material for heavenly battles, so that, by fighting against it and overcoming it, they may be counted as victors.
And through the victories they carry away from the arena of their struggle against it, they may be inscribed as conquerors in the Jerusalem above.
For the desire for sexual union has remained in disciples not so that they should engage in sexual union,
but so that, through the heat of natural desire, they may experience the power of the heat of spiritual desire.
And when the fire of transgression flares up in their bodily members, through it they may discern the burning fire of Jesus that is mingled with their souls.
And through pleasure that is contrary to nature, they may taste the pleasure of true nature. And through the impulse that ends as soon as it begins,
they may gain a taste of the delight of the living impulse, which, once it begins to yearn for the lovely sight of Christ’s beauty,
continues without end in the soul in which it begins, provided that the soul is purified so as to become its dwelling place.
For the fire of this natural desire is hotter than all the other desires.
Along with its heat, a perishable pleasure is also mixed into it, so that two things may be learned from this one thing:
the sweetness of Christ’s love and the approaching end of corrupting desire. For the fire of the Spirit could have—
that fire which has been mingled with us—consumed and extinguished this fire of natural desire.
But then the will would have been fruitless, and the freedom within us would have been without the labors of earnest effort.
It was fitting, then, that an adversary was set against free will,
so that, when he is defeated by it in a struggle of endurance, it may be shown to be free, its strength may be known, and its authority recognized.
Therefore, let us not grow lax and allow this desire, which is preserved within us for our benefit, to become a cause of harm to us.
For anyone who makes a profit of losses from benefits is foolish and ignorant.
And anyone who takes what has been given to us as material for good and directs it toward evil is wicked and opposed to good.
Let us therefore be earnest in the battle against this evil desire, which, although it is good within worldly marriage,
is considered evil if acted upon by disciples. For not everything is fitting for everyone,
even if it is very fine and good in its own nature. For wealth is good in the nature in which the Creator made it.
But if monks acquire it—those who have been commanded not to have two tunics
and not to worry about tomorrow—possessing it is evil for them.
Eating meat and drinking wine are also pure for those who are committed to a worldly way of life.
But for those who have willingly given themselves to the covenant of the chosen life of discipleship to Christ,
it is not fitting to partake of these things without a compelling necessity.
The governing offices and authorities of this world are also good and fitting,
because it is written, “There is no authority that is not from God.” But for those who have withdrawn from life among people
and have taken great and lofty vows upon themselves, it is shameful and disgraceful to desire human ranks.
Nor is living in cities and villages blameworthy, or dwelling in the world and conducting one’s life among other people.
But for those who have stripped themselves of possessions out of love for God and have once renounced the world by their own free choice,
and have gone out to live apart from it as monks and ascetics, living and associating with other people is a matter for accusation and blame.
And there are many other things like these, whose practice is blameless for those who have not previously bound themselves by a covenant opposed to them,
For those who have vowed to abstain from them, they are blameworthy if practiced.
This desire for marriage, then, also belongs to this order, and the Creator rightly placed it in nature.
For it sustains the world, and it has been the root and increase of human nature.
It restores and gives back to the human race what death, imposed by the sentence of judgment, snatches away and takes from them.
But consider, disciple: although it was indeed placed in nature, it was awakened through the transgression of the commandment.
Its stirring became apparent through the eating of the fruit, so that, as through [?], we might learn beforehand
