that it holds sway only in the world of bodily beings, while it serves no purpose at all in the world of spiritual beings.
For patterns of both ways of life were seen in the ancestors of our race themselves: that of spiritual beings and that of bodily beings, that of the world of spirit
and that of the world of the body, that of the first Adam and that of the last Adam. For before they ate the food by which they transgressed the commandment,
through which the desire that had been hidden within their limbs was also stirred, their entire way of life was spiritual.
In everything they were moved spiritually, with holy thoughts and pure reflections,
with understanding worthy of God, with a mind pure and clear of the ugly stirrings of desire.
Their life within Paradise followed the pattern of the spiritual powers.
They were bodily only in outward appearance, but inwardly, with spiritual understanding, they dwelt in heaven.
For the Creator first gave Adam a taste of spiritual things, because he wanted him to become their heir.
For although all these worldly things came into being and were established through the Maker’s word,
Adam in his freedom desired them, and his will chose them and went out after them.
This is evident from his eating of the fruit, which took place in transgression of the commandment. For his eating of that fruit
is the beginning of all desires, according to the words of our teacher the apostle, who said, “I would not even have known desire if the law had not said,
‘Do not covet.’ Through this commandment,” he says, “sin found an opportunity and produced every kind of desire in me.”
Thus, in us, the desire of the spirit precedes the desire of the body, as the account of the ancestor of our race himself shows.
For Adam descended from above to below, and left the desire of the spirit for the desire of the body.
From the way of life of heavenly beings, he was brought down to the way of life of earthly beings.
From the sight of God’s beauty, of which one can never have enough, he turned to contemplate the sight of his wife’s beauty.
For until Adam turned outward, outward things did not appear to him; and until he turned his soul toward the world,
The desirable things of the world were not set before his sight; his eating of the fruit became the cause and beginning of them all.
And just as there all desires were born from the belly, so here too all evils begin from it.
The first thorn that sprouts from the field of gluttony is sexual immorality. As soon as it sprouts, it becomes like a thorn in the eye to the mind's sight.
It prevents the mind from gazing toward God. For this desire darkens not only the sight of those who have not seen,
but also that of those who have often beheld divine beauties, if they happen to be seized by this passion.
Their thoughts are blinded, and it stands before them like a veil, preventing them from seeing that desirable beauty of Christ.
They struggle to find what they have lost, and they find it only with difficulty and toil.
For there are those who are completely blind, like people born blind from their mothers' wombs.
And there are those who became blind after they were born and had seen the light; through the injury that later befell them,
the clear sight of their thoughts was blinded. Yet the memory of the heavenly light remains with them, even at the time when they suffer the injury.
And just as someone who becomes blind remembers the natural light that he used to see before his blindness,
so too someone blinded by the passions remembers the spiritual light that he used to see before this.
The person deemed worthy to see this light does not receive it merely as something heard about, but as someone remembering its former brightness.
And when he compares his recent blindness with it, he sighs over the height from which he has been brought down and the desire he has exchanged for another.
Therefore those who have seen and experienced this spiritual light need greater care than those who have never seen or experienced it at all.
Just as a rich person needs to take greater care over his wealth than a poor person who possesses nothing,
so too someone who, through the purity of his soul, has found the beauty of the divine vision needs constant vigilance, so that he does not lose what he has found.
For just as a person turns his eyes from what is before him and looks behind him, or turns from gazing toward the sun to looking into darkness,
so it is with the mind that gazes at God when it turns away from him and gazes at a shameful desire.
For until the soul loses the beauty of its own being, it is not brought down to desiring the body's perishable beauty.
For lack of beauty, it longs for beauty; and for lack of a vision, it gazes at a sight.
And because the desirable splendor of Christ's beauty is not imprinted before it, it is captivated by the sight of the body's splendor.
And because wakefulness is not awake within it, sleep is awake within it.
And because the fire of spiritual love is cold within it, the fire of bodily love flares up within it.
For until a person becomes aware of the beauty of his soul, he does not begin to perceive Christ's beauty, of which one can never have enough.
He whose nature is such that he naturally binds to himself in love every soul that perceives him and sees him.
For just as love of bodily beauty is naturally stirred in the limbs of those who desire it,
so too, anyone who reaches the beauty of Christ, whom he desires, is stirred to love him as though by the compulsion of nature,
and nothing can sever him from that bond of love. For if someone who is bound by bodily desire,
and by the beautiful appearance of a perishable body, surrounded on every side by reasons for its dissolution,
its repulsiveness and its perishability, disregards everything and despises everyone's correction and rebuke,
and the bodily love within him overcomes the force of every fear that battles against him on every side,
how much more will the soul that has loved Christ and become fervently devoted to the sight of his lovely beauty
be freed from every yoke of fear, and break through and pass beyond the constraint of all laws,
and all beautiful things will become hateful in its eyes when it compares them with the sight of the beauty of the one it loves.
For just as someone may be gripped by natural desire and, for lack of access to a beautiful face,
love a blind woman, ugly in form and hideous in face, but then happen to gaze upon a beautiful face
and look upon another body's desirable beauty, comparing the beauty he has found
with that former ugliness by whose love he had been bound, he despises and rejects that former desire,
and reproaches himself for what he had attached his love to. From then on, passion for the second beauty takes control of all his impulses,
and he is entirely captivated and swallowed up in that desire, especially when he compares it with that former ugliness he used to love.
So it also happens to the mind whenever, for lack of beauty, it becomes captivated by bodily beauty.
That is, for lack of seeing Christ's beauty, it is ensnared by the sight of bodily beauty and desires something unworthy of desire,
and is set ablaze by the fire of love for perishable nature—a love that should not even be called love, but an ugly and repulsive passion.
But if it should happen that this same person, whether through love arising from his own will, through what others show him, or through the action of grace,
has the desirable beauty of that uncreated Being revealed to him and perceives this imperishable beauty,
he immediately forgets natural beauty, and that loveliness turns before his eyes into utter repulsiveness.
He rebukes himself for what he had been bound to in love, for the compulsion to which he had been enslaved, and for the weakness that had overcome his strength.
He reproaches his own life for the laxity through which he became enslaved to love of a perishable body.
For everything is exchanged for its counterpart: pleasure for pleasure, honor for honor.
Wealth with wealth, glory with glory, pleasure with pleasure, desire with desire, beauty with beauty.
And when all these are compared with one another—the things above with the things below—
those who perceive the higher things despise even the choicest of all the things beneath them.
They long for the things that are lofty, glorious, splendid, exalted, and beautiful.
For this is the nature of the soul's desire: to desire things higher than itself. Whenever it desires in this way, it desires according to its nature.
But whenever it desires things inferior to itself, its desire is contrary to its nature. This means
that its discernment has been obscured through involvement with something opposed to it, and then it has desired that very thing which is its opposite.
Or if it desires that thing, it is because its desire has deteriorated. For no one who has seen the sun
abandons it and longs for darkness instead, unless deeds suited to darkness have been stirred up within him,
and, joining the gloom of sin to natural darkness, he desires darkness while in darkness.
It is clear that this desire of his is blind and without sight: he does not discern what he desires in exchange for what.
For it is degradation for someone to be captivated by the sight of what the body desires.
Especially when those who have been freed from the passions turn back and become enslaved to them, and, after being found worthy to see spiritual beauty,
are captivated by love of bodily beauty. Such people rightly deserve to be hated for what they have exchanged for what.
Instead of the beauty of the king's daughter, who is more splendid than all, they have desired a poor, blind woman, uglier than all.
Now, if someone who is worthy to perceive the soul's beauty cannot have enough of it, how much more will it remain inexhaustibly desirable
to the soul—the beauty of Christ, who is by nature desirable and lovable beauty!
There is no beauty comparable to his beauty, no sight resembling the sight of him, and no splendor as lovable as his.
There is no likeness as beloved as his image, and no forms as desirable as his.
For he is desirable in his entirety. There is no part of him that is beautiful and another, opposite to it, that is hateful and ugly,
as happens with a perishable body, in which, although one limb is beautiful,
another diminishes its beauty by its ugliness. Sometimes the face is splendid but the feet are deformed.
It may happen that the eyes are beautiful, while the other organs of sense are inferior, deficient, or marred.
The limbs may be beautifully proportioned, yet some other fault is found in the person's stature.
In short, bodily beauty cannot be entirely perfect, free and clear of defects.
For this too was wisely arranged by the Creator: that bodily beauty should not be perfect in its beauty,
so that anyone seized by desire for it might soon be freed from it.
For when an ugly bodily part is placed beside a beautiful one, and an unattractive one beside a lovely one, anyone seized by desire for the beautiful one
may be restrained by the ugly appearance of the one joined to it, and through that very thing his desire for this beauty may be dissolved.
Thus a rebuke will stand beside anyone seized by his passion, and the remedy will be mixed with the pain itself.
Health will be found beside sickness, and ugliness will peer out from within beauty.
These things were put together in this way by divine wisdom, because it is not his will—
the will of the Cause of everything, the Beauty of all beauties—that the beauty of our soul should desire an alien beauty outside himself.
And if, through the mind’s slumber, ugliness should happen to appear to us in place of beauty, and through the sight of lovely bodily parts
we should be caught in corrupting desire, release from this desire will come from two causes:
from the ugliness of unattractive bodily parts, and from the splendid beauty of the heavenly vision. Thus, while ugliness drives us away from below,
and contemplation of the desirable vision welcomes us from above, we may be mingled with and swallowed up in this beauty of which one can never have enough,
and it may be poured out in its entirety upon our whole being and mingle within us, and the image of its spiritual nature may take shape in our soul.
Let us not, then, go astray and desire things unworthy of desire, and lose the spiritual desire mingled within our soul.
For Adam desired the beauty of the fruit, and from it he was led to gaze upon Eve’s beauty.
The appetite of the belly entered and awakened the desire of the body. Along with the desire for sexual union, other desires also sprouted within us.
For this desire was planted in us to preserve the human race.
But those who are not appointed to this task of perpetuating the world ought to overcome the stirring of this desire.
For the promise to the disciples placed them outside the world, and in every respect their way of life made them strangers to it and beyond it.
That is, they came to be above the world, as though standing on the heights of righteousness, in accordance with our Savior’s promise to them.
And those who have once departed from the world ought also to be outside the desire
that perpetuates the world. For these two desires, which are linked to one another—
I mean the appetite of the belly and the desire for sexual union—are seen to act differently in us.
For one sustains our individual life, while the other preserves the life of our species.
For the appetite of the belly sustains our individual life, while the desire for sexual union preserves our species through the succession of generations.
And if it were possible for our lives to be sustained in this world without bodily necessities,
the commandment of our Life-giver would have forbidden us even food and drink.
But because this is impossible, since the conditions for sustaining our lives were established in this way by the Creator’s command,
he restrains us from marriage. For he did not place us in the world to perpetuate the world,
but only so that it might be an arena for us, from which we might carry off a crown of victory through spiritual combat.
And because anyone who fights needs an opponent, since otherwise there can be no combat,
he left desire in our bodily members to be our opponent, so that when it is fought and defeated, the athlete’s victory may be revealed.
But if we happen to lose, let his feebleness be blamed, because he was defeated through his own weakness, not through his opponent’s strength.
For desire does not defeat us because it is stronger than we are, but because of our own weakness and feebleness.
For if desire possessed the power to conquer by its very nature, it would conquer everyone.
And it would conquer at all times. As it is, however, this is not so: sometimes it conquers, and sometimes it is conquered.
Sometimes it suffers defeat, and at other times it inflicts defeat. Through its being conquered, the strength of our will is revealed.
But through its conquering and defeating us, the feebleness of our free will is revealed, along with our disregard and neglect of ourselves.
For until desire draws strength from you, it cannot conquer you.
Indeed, it does not even dare to stand against you in battle until your will gives it permission. Test this in your own experience:
as long as you wish, it lies asleep, and whenever you want, you awaken it. But if a natural impulse should happen to awaken it against your will,
it is easy for you to extinguish its fire with a little puff of breath, provided there is strength in your soul
to send such a puff against it. It is not, however, extinguished by a blast of bodily strength—
the body in which, whenever desire is stirred, it subjects all the senses to its own will.
For the body, which is conquered by desire, cannot blow against it. And even if it blows, it does not extinguish it.
But when the soul stands firm in the strength of its own nature and takes control of the discernment of its thoughts,
and gathers all its impulses to itself, so that they move for it and not for the body, then, with great strength, whenever it wishes,
it sends a blast of rebuke against desire, and swiftly, like the blink of an eye, extinguishes the natural fire that has stirred in the bodily members.
For whenever the body is governed by the soul, their entire conduct is orderly and sound.
And it conducts itself as befits a human being, with the orderliness appropriate to rational beings.
But when the body's desires govern the soul, a person lives the life of animals.
Even the impulses of his desires are acted upon by him without awareness.
Because of this, he is also deprived of the remorse that accompanies discernment.
For as long as the soul is entangled with the body in its thoughts, it cannot govern it, nor can it see its own self.
Neither do the body's desires trouble it, nor do its own passions confront it.
But like a blind person who is deprived of the sight of himself and of the sight of everything else,
so too the soul, when it has been blinded by sinful passions, sees neither itself nor anything outside itself.
We must therefore separate the soul from the body before the separation of the body from the soul takes place.
For this natural union was established in us by the Creator.
It is not ours to dissolve it, unless someone wishes to be lost to divine life.
But this separation of the soul's thoughts from the body has been placed within the power of our free will.
Whenever we wish, it is easy for us to separate our soul's thoughts from our body. This very separation
we have learned from the Holy Scriptures, and from them we have received strength to make the soul dwell alone within the house of the body.
Perhaps it was this that the Spirit of God was making known in a riddle when he said, “He settles the solitary person in a house.”
For here he fittingly calls good thought “solitary,” because, although it dwells in the body, it does not share in its passions.
Nor does it forge a bond of love with those things that are unworthy of its friendship.
Instead, moving on its own and within itself in solitude, in wonder at the greatness of God's glory,
it dwells within a house of silence. The name “solitary” belongs to holy thought of this kind.
For just as a person is called solitary when he estranges himself from the whole world and rises above its giving and taking,
its wealth and comforts, and everything in it, so too that thought is called solitary which, while dwelling within the body,
is estranged and far removed from all its desires and the activities that serve its comforts, and remains alone with itself,
meditating within itself. Through persistence in this meditation, the beauty of its soul and the splendor and radiance of its own self are revealed to it.
For the prophet aptly offered God's solitude in relation to everything as an illustration of the solitude of this thought.
For just as God, although mingled with everything, is distant and far removed from everything in the solitude of his nature,
so too this solitary thought, although mingled with the body, remains far removed from the body.
“God,” it says, “is in his holy dwelling.” Then it adds: “God settles the solitary in a home.”
What need was there to place this statement beside that one, except to draw from the statement about God a testimony to the solitude of thought?
For just as God is in his holy dwelling—that is, within himself—with everything separate and far from him, although he is near to everything,
so too the solitary mind is near to everything, while everything is far from it. For this is also how it should be.
Thought itself, through the freedom inherent in its nature, should approach everything, so that it may perceive and discover the knowledge sown in everything.
But it should not allow anything to approach it. For God too, through the boundlessness of his nature, is near to everything,
while everything is far from him because it is limited. The mind, which has freedom, should act in the same way:
while it is near to everything because of its freedom, everything should remain far from it because it is not suited to it—that is, bodily things.
For unless thought remains in its solitude, it cannot even gather to itself the power of its nature.
For as long as it is mingled with the body, its power is stolen away and scattered among the body's members.
It becomes impoverished and deprived of its own strength. It becomes enslaved to desires, receiving orders rather than giving them.
For whenever the soul joins with the body and throws itself into the impulses of its wishes, it becomes enslaved to the body's desire rather than its own.
That is, together with the body it desires the perishable things that the body desires, and it becomes estranged from the healthy desire of its own nature.
Now the healthy desire of the soul is this, and it gives us a test of when the soul is moved by the desire of its own nature:
whenever we desire good things and noble impulses spring up within our soul, the soul is moved by the desire of its own nature.
And therefore it desires virtuous and spiritual things through the practice of good deeds.
For the desire of the body is not strong enough to overcome the desire of the spirit.
Rather, this desire draws strength from the soul itself to fight against it.
For desire on its own is weak, and for this reason it enlists other things to help it,
so that what it cannot accomplish by its own strength, it may accomplish with the help of other things.
The things that assist this desire are these: the appetite of the belly, pleasures, amusement,
ornate clothing, social interactions, talk drawn from lustful desires, recounting forms of sexual immorality,
beautiful faces, looking at the body's beauty, a wandering mind, remembering things.
Desire calls these and similar things to its aid, and then begins to fight against the soul and array a battle of impulses against it.
These things reveal the weakness of desire, for if it could conquer on its own, it would have no need of them.
But what is required of you, disciple, if you want to overcome the lust that fights against you?
First, pluck its wings, destroy the forces it has called to its aid, and cut off its limbs.
Expose and pull up its roots, and uproot its foundations. Once it is left alone, you will overcome it without effort.
For when lust begins to fight against you, do not bring it the fuel by which it bursts into flame.
Instead, gather up everything that feeds it and put it far away from it.
Once it has burned by itself for a sufficient time, it dies down and fades away where it is.
First, then, take food and drink away from it. Eat bread by weight.
Drink water by measure. Drive bodily comforts away from you. Take upon yourself hardships chosen with discernment.
Yoke your body beneath the weight of hard work. Let it be tormented by hunger, distressed by thirst, and worn out by keeping vigil.
Let it seek to sleep, but do not allow it. If it wants to snatch a nap, drive sleep away from it.
If its need compels it to seek nourishment, reckon with it, and only then give it something.
In short, do not give it complete ease in anything, because comforts undoubtedly give birth to lust.
Along with these things, also cut off those earlier causes that I mentioned to you.
Do not lend your ear to talk about lust. Do not take pleasure in accounts of its various forms when they are related in your presence.
Do not keep looking at the face of the person for whom you are gripped by passion. Remove the sharply defined image of that person's attractiveness from your mind.
Completely uproot from your soul the memory of the beauty that captivated you. For as long as its memory remains within you,
it sets you on fire. Just as fire catches hold of fuel when it is brought near, so lust also catches hold and bursts into flame in the body's members
through looking at and occupying yourself with these matters. Once it has caught fire, not everyone is able to put it out.
Fight, then, and overcome the small things, so that the great ones do not overcome you.
If, then, you distance yourself from involvement in these things I have mentioned to you,
and drive away from you the things that cause lust, you shut the door in lust's face, and it does not enter and rule over you.
But if you weaken before these feeble things and are overcome by them, how much more will you be defeated and brought low by lust itself!
But so that your struggle does not increase and you do not fall into a battle from which you may or may not emerge,
put far away from you these things that overthrow you and bring you into battle. Become a stranger to them, so that you may become a stranger to lust.
Trample the daughters, so that you may also trample the mother. Cut off the limbs, so that you may also cut off the head.
Pluck the wings, so that the body may remain in the depths of guilt. Do not speak of sexual immorality, lest you come to commit it.
Do not harbor the memory of lust within your soul, lest you fulfill that lust in action.
Do not burden your stomach with too much food, lest the fire of lust burn in your limbs.
Do not let an abundance of wine flood your limbs, lest an abundance of arousal pour through your whole being.
Do not take pleasure in richly flavored foods, lest the sweetness of lust become pleasant to you.
Turn your eyes away from a beautiful sight, so that your soul may be emptied of its stirrings.
Shut the door of your hearing against lustful talk, lest the house of your soul become a permanent dwelling for lust.
Do not delight in the beautiful appearance of your own body, and do not gaze at the beauty of others’ appearance. Neither cause others to stumble nor stumble yourself.
Neither cause others to fall nor fall yourself. Neither defile others nor be defiled. Neither attach yourself to others nor let others attach themselves to you. Flee, so that they may flee from you.
Clothe yourself in anger against lust, and drive it from the house of your soul as you would an enemy.
When lust arises, use anger instead of love, because even love itself often becomes a path to lust.
For many have been ensnared through spiritual love and have turned to bodily love.
Although the beginning of their love was beautiful, its end became ugly and shameful.
Let your passions fight against your passions—those that you recognize as opposed to one another.
Whenever you feel that one of the evil passions is wearing you down, set the passion that is its enemy against it.
Above all, you must fight this shameful passion of lust with the passions opposed to it.
For the passion of anger is evil, but when lust arises it is greatly needed. The onrush of rage is also harsh.
But at that moment of battle it is very useful to you. Along with these things, you will not even be held accountable for stirring up hatred within yourself.
For hatred too is a great help at the time when bodily love is aroused.
By every means, then, keep this passion before your eyes when lust is stirred up, so that you may rescue your life from death,
and your soul from complete destruction, taking as an example for your battle at that time
those people who fight to the death for the sake of their bodily lives.
For there are many who, out of fear of death, fight to the death,
whether against a wild animal, robbers, enemies, or a deadly creeping creature.
They do not engage in this battle halfheartedly, but direct all their strength toward saving their lives.
And every faculty that strength sets in motion in soul and body, they exercise at that moment.
They put on menace, anger, and fury, shouting and combat. They also raise a voice full of terror.
They become fierce and change the peaceful expression of their faces into the menace of anger.
With hands and feet, with thought and limbs—that is, with their whole being, in soul and body—they wage their struggle.
And because they are afraid of dying, they approach the very boundary of death out of fear of it.
All these things happen so that mortal lives may be rescued from death.
Following their example, then, you too must exert yourself for the life of your soul.
Be menacing and full of anger, stern and furious when lust arises. Do not say, “These things are not fitting for me.”
For at that moment they are very fitting for you, because there is no battle without fury, and no contest is brought to completion without fierceness.
If you are standing in battle, you ought to clothe yourself in fury, so that at the very sight of you there may be trembling,
and the enemy fighting against you may flee. For anyone who smiles at his enemy hates his own soul.
Therefore, do not smile at lust, lest you lay her down beside you. Look at her with a scowling eye,
and immediately she will flee from you like a prostitute in the marketplace. For lust, too, is like a prostitute.
When she is stirred in the body's limbs, if the mind smiles at her, she immediately seizes it and forces it into intercourse with her,
and takes her defiling yoke and places it upon the mind, so that it becomes her slave and subject, rather than her commander.
But if the mind remembers itself and clothes itself in an appearance of dignity, and, in opposition to the shamelessness of lust,
puts on the garment of chastity and appears before her with a dignified and fearsome face, lust immediately leaves and departs,
not only from the mind's presence, but also from the place where she was stirred—that is, from all the limbs of the body.
And as though leaving a house that is not hers, she flees and goes out in shame.
But because not everyone sees the disgracefulness of this deed, when a chaste mind becomes subject to impure lust
and becomes something trampled beneath her feet, let the disciple look at the little illustration I give and understand.
For suppose that someone renowned for chastity, or for an honorable way of life and honorable labors,
were to carry one of the prostitutes on his shoulder through the city streets, and walk in a display of shamelessness through the streets and colonnades of the city:
this would cause horror among all who saw it, and anguish of heart would seize everyone over what was happening.
The story would become a subject of talk and retelling wherever it was heard. Through this visible illustration, let us also examine the hidden mind.
When he subjects his chastity to base desire and gives himself to be a seat and dwelling for it to live in.
This sight, then, is shameful and repulsive, even more so than what takes place in the city streets.
For there one body bears another body, and one body joins another body of its own kind.
Here, however, it is not so. Rather, spiritual thought is defiled through union with fleshly desire.
There comes to be an unlawful union, a joining that does not take place according to nature.
For when thought commits fornication with desire, this is unlawful fornication.
But there are distinctions even within fornication itself. There is fornication of the body, and there is fornication of the soul.
There is also fornication of the spirit. And there is union of the body, union of the soul, and union of the spirit.
For fornication of the body is the act of adultery that takes place unlawfully with a woman who is not one's own.
And fornication of the soul is when it secretly joins its thoughts with the desire for fornication,
even when the act is not openly carried out. Fornication of the spirit is when the soul enters into fellowship with demons,
or accepts agreement with foreign teachings. Then again, union of the body is union with a lawful wife.
Union of the soul is when it receives and mingles with knowledge of the natures of things,
and with insights into the governance of everything that moves within this life.
Union of the spirit is when divine teaching and all spiritual things are mingled within it.
Let us therefore take care first to be freed from the fornication of thoughts, which is fornication of the soul,
and we will also be freed from fornication of the body. For it is not good for thought to enter into union with the body.
Rather, the body should become the soul's partner in diligence. Lift your soul from its attachment to the body to the height of its own nature,
so that, as it rises to the height of purity of conduct, it may also raise the body with it from the depths of lusts.
The soul has been appointed queen over the body. Like a wise guide and charioteer,
it should hold the reins of all its senses. It is not fitting for your soul to do what your body loves.
Rather, your body should submit to the deeds that the soul loves, which are the acceptable will of God,
as the soul turns it from all its heaviness to the lightness of its own chaste conduct,
and makes it soar in the clear air of its holiness, exchanging its slackness for the soul's diligence,
its heaviness for the soul's lightness, its love for the soul's love, its desire for the soul's desire, and its needs for the soul's needs.
and its coarseness into her fineness, its bodily nature into her spiritual nature, and its hunger into her fullness.
In short, through knowledge she exchanges all its qualities for all the qualities of the spirit that are stirred within her.
For whenever the soul joins herself to the body, this union is adultery and fornication.
But if the body attaches itself to the soul in complete harmony, and is raised from below to above in a proper marriage,
this is a lawful union, which the Creator has established by nature in the person of each one of us.
For this natural union of men with women was also established in the beginning by the Creator’s command.
Whenever it takes place according to the Creator’s will, it is called a lawful union. But if it is practiced in another way,
it is called adultery and fornication. This allegory is depicted symbolically in the soul and the body:
if the soul joins herself to the body, it is fornication. But if the body joins itself to the soul, it is a lawful marriage.
The passage of Scripture that says, “A man shall leave his father and his mother and attach himself to his wife,” also points toward this meaning.
For it does not say of the woman that she should leave her parents and attach herself to the man,
although this is indeed what is practiced according to the world’s custom: women leave their natural parents and attach themselves to their husbands.
And judging from custom, it appears that what takes place in natural life is the opposite of what Scripture says.
Therefore, the statement made about the man is an allegory applied to the body:
it should leave everything in which it finds comfort and attach itself to the soul. For if Scripture had said
that the woman should leave her parents and attach herself to the man, it would have been teaching the soul to enter into union with the body.
But as it says of the man that he should leave his parents and attach himself to his wife, the statement depicts a mystery of instruction for us.
It urges the body to renounce its comforts and hate its desires, and to share with the soul in all good things.
For when the body is united with the soul, and the soul with the Spirit, and through the Spirit with the Trinity, there is fulfilled in practice
the saying, “The Lord is over all and in us all,” and the saying, “You are the Lord’s temple, and the Spirit of God dwells in you.”
Paul also warns the soul that allows the body to become a servant of fornication, saying,
“Whoever destroys God’s temple, God will destroy him.” Here, then, he teaches the soul
not to let the body be corrupted through attachment to fornication, because the harm resulting from this also reaches her.
For when the body is corrupted by the desires of its nature, the soul too is condemned with it to eternal judgment.
And he rightly places this destruction upon the soul, although God has decreed it against both of them, the soul and the body.
For the soul also corrupted it by allowing it to sink down toward the desires of its own nature.
Although the soul could have restrained it, it did not restrain it. And although it could have given it a taste of the sweetness of its own desire,
it took pleasure instead in the sweetness of the body's own corruptible desire, whose very movements, passions, and gestures are shameful.
For when desire is stirred, it throws the whole bodily organism into turmoil, and bends and lowers a person's vigor beneath the practice of sin.
It destroys his knowledge, dims his discernment, and darkens his understanding. For until the soul surrenders its will
to become enslaved to the gratification of desire, desire cannot overpower it and dim the light of its understanding.
For desire has this undertaking, as does the enemy who helps it:
to extinguish the light of knowledge within the soul's house, so that desire may easily carry out its shameful deeds as though in darkness.
For just as goodness longs for the light, so desire rejoices at the coming of darkness.
For this reason it sends out its smoke and blows against the soul's light, extinguishing it.
And when the whole person is left in gloom, he does everything, openly and secretly, as though in darkness.
For just as the bodily eye feels shame before the light and extinguishes it, and then approaches sinful deeds,
so the soul's sight also feels shame before the hidden vision of God within it.
For this reason desire extinguishes this light by which the soul ordinarily sees God, and then leads the soul into partnership in its activity.
For the soul is ashamed to approach sinful deeds as long as the light of the vision of God rests within it.
In the same way, the body feels shame before its partner, and one person's gaze feels shame before another's, as long as natural light lies before their sight.
And just as sin is practiced freely in darkness, without concealment,
so the soul shamelessly and brazenly commits fornication with the body once it has extinguished within itself the light of the remembrance of God.
For the soul extinguishes the light so that this sin may be pleasurable to it, because as long as it remembers God, it does not sin.
And if it happens to sink into a sinful act through drowsiness, its desire gives it no pleasure.
For the fear of God strips away and removes from it the pleasure of the act.
This light of the remembrance of God, then, does two things within the soul:
either it restrains the soul from sinning, or, if the soul gives way to desire and sins, it carries out sinful deeds with fear, trembling, and alarm.
For just as the body becomes alarmed during a sinful act when it knows that witnesses will soon arrive,
so the soul also becomes alarmed and afraid at the coming of the vision of God.
And since this light alone can restrain the soul from this wrongdoing,
the soul should always keep it close and let it rest within itself continually.
It should not let the remembrance of God depart from it, but should cling to the sweetness of communion with him.
For as long as it is bound to communion with him, it does not lower itself to communion with lust.
And as long as this light of the vision of God burns within it, darkness does not enter its radiant regions and take control.
And as long as the soul’s desire is mingled with the spirit’s desire, it does not mingle its thoughts with the body’s desire.
For a soul deserves ridicule when it abandons the desire for what belongs to its own nature and stoops to desire what is not its own.
For a wise soul, the body’s desire serves as an example, so that the soul too may stir up its own desire within itself.
Indeed, if the body desires what belongs to it, does the soul not desire what belongs to itself? And if the body lives through the movements of its nature,
does the soul not live through its living movements? And if the body, whose desire is hindered by many things, overcomes them all and is moved by that desire—
that is, it arouses this desire within itself—does the soul, which is free from all obstacles, not stir with the beautiful desire of its own nature?
Therefore, the disciple should not move on even from the stirring of this bodily desire
without gaining knowledge from it. Rather, when he sees that it has awakened, he should awaken his soul through knowledge
and become its observer. And if he has control over his own freedom and stands firm in the strength of the soul’s nature,
he is neither disturbed nor frightened by this desire even when it awakens in his limbs. Instead, he stands above it as an observer,
watching how it has awakened, from what causes, how strong its onset is, and how it grows.
He allows its heat to take control of his bodily limbs and spread fully throughout his body.
As it grows in his limbs, he increases thoughts of resolve in his soul to the same degree.
And as it grows hot, he in turn kindles the soul’s desire against it, placing that desire as though in an arena.
He himself sits as an observer on the heights of knowledge. For this desire stretches out its hands and takes hold of all the body’s limbs,
and wrestles with the body like an athlete with his opponent, while the mind sits as an observer on the heights of knowledge.
From the contest itself, the mind gathers instruction and learns how both sides win and how defeat can befall either side.
While remaining free from the struggle itself, it gains knowledge of the contest.
For such a mind does not allow itself to enter and become caught up in the desire that struggles with the body.
Otherwise, it cannot observe the struggle, nor can it gather and acquire instruction from it.
For just as the body cannot be a spectator of its own struggle while it is engaged in the contest,
and desire cannot watch itself while it is drawn up for battle against the body,
so neither can the mind be a spectator of this struggle if it allows itself to become entangled in the passion of desire.
For the passion of desire is blind, and it also blinds anyone caught in it.
For desire blinds the mind’s eye, lest, being able to see, it free itself from desire’s yoke.
So if you have confidence in the strength of your mind, do not be afraid when desire stirs in your limbs.
For it becomes a source of many good things for you, if you possess the knowledge that gains profit from losses.
First, it provides you with material for a struggle. For if you have no enemy, there is no struggle.
And if there is no struggle, victory cannot be known.
And if victory is not revealed at the end of the contest, the crown of triumph and praise is not given.
Take courage, then, in your battle, and do not lose heart because desire is stirring within you.
But take care that it finds no outlets in improper conduct.
Nor should the mind secretly dwell on it and commit sexual immorality without a body, with an image that has no actual existence.
For this is desire’s habit: when no real body is near it, it commits sexual immorality with the shadow of an image,
and with the likeness of a person instead of the person. The one committing sexual immorality embraces in his mind something that is not near him.

Instead of joining himself to the image with his body, he joins himself to it in his soul. Instead of committing adultery with his limbs, he does so with his thoughts. Instead of defiling her body, he defiles his own soul.
For when the passion of sexual immorality takes hold and flares up within his thoughts, its excess makes him discharge his semen even without a physical object.
And although he has no external stimulus, desire itself, through its abundance, presses to find an outlet.
It seeks opportunities and finds ways, and kindles in the body the fire of destructive arousal.
For just as divine desire seeks opportunities through which to carry out its wishes and please God,
so too the desire for sexual immorality seeks ways to obtain its pleasures and provoke God to anger.
But set desire against desire in battle, discerning mind, and the desire of the body will soon be defeated by the desire of the spirit,
because spiritual things are stronger in every way than bodily things. And while you hold the reins of desire and of the body,
which struggle against one another, and watch their struggle from the height where you sit in knowledge,
you win a crown from your position between the two. That is, the body that shares in the soul’s life receives a crown,
For it, life without decay is also reserved through its union with her. For the body is naturally united with the soul.
Desire, however, entered from outside through the transgression of the commandment. And for this reason, to separate the body from the soul—
we cannot. But we can cut off desire and cast it out of the body, if we wish.
But the body was not created to be a home for evil desire in the same way that it is fitted to be a dwelling for the soul.
For if the body had been made by the Creator to be a dwelling for desire,
the divine commandments would not have driven desire out of it on every side, crying out with various threatening voices from every direction.
There, judgment; there, threats; there, torment; there, hell; there, retribution.
There, gnashing of teeth; there, endless scourging; and there, punishment without end.
Along with this, it is also chastened by pains close at hand and scourged by the illnesses that befall it.
And ravenous death suddenly removes it from life, while fear accompanies it.
Terror surrounds it, and losses and afflictions befall it.
At the beginning, desire is inactive within it because of infancy and childhood, and at the end it dies down within it because of old age.
Divine wisdom devised these and similar means to eliminate evil desire from the body,
so that, when it sees the afflictions upon it and the constant torments that accompany its life, it may extinguish the inflaming desire in its members.
That is, so that the fire spread throughout all its members may cool and die out within it, like a flame that has caught in brushwood,
and like a fire that displays its blaze amid abundant fuel. For just as kindling is before fire,
so the members are before desire. And just as fire destroys fuel when it takes hold of it,
so desire also destroys the body's members when it takes hold of them. For the final result of fire's burning
is ash, and the final result of desire in the members is destruction. Therefore, do not conceal fire among pieces of wood, or desire within the members.
For just as naphtha and oil increase the burning of fire, so food and drink intensify the blaze of desire.
And just as fire is extinguished by water, so desire is also extinguished by ascetic discipline.
For if you throw plenty of water on a fire, it extinguishes it. But if you pour naphtha or oil over it, you make it flare up.
Likewise, if you supply desire with nourishment by eating food and drinking wine,
you add fire to fire and heap flame upon flame.
But if you reduce the body's food and drink, its natural desire will subside.
And all its desires die down and grow cold. So let desire stir in your body, not for your condemnation but for your victory.
Not so that it becomes a cause of shame for you, but so that it brings you crowns of victory.
Not so that through it you prove foolish and ignorant, but so that from it you gather understanding and wisdom.
Not so that it stirs within you to blind your discernment, but so that it becomes a polishing stone for you, clearing the eye of your thoughts.
So that what is written may be fulfilled in you, O mind: “The wise person sits on a secure height, but fools will fall into a pit.”
So when you sit on the height of knowledge, let desire and the body be subdued beneath you.
Be an observer of their struggle, not a partner in their desire.
Be watchful over the desire of your nature, O mind, as you observe the struggle of fleshly desire.
Let it be subject to you in everything, like the earth pressed down beneath the mountains.
Let your will stir it, and let your will quiet it. Let its course, too, be under your watchful gaze.
For the wise, the stirring of desire becomes an occasion for learning and material for knowledge. For passions stir within them so that they may gain experience of the passions,
and test their strength against them, and provide material for putting their knowledge into practice: when these things occur,
and to what extent they take place, when the intellect, in its natural freedom, is above the passions,
and commands them as a master commands his servants, and they obey it, as it places the yoke of its mastery upon them,
and turns their gaze toward the movement of its signals, so that they follow its word and are ready to obey its command.
And while it remains in its natural freedom, they serve like slaves, carrying out the will expressed in its word.
What teaching, then, is as excellent as this, through which a person becomes victorious over his own passions?
For these passions do not merely make you victorious, but also wise and knowledgeable,
if you observe them rather than act on them, and free yourself from their pleasure while binding yourself to the knowledge gained from them.
For as long as thought is held captive by the sweetness of desire, it cannot observe the struggle and gather knowledge.
Instead, it turns toward pleasure that passes away. For desire was placed within us for combat, not for condemnation,
and to be conquered by us, not to conquer us; and so that through training against it we might become wise, not so that it might show us to be foolish and ignorant.
For all the learning we find outside ourselves has its material conveyed to us through words.
But the learning and knowledge we acquire through victory over our passions has the truth of its wisdom confirmed for us through practical experience.
For this reason, this teaching is also trustworthy and true, and when the soul finds this wisdom, it is much sweeter to it than the wisdom that comes from outside.
For it is something inward, and the soul finds rest in it from within itself.
Its delight comes from within itself, not from causes outside it.
For when we gather knowledge from outside, the source of our knowledge lies outside us.
But when we find instruction of this kind through experiencing our own passions, the instruction we gather is sound and trustworthy.
We can rely on it, and it is preserved. For if things outside us provide material for our knowledge,
how much more will those things that arise from us and stir within us become a source of instruction in wisdom for us,
provided that we allow desire to stir within us for this experience, and not for the gratification of desire itself.
Therefore, observe yourself with discerning knowledge. Distinguish between yourself and your passion, and understand the difference,
so that you may run and discover your own purity. Do not let desire find rest within you, lest it constantly demand gratification from you.
Do not bring it to fulfillment when it begins, lest, after its fulfillment, it demand another beginning from you.
Cut off its flow, and its spring is stopped up. Block its path, and the impulse that gives rise to it immediately becomes still.
For desire is never satisfied. That is why the more it is fed, the hungrier it becomes, and the more it drinks, the thirstier it becomes.
For as long as desire fulfills its wishes within you, its demands on you never end.
Do not say, “I will do what it wants now, and fight against it another time.” For if you are defeated by it once,
it will defeat you every time. And as it grows stronger through its activity, your own strength grows weaker.
Do not grow lax and give your strength to desire so that it may become strong through it. Instead, use the strength of your nature yourself, and let desire remain in the weakness that belongs to it.
Let the heat of desire be an instructive example for you, so that spiritual desire may awaken within you and grow equally hot.
For just as the body is set ablaze by its natural desire, so too the natural desire of the spiritual life is set ablaze and grows hot.
For as long as the desire of the spirit burns hot within you, there is no way for bodily desire to awaken within you.
And if you have not experienced this in practice, learn from its opposite.
For whenever bodily desire boils within you, you yourself perceive that at that moment the desire of the spirit has entirely ceased within you.
Indeed, bodily desire would not have awakened if it had not found the desire of the spirit asleep.
For when either one sleeps, its counterpart awakens. For this reason they constantly watch one another,
so that when the impulses of the first have withdrawn, those of its opposite may come in after it.
For just as a thief watches and waits for the master of the house to fall asleep, so bodily desire waits for the desire of the spirit to fall asleep.
And when it sees a little negligence and contempt, and that a person has been deprived of the taste of experiencing divine desire,
the desire of the flesh immediately awakens and begins to surge and rise through all the limbs.
And if a person is negligent and gives way to it, it spreads like night through the house of his own being and darkens it.
For just as the shadows on the earth increase and grow stronger as the sun inclines westward on its course,
until it sets and its rays are cut off, and then the shadows of night rise fully and cover creation,
so too the darkness of fleshly desire constantly watches the course of the light of spiritual desire.
And as it sees that light moving downward, it too begins moving upward:
degree for degree, measure for measure, notch for notch,
until this light sets completely, grows dim, and draws back to itself the rays of its spirituality.
Then the shadow of desire rises fully and covers the soul, and a gloomy night falls within the luminous house.
From this point a person begins to stumble over everything, because he cannot see and distinguish the things placed before him.
For just as the distinctness of everything is concealed in the gloom of night, so in the gloom of desire
all the soul’s perceptions are darkened, and the power of its knowledge is impoverished—especially if it has experienced the knowledge of the Spirit.
For just as darkness is opposed to light, so this passion of desire is opposed to the knowledge of the Spirit.
For even when the mind turns to observe the movements of desire, it does not look at it with a spiritual eye,
but with its seeing faculty, which examines things through the knowledge of the soul. And when it looks in this way,
it gathers knowledge from the struggle itself. For when the intellect looks spiritually upon God,
nothing opposed to him appears to it. Nor does it lower itself to look at desire.
For wonder at the greatness of God’s glory does not allow it to turn and look at the things that lie behind it,
because the vision of the delight it has tasted is enough to hold it unwaveringly to itself.
And again, suppose someone says that it looks at desire to gain instruction: the mind does not gather instruction of this kind from opposing things,
but through a simple movement of the knowledge that it has acquired after becoming free from the passions.
This is also how the angels know everything: not by comparing one thing with another
and setting things that oppose one another side by side, but by moving in knowledge through simple and undivided thought.
But let anyone who wishes to observe desire also beware of this thought.
For fear that, while he has not yet been completely freed from the passions, when he lowers himself to acquire knowledge,
he may be seized by the pleasure of hateful passions. For at that time the mind itself is also engaged in a struggle.
Just as the body and desire are engaged in battle, so the mind itself is also fighting, so that it may not be seized by love for something it sees.
But if the mind is confident that it can contemplate the passion of desire without passion—otherwise, it is better for it to flee rather than look.
For if someone recognizes his weakness, it is better for him to flee than to become enslaved to his enemies.
For fighting and gaining victory are a demonstration of strength and a sign of diligence.
But if he is seized by the pleasure of passion and drawn away from the love of knowledge, it is better for him to be freed at least from passion,
rather than to be enslaved to it while receiving no knowledge. For it is not even possible for him to find knowledge if he is held captive by passion.
For the natural eye, which hastens to investigate the knowledge of things, is blinded.
And he is seized by the pleasure of passion, not by the pleasure of discernment.
For just as good things differ from one another, so their tastes differ from one another.
Everyone chooses whichever he desires and is seized by the passion he seeks. Some are seized by the passion of desire,
and others by the passion for knowledge. Someone held captive by passion through the pleasure of desire is not concerned with gathering knowledge from it.
Likewise, someone held captive by the sweetness of knowledge does not turn toward the pleasure of desire, which takes captive whatever it takes captive.
All the parts of the soul and body gather around the passion that is strong within it, to nurture and serve it.
For this reason, you find many lovers of knowledge who are free from this passion of desire.
Yet their victory is not a complete victory, because they have overcome passion by means of passion, not through the discernment of divine knowledge.
But for us, it is not only victory over desire that is required; we must also know the cause through which we gain victory.
For the victory, too, will take its name from its cause. If the cause is from God,
then the victory is also divine. But if it is directed toward the world, or comes from love of knowledge, or from empty glory,
or is intended to prevent one of the other passions from impoverishing a person through it, when he overcomes the passion of sexual immorality,
this victory should be considered weak, because it is seen as either weak or strong according to its cause.
Those who overcome passions by means of passions suppress them but do not pass beyond them.
But someone who overcomes the passions without passion gains a victory free from passion.
For how can something composed of the passions themselves be called a victory over the passions?
And how can it be called their conqueror when it has sprung from the very root from which they grow? For if, because the contemplation of knowledge is strong within you,
you overcome the passion of sexual immorality, the passion had its moment and overcame its counterpart.
But another moment comes for that other passion too, and it overcomes the first. And when they thus overcome one another and are overcome by one another,
righteous victory is taken away from their midst. For this is the victory that takes place justly: when good overcomes evil,
and the desire of the spirit overcomes the desire of the body, and light overcomes darkness, and knowledge overcomes ignorance, and likewise with all the rest.
But this is the victory that takes place unjustly: when evil overcomes good, and darkness overcomes light, and ignorance overcomes knowledge.
The victory that stands between these two is that of the passions opposed to one another.
It is not a victory of divine triumph when the passions themselves overcome one another and are overcome by one another,
and the establishment of one brings about the undoing of another. For example, there are some who, because of the passion of love of money,
fight against the appetite of the belly. And there is someone who, for the sake of empty glory, overcomes this desire for sexual immorality.
And there is someone who, because of the desire for human praise, fights against the desire for possessions.
And there is someone who, because of the passion of love of honor, restrains himself from the passion for many social interactions.
And there is someone who, because of the desire for leadership, wages war against the love of comfort.
Although both these and those are evils, they overcome one another and are overcome by one another.
But it is not counted as a genuine victory when one passion fights against another passion and overcomes it.
Desires therefore stir within the body, and evil passions are also aroused within the soul.
And just as their natures are opposed to one another, so their passions are also opposed to one another.
For all the body's desires, so to speak, are opposed to the soul's passions.
And again, for the most part, all the evil passions that spring from the soul are opposed to the body's desires.
For there are bodily passions, and there are passions of the soul.
The bodily ones are those that spring from the body, while those of the soul are those that sprout from the soul.
And all the bodily passions, if someone examines them with understanding, support one another.
For the passion of gluttony has its origin in the body, and it supports the passion of sexual immorality.
This too is itself a bodily passion. Likewise, adornment with clothing and the passion for human pleasures,
and all the things that follow these and are found in connection with the body, support the passion of sexual immorality.
The passion of love of money stands between the others. Sometimes it supports bodily desires, and sometimes it assists the passions of the soul.
For through lavish spending it supports gluttony, sexual immorality, and fine clothing,
as well as entertainments, the sounds of singing, and the pleasure of human company.
All these are offspring of the body. But in other respects it also assists the passions of the soul,
supporting the love of leadership and also the passion of vainglory,
if someone wishes to gain praise in this way, and the world's honor and acclaim. It also nurtures pride
and lends a hand to envy, along with other things like these, whose impulses have their source in the soul.
Thus this passion of love of money is a bond that gathers together different passions.
Yet in another form it can also be found opposing the passions of both soul and body,
if someone examines it closely and with understanding.
For, in order to grow and become strong itself, it restrains desires in the body and likewise the soul's passions in the soul.
All these passions of the soul also support one another.
For just as the discussion has shown that bodily desires support one another,
the very same thing is found with the passions of the soul. Honor, for example, supports vainglory.
Vain pride, in turn, supports pride, and pride urges a person toward leadership and authority.
All these support one another in this way. Yet there are also other perspectives and, in turn, opposing aspects
of these very passions. But along the path that our discussion is now following, they support and assist one another.
For just as one good thing supports another, so one evil thing also fosters another.
But because the paths of the passions are subtle, and they have different outlets, impulses, aims, and forms,
let no one judge my words by looking at other aims,
in which these passions of body and soul, and the intermediate passion of love of money, stand opposed to one another.
Rather, let whoever judges our discussion examine it from the perspective set before us, and he will find that it is just as we have written.
The human being from whom all the passions spring is one.
For sin itself is also one, even though it is divided into many forms.
And his constitution is made up of the members of opposing passions. But now we are speaking about the passion of sexual immorality, which prompted our discussion.
so that we may wake up and watch it. For anyone overcome by it is clearly not truly awake.
For just as happens to those who are asleep, who dream [?] in their sleep without conscious discernment,
yet feel the pleasure of desire even while asleep, so too someone who gives himself over to this passion, allowing his desires to work through it,
is plunged, as it were, into a deep sleep. At that moment he has no sound understanding,
no wakeful discernment, no clear awareness, and no well-ordered mind. Instead, in the same way
that his bodily senses are confused and the joints of his limbs grow slack from the stirrings of desire,
so too the thoughts of his soul are confused, his mind grows dark, and his discernment is taken away.
And just as all the members of the body turn to become servants of desire,
so too all the thoughts of the soul are drawn down toward bodily pleasure and submerged in it.
They are swallowed up in the sweetness of corruptible desire.
At that moment a person does everything like someone asleep. Understand from his actions that he is plunged into sleep.
For when neither fear of God, nor shame before other people, nor remembrance of punishment far off,
nor recollection of judgment close at hand, nor remorse, nor shame is before his eyes at that moment,
and he neither reflects on any of these things nor lets them enter his mind, is it not clear that he is plunged, as it were, into a deep sleep,
and does everything without awareness, as though drowsy? We can also recognize this from another consideration:
immediately upon the completion of the act of desire, remorse enters the soul.
Sorrow over what it has done arises within it. And the understanding it lacked during the passion
comes to it afterward, so that it suffers, is distressed, mourns, and grieves, regretting its shameful deeds.
It realizes that what it has done deserves blame. The recollection of judgment and condemnation stirs within it.
The penalties to come are pictured before its eyes. And, as though in light and wakefulness, it sees
what it did not see while it was asleep in passion. It thinks about God and recalls judgment.
It remembers punishment and despises desire. It reproaches itself for how it was carried away, overcome by the apparition of a dream,
and defeated by a passing shadow; though it is something, it was enslaved by nothing.
These and similar good recollections that come to it after desire has been fulfilled
show that it has returned from sleep to wakefulness and has regained a sound recollection of itself.
And from the stupor of sleep and from the death of sin it returned to the dwelling of life. Therefore, at a time of lust,
a person needs vigilance more than anything else, and to look at the thing that overcomes him and see how contemptible and despicable it is.
For a short time is enough to satisfy lust and to feel remorse over engaging in its vile act.
For we see that none of the things people desire is so quickly fulfilled as the pleasure of lust.
And this very fact—that its satisfaction lasts only a brief instant and its pleasure only a short time—
should have made us despise it and not fall into its destructive enticement.
For I know of no other desire that is as devoid of benefit as this desire,
whose weakness is apparent from every side. As for its benefit, it has none.
As for the duration of its pleasure, it is brief. As for its delight, it is like a shadow. As for the movements of its [?], they are shameful.
As for the causes that stir it up, they are weak. As for its behavior, it resembles that of animals.
As for its postures, they are those of a beast. As for remorse, it is close at hand. As for fear, it accompanies it.
As for shame, it lives with it. As for anxiety, it is found beside it.
As for terror, it is its companion. As for losses, they accompany it. As for injuries, they are close at hand.
As for a bad reputation, it is crowned with it. As for mockery, it accompanies it at all times. As for derision, it is laughed at by everyone.
And however you look at lust, losses accompany it. On account of which of these things, then, should it overcome us, and why should it overpower us?
Its enticements are strong; for that very reason we ought all the more to despise it.
But because of our low condition, it evidently overcomes us in the very respect in which we ought all the more to overcome it.
And if it seems powerful within us, it is because the strength of our soul is weak within us.
For whatever strength lust has, it takes from the soul. And when strength has been stripped from the soul, weakness remains with it.
And what soul is more wretched than this one, whose strength others use while it is clothed in the weakness of others?
For the spiritual nature of our soul naturally possesses strength against desires, and it can easily overcome them if it wishes.
For just as weakness, dissolution, and decay are naturally associated with the nature of the body,
so strength and steadfastness in good things are associated with the spiritual nature.
And if it exercises strength, it draws that strength from its own nature. But along with this, the soul
is also accompanied by the grace of the Spirit, which gives it help and strength if it entrusts its good will to that grace.
For just as a strong man takes a child's hand and lifts him in his weakness with the support of his strength,
so the Holy Spirit takes hold of the soul's thoughts and lifts it up, as though by the hand, so that it may rise toward spiritual things.
Through its companionship with the Spirit, the soul also gains a lightness beyond what it has by nature.
Whoever entrusts himself to the Spirit to be his teacher remains beyond harm throughout the whole course of his life.
For this reason Paul also teaches us to live in the Spirit and surrender ourselves to the Spirit.
For whoever lives in the Spirit and surrenders to the Spirit becomes spiritual in his whole way of life.
He is guided by the Spirit's stirrings, and his thoughts and actions accord with the Spirit's wishes.
For we are overcome by desire not because we lack a helper, but because we do not seek the helper's assistance.
For just as desire itself, whenever it wishes to overcome us, calls others to its aid,
and then fights and overcomes us, so we too, if we are determined to fight and overcome it,
should call to our aid the divine power and the assistance of the grace within us. Then we will easily overcome the desire that fights against us.
For the more our soul is purified of thoughts of desire, the more firmly it stands in its natural strength.
And the more it rises to stand in its natural strength, the more it becomes worthy to receive divine power to assist it.
Once it has such support, it is not easily overcome by the desires that fight against it.
Guard yourself, then, against the causes that lead you toward desire.
Block the channels and conduits that gather a foreign stream against you from every direction.
Once you have cut off the causes that nourish the ailments, your sores will dry up by themselves, even if you apply no medicines to them.
Little by little, the putrefaction in them will cease and disappear. For this desire within us is nourished by causes outside us,
which are many and differ from one another. Each of them supplies desire with a particular strength.
If you cut off these causes, desire itself will also cease and come to an end.
For desire does not even exist without these things, nor does it remain within us if its causes are removed.
For desire sometimes begins in the body, and sometimes in the stirrings of thoughts,
and sometimes in causes outside us, whether through sight, through hearing, or through things like these.
We must examine it with discernment and cut it off at its source before it advances.
For if it is aroused within us by external causes, let us cut ourselves off from dealings with other people.
And let us keep away from the sight of those people who encourage it. By this means we block its entry into us.
But if its stirring comes from the boiling heat of the body, we ought to weaken the body.
And let us reduce its strength with a little poor food and with drinking water in moderation,
along with the other hardships that ordinarily lessen the body's heat.
But if we perceive that lust began with a thought, we ought to recognize that the mind is idle, without meditation on God.
And because it has no movements of its own, foreign movements from outside it have entered it.
And if it appears to us that the thought of lust was stirred up in us because we ceased meditating on good things,
let us take care to occupy the mind with meditation on spiritual things and with the study of divine knowledge.
And at such a time let us devote ourselves to reading the Scriptures and listening to accounts of resolute and mighty people,
continually picturing their likenesses before our eyes and awakening in ourselves a desire to imitate them.
And let us also persevere in prayer, which gives strength to the mind more than anything else.
For this is the distinctive work of prayer: to clothe the mind with invincible strength.
For just as, when we withdraw from the mind's empty occupations and turn away from sights that encourage laxity,
we purify our thoughts and thereby gather ourselves inward, so too, when in prayer,
after gathering the mind together, we persevere, our thought receives strength to overcome courageously the passions that battle against it.
These, then, are the three ways in which lust gains control over our lives.
And if we wisely know how to shut the door against them and apply to each one the remedy it requires,
we cast lust out of ourselves and remain in purity of soul.
And we conduct ourselves with invincible strength of mind, so that after this
the soul is also deemed worthy of the blessedness of exalted contemplation, and it gains an awareness of spiritual things that is beyond the body.
And just as the body is moved by things belonging to its nature and finds rest in them, so too the soul takes delight in spiritual movements,
and rejoices in the light of living knowledge that is above the world. May all the disciples of the faith be deemed worthy of this,
by the grace of Christ, the God of all, to whom be glory forever. Amen.
Here ends the discourse on the lust for sexual immorality.
Notes on the Syriac text:
Discourse Thirteen: On sexual immorality and the evil passion of bodily desire. In it he explains
how much strenuous training is required of us who fight in this battle,
and how they may guard against its manifest passions beforehand, at the stage of hidden impulses, so that they may also be freed from its manifest passions,
until they keep clear of it and its passions by every means, both inwardly and outwardly.
As I considered the hateful passions that hinder the soul from divine knowledge and purity of prayer,
I found that this passion of sexual immorality hinders good things more than many others do.
It rules especially strongly and blazes up in people who lack endurance.
For when this passion finds an occasion in the heat of the body,
and finds thoughts unoccupied with meditation on God and the pursuit of excellent knowledge,
the fire of this passion, like a flame in brushwood, catches hold and takes control of all the body's members.
For this destructive passion is hotter and swifter than all the others.
The soul needs great courage when it draws up for battle against her, so that she may fight and defeat it,
while also calling on the grace of God to help her in this struggle.
The person fighting this battle must take care to struggle and uproot this passion from his thoughts,
and pull the roots of its growth out of the depths of his heart. For that is where it enters, takes hold, and makes its home.
When it is uprooted from there, all its branches extending over the rest of the body's members wither.
But if this passion should rule within the soul for a long time and become firmly established in her through constant practice,
it darkens her powers of discernment and does not even let her recognize it as a passion.
Instead, the mind considers this desire blameless, like other things whose practice is not blameworthy.
For sin also undertakes this task: to uproot from the soul the thought that recognizes it as sin,
so that it may operate without fear or anxiety in inward thoughts and outward deeds.
For as long as we see sin in others, and it is not being practiced in our own persons, we use the judgment of righteousness within us
to declare that it is sin. But if we ourselves should happen to commit it, awareness of its activity is uprooted from our soul,
and the eye of discernment, through which we see the ugliness of its activity, is blinded.
Let us therefore take care not to stumble and fall into this desire. But if we should happen to be caught in it through the enticements of occasions,
Let us not fail to recognize and discern that this is sin, especially when it lies secretly concealed within us in our thoughts.
For many people suppose that desire in one's thoughts is not sin.
Yet it is not merely sin in an ordinary sense; it is the root of all sinful actions.
For the heart is the source of all thoughts, and from it arise impulses toward good and evil.
Whatever puts down roots and takes hold in it, whether good or evil, also bears fruit that becomes visible outwardly.
For when desire is stifled in the heart, it can awaken there at any time.
And just as a tree is cut down and its root remains in the ground, and with the moisture of water it sprouts again and grows,
so too, when desire is cut off and its root remains within the mind,
through the moisture supplied by food and drink, it sprouts again and grows in the thoughts and bodily members.
Here we especially need to struggle against this hidden desire, much more than against desire that is openly acted upon.
For in the latter case there are many things that hinder it: being seen by many people, shame, and modesty,
and laws imposing punishment. Moreover, the very people on whom the passion of desire fixes itself may happen to be unwilling.
Because all these things hinder desire from being acted upon, our struggle against it in outward conduct is, in a sense, not very difficult.
For we do not fight against it alone; we have all these helpers.
Even when we want to carry out the sinful act and devise many ways to accomplish it, these things and others like them hinder us.
Although desire is active within us because we willingly consent to it, it is restrained outwardly by the things that hinder it.
And although people consider us chaste because of our outward conduct,
God, who examines our hidden thoughts, counts us as sexually immoral because of what we will.
Although we do not sin in one another's presence, our sin is plain to God's knowledge. Let us therefore guard against both,
so that we may neither be disgraced in people's eyes nor stand ashamed before God.
Let our first concern be to please God, for this also gives rise to confidence before other people.
For not committing sexual sin openly does not prevent someone from being counted as sexually immoral in secret.
But being freed from thoughts of sexual immorality also shows a person to be chaste in outward conduct.
For action is not the root of thoughts; rather, thought is the root and cause of actions.
For in the heart, the source of thoughts, resides the will for everything. Thus God's will too finds rest there.
And because the streams of actions branch out from it as from a great spring, we must keep it clear so that it does not become muddy.
For just as, when the source of a spring is muddy, all the streams flowing from it are also muddy and murky,
so, when the heart is disturbed by lust, all the senses are troubled, all the limbs are disturbed, the whole person is thrown into turmoil, and the mind is confused.
Thoughts are jumbled, and each of the body's limbs shows by its appearance that it is enslaved to the lust hidden in the heart.
For whatever begins in the heart, whether in good things or in evil things,
