is what is counted as sin or as righteousness by the judgment of divine knowledge.
For this reason our Lord too, wishing to remove lust by its root and not merely cut it off from outward actions, said:
“Everyone who looks at a woman to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart.” He put the matter this way here, comparing adultery with adultery,
and the judgment of the law concerning sinful deeds with the exactness of his own knowledge.
“You have heard,” he says, “that it was said to those of old, ‘Do not commit adultery.’” For those of old, the law restrained the acting out of lust.
The commandment held them in check so that their sexual immorality would not appear in their outward limbs.
For because they did not have the strength to uproot sexually immoral thoughts from within the heart,
the lawgiver left the first thing aside and moved on to the second.
And because they were unable to cleanse the heart of the thought of adultery, he compelled them by the binding force of the commandment at least to keep the body from committing the act.
He established righteousness for them in the outward realm, where there are many reasons that support this restraint.
But our Lord does not seek to remove adultery from the outside, but from the place where he himself sees.
For God's sight is unique, and where he sees, human sight does not see,
because human beings cannot know the hidden thoughts within the soul. Just as, he says, the sight of other people restrains you
from the outward act of adultery, let my sight also restrain you from the thought that desires adultery.
And cleanse the spiritual realm of your soul, so that it may resemble my sight, which looks into it.
For just as my gaze upon you is free from error and conjecture,
so let the place that receives this gaze also be free from the passion of sexual immorality.
For in my judgment, lust is adultery, and the thought's consent is what puts the body to work.
For I do not need to see lust carried out in action before I count it as adultery.
For the thought that desires adultery has already committed adultery. And everyone who looks at a woman to lust after her,
He has already committed adultery with her in his heart. For he has practiced adultery where it was easy for him to do so.
For the fact that the deed did not appear openly does not mean that his will restrained him; rather, he was hindered by other circumstances.
From this it is clear that the victory belongs not to his will, but to those circumstances that hindered him.
But the gaze of God's knowledge looks into our thoughts, beyond the circumstances.
He examines the very depths of the mind, where human beings cannot easily see, nor can they easily understand even if they try to investigate.
For this belongs to God alone: to search the heart and know hidden things.
And just as it belongs to him to know our hidden things, so it belongs to us to purify our hearts before his sight.
For many who do not commit adultery in deed are adulterers in their will, and continually practice sexual immorality within their souls.
For they continually conceive and give birth to images of every variety, and constantly commit sexual immorality with beautiful faces, without bodily union.
They do not consider that even if human beings do not see, God examines the hidden things in their thoughts.
For sometimes the thought itself is sin, and sometimes it is the carrying out of the deed.
For a thought that fully consents to evil is sin as far as its will is concerned, even if it does nothing in deed.
But our Lord laid this commandment upon us as people capable of strength: everyone who looks at a woman in order to desire her has committed adultery with her in his heart.
This is so that we may uproot sin and cut away and remove destructive desire from the depths of the heart.
For he did not tell you not to see, but not to look in order to desire. The eye looks at everything, but it does not desire everything.
In the same way, let a woman's beauty be before your eyes like the sight of anything else, and do not be caught by this beauty.
For if the soul could see the beauty of its own nature, it would not crave the beauty of the body.
For its own beauty would be enough to hold its thoughts captive through the delight of beholding it. And when it saw itself
and gazed closely at the beauty of its nature, a desire to possess itself would also awaken within it,
so that it might possess its own being more than anything else, and commune with itself in complete purity.
He says, "Do not entertain an alien desire in your heart, and do not let the eye of your mind gaze at beauty outside yourself."
For it is a disgrace for the soul to be bound by the desire of the flesh. If it is shackled by this, its bondage is foreign to its nature.
And because it has taken on the mindset of the flesh, its gaze too has desired what is outside its nature.
For there is adultery of the body, and there is adultery of the soul. Whenever the soul lusts in thought, this is its own distinct adultery.
For just as, in the case of the body, the act itself bears the name of adultery, so, in the case of the soul,
A man's thought is his deed. In spirit, there is no escaping the charge of adultery for someone who thinks of committing adultery, because in his soul he has carried out the sinful deed.
And just as the soul's nature is higher than the body's, so the soul's sexual immorality is more serious than the body's.
Again, the bitterness of this wrongdoing can be seen in another way: he has not committed sexual immorality with the body, in which desire is naturally mingled,
but has subjected the soul to something foreign to its nature. And without knowledge of its own desire,
it has been brought down to crave a desire that is not its own. Furthermore, the body's sexual immorality has its appointed times,
and there are intervals and interruptions in its desire: sometimes a person sins, and sometimes he rests from his sin.
But someone who commits sexual immorality in his soul has no rest from practicing this wrongdoing, because desire is continually mingled within his soul.
And if he happens to stop thinking about it, it is not because he regrets it,
but because another passion has grown strong within him and carried his mind off to some other thought. For victory over desire
is not recognized by this: that through engagement with another thought, someone stops dwelling on sexual immorality,
but when he overcomes it on its own, with readiness to overcome it established in us beforehand.
For there are many in whom thoughts of sexual immorality grow quiet because other thoughts come and put them to sleep.
And when these incoming thoughts have also finished their work and grown quiet, the thought of sexual immorality is found in its place.
For it had not actually departed from there before. Rather, like a body in darkness, it too was hidden in the shadow of another passion.
And after the shadow that covered it has passed away, then the body of sexual immorality is seen, lodged within the soul.
Let us therefore flee, my brothers, especially from this sexual immorality that is not considered sexual immorality.
For many flee from an evil whose practice is obvious.
But people are all the more caught unawares by what is not considered a sin.
For it is not only something that is not seen to be evil that is evil; rather, whatever God has judged to be evil, that above all we should consider evil.
For indeed, the evil of every sinful deed is apparent to a person before he is caught in it.
But once he has become enslaved to it and has personally practiced it for a long time without repentance,
his awareness of its evil is taken away from him, so that he neither recognizes nor sees its ugliness, because he has lost his discernment.
For sin not only defiles the person; it also blinds discernment.
It makes someone who once saw unable to see, someone who once knew unable to know, and someone who once discerned unable to discern.
And that little which used to be seen and known as though in the light is hidden from sight when the darkness of sin is poured into the soul.
For just as everything in darkness is hidden from sight, even darkness itself,
so too everything is hidden from the soul over which the gloom of sin is spread,
even sin itself, so that it is not recognized as sin. For recognizing one's sin is the first step toward release from sin.
For once someone realizes that he is bound, he devises ways to free himself.
But if he does not even know that he is bound and shackled, how will he devise ways to seek release for himself?
“Do not,” it says, “look at a woman with desire for her. Otherwise you are committing adultery with her.” Look at her with a pure eye, as at a beautiful work of God.
And praise the wise maker, who fashioned such a thing from such material and adorned what he willed.
What beauty he has made from lowly material, and from ordinary dust, beauty that captivates those who see it! And see, from the beauty of the work,
the beauty of its maker. And as you marvel at the lowly material, which has been so richly adorned and become glorious,
wonder and stand amazed at him who is glorious by nature, whose beautiful appearance those deemed worthy to look upon him can never see enough of.
Therefore, take care to purify your soul, so that your body too may be pure along with it.
Be holy in body and spirit, because you are a dwelling place for the Spirit of God.
For your prayer too becomes pure and light when your thoughts are purified of the passion of sexual immorality.
Along with this, the light of the knowledge of Christ shines more brightly within you when the eye of your soul is purified so that he may dwell in it.
For just as a healthy body is ready for any task, so a mind purified of evils readily becomes a dwelling place for divine impulses.
And just as sickness weakens the body and makes it unfit for anything, so too sinful thoughts
weaken the soul's strength and leave it without divine impulses.
For this thought of sexual immorality casts foulness into the soul,
so that it is changed from the sweetness and loveliness it once possessed, and a foul smell rises from it.
The treasure of divine thoughts is not deposited in a soul like this.
For just as substances that naturally have a sweet smell are placed in clean vessels suited to them,
so too divine knowledge dwells within a soul purified of sinful thoughts,
and especially within a soul freed from this passion.
For more than all the other passions, it distracts and confuses the thoughts.
Thus Solomon too depicted this very passion of sexual immorality and likened it to things of this sort.
“There are three things,” he says, “that are hidden from me, and four that I do not understand: the way of an eagle in the sky,
and the way of a snake on a rock, and the way of a ship in the heart of the sea, and the way of a man in his youth.
Such is the way of an adulterous woman: she eats and wipes her mouth and says, ‘I have done nothing.’”
For he illustrates sexual desire by an adulterous woman, whose ways and paths are unknown.
For she casts her gaze indiscriminately upon everyone, stumbles over everyone, and commits sexual immorality in everything, outside the order of nature.
For such is the intoxication of desire when it takes control of the thoughts: it has no known road,
nor any path that is clear and distinct. You want to trace its course, but you cannot.
For this sexual desire wanders within the soul and turns easily in every direction, while the traces of its steps remain unknown.
Its way is not visible to those who watch, like that of an eagle in the sky, a snake on a rock, and the way of a ship in the heart of the sea.
The wise Solomon rightly included the young man as an illustration too, in the likeness of these first three.
For as the sea is to the ship, the air to the eagle, and the rock to the snake, so also is the young man to desire.
For the eagle cuts freely through the air, the snake moves over the rock without hindrance, and the ship travels easily through the heart of the sea.
So too, during youth, thoughts of sexual immorality are easily brought to fulfillment within the soul.
If someone calls youth the road of sexual immorality, he is not mistaken. That is, he too calls it what Solomon called it.
The easy road for the snake, he says, is the rock: it stumbles over nothing on it, nor does the weight of the earth there hinder its movement.
Again, the eagle’s road is the air, and the ship’s is the sea. In the same way, youth is the road of sexual immorality,
along which it flies wherever it wishes, as though on wings, and runs everywhere on swift feet.
For because the body’s heat is great during youth, it provides abundant fuel for the flame of desire.
When fire draws its impetus from fire—that is, when this desire draws it from the fire of nature—it produces a mighty blaze of sin.
For this reason, this stage of life must be met with constant warfare,
and blows, labors, hardships, little food, and little drink.
Then, when the fuel on which desire catches fire is removed, desire itself also disappears and dies out.
Everyone who wishes to observe such things perceives this through practical experience.
Therefore, anyone who wishes to overcome this desire should take measures to remove from its reach the kindling
and the fuel that sets it alight, and then it will not catch fire in him. For desire enters along with these causes.
Or through looking at women, or through conversation that constantly dwells on matters concerning lust.
Or through food and drink given to the body beyond what it needs.
If you remove these three things and occupy yourself with the knowledge of God, not even a lustful thought will trouble you.
For as long as the body does not stir up lust through its heat, and the soul does not dwell on it out of idleness, where can it find an opportunity to awaken?
For either the body kindles it with its heat, or the soul dwells on it because it lacks thoughts of knowledge.
Apart from these two things, lust has nowhere to lay its head.
For when it finds the body deadened by toil and the soul alive in meditation on God, it immediately turns back,
and finds nowhere to stay. For if the pain of lust makes you suffer, recognize its cause and cut it off.
Why do you let yourself be tormented, without understanding, by an illness that is easy to cure?
Indeed, I am not convinced that there is any other passion as easy to cure as this one.
For food does not cause you to sin when it is taken in proper measure to sustain your life.
But it is sin when it leads you toward lust. As long as you eat for yourself, there is no sin in your eating.
But if you eat for lust, your eating is sinful. How, then, can you know when you are eating for sin and when for yourself?
For as long as lust is stirring in the parts of your body and troubling you, if you eat, your food belongs to it.
It is lust that grows and becomes stronger through it, not your strength and your life. For lust is mingled with your life for the preservation of your life.
That is, so that through you your life may be passed on to others.
But the will that overcomes the love of life will all the more overcome lust and bring it into subjection.
For you have no authority to give your life to others, because it does not belong to you, but to Christ.
For companionship and marriage in this world bring human offspring into being and pass life from one person to another,
so that a human being comes from a human being, and a living being gives birth to another living being like itself. And when did these things apply? When our lives belonged to us.
For at that time we had authority to share them with others through the union of marriage.
But now, because we live by the spiritual life of Christ, we have no authority to give others a life that is not our own.
For we do not belong to ourselves. “You do not belong to yourselves,” the apostle told us, “for you were bought at a price.”
“Therefore glorify God in your body and in your spirit, which belong to God.”
You see that both spirit and body belong to God, and we have authority over neither of them. And someone who has no authority over his own life,
How can he share them with others in sexual intercourse—that is, how can he bring forth through them another person by human procreation?
Spiritual birth was therefore revealed in the world in order to abolish bodily birth.
And another womb, that of baptism, was established to make the natural womb cease bearing children.
If all humanity had been capable of keeping this commandment, this would have been the desire and delight of the will of the divine Majesty.
But because our Savior saw humanity’s weakness, that it was incapable of doing this,
he set his will before everyone, so that there might be at least a few who would carry it out.
Do not look only at this: that the childbearing womb was originally fashioned by God.
But consider this as well: that another womb was created in place of that first one.
It gives birth to spiritual people instead of bodily people, in accordance with the perfect will of God.
For this is the good and perfect will acceptable to God: that all bodily people should become spiritual.
For this purpose he also came into the world: to make human beings into a new creation.
But do not look at the fact that he did not abolish marriage or cut off the flow of desire and suppose that perhaps he takes delight in these things.
For look: neither did he do away with this whole world, nor did he take away its comfort, wealth, and power.
Instead, he left it as it was in its original condition and commanded you to be a stranger to it and to take it off like a worn-out garment.
For the fact that he has allowed things to remain as they are—the world, its comforts, or the desire within you—
must not become a cause of error for you, so that your soul becomes bound by something from which it was once set free.
For these things were left to provide material for your struggle, not for your desire,
and so that through them your strong will and your God-loving mind might be tested. For the world remains in order to kindle in you a longing for another world.
Wealth and power remain in order to awaken in you a longing for possessions that do not perish and honor that does not pass away.
Comforts also remain in the world so that you may yearn for that taste of spiritual life.
Desire also remains within your body so that it may provide material for your good will,
so that little by little you may take it away from the body and direct it toward the soul.
Therefore, do not give your desire a share with the body, and do not allow your natural pleasure to be dissolved,
or the joy and delight within you to be abolished. Instead, carry them as though from one house to another, from the body to the soul.
For just as someone carries his valuable belongings out of a house that he knows is going to collapse,
And he carries them to another one, new and secure, which you can trust not to fall or give way.
In the same way, take all those passions that belong to the body, which, by their very names, are material for good things,
and bring them in and place them within the dwelling of your soul, in that house which does not fall, come apart, or decay.
Take warmth from the body and place it upon the soul. Take desire from it and mingle it with the desire of the soul.
Take its strength and mix it with the soul’s vigor. Turn everything that belongs to it into something belonging to the soul.
And make every effort to do these things, especially in youth, when the passions begin to show themselves.
For you do not have them in childhood or in old age. And how can you easily take something that does not exist and give it to others?
For the time of the passions is the time of youth. But this is also the time of vigor.
And it is fitting that vigor has appeared along with the passions, so that through it you may fight,
rescue your good things from your body, and pick up and carry your wealth from one place to another.
For someone who fights and overcomes his desires in his youth can become strong in his soul.
And he alone can advance in the full growth of good things, because he has something to give and something to receive.
For old age is inactive in both, while childhood has not yet reached either of them.
Do not wait for desire to subside on its own and gradually cease as your nature declines.
For you deserve no credit for this. Just as your natural death is not called martyrdom for God,
since you are undergoing the sentence imposed upon your life, and you gain no renown or praise through this,
so neither do you have anything to boast about when desire ceases along with strength, whether through old age or through illness.
Rather, your victory comes when you cool it while it is hot and extinguish it while it is blazing.
And as soon as it begins to stir in your limbs, prepare the shoulder of your mind, lift it up, carry it away, and place it upon the soul’s desire,
saying to it in this way: “Why do you stir where you are corrupted,
and where the sensation of your pleasure immediately ceases? Instead, come and stir in the place that belongs to your nature,
where the sweetness of your desire does not dissolve and cease, and where regret does not approach when you reach your end,
where weakness does not enter the soul in your wake, and where the warmth of nature does not cool after your activity is fulfilled.
Instead, you always remain vigorous, your pleasant taste is preserved unchanged, and boldness and confidence are strengthened through you,
when you desire—not those things that are unworthy of you, those things that deserve disgrace and blame.”
But these things that you are naturally stirred to desire—desire for them is itself praiseworthy, and day by day it grows stronger and greater.
This is excellent desire, and you advance forward. For in relation to the body, your time is short.
But in relation to the soul, you have no end. Rather, your pleasure endures immortally for as long as the soul lives.
For in relation to the body, union with another body sets you aflame; but in relation to the soul, union with the Holy Spirit kindles you.
Therefore, do not attach yourself to a corruptible body, for unless the soul loses its powers of discernment,
and the body's corruption and ugliness are hidden from its eyes, there is no room for you even to be stirred there.
But if it should happen that, while you are pursuing your pleasure, discernment dawns upon the soul,
your activity immediately ceases, and there is no outlet for your corruptible pleasures.
Let us say these things and others like them to desire when you bring it from the body into the realm of the soul.
Let it therefore receive good assurances and promises from you that it is going to receive something better than what it leaves behind.
For just as desire is naturally placed within the body, so desire for excellent things is placed within the soul.
When the soul desires naturally, its desire is for spiritual things. And when it enters into a lawful union,
it unites with the Spirit, and from this union it brings forth holy and pure children.
Just as bodily union produces pleasure in the limbs and stirs a corruptible heat throughout the whole body,
so also, when the soul unites with the Spirit, it receives spiritual pleasure.
It gains fervor with swiftness and strength, to fight against the evils that oppose its pleasure.
When the soul tastes this sweetness that comes to it from union with the Spirit, the desire for sexual union dies completely within it.
You should know from experience that it is through a lack of awareness of the desire of the Spirit that the desire of the flesh is awakened in your limbs.
It is impossible for both to burn within you at once. For as long as the desire of the Spirit is hot within you, that of the body is cold.
And as long as the desire of the body is hot within you, that of the Spirit is cold. For the two desires are set against each other.
The desire of the body opposes the desire of the Spirit. And just as they differ from each other,
so all their activities differ from one another. One takes hold of the limbs, while the other burns in the thoughts.
The instrument of the one is the physical body, and that of the other is the nature of the soul. Disorder accompanies the one, and order the other.
When the one is satisfied, it darkens the light of the thoughts and removes knowledge and wisdom from the mind.
But the other fills the mind with light and gathers knowledge and the wisdom of the Spirit within the soul.
And bodily desire, once satisfied, makes a person weak and full of regret, so that he is ashamed before everyone, even himself,
and afraid of everything. But spiritual desire places strength and courage within the soul, along with contempt for everything visible,
boldness before other people, and a pure gaze toward God,
and confidence that a person comes to have in himself. Bodily desire, however, is a teacher of foolishness.
For a person who constantly serves this desire cannot be wise. But spiritual desire
not only gives a person natural knowledge of the world, but also imbues his mind with the living stirrings of the spirit.
And it clothes a person with readiness and preparedness for everything good.
For it makes his mind alert and swift for every spiritual work.
And all the movements of his soul are stirred with courage, strength, and vigor.
This desire does not even allow bodily sluggishness to come near a person.
For if the body happens to suffer sluggishness because of its natural coldness, or because of pain and weakness,
the fervor of this desire immediately warms it, and with its warmth drives away the body's coldness.
As a result, the person becomes alert and ready for divine activities.
For spiritual people do not carry out their active way of life through the natural warmth of the body,
but because they are fervent in spirit, they are swift and ready for such works.
So Paul also commands us to awaken within ourselves this very fervor of spirit, through which all spiritual activities are accomplished.
And through the strength that comes from it, we complete our course along this path. He says, “Be fervent in spirit.”
For because bodily desire also has its fervor, Paul makes the distinction for us in his words and teaches us in which desire we should be fervent.
He says, “Be fervent in spiritual desire, so that your entire course and your work may be spiritual.”
For just as the warmth of the blood drives out of the body the sluggishness produced by the coldness of phlegm,
so spiritual fervor drives out of the soul and body the apathy born of forgetfulness and lack of love for God.
And just as natural warmth, when it rises, approaches the heart, and mingles with it, makes a person eager, ready, alert, and swift
in worldly activities, so also spiritual warmth, when it approaches the mind of the soul,
urges a person toward heavenly things instead of worldly things: to build himself up, to accumulate spiritual profit,
to pronounce judgment against those who plunder his inheritance, and to long for fellowship that does not perish.
To be a father to immortal children, to care for them, acquire them, think about them, gather them, cherish them, and guard them.
All these things are spiritual and heavenly. A person therefore calls all these things to mind through fervor of spirit.
Paul rightly taught us to be fervent in spirit. For just as cold is dispelled and comes to an end before warmth,
so, before the fervor of this spiritual warmth, sluggishness flees, disdain is driven away, and discouragement comes to an end.
Conceit is dispelled, error is removed, and all the shadows of sin turn away to hide themselves completely.
And just as natural strength is generated by warmth, while weakness takes hold of the limbs through cold,
so through spiritual warmth the soul acquires strength, readiness, and courage.
And it completely drives away all the sluggishness that affects the soul or the body in doing good deeds.
And just as the intensity of a fire's burning and the abundance of its light correspond to the size of its blaze,
so, according to the measure of warmth found within the soul,
are its fervor for spiritual things, its knowledge, and its wisdom that has command over divine treasures.
Therefore, while there is still warmth within your body and natural desire is alive in your limbs,
make an effort to kindle spiritual warmth within yourself, and awaken divine desire in your thoughts,
so that, as desire vies with desire and flame contends with flame, spiritual desire may grow strong and gain the victory—the desire to which victory naturally belongs.
For while you have strength to serve bodily desire, use that very strength diligently and make it a servant of spiritual desire.
For the Holy Spirit does not perform her works in idle bodies.
Nor does she cause insights into divine wisdom to dawn in people who have grown cold through old age.
For someone who, in the time of his youth, spends his strength serving evil desires
does not receive divine knowledge in the feeble time of his old age. Rather, when his natural vigor has left him
and he has reached old age, he becomes utterly inactive, growing cold and feeble alike in soul and body.
But if you want the warmth of your youth to remain available to you in your old age,
work with all your strength in your youth, and entrust this warmth to the keeping of your soul.
And because the soul itself does not grow old along with the body, when the body grows weak in old age, you will draw from the treasury of your soul,
and in your old age you will be sustained by these deposits that you entrusted to the soul.
And when the body's strength has grown weak, you will find strength with the soul.
And when its warmth cools, you are warmed in your deeds by its own fervor.
And when the strength of your limbs is exhausted, you are strengthened in your deeds by your thoughts.
And when natural desire ceases along with the body's warmth, the desire of the spirit remains with you,
which continually enters into union and brings forth spiritual children. For the time of sowing is one thing, and the time of harvest another.
Therefore sow good things in your soul during your youth, so that you may reap them from it in your old age.
Therefore, if you desire to enter into marriage, take care to establish within yourself this desire, which conceives and gives birth even in old age.
For bodily union does not hold sway at all times.
Nor does natural desire remain in the limbs at every age. But the desire of the spirit is not like this.
Rather, all times belong to it, provided that it has its appointed time—the time of youth.
Therefore cross over from the body to the soul while there is still a bridge for crossing, while your feet still have strength to walk,
while you still have light to walk by, before the shadows of old age fall upon you
and you are left within the body's territory. Therefore stir up anger within yourself against desire.
And because affection accompanies desire whenever it is stirred, take anger and wrath as your allies and go out against it.
And just as you need affection against anger, so you need anger against desire.
For desire comes peacefully and calmly, accompanied by slackness, dawdling, and languor,
by frivolous gestures, and by shameful movements and gestures, which are the opposites of diligence.
But when desire peers at you in these guises, put on the armor of anger and go out against it.
For just as the sluggishness of sleeping children is driven into swift flight
before someone who peers at them with a terrifying face and frightens them,
so you too will drive away desire's childishness and wantonness if you show it a face full of anger and menace.
Therefore pluck the flowers of virtue from the noonday of youth. Gather, bring in, and store up fruits and pulses for yourself, so that they may be kept for you for the winter of old age.
For a person who lives entirely in the body becomes completely inactive in old age.
But whoever burns with the desire of the spirit in youth continues unchanged until the end of life.
For the body cannot preserve its natural faculties endlessly.
Some of them cease before life ends, while others come to an end with life.
But they are all released and taken away from the body and redirected toward the soul, if there is a discerning mind that knows how to redirect them.
For even natural life, although it is visibly dissolved by natural death, is nevertheless preserved in the spirit with the soul.
So too, in the same way, the rest of the body's natural capacities, which cease with old age and disappear from the body,
when entrusted into the soul's hands, endure along with the soul's endless life.
Desire therefore has no power to persuade you unless it recruits your will as its persuader.
For this reason, as though aware of its own weakness, it does not approach you without your consent.
But when you enlist thought as its accomplice, then it enters and kindles its fire in your limbs.
But when you sense the destructive fire taking control within your body, kindle the living fire within your soul.
And when you sense that your limbs have been bound over to the service of desire, occupy your thoughts with the service of knowing the divine mysteries.
Do not, then, let desire come and find you idle, and it will not accomplish its wishes in you.
Let it find you alive in the spirit, so that its fire may be extinguished by the fire within you.
Wherever it finds an opportunity, cut it off there. And wherever it begins to enter you,
shut the door against it there and keep it locked outside. For hateful desire enters us from outside.
For the desire naturally implanted in us, whether of the soul or of the body, has been placed in us to serve good things.
For the soul too has the capacity to long for God.
And the body, in turn, has the capacity to be moved by its natural desire. Desire has fittingly been set opposite desire,
so that, when they mingle with one another, they may produce a single activity of pure and holy desire.
For the causes that stir the soul's desire are from above.
But those that stir the body's desire are from below, where the body's nature itself also comes from.
Yet he did not create it for this purpose, to desire these things, but to desire spiritual things in fellowship with the soul.
For although it is indeed formed from the earth and sustained by various mixtures, it was not formed for the earth.
That is, it was not formed to be named or called the earth's body. Rather, it was created by the Creator to belong to the soul.
That is, to serve its wishes in everything and to share in all good things.
Therefore we must not think that our body's activities belong to the place from which our body comes,
but we must direct the aim of its actions toward that for which it was made. For it was made for the spirit, not for the earth.
And that it should be spiritual, perfected and not subject to decay. For it is called a body so that this name may make it known that it was taken from the earth.
It is also called a human being, so that this may reveal that it is joined to a living soul.
For this individual human being is rightly called by three names: the names of its separate parts and the common name—body, soul, and human being.
Through the name “body,” its bodily nature is made known, namely, that it is from the earth; and through the name “soul,” the living nature that dwells in it is revealed.
And through the designation “human being,” we learn of the combination of the individual being constituted from both.
For because the body has no thoughts, and the soul has no visible actions,
they were rightly combined with one another: that which is the spring of thoughts,
with that which is the instrument for carrying out deeds, so that an embodiment of virtue might be constituted from both.
Thus, whoever wishes to belittle the body because it has no thoughts should honor it because it carries out deeds;
and whoever wishes to despise the soul because it does not carry out good things through visible actions,
let it become great in his eyes, because it is the source of the thoughts behind good things.
For the desire of the spirit is ardent, just as the desire of the body is also ardent. But they are not so in the same measure:
the ardor of the soul’s desire corresponds to its subtlety, while the fire of the body’s desire is correspondingly cool in proportion to its coarseness.
And if it seems ardent in those who are bodily minded and weak, this is not because its nature is powerful and ardent,
but because their will is weak and cold. Understand how cool the ardor of bodily desire is,
and how ardent the soul’s desire is, from the things that happen to both.
For look: whenever bodily desire is stirred in the limbs, even the sight of other people cools it,
as do news of battle, if it is heard; a threat from someone, if it is spoken against it; sudden alarm;
and another passion opposed to it, if it is stirred up in the person;
correction and rebuke from friends or relatives; recollection of judgment by other people;
remembrance of the corruptibility of human nature; reflection on the unattractive features of the person to whom the desire is attached;
hunger, thirst, excessive heat and cold; and illness and pain, if they occur.
And many other things like these, whenever they occur, easily quench and put an end to the ardor of bodily desire.
But as for the soul’s ardent, spiritual desire, whenever it takes full hold of the soul’s thoughts, nothing is capable of quenching it,
as those in whom the divine fire of this desire has taken hold testify by their very deeds.
The whole world fought against them and could not extinguish their desire. And kings, leaders, and rulers,
not only with threatening words, but also with afflictions and harsh tortures,
confinement, beatings, imprisonment, and severe punishments of every kind,
fire, combs for tearing flesh, swords, wild animals, and everything that causes suffering and pain among the afflictions of this present life.
Yet none of all these things, or anything like them, could weaken and cool the burning power of this desire.
Instead, the opposite happened: these very things became fuel for the fire of their desire.
And just as fire is fed by wood, kindling, and the richness of oil,
so too the good desire within them was fed by afflictions and torments.
And whenever fire was brought near their bodies, that fire of divine desire within them
grew still stronger and blazed more fiercely, especially because it was overcoming its opponents.
For victory over harmful things usually strengthens and fortifies a person in love for what he loves.
For when he has removed the stumbling blocks before him and cleared the rocks from before his feet, he walks easily and runs without hindrance.
And when he has brought his enemies under his power, his strength becomes still greater.
For the strength taken from his enemies is added to him, and the power they lose passes to him.
Now when the soul's desire struggles against the desire of the flesh, it not only cools the flesh's heat,
but turns that very heat toward itself, so that it may serve its will
and mingle with it in spiritual fervor, rather than serve the body's desire through union with another.
For this reason the Creator also made the body's desire hot, because the desire placed within the soul
is also hot. Thus, whenever the soul wishes to be moved by the desire belonging to its nature,
it brings the heat of bodily desire into partnership with itself, turning it toward its good will, and in this way performs a good deed.
And not only in this, but also in each of the faculties of its nature: whenever the soul wishes to act in relation to external things,
it turns to the bodily organs that correspond to its hidden faculties, seeing through the eye and hearing through the ear,
along with all the remaining senses and organs, which serve its inward will.
And just as in these things, so also whenever it wishes to desire something, it joins the body's desire to its spiritual desire,
and puts it to work in divine love, blazing with love for a life of righteousness.
So that the signs of this desire’s burning may be seen even in the body’s outward members.
Not in shameful movements or in the act of satisfying foolish desire, but in their being calm even while they are hot,
and peaceful even while they boil. Therefore, let the heat of desire that is mingled in our members not become a cause of condemnation for us.
Instead, let us consider the purpose for which the Creator mingled it within us, and let us use it according to this order.
But when bodily desire burns within the body, it is opposed to chastity.
For when it is mingled with the soul’s desire, it helps virginity.
It is right, therefore, that the power of desire should not be scattered outward, but gathered and contained within the soul’s desire,
so that, when they are mingled with one another like light with light, they may kindle one light perfected in chastity.
But the things that nourish each of these desires differ from one another.
For through fasting, ascetic discipline, keeping vigil, prayer, beatings, and bodily labors, the soul’s desire increases and grows strong.
But through their opposites—comforts, pleasures, luxuries, food, drink, and fine clothing,
and association with frivolous and undisciplined people—the body’s desire grows and blazes within us.
Yet it does not follow that, because the body grows weak through labors, the soul is thereby weakened along with it.
Rather, the more it is weakened, the more the soul gains strength and grows mighty. Indeed, the soul weakens it especially for this reason: so that the soul itself may become strong.
For there is a difference between the body growing weak by its own nature and the soul itself weakening it,
with the purpose that the soul may stand in the strength of its own nature. For when the soul weakens the body in this way,
and brings down its mighty strength through hardships, what Paul said is fulfilled in them:
As the outward person wastes away, the inward person is renewed day by day.
For this reason Solomon also advises us to begin, from our childhood, the labors undertaken for the sake of good things, and to train ourselves in this teaching from the beginning of our growth,
so that we may conquer what is within us but does not agree with us, and subject the desire that opposes our desire.
Thus everyone who, in the time of their strength, conquers the weakness within them is found strong in the time of their weakness.
That is, if someone takes on the discipline of the elderly in youth, they will find the strength of the young in old age.
Therefore, disciple, gather provisions for your old age from the field of your youth,
so that, when you cease from bodily labor, you may find rest for your soul. For you will not have to fight throughout your whole life.
Your Creator, out of compassion for you, has set a definite time limit for your struggle.
But make your delight endless. For at the beginning and at the end you are free from battle.
Either because desire has not yet been stirred, or because it has cooled after being stirred.
For whether you wish it or not, in your old age you find yourself inactive.
Because of the body's weakness, you cannot fulfill your desire. It is not you who extinguish desire; rather, it dies out within you.
For the fire of desire, which the Creator placed in the body's nature for the propagation [?] of the human race,
ceases toward the end of a person's life, in old age.
For a person is not capable of reproduction throughout his entire life: he cannot do this either in childhood or in old age.
In this he resembles not only himself, but also livestock, wild animals, birds, and plants.
For these kinds of living things are also like this: neither in their youth nor in their old age do they produce offspring of their own kinds.
For each kind has its limits, and its reproductive capacity is also subject to a limit.
Especially because the offspring itself is carried in the body and by means of the body, and therefore is limited just as the body is.
For just as the body's life is limited, so too is its strength. Its strength is not even evident throughout the entire span of its life.
For, as I said, it possesses reproductive power neither at the beginning nor at the end of its life.
But because the soul has no composite structure, it has no old age. The warmth of its desire never ceases unless the sickness of wickedness befalls it.
For just as the body grows old or weak through the mixture of its constituent parts, so too the soul becomes sick and weak through sin and wickedness.
Through its weakness, the warmth of its desire dies out. As a result, it cannot even produce fruit.
Therefore, whoever weakens desire in his youth will be found strong in his soul in old age.
After he finishes his battle, his strength remains with him. This also happens to the warriors of this world.
For they possess their strength not only while standing in battle formation and fighting their enemies,
but even after the battle ends, their strength is evident in them. Their strength does not come to an end along with their fighting.
Even though its activity was more evident during the fighting itself, because it is aided and brought into action by bursts of zeal.
So too with you, whose soul is clothed in the strength of chastity, to serve as your equipment for the battle against sexual immorality:
do not suppose that when your battle ends, the time of your strength also ends.
Rather, at the end of the battle it is renewed all the more, even if no longer for fighting, but for doing good.
For by this strength you accomplish both things: you fight against sexual immorality, and you build up chastity.
For just as a craftsman, when an old building is entrusted to him to renovate, tears it down by his own strength and builds it up by his own strength,
so too both your new building and the demolition of your old building are accomplished by that same strength of yours,
when you tear down sexual immorality, which is the road to every evil, and build up chastity, which is the smooth road leading up to heaven.
For what evil is not found in sexual immorality? And what shameful thing does not enter through its door?
If it is gluttony, it strengthens sexual immorality; if it is the love of gold, it serves it. Anger and rage accompany it,
and through them it fights against its opponents. Distress follows in its footsteps, and shame accompanies the completion of its deeds.
Perhaps even vainglory, which is thought to be its opponent, is a helper in its shameful work.
For how often have many people turned from vainglory to the passion of sexual immorality! After completing their labors,
when they thought they had reached the hall of rest, because they were caught in vainglory through their negligence, it dulled their minds
and darkened their vision, which had been purified through victory over the body's desires,
and turned them toward the desire for sexual immorality, which they had conquered at the beginning of their struggle.
Therefore, anyone who calls sexual immorality the road to every evil is not mistaken.
By sexual immorality I mean not only that of the body, but still more that of the soul.
For a layperson, adultery consists in the act, but for a monk, in thoughts. To the layperson it was said, "Do not commit adultery,"
but to the monk, "Do not lust." The layperson knows nothing at all of the battle against thoughts.
For this reason, he does not vigorously conquer his desire, but satisfies it lawfully—
the desire that belongs to nature. The monk, however, does not have this permission.
His victory is not shown by refraining from the act; rather, his triumph is proclaimed by his conquest of the thought.
For because he is a spiritual laborer for Christ, his victory too is accomplished spiritually, in his inward thoughts.
Through his endurance he purifies the dwelling of his soul. When he drives the thought out of there, the whole house of his soul is seen in the light.
And wherever there is light, the darkness of sin does not enter, because sin is practiced in darkness,
just as righteousness is practiced in light. Therefore, do not let this destructive passion bring you down, or subtly gain control over your thoughts.
For it has abundant fuel at hand in you, especially when you live among other people,
as it grows through the memory of various faces and through bodily beauty and appearance.
For because the desire for sexual immorality is born of the flesh, it also desires the flesh.
Just as the appetite of the belly longs for different flavors, so the passion of lust desires people of beautiful appearance.
Its love does not linger over the appearance of any one of them, because it does not love people, but beauty for the sake of passion.
But when its excitement increases, it no longer depends even on beauty of appearance. Instead, it grows and strengthens on its own.
Once it has secretly subdued the soul's strength, it openly overcomes the body's endurance as well.
But if it is defeated even by the body while awake, it turns to fighting through sleep.
Through sleep it stains the soul and fills it with memories of those people who were driven from it while awake.
It makes a person suffer defeat involuntarily during sleep. For this reason you need ascetic discipline,
so that through it you may reduce the body's excess, and lust may find no material in your bodily members, even during sleep.
For this passion's habit is first to wage war through the members of the body, stirring a person to desire like an animal.
But if a person acquires discernment and restrains the impulses of his bodily members from acting,
it turns and enters his mind, secretly exciting it so that through it the bodily members too may be stirred to carry out desire.
But if it is defeated by the thoughts as well—and it is certainly defeated whenever the mind looks toward God,
and endurance and ascetic discipline are also present with it—then this same evil passion turns to sleep,
and through sleep it fights against the soul's endurance. Yet if even this happens to us, we must not let it pass without repentance.
This is especially so if images of people have been imprinted on our mind, which clearly shows that this is a remnant of our waking state.
But if the body's discharge occurs without images of people, it comes from the excess present in the bodily members.
For because the body has not been subdued by ascetic discipline, desire has found material in its members.
But if we are entirely unaware of what is happening, this is an excessive depth of sleep.
Therefore the disciple must overcome this passion in every way: in action, in thought, and in discharge during sleep.
Being defeated during sleep is an indication that he has not overcome it in thought.
And not having overcome it in thought is evidence that he is being defeated in action.
For this reason, less food and less sleep are useful, so that excess may not wage war in the body and we may not be defeated involuntarily in a dream.
For just as this does not happen, even during sleep, to those who are weak and advanced in years,
because the discharge of lust has already disappeared and dried up in their bodily members,
so too nocturnal lust does not happen to a body weakened by the labors of ascetic discipline.
For even if thoughts stir and demons provoke, no fuel is found in the bodily members for desire to run its course.
For solitaries struggle even against sleep, just as they struggle against desire and food.
For sleep, like these other things, dulls the mind and increases desire.
But if someone supplies the body with food only to meet its need,
and likewise gives us sleep, he is freed from the passion of sexual immorality as far as possible.
But if his wakefulness is not spent in wandering thoughts, but with a mind that is collected, singing psalms and praying,
he drives this passion even from his thoughts. And if it leaves the soul, it does not remain with the body either.
“Put to death, then, your members that are on earth,” blessed Paul commands us.
And if the bodily members die according to the apostle’s teaching, there is no room in them for the stirring of desire.
For what can desire do in a dead body? The apostle’s own statement shows that the bodily members can indeed die.
For he would not command something that could not be done. More particularly, he said, “Your members that are on earth,”
as though we had other members in heaven or from heaven. This, then, is what the saying “Put to death your members that are on earth” means.
For because desires come from the earth, they rule over the bodily members that come from the earth.
But if we put these bodily members to death by persevering in fasting, abstinence, and ascetic discipline,
and, along with these, through constant vigils and wakefulness in prayer, desires that come from the earth are no longer admitted into them.
For what can the passions do to dead bodily members?
For he calls the members of the new person “members in heaven,” and he said that they are from heaven.
“As is the one from the earth,” he says, “so also are those who are earthly. And as is the one from heaven, so also are those who are heavenly.”
Thus he calls the members of the new person heavenly, and the old passions ought not to rule over them.
For those passions do not suit them and do not belong to them.
How, then, can the passion of sexual immorality rule over a member of the new person, who has become one body with Christ?
But it is not only because of the greatness of the gift bestowed on us,
and because of the greatness of our honor, that I say we ought to overcome this passion of sexual immorality, but also because of the things that accompany the passion itself.
These are shame, distress, remorse, loss of confidence, darkening of the mind, and dullness of thought,
and confusion of the thoughts. All these things, then, and others like them enter the soul in the wake of the passion of sexual immorality.
But if we endure and overcome, and establish within ourselves the beautiful image of chastity, then, after overcoming this desire, the soul is immediately filled with joy.
And with confidence before God and other people, and it delights in the peace of its thoughts.
It receives the light of divine knowledge, is also clothed with strength, and is filled with trust.
And from this victory such rest comes to the soul as we cannot explain in words.
For the soul itself did not obtain it through words. What is obtained through action also gives delight through actual experience.
And things acquired through words also bring joy through words.
Therefore, since the victory over desire came about through the soul’s strength together with the help of grace,
the delight that comes to it afterward is likewise given to it in the same way:
it comes from the health of its nature and from the gift of God’s grace.
For just as the body’s delight and rest are twofold, since sometimes it takes delight in its natural health,
and sometimes it receives pleasures from food and desirable things outside itself, so it also happens with the soul.
Sometimes, when it remains in purity of mind and possesses its natural health, it feels the delight of that health.
And sometimes, when it is found worthy of God’s grace and of the contemplation of spiritual revelations, it receives this delight.
It knows that it is taking delight in it and feels the spiritual sweetness poured out through all its parts.
But there is no way for it to put this delight and the spiritual sweetness it has felt into speech or verbal instruction.
For it received the taste of this delight spiritually. For when, from the tastes of material things and from the seasonings of substances,
the body receives the pleasure of food, or is stirred to the pleasure of desire by seeing a face,
or its hearing delights in the sweet sounds of singing, with the changing melodies of the song,
or the body receives the pleasure of rest from touching something soft—all these things, because they are bodily,
and delight the body materially and through actual experience, allow a person to express this pleasure in words.
And because bodily things have delighted and refreshed the body, a person can speak as much as desired about their pleasure in articulated, embodied speech.
But the soul’s delight does not come from material things, or from their bodily activity, or from their perishable tastes.
Rather, its delight comes from the spiritual contemplation of everything—a contemplation that it can perceive
when it has attained the health of its nature. It cannot describe in words this pleasure that comes to it.
Instead, it delights in secret and rejoices invisibly, because its joy does not come from itself.
For just as the soul is within the body and, through the power of its life, enables the body to feel the pleasure of everything,
so spiritual contemplation is within the soul and habitually gives the soul delight.
Whenever the soul takes delight in this way, its delight is natural.
It receives pleasure in keeping with the order of its nature, because the soul’s world is within it, just as the body’s world is outside it.
But whenever the soul takes delight outside its nature, it receives that delight from the body or from the world.
For this is how such delight comes to it: either it finds satisfaction in the body’s desires when they are fulfilled,
whether through gluttony or through indulging the passion of sexual immorality, or through the things it receives from the world:
praise, acclaim, the sounds of singing, and the pleasure of physically seeing visible things.
All these things in which the soul takes delight, whether from the body or from the world, give it delight outside its nature.
It finds satisfaction not on account of its health, but on account of its sickness.
For there are desires that serve the health of the soul or the body, just as there are those that serve their sickness.
It is clear, then, that whenever the soul takes delight in evil desires, its delight is outside its nature.
It has found satisfaction not in something suited to it, but in something foreign to the health of its nature. For consider: whenever its body commits adultery
and performs this unlawful act, the soul apparently receives pleasure from it.
And again, whenever the soul struggles and overcomes its body’s desire, and achieves this victory with a good purpose
and with discernment acceptable to God, it also receives pleasure after this victory.
Thus it receives pleasure both from fulfilling desire and from overcoming desire, from both alike.
But the pleasure it received from the body, as I have said many times, is outside the order of nature.
The pleasure that comes to it through overcoming desire, however, is a natural pleasure.
It experiences this delight as a healthy soul, and enjoys this pleasure in a lawful and natural way.
For those who overcome the assault of desire with a spiritual purpose experience what I am speaking of.
Although they experience their delight, they cannot express it. For how could they express it, since they did not enjoy it bodily?
But since all the things of the spirit are not bodily, let us seek them in their own place, and there they are found.
Where they are found, there they are enjoyed. And where their delight is, there also is their joy:
a joy that gladdens but is not seen, a joy accompanied also by power.
For just as there, whenever desire overcomes the soul, it shows the soul to be weak, miserable, and clothed in shame,
so here too, whenever the soul overcomes desire, it is filled with strength, joy, and confidence after this victory,
and acquires a clear eye, so that it can freely perceive spiritual knowledge, which is mingled with all visible things.
But just as bodily pleasure is experienced by those who fulfill the body's desires,
so too spiritual pleasure is enjoyed by those who serve the soul's spiritual desires.
And just as the soul in its sickness experiences the pleasure that comes from the body's desires,
so too the soul in its health experiences this pleasure. And if someone wants to experience what is being spoken of through written words,
he is seeking something outside its proper place and time, and he will not find the fruit he seeks,
because he is not seeking to pick it from its own tree. For just as every fruit is found on its own tree
and is picked from there, so too spiritual things are seen in their proper places.
And these rational and spiritual fruits, which delight our nature, are found on their own tree.
Thus, after overcoming the passion of sexual immorality, the soul picks the spiritual fruit that delights and enlightens it.
Whoever seeks it finds it after overcoming this passion—a victory achieved not only in the body but also in the soul.
For sometimes this desire fights against the body, and sometimes it wages war against the soul's thoughts.
For as long as its fire burns in the limbs, it does not fight against the thoughts. Indeed, how can it fight against something that does not oppose it?
For as long as the thoughts are subject to desire and serve its will, it commands all the limbs like a mistress
and freely fulfills all its pleasures within the domain of the body where it dwells.
But if the mind becomes watchful over itself and perceives that a foreign power is dwelling within the domain of its body,
and that thieving and plundering passions are living in its limbs, it then prepares to drive them out
and begins to stir up a battle to expel the foreigners found within its house.
And because the desires find their dwellings pleasant, they too fight to avoid being driven out.
From this arises the battle of the thoughts against the passions, and of the passions against the thoughts. And victory is found on the side with greater strength.
Desire in the limbs, then, is fulfilled by action, and it does not always get to act as it wishes.
But as for desire hidden in the thoughts, nothing prevents it from being put into action except the vision of God alone.
For this reason the prophet also pronounces woe upon those who defile themselves on their beds, and exposes their foolish thoughts.
Those who think and say, “The walls of my house surround me, and the roof of my house shelters me.”
He does not know that the Lord’s eyes are ten thousand times brighter than the sun, and that he sees all human thoughts.
Although the saying, in its literal sense, seems to refer to someone who does wrong secretly on his bed inside his house—
those who satisfy their desires in the darkness of their dwellings and hide themselves from human sight—
yet that prophet’s saying rebukes still more the thought that secretly commits adultery within the soul.
Instead of walls, the body’s limbs surround it, and instead of a roof, the vessel of the heart shelters it.
While he dwells concealed and hidden in this place and commits his adultery here, he thinks that no one sees him.
Yet he is fleeing not from sin but from human sight. He does not understand that nothing can hide from God’s radiant sight.
For God’s sight, which examines hidden things, is ten thousand times brighter than the sunlight.
Just as nothing is concealed from the sunlight, but everything on which it shines
it reveals and brings into view, so too the seeing eye of God’s knowledge
examines people’s secrets and looks into the thoughts concealed within the mind.
Even when the thought does not commit adultery in deeds, it counts him an adulterer because of his will, and judges the thought by his consent, not by his deeds.
For some take pleasure in the act, and some take pleasure in its imagined likeness. There is adultery that takes place in the body,
and there is adultery that is carried out in the soul. Whoever, then, drives adultery out of his heart clearly does not allow it in his body either.
For thoughts are the root of deeds.
Just as, if a tree is shaken at its root and its rootstock, firmly set within the earth, is loosened,
its leaves immediately droop, its fruits wither, and its whole appearance changes, so too, if the root of desire
is shaken and loosened from the heart, outward deeds also immediately begin to dry up.
For just as a root is within the earth, so thought is within the heart, nourishing outward deeds,
whether good or evil. Just as trees are nourished by water, so deeds are nourished by the watering of thoughts.
And just as plants set beside a spring dry up if that spring happens to run dry,
so the deeds of lust, planted beside the spring of the heart, wither—
though they drink from it and are nourished by it—if someone blocks up the very source of evil thought.
For cutting desire off from thought is complete victory in deeds.
This desire in the thoughts knows no fixed times. Rather, it is stirred at every moment and fulfilled at every moment.
Especially when it has things outside it that supply it with fuel.
Therefore, let us be especially watchful here and examine things wisely; and wherever desire peers in at us,
let us shut the door against it there. For desire is mingled with the very movement of our life.
As long as life moves in our body, desire too moves and flutters within it.
But just as death stills the movement of natural life, so putting the old self to death silences the impulses of desire.
If, then, desire rises against us from the body's natural impulses, let us recognize that the body needs to be disciplined and subdued,
and let us remember the apostle's helpful saying, which he addressed to us by speaking of himself: “I subdue my body and bring it into subjection.”
As we reflect on this, let us bring our body into subjection and subdue the animal desire that stirs and leaps within it,
by laying on it the burden of prolonged fasting, little food, and little drink.
And if these are sufficient to subdue it when applied in moderation—but if not, let us double and increase them.
And if even then they are not sufficient by themselves to bring it into subjection, let us look for other measures harsher than these and use them against it as well.
More than anything else, however, drinking little is needed for this battle against lusts.
Especially because this desire for sexual immorality is nourished by moisture.
And if moisture nourishes it, then the dryness that comes from drinking little dries it up and quenches it.
Thus Gideon the warrior also sent away from battle those who knelt on their knees and drank their fill of water.
But those who drank little, lapping water from their hands into their mouths, he took with him into battle against the Midianites.
He did not devise and carry this out casually; rather, God commanded him to do so.
For when he gathered a large force for battle, to march against the camp of Midian, which was likened to the passion of sexual immorality,
God commanded him to sound the horn, warn the people, and proclaim before them: “Let everyone who is afraid and trembling turn back.”
At this proclamation, most of the people who were with him turned back.
This showed that not everyone called to battle is fit for battle.
And because there were still among them those who eagerly desired victory,
but were afraid of the toil required for it, God told him to test these people too.
And after he tested them with water, those who knelt on their knees and drank a great deal of water,
He sent them back from battle, because drinking one's fill of water is not helpful in the battle against lust.
But he took with him into combat the few who drank a little hurriedly, lapping it up as they brought their hands to their mouths,
against that camp which represented sexual immorality. That this is so, as has been said, is attested by the account
in the book of Moses, which says that the people committed sexual immorality with the daughters of Midian and ate their fill of the sacrifices to their gods.
For since everything that happened to them is a pattern of our spiritual way of life,
everything written about them points to these things concerning us, as Paul said:
“Let us not commit sexual immorality as some of them did, and twenty-four thousand fell in a single day.”
So this undisciplined generation that came out of Egypt, when the battle against sexual immorality confronted them, could not stand against it.
Instead, they were overcome by the beauty of the daughters of Midian and committed sexual immorality with them.
In the wake of this sexual immorality, a plague suddenly overtook them at that time. But because there the sexually immoral perished
through the punishment that suddenly came upon them, while the passion of sexual immorality itself was not put down in an orderly way,
here, through the leader Gideon, he does not destroy the sexually immoral, but does away with sexual immorality itself.
For this reason, when he was about to destroy this camp that had led
that former people into sin, since, as I said, a symbol of sexual immorality is displayed in it,
he took a few men with him into battle against this passion: those who had hurriedly drunk a little water.
By this they showed that they were capable of facing this battle, which also proved true
in practice. When he had prepared them for combat, he put jars, horns, and torches into their hands.
They hid the torches inside the jars and held the horns in their right hands and the jars in their left hands.
As soon as they blew the horns, the jars were broken and the light of the torches appeared.
The sound of the horn is a symbol of God's commandment,
which cries out in all his Scriptures against this passion of sexual immorality, as in: “Let us not commit sexual immorality as some of them did.”
And as in: “Let no one among you be sexually immoral or undisciplined like Esau, who sold his birthright for a single meal.”
And as in: “Do not be deceived: neither the sexually immoral, nor adulterers, nor idol worshipers, nor those who corrupt themselves, nor men who sleep with males,
nor thieves, nor the greedy, nor drunkards, nor robbers will inherit the kingdom of God.”
And as in this other statement he made: “Everyone who is sexually immoral or impure,
Or a greedy person, who is an idol worshiper, has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God.
And as our Lord said, everyone who looks at a woman with desire for her has already committed adultery with her in his heart. And again, James the apostle said in his letter:
“Where do the battles and quarrels among you come from, if not from the desires that wage war in your bodily members?”
And again Peter said, “If a deadly desire assails you, do not think that something strange is happening to you,
for you are indeed being tested.” And again, God cried out with his voice to the Jewish people:
“Do not covet your neighbor’s wife.” Now the symbols of these holy sayings spoken against the passion of sexual immorality were
those horns that sounded against the camp of Midian. For there, along with the sound of the horns, the jars were immediately shattered.
For Gideon had commanded all the people as follows: “As soon as you hear me sounding the horn,
sound yours too and break the jars, so that the light of the torches hidden inside the jars may be seen.”
All these things are symbols of our spiritual way of life.
For the sound of the horns signifies the divine commandments. As soon as someone uses these with the voice of his soul
and cries out forcefully against the passion of sexual immorality, this desire is immediately driven away and brought to an end by the divine voice.
And just as the jars there were shattered at the sound of the horns, so here too, upon hearing the commandment,
this desire for sexual immorality is shattered and brought to an end. And just as, when the jar there was broken, the light hidden in it became visible,
so here too, when sexual immorality is brought to an end, the light of the knowledge of Christ dawns in the soul. All three are thus understood:
The sound of the horn represents the commandment of God, and the shattered jar represents the passion of sexual immorality,
which is itself also easy and simple to break. And the torch that became visible when the jar was broken represents the light of divine knowledge,
which dawns in the soul when sexual immorality is brought to an end. These things are understood more fully by those who have experienced them.
This, then, is the teaching that Gideon’s battle shows us, and these are the symbols it makes known to us.
And for this reason those who went to carry this battle through drank only a little water,
so that, as we consider them, we may imitate them and not drink water to the full, nor should anyone fighting this struggle fill his stomach with food.
Nor should he be overcome even by a desire for ordinary foods and indulge in filling his stomach. Rather, he should remember Esau,
who is condemned by Paul’s words and called sexually immoral and lax, because he sold his birthright for a single meal.
Yet Esau was not blamed in this passage because the meal was lavish or very costly,
but because of his laxity. For that meal was made of lentils.
And because he was overcome by his desire and greedily fed on them, he was called sexually immoral and weak.
Paul rightly called this surrender to desire sexual immorality.
For someone who was overcome by the sight of a dish of lentils would be overcome all the more by lovely beauty.
Let us also consider the word of God spoken to the Jewish people: it forbids not only the act of adultery,
but also desire in one's thoughts. For he did not say, “Do not commit adultery with your neighbor's wife,” but, “Do not desire your neighbor's wife.”
Although their chosen community was still a child, the commandment he gave them was perfect and complete, for against desire in their thoughts,
even more than against the act of adultery itself, he warned them. “Do not desire,” he says, for if you do not desire, neither will you commit adultery.
And our Lord said, “Everyone who looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart.”
For someone may look without intending adultery, but simply look and see.
But someone who looks with the intention of committing adultery is an adulterer by virtue of his will and desire. These two sayings agree with one another:
the one that says, “Do not desire your neighbor's wife,” and this one spoken by our Lord against adultery in one's thoughts. For there he said, “Do not desire,”
and here he said not to look with the intention of desiring. For sight alone does not cause sin unless the inward will also consents to it.
For one person looks in order to commit adultery, while another looks in order to see. Simple seeing, then, belongs to the nature of the eye.
But a lustful look does not belong to the eye alone, but to the will and the mind.
For if David had not looked, he would not have desired; and if he had not desired, he would not have committed adultery.
“He went up,” it says, “to the roof of his royal palace and saw a woman bathing, and desired her. He sent for her, had her brought to him, and committed adultery with her.”
For if he had looked without further intention, he would not have desired; and if he had not desired, neither would he have committed adultery.
Let us therefore close even the gate of sight against desire, for sight paints alluring images within the soul to no small degree.
For this reason desire itself is stirred in various ways in our bodily members and longs for different people.
This happens to the soul when the vision of God is not set before its eyes.
For if remembrance of God is present within it, all memories of evil desire are easily driven out of it,
and it does not turn away from the sight of that beauty of which one can never have enough to contemplate perishable beauty.
For it greatly helps us suppress desire when we consider the perishability of nature itself,
and the other filthy and repulsive things from which the conscience recoils, things that cling to the nature of the body.
And if someone considers their foulness, these things too do no little to quench the heat of desire.
For just as David, the prophet of God, said of human nature when he was rebuking its pride:
“A human being is like a breath, and his days pass like a shadow”; and again, when he was putting an end to reliance on it,
so that no one would place his hope in his fellow human being, he said, “Do not trust in a human being or in a ruler,
who has no power to save. His spirit goes out, and he returns to his earth, and on that day all his thoughts perish”;
so let us also act toward the passion of sexual immorality. Whenever it burns within us and disturbs our thoughts, let us set against it
either the remembrance of God and the fear of his judgment, or let us use the repetition of the words of Scripture against it.
Or let us reflect on the corruptibility, weakness, and sufferings of human nature itself.
For when someone considers these things wisely and looks at their outcome with all the strength of his soul,
and sees the discharges, filth, and pains that afflict the body, and the abundance of uncleanness in its limbs,
and the other things like these that accompany the body, he can also extinguish his desire by means of them,
despising it and treating it with contempt, because he sees what sorts of things it makes him dependent on.
But when the mind reflects on the filth and foulness of human nature, let it take care that human nature does not become contemptible in its eyes.
For we stir up these thoughts within it not so that we may despise human nature, but so that we may curb its desire.
And if it also needs a strengthening perspective and an encouraging vision, let it remember the righteous people of old,
not only those from the revelation of our Savior onward, but especially those before his coming.
For although perfection had not yet been handed down to human beings, nor had they been found worthy of the way of life of the world to come,
even so, chastity was more precious in their eyes than marriage.
Each of them honored sexual abstinence more than marital intercourse. For Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob,
who are the patriarchs of the faithful people and welcoming halls for all the righteous,
who abounded in their faith and compassion, evidently desired, more than marriage—which sustains human procreation—
purity and abstinence from marital intercourse. And after them came Joseph the chaste,
who, though young in years, displayed the discernment of the aged through his endurance.
Although he had no teacher to instruct him, no tutor to enlighten him, and no father to watch over him,
nor any kindly oversight to help him, the remembrance of God sufficed for him in place of all these.
And in his own person he was already putting into practice what was later expressed in the words, “I have set the Lord before me at all times, so that I may not be shaken.”
And when his master's wife was captivated by love for him because of his physical beauty,
and was trying to entice him into committing sin, he was already learning the philosophy of Christ's teaching,
and was persevering so that he would not be overcome by his desire, as he faced a twofold battle, from within and from without.
For from without, his master's wife was fighting against him with her beauty, her words, and the enticements of her proximity.
And from within, bodily desire was fiercely waging war. Yet as he stood between these two fierce struggles,
