he overcame them both through the strength of his endurance. Consider, then, the distress his soul was in at that time,
when wave after wave of desire, stirred up by outward enticements, was beating against him.
But they could not overturn the mighty rock of his endurance.
For just as a ship is tossed about and shaken by the waves that come against it, so the ship of Joseph's soul was also being shaken.
But because his soul's anchor was set above in heaven, as Paul says, and was not cast down into the depths,
his thought was continually rising to the heights. And against the desire that had been stirred up against him,
he in turn stirred up his remembrance of God, and the prospect of God's judgment made him recoil from it.
He said to the woman who was enticing him impurely, "My master has given me authority over his whole household and has withheld nothing from me,
except you alone, because you are his wife. How, then, could I do this great evil and sin against the Lord?"
For to him, sinning against God was worse than all bitter judgments and fierce, harsh torments.
And perhaps it was not God's judgment that restrained him from sinning, but the very wish not to sin against God.
For what punishment pains the soul, if it has any awareness of divine life, as much as offending God?
For Joseph called sinning against God a great evil, and it is indeed a great downfall.
There is no cure, except through God's grace, for a person's sinning against God himself.
As divine Scripture also says, "If a man sins against the Lord, to whom can he appeal?"
But wise and chaste Joseph regarded sinning against his master—if he were to sin with his wife—as a sin against God.
For God's commandment would be broken by transgressing the law of nature.
For although the command, "Do not covet or commit adultery with your neighbor's wife," had not yet been heard, the substance of that command was woven into nature itself.
For the saying, "Do not do to your neighbor what you yourself hate," is written in nature itself.
And it was inscribed in letters on everyone's conscience by God's creative power, so that each person's law would be within them.
And no one can say, “I have not yet learned to read, nor have I read and become familiar with written letters.”
For God’s power as Creator has been engraved on the tablets of the heart. As a person grows in bodily stature, he studies this very book.
Joseph too, when he was only twenty years old—for that was his age when this battle arose against him—
was secretly studying these writings. He recited to his master’s wife the teaching he had received from them:
“How,” he said, “could I do this evil and sin against God? How could I condemn myself by something I have already judged?
How could I make myself guilty through something I have already recognized as deserving condemnation?”
For Joseph was fulfilling in practice that blessing which Paul pronounces on anyone who does not condemn himself in what he has approved.
At a young age he displayed a victory beyond his years. And perhaps Moses took from him what he said:
“Everyone who passes into the census, from twenty years old and upward, shall give an offering to the Lord.”
Here is a helpful and encouraging example for the disciple against whom fleshly desire wages war.
Yet the circumstances are certainly not equal or comparable, because Joseph’s commitment was not like yours.
For providence had not set him apart to be a virgin and celibate, but to become the father of a numerous people,
as the outcome itself showed. Moreover, he had no example before him there,
nor another person’s example to look to for help, nor a written law restraining him from this.
For Moses had not yet been named, nor had any of the prophets spoken.
Nor had the commandments of Christ our Savior, which teach perfection, yet been heard in the world.
Nor was the practice of asceticism available there, which itself is also a powerful suppressor of desire.
Nor was he kept from seeing and associating with women, something that itself also inflames desire.
Rather, so to speak, he was fighting desire let loose; that is, he was struggling with a vicious, unchained lion.
And in a new struggle within the contest of endurance, he was winning the victory.
But for the monk or solitary, or anyone who has set himself apart by a pledge to God,
to whom these words are addressed, there are many things that help them. First is the very covenant they have made with God.
For this remembrance alone is enough to teach us divine philosophy.
Along with these things, life in the desert itself is far removed and sheltered from all disturbing dealings.
And if, instead, he lives in a community of many or of few, there are these walls that surround him and keep him enclosed, away from the distractions of the world.
For anyone who wishes to prove victorious in the battle against this passion must also abstain from the company of women,
and from looking at faces that stir up desire. For just as gluttony craves different kinds of food,
so too this impure passion of sexual immorality craves beautiful faces.
Its desire is bound to beautiful flesh, and as long as such a sight is kept far from him,
even the memory of that sight dies within him. Once he has forgotten the images, he no longer commits sexual sin with them in his soul.
It is therefore not without reason that monasteries for recluses and dwellings for solitaries have been established, and that many are kept from seeing women and keeping their company.
Rather, it is so that, deprived of these things, the mind may be purified and recover its strength.
Then, when it stands in its own strength, it may resolutely face the battle against sexual immorality,
if that battle should happen to arise against it, whether from the stimulation of nature or from the incitement of demons.
Indeed, is not the memory of Joseph, who was young, still a boy,
and was being urged by his mistress to commit the hateful act of adultery, enough to strengthen every disciple against whom desire wages war?
And if victory should be won here, it deserves less praise than Joseph's, because there are many sources of support.
And the more supporters the combatant has, the more his weakness becomes apparent.
For after the account of Joseph, there were written accounts of the holiness of Moses, the chastity of Joshua, and the Nazirite consecration of Samson,
and his fall, which weakened his strength; the upbringing of Samuel; the sin of David and the punishment for it;
the virginity of Elijah; the renunciation and purity of Elisha; and the renowned companies of the sons of the prophets,
who lived in the mountains in the manner of monks, and through endurance lived lives estranged from the world.
And every example that teaches chastity and virginity was written down and made known after Joseph's deed,
so that he might be shown to be victorious and triumphant, since he fought and conquered without an example,
while we are weak and deserving of every punishment if, after all these examples, we stumble and fall.
For the passion of sexual immorality, as the fathers teach, is a veil before the mind's sight, preventing it from contemplating divine things.
Just as someone might spread a cloth over writings, so that they cannot be seen by the eye and read,
so too this passion becomes a veil before the mind, preventing it from contemplating spiritual things.
It darkens the mind not only when it is carried out in action, but even if it lingers in thought while the soul takes pleasure in it.
For we must first purify the dwelling place of the mind, and then the outward members of the body are also kept safe.
For the desire of the bodily members is situated in the middle: inward from it is the mind’s discernment, and outward from it is the sight that arouses it.
If it listens and submits to the mind, the mind transforms it into spiritual desire.
But if it receives recollections from outside and grows, it stirs up a struggle and disturbs the clarity of thoughts.
The more it weakens the mind, the stronger it becomes, and it has things that strengthen it.
All bodily and sensory things, those that come from the world, nourish it.
For there are some who struggle and are defeated, and there are some who do not fight at all.
Neither the person who satisfies his desires nor the person who completely overcomes his desire is fighting.
The first is not fighting because he has not begun, and the last because he has finished. The whole struggle belongs to the person in between.
For this reason Paul also calls those who have finished this struggle dead.
He says, “You have died to the law through the body of Christ, so that you might belong to another, the one who rose from the dead,
so that you might bear fruit for God.” And when explaining the cause of the struggle that befalls the person in between, he said, “When we were in the flesh,
the sinful passions that came through the law were active in our bodily members, so that we bore fruit for death.”
Those who live in the flesh, he says, are always defeated by desire and bear fruit for death.
But those who conduct themselves according to the law stand on the battlefield,
with the law in which they stand serving as their helper and source of strength.
But when, even in this intermediate position, they fulfill the law and gain the victory, Paul says to them,
“Now we have been released from the law and have died to what held us,
so that from now on we may serve in the newness of the Spirit and not in the oldness of the written code.” For in the new life there is no desire.
Where there is no desire, there is no struggle; and where there is no struggle, there the peace that our Savior brought to the world is known.
Thus a new peace is seen in the new person, because this is the person who conducts himself in the new life.
In this state there is no struggle with desires. Rather, just as the person who lives in the flesh
has no awareness of sin, so also the person who conducts himself in the Spirit remains free from susceptibility to sin.
For lack of awareness does not know that it has sinned, while freedom from susceptibility does not remember sin.
For in both places the old person takes off his desires: in baptism and in the grave.
The person who takes off his desires in baptism is called to adoption as a son.
But whoever serves them throughout his life and abandons them in battle is summoned to judgment in the sudden rush of the resurrection.
Whoever, after his baptism, lives according to the Spirit is truly a new person,
who has not put on again the old way of life that he took off through baptism. Such a person has no battle with desire,
because he is dead to the world. For Paul said, “I would not have known desire if the law had not told me, ‘Do not desire.’”
Therefore, whoever lives as a new person does not know desire. He does not live by enduring desire, but without being affected by it,
just as Adam was before the law was laid down for him.
He did not know desire, because it had not come to life and begun to stir.
For the commandment brought about a stirring, and that stirring received the law.
And the law said, “Do not desire.” For when he heard “Do not desire,” he became acquainted with desire.
And he learned about sin through the commandment that forbids sin—the very thing that happens to those who are free from bodily desire.
When a discourse against desire is addressed to them, describing its shameful forms, its degrading practices,
and its powerful impulses, the very things said to put an end to it cause it to flare up all the more.
For through the things opposed to it, they are led to support it and are inflamed with its passion.
This happened to Adam too, or to anyone who is free from desire when the words “Do not desire” are addressed to him.
For thoughts habitually take in memories, and memories stir up desire.
The disciple must therefore keep away from conversations and sights, so that he does not take in memories, and those memories stir up desires
and disturb his thoughts. Once the mind is disturbed, it can no longer see God.
“Do not let sin reign in your dead body,” he says, “so that you obey it through the body's desires.”
For if, according to Paul's teaching, they are dead—
I mean those who live in the Spirit—then clearly the desire within them is also dead. And it is a disgrace to the mind,
not only to be defeated, but even to engage in battle. But how can someone who has died fight?
These things are hard to understand for those who have not experienced them. We, however, do not write these things from experience,
but on the strength of Paul's teaching. “The law,” he says, “has authority over a person as long as he lives.
For a woman is bound by law to her husband as long as he lives. But if her husband dies, she is freed from the law concerning her husband.
But if she joins herself to another man while her husband is alive, she becomes an adulteress.”
But if her husband dies, she is freed from the law and is not an adulteress if she marries another man.
What, then, is the point of this illustration, and what does the apostle teach us through these things?
“You too,” he says, “have died to the law through the body of Christ, so that you may belong to another, the one who rose from the dead.”
“As long as you were members of the first Adam,” he says, “the one who received the first commandment, you were subject to the law.”
But now that you have become members of another—that is, of Christ, who rose from the dead—the law has no authority over you.
For the one whose members you are is not subject to the law,
because, as God, he is above the law. And when he became a human being subject to the law,
he kept the law and fulfilled all its commandments, and he went out into the freedom that is above the law,
the freedom spoken of by our Lord: “If the Son sets you free, you will truly be free.”
“Now,” he says, “that we have been released from the law and have died to what held us captive, let us henceforth serve in the newness of the Spirit and not in the oldness of the written code.”
But, as I see it, these words of the apostle are familiar and clear to anyone who lives the life of the new person.
Anyone who lives this way is not merely a hearer of the words, but one who sees their power.
For sight is more reliable for seeing and understanding what takes place.
For we clearly recognize the things that are seen with the eye.
So too, those who are found living the life of the new person become eyewitnesses of the apostle’s words,
and not merely hearers. For he too was not writing on the basis of what he had heard from others. For it was not from a human being,
nor through a human being, that he received this teaching, but, as he said, through a revelation of Jesus Christ.
And revelation, as is well known, discloses hidden things.
For just as physical sight sees visible things, so too a pure mind beholds spiritual things.
Purity of mind, as I have said many times, is acquired by putting to death all the deeds of the old person.
Paul therefore rightly said that a woman is bound by the law as long as her husband lives.
Here he figuratively calls the soul that has not been freed from the deeds of the old person a woman.
And he calls the law to which she is subject her husband. Through her attachment and obedience to it, she is kept from other men.
But if this woman’s husband should happen to die—the one by whose law of union she had been bound—
she is freed to belong to whomever she wishes, just as also happened to the law through the freedom of Christ.
For every soul that was subject to it, being bound by sinful deeds, has been set free through Christ’s way of life.
It does not refrain from sin because the law guards it, but because it has been united with Christ.
Thus it is not to hold back from evil out of fear of punishment, but to practice goodness out of love for it.
For the constraint of the law is not as powerful in restraining the soul from evil
as goodness is powerful in binding the soul to itself, once the soul has experienced the sweetness of its taste.
“You have died to the law through the body of Christ,” he says. It is as though someone were to say:
“Because you have been placed in another body, you have been freed from subjection to the law.”
For the law’s authority is over the old human being,
who had his beginning in the first Adam’s transgression of the commandment, as Paul said: “The first Adam became a living soul,
and the last Adam a life-giving spirit.” Since, then, there are two Adams according to Paul’s teaching,
one who was governed by a living soul and over whom the law had authority, and another who is a life-giving spirit, above the law,
Paul rightly said, “A woman is bound by the law as long as her husband lives.”
Thus the soul that lives according to its natural life is subject to the law, but the soul that is moved by the living Spirit is above the law.
For the Spirit, who is the giver of the law, is not subject to the law.
And those who are deemed worthy to be guided by the Spirit are above sinful thoughts, impulses, and deeds.
They refrain from practicing sin not because they fear the law, but because they are dead to sin.
“You have died to the law through the body of Christ,” he says, “so that you may belong to another, the one who rose from the dead.”
For just as the limbs attached to a natural body feel only the pain or suffering that occurs in their own body,
and, if their body is healthy, enjoy its health, but neither suffer nor feel the illness in the bodies of others,
so also the new members who have been placed in the body of the one who rose from the dead, Christ our Lord,
experience the spiritual life and true health that belong by nature to the body to which they are joined,
while they do not feel the suffering caused by sins in the body of the old human being.
In the same way, the body of any individual does not feel the pains and illnesses of another body.
And although all the deeds of the old human being prevent the mind from experiencing the way of life of the new human being,
this passion of sexual immorality does so more than all the others. Concerning this Paul said:
For every sin a person commits is outside his body, but the person who commits sexual immorality sins against his own body.
Here, by “body” he means the body of Christ, in which the person has been found worthy to become a member, as he said:
“You have died to the law through the body of Christ, so that you might become members of another, who rose from the dead.”
And again he said, “The body is not for sexual immorality but for our Lord, and our Lord for the body.”
Therefore, according to Paul's statement, the body of someone who lives according to the conduct of the new person belongs to our Lord.
And just as there was no passion of sexual immorality in our Lord's own body, so also, in someone whose body has become a member of Christ's body,
the passion of sexual immorality should not be stirred up, because it is our Lord's body, having become so through a new union.
And how did this come about—that the body should not be for sexual immorality but for our Lord, and our Lord for the body? He said, “God raised our Lord
and will raise us by his power.” For just as God the Father raised his Son from death to the immortality of another life,
so we too have all risen with him by his power. Just as, after his resurrection, he no longer lived according to our way of life,
so neither should we, who have risen with him by his power, live a life enslaved to the passions of the old person.
And why should we not conduct ourselves in a new life? He immediately introduces a statement full of rebuke and instruction, saying:
“Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ?” Here Paul not only teaches us but also rebukes us,
and shows that there is no way for a member to live apart from its body.
For all the members situated in the natural body are sustained in it and receive their life from it.
Likewise you too, whose bodies have become members of Christ's body, receive from him everything that sustains you: life,
joy, purity, holiness, freedom from all evils, freedom from sinful passions,
kindness, tranquility, peace, love, activity in all spiritual things,
and, in short, everything that this body has to give its members. And if this is the proper conduct of the new person,
then he does good, not under compulsion from the law that restrains evil, but because this is appropriate to the order in which he has been placed.
For in Christ's incarnation from the Virgin, the members of his own body came to belong to him.
For his becoming human showed this and brought it to light. But in the birth through baptism,
which resembles the birth from the Virgin, those who are baptized do not become his members through his incarnation,
but through his ordering of salvation. And each of those who are baptized, while in his own individual existence he is a body and a soul
and a human being counted as a distinct individual, becomes a member in the body of Christ.
And although this union is not visible to human beings, as the union that took place in his incarnation from the Virgin was visible.
For there the Son of God appeared openly after being hidden, and appeared as a composite being after being without a body.
Here, however, bodily human beings become spiritual human beings.
And whereas each of them, in his own person, is a body with many members, in the body of Christ
he is counted as a member, invisibly joined and placed within that body in a way beyond words,
and becomes a spiritual member in the body of God, according to the apostle's statement: “Your bodies are members of Christ.”
How, then, can a member of Christ overcome lust while fighting against it?
For if this battle with lust existed in the holy body of Christ,
there would also be a way out for those who, though they are members of that body, are disturbed by lust.
But the apostolic word commands us not only to refrain from sexual immorality, but also not to be receptive to the passion of sexual immorality,
and not to be disturbed by lust at all, nor to enter into battle. For a dead person does not fight.
For life admits sensation, and sensation arouses lust.
But if the old life is absent, sensation is absent too. And if sensation is absent, lust is not admitted either.
Nor, consequently, is any battle stirred up against lust. For how can someone fight against something that does not exist?
“Shall I take a member of Christ,” he says, “and make it a member of sexual immorality?” He says, “Shall I take.”
It is as though someone were saying that, as long as it remains within the body, there is no possibility of its becoming a member of sexual immorality.
For even a member placed in a natural body, as long as it remains in its place,
cannot possibly receive life from another, foreign body, but only from its own body.
But if someone cuts it off from there, he cannot attach it to another body while it is alive.
Instead, when it is cut off, it leaves its life with its body and remains dead and without sensation in the hand of the person holding it.
It was in this sense that Paul said, “Shall I take a member of Christ and make it a member of sexual immorality?”
It is as though someone were saying, “Unless it is taken away from there, it does not become a member of sexual immorality.”
But if he commits sexual immorality while he is within the body—that is, if he becomes receptive to this passion of sexual immorality—he sins against his whole body.
That is, he causes his whole body to suffer. For just as, when one of the body's members receives a wound,
its pain spreads to all the body's remaining members, so too the member that admits the passion of sexual immorality,
Since he is placed in Christ’s body, he causes the whole body suffering and pain. This is what he meant when he said that he sins against his body.
As someone might put it, the sin lies not only in his causing pain through the passion for sexual immorality, but also in his making the whole body suffer.
For if someone strikes another person’s body, the blow he strikes makes him guilty of sin,
and the law commands that he immediately receive punishment as a guilty person, saying, “Wound for wound, burn for burn, and stripe for stripe,”
then it is clear that a member placed in Christ’s body also causes the whole body pain if it is seized by the passion for sexual immorality.
For this reason Paul rightly said that he sins against his body.
For no other sin can defile the soul and body in the way that the passion for sexual immorality does.
For this reason Moses too, showing exceptional caution against this passion, said:
“A man from whom semen comes out shall be unclean.” He made the condemnation this severe:
it defiles him not only when he is stirred by his own will and proceeds to an act of adulterous sexual immorality,
but even if semen simply comes out of him. Along with this, there is also another point:
wherever he gives instructions about those parts of sacrificial animals that are set apart to be offered to God,
he also carefully insists on this: the two kidneys and the fat covering them must be burned.
Nowhere does he set these apart as food for the priests or the high priests.
Instead, he hands them over to be burned in the fire, along with the remaining parts that symbolize sinful deeds.
“Take,” he says, “the fat, the fat tail, all the fat covering the internal organs, the lobe of the liver, and the two kidneys and their fat,
and burn all these in the fire.” Yet along with all of them, and before all of them,
come the two kidneys and their fat, which are the passions of sexual immorality and adultery.
“Let the kidneys be burned,” he says, together with their fat, which is a sign of the mind’s dullness,
which does not allow the ugly sight of these passions to be seen.
If, then, the old law burns the passion for sexual immorality with fire, and declares that anyone from whom semen simply comes out
is unclean, and also burns the adulterer and adulteress with fire, and our Lord, in the teaching of his gospel,
forbade not only adultery itself [?], but also the thought that leads to adultery, and Paul said,
“Neither the sexually immoral nor adulterers will inherit the kingdom of God,” and again, “Whoever joins himself to a prostitute becomes one body with her,”
and, “Whoever commits sexual immorality sins against his body,” and again he says, “Shall I take a member of Christ and make it a member of sexual immorality?”
Along with the words of the Scriptures, practical experience also teaches those who observe their own passions.
What disciple who wishes to live righteously and holily would not guard against the downfall brought about by this passion?
And let us receive with lively and attentive hearing the voice of God calling to us: “Be holy, just as I too am holy.”
We would not, then, have been required by God's command to have holiness resembling his holiness,
if he had not also given us the Spirit who sanctifies us, who has become a soul to our soul and causes it not to be guided by its own thoughts
or to descend to the pleasure of bodily desires, but to rise toward its purity and holiness
and receive the radiance of its glory, which purifies and sanctifies its thoughts.
For if old age and illnesses restrain and extinguish this desire,
how much more does a sound will that loves spiritual things and longs for divine holiness!
For old age and illness do not uproot desire, but weaken it and put it to sleep.
But this will, which is perfected through the power of the Holy Spirit, completely uproots desire.
It establishes a person in freedom from passion and causes all his thoughts to move among spiritual things.
It removes from him not only [?] the turmoil of the passions, but also awareness of things perceived by the senses.
And just as someone firmly held by love for this passion has his love for other things extinguished,
so too someone who casts it off entirely and binds himself completely to the love of spiritual things
does not admit awareness of things that stir up this passion.
But you, disciple, since you have not yet attained these things,
meditate on what has been written for you above and put it into practice, closing the entrances of desire,
which are outward sights and interactions, and also stopping up its source, which is the passion and natural health of the body.
Purify your thoughts as well, for they so often assist desire and stir it up within the body's members.
And if you cut it off by these three means, so that no thought dwells on it and the body's members are not stirred by it,
and it has no entrance from outside, you will remain in undisturbed quiet,
and your ship's voyage to the harbor of peace will be without waves or storms, with the rest of its gains also kept safe aboard it.
Through this you will become like the heavenly powers, and while you remain in the body, you will move in the spirit.
While you are in one world, you will conduct your life in another. You will also perceive the reason for Christ's coming into the world.
This is unknown to all who live in the flesh; they hear only talk about his mysteries.
Yet they do not perceive the power of his mysteries. May we not be deprived of the knowledge that perceives the power of these holy mysteries.
And may we not be strangers to the practice of the divine commandments.
And may we not be deprived of spiritual contemplation of visible and spiritual things.
By the grace of him who came for the salvation, liberation, and renewal of all: Jesus Christ, the Only-Begotten, God the Word.
To him be glory from all who have received his salvation, experienced his salvation, and become mediators of his gifts,
through all the generations of the worlds of light and the realms of the Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.
Here ends the discourse on sexual immorality and bodily desire, which is the thirteenth.
